case20v1-ethics.dark.patterns:
Tarazu and the Diwali Checkout

A case on the thirteen dark patterns named in India's CCPA guidelines

1. Opening

At 8.10 on the morning of Monday 19 October 2026, Ezhilarasi Lalgudi, chief product officer of Tarazu, opened the readout that her data scientist in Toronto had sent overnight. It covered ten versions of five checkout changes planned for the Diwali campaign, which opens on Tuesday 27 October and runs twelve days before the festival on Sunday 8 November. The numbers were the best the growth team had seen all year.

In the next window she had the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, issued by India's Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) in November 2023. Their annexure names thirteen practices. She had counted five of them in the plan.

The release build had to be cut by 6 pm on Friday 23 October (Figure 1). She had to decide which version of each change would ship. The full team was due on a call at 7.30 that evening, which is 4.00 pm in Berlin and 10.00 am in Toronto.

Figure 1. Timeline of the decision. Scale: 17 px per calendar day from 28 September.

2. Company background

Tarazu was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 to deliver groceries and household essentials in under 40 minutes from neighbourhood dark stores. By October 2026 it ran 410 stores in nine cities, including Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and the Delhi NCR, and served 31 lakh monthly customers. A typical day brought 1.1 lakh orders at an average basket of ₹540, an annualised gross order value above ₹2,000 crore. It had raised ₹620 crore in three rounds and had not yet reported a profitable quarter.

The category is crowded. Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart compete on speed, BigBasket and JioMart on range and price, and all spend heavily around Diwali, when baskets grow and gifting opens up. Tarazu took payments through UPI and Razorpay. Its membership, Tarazu Plus, gave free delivery for ₹299 a quarter after a seven-day free trial. Investors judged the company on order growth and on the share of customers taking Plus. Both had slowed through the monsoon quarter, and the Diwali campaign was meant to restart them.

3. The situation

From 28 September to 11 October the growth team ran ten arms against one control, each on 1,00,000 sessions, each changing a single thing. In five arms the change was the version built for maximum effect. In the other five it was an alternative built to do the same job without the feature in question. Exhibit 2 gives the results. The control turned those sessions into 6,200 orders at ₹540.

Ezhilarasi had asked Edith Lakkireddy, the product designer in Berlin, to compare the effect-maximising versions with the CCPA annexure. Exhibit 1 is her mapping, finished on 16 October, before the readout.

The effect-maximising versions earned ₹3,94,418 of extra billings per 1,00,000 sessions and the alternatives ₹1,09,895. Finance expected 3 crore sessions in the campaign window, which is 300 lots of 1,00,000. Scaled that way, the figures become ₹11.83 crore and ₹3.30 crore. They are billings, not profit, and they assume the effects scale in a straight line and do not interact, which five separate arms cannot confirm.

Ezekiel Lingamneni, the data scientist in Toronto, added support tickets (Exhibit 3). The control drew 18.1 tickets per 1,000 orders. He cautioned that every alternative, and the offer-clock and mithai effect-maximising arms, sat within a few tickets of control and should not be read as different. The Plus cancellation arm drew 322 tickets against the control's 112, and most were requests to cancel.

One more fact mattered. Under the RBI's e-mandate rules and NPCI's UPI AutoPay, a customer's bank sends a pre-debit notice before each renewal whatever Tarazu does. The alternative Plus design added Tarazu's own reminder three days earlier.

Edith said from Berlin, where the debate on manipulative design is older, that she could not put her name to the effect-maximising screens. Eraivan Lankapalli, the growth head in Pune, replied that the quarter's targets had been set on these numbers, that every Diwali app on a customer's phone pushed the same buttons, and that a customer who dislikes a screen can always decline it. Ezekiel noted that the test had run for only fourteen days, so longer effects such as repeat orders and churn were unmeasured.

4. The people

Ezhilarasi Lalgudi, chief product officer, Bengaluru. She owns the checkout and signs the release. She wants the campaign to restart growth and does not want to explain a regulator's notice to the board.

Eraivan Lankapalli, head of growth, Pune. His bonus and his team's targets rest on orders and Plus take-up. He wants the versions that tested best and argues that customers can always decline.

Edith Lakkireddy, senior product designer, Berlin. She mapped the pack to the annexure. She wants screens she can defend to a user and offers to redesign anything inside the week.

Ezekiel Lingamneni, data scientist, Toronto. He wants the decision made on measured effects, tickets included, and flags that his arms ran only fourteen days.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. The thirteen practices in the CCPA annexure, with the design review's notes on the Diwali pack

6. The options

Option A: ship the effect-maximising versions. This keeps the full tested lift, ₹11.83 crore of extra billings across the window, and needs no new work. The cost is exposure. The CCPA can direct a platform to stop a practice and refund consumers; in June 2025 it also urged e-commerce platforms to audit themselves. If the Plus charges alone were refunded, the 72 extra paid conversions per 1,00,000 sessions become 21,600 charges of ₹299, about ₹0.65 crore. Edith would not support the release.

Option B: ship the alternatives now. Every alternative was built and tested, so the 23 October cut is feasible. It keeps ₹3.30 crore of billings, well under half of Option A's, and it would put Eraivan's quarter target at risk. A fuller audit of the rest of the app would follow after Diwali.

Option C: freeze the pack and commission a full audit. An outside firm would review all screens against the thirteen practices in about six weeks for ₹18 lakh. Nothing new ships for Diwali and the extra billings are zero, but nothing doubtful ships either.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which features in the pack match a named practice, and what would you need to see to call a close case either way?
  2. Read Exhibit 2 row by row. What did each effect-maximising version earn, and what did its alternative keep?
  3. Billings and tickets are measured on different bases. How should Ezhilarasi weigh them, and which costs does neither capture?
  4. What would you tell the 7.30 pm call, and what evidence would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

The CCPA's annexure turns an argument about intent into a checklist about what a screen does to a user's choice. A pattern is named by its effect: a clock that resets, a box already ticked, a cancel button that is hard to find. Whether the team meant harm, and whether it worked, do not settle the matter. That is why a product manager can use the list as a design review before launch, not as a defence afterwards.

One defensible path is Option B. It meets the build deadline, keeps a measured share of the lift, removes every named practice from the pack and leaves a record that the team checked. Ezhilarasi would then schedule the wider audit for after Diwali, cover the app's older screens, and track tickets per 1,000 orders as a guardrail in the campaign dashboard. Other answers can be defended if they state which risk they accept and why.
case40v1-ethics.dark.patterns:
Indian School of Business · Case study

Vanavil and the Thirteen

A dark-patterns decision falls due the week a festive sale opens, in a checkout that forty-two other retailers also run.

1. Sunday night, Koramangala

The rain had started again over Koramangala by the time Gowthami Mudaliar reached page nine of the audit, and she had read the same three lines four times. It was Sunday, 18 October 2026. Vanavil's audit of its own product against the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns, finalised on 9 October, found eleven of the thirteen named patterns present — ten in the app she had run for two and a half years.

Four dates were stacked on her calendar. The executive committee met at 09:30 IST on Monday, 19 October, and expected her recommendation. The board met on Thursday, 22 October. The self-declaration to the Department of Consumer Affairs was due on Friday, 30 October. And on Saturday, 24 October the Festive Edit sale opened for the run into Diwali on 8 November, the fortnight in which Vanavil booked about a tenth of its annual orders.

Her chief executive wanted a clean filing. Her growth lead had a spreadsheet saying a clean filing cost ₹193.1 crore a year. Her data scientist in Toronto had a six-week experiment that said, as far as she could tell, almost nothing. And her sales head in New Jersey had written that six Gulf contracts would not permit the change before February.

2. How Vanavil got here

Vanavil Commerce Private Limited was founded in Chennai in 2016 by Gyaneshwar Muthuraman, a former category head who had watched Indian beauty buying move from counters to phones. It opened with 180 brands and a promise about authenticity. By the year ended 31 March 2026 it carried 4,100 brands, moved ₹3,640 crore of gross merchandise value across 2.95 crore orders, and recorded net revenue of ₹1,180 crore and contribution of ₹412 crore against an EBITDA loss of ₹96 crore. Head office moved to Bengaluru in 2019.

The decision that now shaped everything was made in March 2025, and had looked like the cleverest thing the company had done. Vanavil extracted its storefront — catalogue, cart, checkout, membership, the whole conversion component library, owned in Pune by Girivasan Mallampalli's team — into a licensable stack, Vanavil Retail Kit, and sold it to retailers who wanted an Indian storefront without building one. By October 2026 Retail Kit ran at forty-two licensees carrying ₹82.1 crore of annual licence revenue. To win the early enterprise deals the licence carried a feature-parity clause: for twenty-four months from go-live the licensee was guaranteed the same components the Vanavil app itself ran. Ten contracts carry it, expiring through 2027.

3. The industry Vanavil sells into

Indian online beauty and personal care in 2026 was fought over by Nykaa, Purplle, Myntra, Amazon, Flipkart, Tata Neu and Reliance Retail's Ajio, with Meesho underneath on price and Zepto and Blinkit pulling the impulse basket into ten-minute delivery. Acquisition cost had risen four years running. Most of the category ran a paid membership, and had learned the same lesson about what a shopper says and what a shopper taps.

The regulatory frame tightened in parallel. The CCPA's 2023 guidelines name thirteen specified dark patterns and make them unfair trade practices under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019; the Department of Consumer Affairs has asked platforms to audit themselves against the list and file self-declarations. The Reserve Bank's e-mandate framework governs the UPI Autopay debit collecting Vanavil Plus at ₹499 a year; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the consent taken for WhatsApp marketing; the Advertising Standards Council of India, the labelling of paid placement.

The exposure was not only Indian. Through Retail Kit the same checkout ran at seven retailers in the Gulf Co-operation Council states and three in South-East Asia. The largest licensee, Vusul Retail Group of Dubai, holds a contract governed by DIFC law, carrying a parity clause and 120 days' notice of any checkout change.

4. The timeline, and what was believed at each point

Exhibit 4 lays out the sequence. In July 2025 the ₹24 handling fee, until then shown in the cart, moved to the payment step; the note at the time called it “disclosed before authorisation and therefore not drip pricing.” It is waived for Plus members; 78 per cent of orders carry it.

On 14 November 2025, after a two-week review, Vanavil filed a self-declaration stating that its checkout complied with the guidelines. The review examined the web checkout. Web carried 9 per cent of orders in the year to March 2026; the app, 91 per cent.

On 10 February 2026 a pre-ticked ₹19 “shipment protection” line shipped into the app. Attachment settled at 23.1 per cent of orders, which the February review paper recorded as latent demand. On 21 April the board approved an FY2027 plan carrying contribution of ₹498 crore. On 18 June the Vastavik Upbhokta Manch, a Delhi consumer collective, complained to the CCPA about the cancellation flow and the pre-tick; a business daily asked for comment six days later.

The cancellation flow, long taken to be two taps, is four taps inside Help, and its last screen defaults to Keep my benefits. In September 2026, 38,900 of 1,12,400 members who opened that screen completed a cancellation (34.6 per cent); 1,180 of the rest raised a ticket. The customer-success macro directs cancellation requests to the website, which has no cancellation control. The ₹21.3 crore first carried for false urgency rested on a test run from 30 March to 12 April 2026, alongside a catalogue-wide price change; Exhibit 2 carries a later re-estimate.

5. The people

Gowthami Mudaliar, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru. Wants a line she can hold in public for two years. Paid partly on contribution, and chairs the trust programme she announced in January. Has not said she approved the pre-tick over her design head's objection.

Gyaneshwar Muthuraman, co-founder and chief executive, Chennai. Says Vanavil should file clean and say so loudly: “we are not that company.” Has not said that a Series D conversation opened in September runs off the FY2027 plan.

Gokulram Maganti, Vice-President, Growth, Bengaluru. Holds Exhibit 2 conservative and disarming in the festive fortnight indefensible. Variable pay is 40 per cent of his package and settles on contribution. Has not said that two of his nine attributions were never replicated.

Gazala Mantravadi, Head of Design, Berlin. Argues all of them should go, as a craft failure rather than a legal one, and has a conference submission in on that. Is 3.5 hours behind IST and has missed four of the last six decision calls. Has not said she built the decline link.

Gnanadeep Mylavarapu, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Says the holdout cannot answer the question asked of it and wants ten weeks spanning the festive window. Has not said that the four clusters dropped mid-test were not dropped at random.

Gandhimathi Manimaran, Head of Customer Success, Singapore. Wants the cancellation fixed this week whatever else is decided, and owns the contact-cost budget. Has not said that the cancellation macro is her own team's.

Govindaraj Moopanar, Senior Vice-President, Retail Kit Sales, Edison, New Jersey. Holds that any checkout change needs its notice and a negotiated credit, and a parity breach invites a claim. His quarter closes on the Vusul renewal. Has not said he sold the parity clause as a feature.

Guhanesh Masilamani, General Counsel, Bengaluru. Wants a narrow, factual filing that characterises nothing. Measured on exposure avoided. Signed the self-declaration of November 2025.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Read the column again. Fifty-five crore of it is a fee we charge and collect. That is a price, not a trick. If a disclosed price is now a dark pattern, say so to the board.”

“The test moved six things at once, over thirty-eight clusters, with four dropped. It can rule out a catastrophe. It cannot tell you whether the growth team's number is right.”

Gnanadeep Mylavarapu, 05:40 IST call, 6 October

“Orders per exposed user fell from 0.600 to 0.580. In the festive fortnight that is not a rounding error, it is the quarter. And the test did not run then.”

Gokulram Maganti, reply, 6 October

“Eleven of thirteen. I built the decline link in January, so I am not outside this. We called it optimisation for two years and the audit has given it the other name.”

Gazala Mantravadi, design review, Berlin, 12 October

“Four taps, then a button that says Keep my benefits. My agents apologise forty times a day for a flow we built on purpose. Fix it this week; argue the rest in November.”

Gandhimathi Manimaran, Singapore, 14 October

“Not one licensee has complained about these components. Three asked for more. Strip the app and not the Kit and I am selling what my own company calls unfair; strip both and I owe six Gulf contracts a hundred and twenty days and a credit.”

Govindaraj Moopanar, Edison, 16 October

“It is one component library. The app and the Kit import the same cart. Removing a pattern in one and not the other is not a toggle, it is a fork — two checkouts to maintain.”

Girivasan Mallampalli, Pune, 15 October

8. The options as Gowthami sees them

She had written four on the back of the audit's cover page, and had not been able to add a fifth.

A. Remediate, then file

Remove the ten in the app, rebuild the cancellation to one tap, relabel the Editor's Pick shelf, make protection and the Plus trial opt-in, and file a declaration describing what went. Girivasan says fourteen engineer-months.

B. Remediate four, disclose the rest as under review

Take the subscription trap, drip pricing, basket sneaking and nagging — the four heaviest in Exhibit 6 — and file a declaration naming the others as under review, with dates. Leaves the festive fortnight intact.

C. Fix the cancellation, re-run the experiment, decide in January

Ship the one-tap cancellation this week, file an audit-in-progress declaration, and give Gnanadeep ten weeks spanning Diwali and December. Decides nothing else before 30 October.

D. Contest the characterisation

Argue that the fee is disclosed before authorisation, the pre-tick is a default and not a sneak, the shelf is labelled in the terms and the countdown reflects a real offer window; fix the cancellation and file as in November 2025.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The filing is due Friday 30 October. The Festive Edit opens Saturday 24 October, and the merchandising freeze bites at 18:00 IST on Wednesday 21 October. Removal costs, as Girivasan has them: fourteen engineer-months at a fully loaded ₹4.1 lakh a month, ₹57.4 lakh; licensee migration support across the forty-two, ₹1.32 crore; counsel and an attestation, ₹46 lakh — ₹2.35 crore in all, against unwind credits of ₹8.06 crore if the parity contracts are touched. The FY2027 plan approved in April carries contribution of ₹498 crore against FY2026's ₹412 crore, and the Series D conversation runs off that plan. Six Gulf contracts need 120 days. Nine working days remain once Dussehra on Tuesday is taken out, and Monday's 09:30 IST committee falls at midnight for Toronto and New Jersey.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Working from Exhibit 1, which of the thirteen named patterns is live in the Vanavil app, and for each, what evidence would you require before calling it a dark pattern and not a design choice?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 speak to overlapping surfaces. Reconcile them: what does each measure, over what base and period, and what can neither tell Gowthami?
  3. What is the largest annual figure Gowthami could honestly put to the board as at risk if the nine surfaces in Exhibit 2 go, and the smallest? Derive both, and state what each assumes.
  4. Exhibit 6 ranks the patterns by consumer contact. What does that ranking establish, and what in its footnote bounds it? To rank the ten by harm instead, what would you measure?
  5. Gowthami has framed this as a decision about the Vanavil app, to be taken before 30 October. Argue that both the unit and the date are wrong, and say what follows for each option.
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October. What do you do before 09:30, what do you file on 30 October, and what exactly do you say to the board on Thursday, including about the self-declaration of November 2025?

11. Sunday, 23:40

The rain had stopped. Gowthami put the audit down, opened the app on her own phone and went to cancel her own Plus membership. She found the screen on the fourth tap. The button under her thumb said Keep my benefits, and she noticed that she had almost pressed it.

She put the phone face down. Gokulram's spreadsheet lay on one side of the desk and Gnanadeep's readout on the other, and the two had been arguing since the readout. Govindaraj's message was unanswered. Guhanesh wanted only what the product does; Gyaneshwar wanted clean.

She had ten hours, and she was still writing the first line.
exp40v2-ethics.dark.patterns:
Ethics, Persuasion & Trust · Dark Patterns Taxonomy · Deep Reading

Two Ways to Build a Maze

The thirteen named patterns are artefacts of two structurally different wrongs. Only one is cured by telling the truth, and the metric that exposes both is not conversion but the behaviour of the marginal convert.

1. Two Rooms, Same Week

On the morning of 11 February 2026, Ritwika Menon, Director of Subscriptions and Retention at Bhulbhulaiya Play — a Mumbai video-streaming service with 4.1 crore monthly active users and roughly ₹1,180 crore in annual subscription revenue — was looking at a slide she had presented proudly nine months earlier. It showed a redesigned cancellation flow lifting quarterly save-rate from 19% to 41%. A subscriber who tapped Manage Plan met a screen whose primary button read "Keep my watchlist", with "Continue to cancel" as grey underlined text two-thirds of the way down; those who continued met a three-question survey, then an offer of two months at half price, then a screen asking them to confirm by typing the word CANCEL. Sign-up, by contrast, was two taps from a UPI autopay mandate.

The slide had been a promotion case. The document in front of her was different: a National Consumer Helpline notice consolidating 214 complaints about that flow over eleven weeks, and a legal memo observing that the Central Consumer Protection Authority's Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 name Subscription Trap and Interface Interference as distinct unfair trade practices, that the CCPA had in mid-2024 advised e-commerce platforms to self-audit against all thirteen, and that Bhulbhulaiya Play had filed no such audit. The lift was worth an estimated ₹74 crore a year, and Ritwika could not tell from any dashboard she owned how much of it was real.

Four days later, 700 kilometres away, Adhiraj Sethuraman, Head of Product at Vyuhrachna Cloud — a Hyderabad workforce-management SaaS with ₹310 crore ARR across 4,100 accounts — was in a procurement call that had gone sideways. A prospective customer's counsel had inserted a clause requiring that "the process to reduce, downgrade or terminate any subscription shall require no more steps, channels or elapsed time than the process to acquire or expand it." Vyuhrachna's console let an administrator add seats instantly; removing seats produced a ticket routed to a retention specialist, who called within two business days. That desk saved 61% of downgrade intents and protected about ₹11.4 crore of ARR a year.

Adhiraj's instinct was that the guidelines did not apply to him, and he was very nearly right: the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 excludes a person availing services for a commercial purpose, which puts most enterprise software outside its reach. What he had not noticed was that 640 of his 4,100 accounts were sole proprietors and two-person firms on a ₹2,400-per-month plan, that the Act's proviso preserves consumer status for purchases made "exclusively for the purpose of earning a livelihood by means of self-employment", and that his retention desk treated them exactly as it treated a 900-seat enterprise. Two product types, two very different exposures, one underlying structure.

2. The Idea, and the Two Wrongs Inside It

A dark pattern is an interface choice that creates a systematic gap between the option the interface makes easiest and the option that best serves the person using it, where the gap exists because it benefits the operator. The term is Harry Brignull's, coined in 2010 for a public gallery of offending screens; his insight was forensic rather than aesthetic — the same tricks recurred across unrelated products, so they were being copied rather than invented, so they worked. The academic period that followed did two things. Colin Gray and colleagues, in 2018, sorted the sprawl into five strategies — nagging, obstruction, sneaking, interface interference, forced action — an ordering that survives in the CCPA list. Arunesh Mathur and colleagues, in 2019, automated the crawl: of roughly 11,000 shopping sites, 1,254 carried at least one of 1,818 instances, establishing a population-level phenomenon rather than a rogue-actor one. Jamie Luguri and Lior Strahilevitz, in 2021, then supplied the causal number the field lacked: acceptance of an unwanted paid data-protection plan ran at 11% in a neutral control, 26% under mild dark patterns and 42% under aggressive ones. The CCPA's contribution, notified on 30 November 2023, was operational rather than conceptual — it narrowed the taxonomy to thirteen named practices and declared each an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, so that a design choice carried a statutory hook rather than a reputational one.

But the thirteen do not form a single family, and this is the analytical move on which everything downstream depends. Some work by making the user believe something false: a stock counter that resets nightly, a fee revealed at the last screen, an advertisement dressed as a review. Others require no false belief at all: the user knows she wants to cancel, knows where the link is, and is simply made to spend six screens getting there. The first family is deception, and its currency is information. The second is what Cass Sunstein named sludge — friction deliberately placed in a path the operator does not want taken — and its currency is effort. Only the first is cured by disclosure.

Four schools disagree about where the wrong lies, and practitioners in one room routinely hold different ones without realising it. The deception school, descending from Brignull and from consumer-protection law, locates it in false belief: it signs "if the user correctly understands what is happening and proceeds anyway, there is no dark pattern", and refuses "a truthful countdown timer is manipulative". The autonomy school, Luguri and Strahilevitz and the behavioural-law tradition, locates it in exploitation of known cognitive limits, truthful or not: it signs "a real scarcity signal placed to trigger loss aversion at the moment of payment is manipulation", and refuses "disclosure cures it". The welfare school, Thaler and Sunstein's, judges outcomes rather than mechanisms — organ-donation defaults prove friction and defaults can serve the user: it signs "sludge is bad because it destroys welfare, and measurable welfare is the test", and refuses "defaults are inherently illegitimate". The symmetry school, proceduralist and the one regulators converge on because it is enforceable, locates the wrong in asymmetry between acquire and exit paths: it signs "cancellation must be no harder than sign-up, regardless of outcomes", and refuses any welfare test, because welfare is unfalsifiable in a compliance proceeding.

These are not four flavours of one claim. On Ritwika's flow the deception school condemns the mis-weighted button and acquits the survey and the offer, both honest; the autonomy school condemns the offer too, as exploitation of maximum ambivalence; the welfare school asks whether saved subscribers watched and renewed, and if so acquits everything; the symmetry school condemns all of it on a count of taps, without reading a screen.

3. Mechanics: What the Marginal Convert Tells You

Expert practice rests on a measurement discipline almost nobody executes by default: never evaluate a persuasive mechanism on the population it touches, only on the users whose behaviour it changed. Define the persuasion lift D as the conversion difference between the patterned flow and a neutral control. The users represented by D — the marginal converts — are the entire causal footprint of the pattern; everyone else would have done the same thing anyway. Honest persuasion leaves marginal converts looking like inframarginal ones downstream; manipulation makes them diverge, and the divergence is the empirical signature. Ritwika's team built the holdout in March 2026: 6% of cancellation-intent sessions went to a neutral flow — one screen, cancel primary, no survey, no offer, no typed confirmation. Over eight weeks the patterned flow saved 41.2% of intents and the neutral flow 18.6%, so D = 22.6 percentage points, or 226 marginal saves per 1,000 intents.

Exhibit 1 — Bhulbhulaiya Play, per 1,000 cancellation intents, eight-week holdout, March–April 2026. Subscription ₹299/month. "Inframarginal saves" are the 186 who would have stayed under either flow.
MeasureInframarginal saves (186)Marginal saves (226)
Still subscribed at day 9074%21%
Viewing hours, first 30 days after save17.42.1
Payment-failure or mandate-revocation at bank1.1%19.4%
Complaint, chargeback or helpline entry0.4%7.6%
App-store rating of 1 or 2 within 60 days0.3%4.9%
Revenue realised per saved user, 90 days₹822₹394

Read the third row carefully; it changed the conversation internally. Nineteen per cent of marginal saves did not churn through the product at all — they went to their bank or UPI app and killed the mandate. The pattern had not retained them; it had moved the cancellation off Bhulbhulaiya Play's surface, where it was measurable and recoverable, onto a rail where it was invisible and irreversible, since a revoked mandate cannot be re-established without a fresh consent journey. That is the most important second-order effect of sludge in Indian subscription products, and it is invisible to the team that builds the sludge, because their dashboard stops at the app boundary.

The arithmetic follows. With roughly 31 lakh cancellation intents a year, D = 22.6pp yields about 7.0 lakh marginal saves at ₹394 over 90 days, or ₹27.6 crore — against the ₹74 crore the slide claimed, which priced marginal saves at the inframarginal user's revenue. Net of complaint servicing and the rating-driven acquisition penalty, the defensible figure is nearer ₹22 crore. Against it sits the regulatory expectation — not principally the penalty, ₹10 lakh for a first contravention under Section 21 and ₹50 lakh for a repeat, rounding error at this scale, but remediation and a possible directed refund to the affected cohort. Let G be the annual net gain and L the loss conditional on enforcement: the pattern is expected-value positive only while the probability of enforcement p satisfies p < p* = G / (G + L). With G = ₹22 crore and L = ₹66 crore refund exposure plus ₹4 crore remediation plus ₹0.5 crore penalty, p* = 22 / 92.5 ≈ 24%.

The step usually left implicit is the last one. Executives asked to approve a growth pattern are shown the lift and never asked what value of p they believe. Making p explicit converts an ethical argument, which product committees are bad at, into a risk argument, which they are good at — the most transferable mechanic on this page. Adhiraj ran the same structure with a different L: statutory exposure near zero on 3,460 accounts and real on 640, but a commercial L in the exit-parity clause, which, once one buyer had drafted it, would appear in every renewal after. His L was a retention mechanism becoming a procurement objection.

4. When the Frame Applies, and When It Misleads

The framework rests on three testable claims, each of which fails in identifiable conditions.

Claim one: a neutral control exists. The marginal-convert method requires a flow with no thumb on the scale — testable by asking whether a designer with no stake in the outcome would build the control screen the same way. Ritwika's passed. Adhiraj's did not: there is no neutral way to downgrade an enterprise contract, because the contract has notice periods, seat minimums and a renewal date, and removing all friction means removing terms both parties negotiated. When friction is contractual rather than designed, the taxonomy misleads, and the right frame is contract fairness, not interface ethics.

Claim two: operator interest and user interest are separable. This holds for Ritwika and fails in safety-adjacent products. A diagnostic app that nags a user with an abnormal result until they book a consultation commits Nagging by the CCPA's definition while serving the user by any reasonable welfare standard. The test: would an independent clinician, told the mechanism, endorse it? If yes, the taxonomy describes the artefact correctly and judges it wrongly.

Claim three: the interface is the locus of choice. Increasingly it is not. When the decision happens inside a conversational agent, a voice flow or a recommendation ranking, there is no screen to audit and no button weight to measure. There the taxonomy is actively misleading, because a team can certify that none of the thirteen artefacts is present while the agent produces exactly the effects the guidelines exist to prevent.

5. Hard Edge Cases

Five situations break the standard treatment, and mature companies handle them by means they rarely describe.

Multi-product estates. Bhulbhulaiya Play sells three things on one login: the plan, a ₹49/month sports add-on and a partner music bundle. Cancellation cancels the plan; finding that the add-on persists takes a different menu. No single pattern describes this — it is an emergent property of account architecture, and the tell is that no team can answer "how many taps to leave us entirely?" Mature estates answer with an account-level exit page listing every live mandate, owned outside any product team and built after an incident rather than before.

Two-sided markets. Bhanwar Mobility, a Pune ride-hailing operator, shows riders "2 cars left near you" and drivers a bar reading "4 more trips to your ₹1,800 bonus", the threshold recalculated daily against that driver's own recent output. The rider side is textbook False Urgency and draws regulatory attention; the driver side is a near-miss mechanic aimed at a worker, not a consumer, and falls outside the guidelines. The seam is organisational: ethics committees are staffed for consumer trust, while the supply side is run by operations, measured on utilisation.

Regulated categories. A pre-ticked credit-insurance box at loan disbursal is Basket Sneaking under the guidelines and also a breach of the RBI's digital-lending rules on explicit borrower consent and Key Fact Statement disclosure — and the sectoral regulator moves faster. Here the taxonomy is rarely the binding constraint, and teams auditing only against the thirteen miss the rule that stops them.

Hardware plus software. Girah Devices sells a ₹14,900 water purifier with a filter subscription; when the subscription lapses the unit reduces flow rate and shows a service warning. Subscription Trap or safety interlock? Both readings are defensible and Girah's engineers disagree. Mature hardware companies separate the functions physically — an interlock triggered by measured filter saturation, a reminder triggered by billing state — so the question is settled by pointing at firmware rather than at intent.

AI-native products. Jaalika AI, a Bengaluru scheduling assistant, has no cancellation screen; users type "I want to stop paying" and the assistant responds. The response is generated, not designed, and the model was tuned on conversations rated highly on session continuation. Nobody wrote a confirm-shaming line; the system learned one. The taxonomy assumes a static artefact that can be screenshotted, while an optimised generative system produces a distribution of behaviours, some fraction of which are dark patterns on any turn. Companies handling this well audit transcripts rather than designs, and treat exit intent as a classifier target with a fixed, non-optimised response.

6. Eight Things Experts See That Competent Practitioners Miss

The marginal convert, not the aggregate. The obvious reading of a save-rate lift is that the flow retained people. The expert reading is that it retained two populations whose downstream behaviour must be measured apart, because honest persuasion and manipulation produce identical aggregate lift and opposite cohort splits. The tell: a team that reports lift but cannot produce 90-day retention by holdout arm. If the split has never been run, assume divergence.

Disclosure is a volume knob, not a switch. Competent teams treat "we disclosed it" as binary, satisfied by the presence of text. Experts treat it as continuous, measured by what a reasonable user notices, and know the elasticity is steep at the top: moving a fee from the terms page to the payment screen changes almost nothing; moving it to the cart line changes everything. The tell: a compliance screenshot with an arrow pointing at text no recorded session ever looked at.

Truth does not cure sludge. The commonest remediation error is fixing a left-column problem with a right-column tool: told to remove a Subscription Trap, a team adds a paragraph explaining how to cancel and closes the issue. Nothing changed; the user always knew how. The tell: a remediation whose success metric is comprehension rather than completion. Ask what fraction of users who began the exit path finished it.

Asymmetry is the only invariant measurable without a lab. Everything else needs a counterfactual. Asymmetry — steps, screens, channels, elapsed time, hours of availability, languages supported — can be counted by one person in an afternoon without instrumentation, and regulators reach for it because it is what they can verify. The tell that a company has internalised this: an exit-parity number sits in the same review as activation, owned by the same person.

Dark patterns are produced by optimisers, not people. The obvious reading is that someone chose to deceive. The expert reading is that an experimentation platform tested forty variants against a conversion objective and shipped the winner, which was dark because darkness maximises that objective in the short run. The tell: a pattern reappears three months after removal in slightly different form, with nobody able to name who reinstated it. Removal that is a design change rather than an objective change will not hold.

The guidelines name artefacts; the Act prohibits practices. Competent teams read the thirteen definitions as a specification to design around, renaming the button and cutting six screens to five. Experts know Section 2(47) prohibits unfair trade practices generally, that the thirteen are illustrations rather than a boundary, and that an artefact engineered to sit just outside every definition while producing the same effect is worse placed than the original, because the engineering is itself evidence. The tell: a review asking "does this meet the definition?" rather than "what will this do?"

Privacy consent and consumer consent are different tests. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires consent that is free, specific, informed and unambiguous, by clear affirmative action; the guidelines ask whether an interface materially misleads or impairs choice. A banner can satisfy one and fail the other, and the two are usually reviewed by people who never compare notes. The tell: a privacy counsel who approved the consent banner and has never seen the checkout.

The durable patterns have no owner and a green dashboard. Expensive patterns get scrutiny because someone proposed them. Durable ones were added by a contractor in 2021, sit behind a flag nobody has opened since, and contribute a line to a weekly review never questioned because it is always green. The tell: ask who would have to approve turning it off. If that takes more than a day to establish, the pattern has no owner — and unowned patterns survive audits.

7. How It Differs by Product Type and Stage

The differences are real in some places and imaginary in others.

Exhibit 2 — Where the exposure concentrates. "Binding constraint" is the rule that actually stops a team, which is frequently not the CCPA guidelines.
ContextDominant patternsBinding constraint
Consumer transactionalDrip Pricing, Basket Sneaking, False UrgencyCCPA guidelines; app-store policy
Consumer subscriptionSubscription Trap, Interface InterferenceCCPA plus payment-rail mandate rules
B2B / enterprise SaaSSaaS Billing, contractual obstructionProcurement terms, not statute
Marketplace / platformDisguised Advertisement, seller-side False UrgencyE-commerce Rules due-diligence duty
Hardware plus serviceSubscription Trap via device stateProduct-safety and warranty law
AI-nativeLearned confirm-shaming, non-deterministic obstructionNothing yet — the gap is the point

The one genuine structural difference is legal rather than behavioural: consumer products face a statutory regime and enterprise products largely do not, which is why Adhiraj's exposure arrives through procurement and Ritwika's through a helpline. The asserted difference — that enterprise buyers are too sophisticated to be manipulated — does not survive contact with evidence, since enterprise buying is done by a procurement officer with limited time and an incumbent-renewal default, precisely the condition under which sludge works. What changes is not susceptibility but recourse: an enterprise customer can write a clause; a consumer cannot.

Stage changes the mix predictably. A seed-stage company reaches for Nagging and Forced Action, cheap to build and immediately visible in activation. A growth-stage company generates Interface Interference and Drip Pricing as the output of experimentation systems rather than of decisions. A late-stage company's characteristic pattern is the unowned one, and its characteristic failure is not adding a dark pattern but being unable to remove one.

8. Three Worked Examples

Kundal Fresh (success). The Ahmedabad quick-commerce operator added a ₹29 "handling fee" and a pre-ticked ₹9 charity round-up in 2024, and removed both in October 2025: the fee moved into the item subtotal, the round-up became opt-in. Conversion fell 1.9pp on 46 lakh monthly orders, about ₹3.1 crore a month of order value, and round-up participation collapsed from 88% to 21% — but revoked round-ups had been generating 14,800 support contacts a month at ₹95 each, and that cost fell 79%. Net monthly impact: minus ₹2.6 crore. Repeat-order frequency then rose from 3.4 to 3.7 per twelve weeks, recovering roughly ₹4.4 crore a month by month five. The instructive detail is the lag — cost immediate, benefit a quarter later — and the change survived only because the CFO had fixed the measurement window in advance.

Antarjaal Bazaar (success, with a caveat). The marketplace found 31% of its 2.8 lakh active sellers using a template with a hard-coded "Only 3 left!" badge. It did not ban the badge; it required the badge to bind to the seller's own inventory feed, so the number became true or vanished. Prevalence fell to 9% in six weeks, conversion on badged listings fell 0.6pp, and returns on them fell 2.2pp — a net gain, because returns cost more than the marginal order earned. The caveat: sellers migrated the claim into the product title, outside the audit's scope, so the platform's due-diligence duty under the E-commerce Rules was not in fact discharged.

Bhulbhulaiya Play's first attempt (failure). In June 2025 Ritwika's team had already answered an internal flag by shipping "one-tap cancel". The button appeared on the first screen as promised, and opened a sheet offering "Pause for 3 months" as the primary action and "Cancel anyway" as secondary text, pause pre-selected — a Subscription Trap remediated into an Interface Interference. Exit-path completion rose from 59% to 63%, which the team read as success; complaints rose 41% the next quarter, because 7,100 users who believed they had cancelled found a charge three months later. Recovery cost ₹1.9 crore in proactive refunds and eleven weeks, and produced the one durable change: an exit-completion metric — the share of users expressing cancellation intent who hold no live mandate 30 days later — reported weekly beside activation and owned by Ritwika. The failure was not the design but a success criterion that measured the absence of a named pattern rather than whether people who wanted to leave had left.

9. Failure Modes and Their Early Warnings

Exhibit 3 — The five failure modes that recur, with the question that catches each one early and what it costs to find it late.
Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching late
Checklist complianceSign-off memo produced from screenshots, not sessionsWho on this team has completed a cancellation on a phone in Hindi?A CCPA direction naming a pattern your own audit cleared
Laundering one pattern into anotherRemediation ships and complaints do not fallDid exit completion rise, or only exit availability?Refund programme; Bhulbhulaiya Play paid ₹1.9 crore
Fixing the flagship surface onlyAggregate complaints fall, per-session complaints rise on one surfaceWhich surface has the worst ratio, and did we test it?Harm concentrates on the least-represented users
Optimiser reintroductionA removed pattern reappears in a variant testWhat did we change about the objective function?Permanent remediation treadmill, no durable fix
Pricing the marginal convert at inframarginal valueBusiness case cites blended LTVWhat is 90-day retention in the holdout arm?Defending a flow worth a third of its claimed value

Across all five the early warning is a measurement artefact, not a moral signal. Nobody notices a dark pattern by feeling uneasy; they notice when a metric that should have moved did not, or when two that should agree diverge. The ethical question is in practice an instrumentation question, which is why teams with good cohort instrumentation catch these problems years before teams with good intentions.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Enumeration versus general standard. The case for naming thirteen patterns is administrability: a named practice can be cited, and firms told what to stop without a multi-year adjudication. The case against is that enumeration invites engineering around the definition and already lags the technology — nothing on the list describes a generative assistant. The enumerationist position fails if enforcement treats the thirteen as merely illustrative and reaches well beyond them; early Indian evidence is mixed.

Does disclosure work? The disclosure school holds that informed users making bad choices is not a regulatory problem, resting on a real finding: much of the measured effect attenuates in experiments once the mechanism is explained. The prohibition school answers that Luguri and Strahilevitz showed aggressive patterns quadrupling acceptance among people who could have read everything, and that attenuation in a laboratory where subjects attend carefully says little about a checkout at 11pm. For disclosure to be right, field studies would have to show plain language closing most of the gap in real transactions. Those studies mostly do not exist.

Does symmetry regulation produce better products? The proceduralist rule — cancellation as easy as sign-up — is enforceable and intuitively fair. The critique is that it is blunt, banning legitimate retention conversation along with obstruction, and less settled than practitioners assume: the US Federal Trade Commission's "click to cancel" rule, adopted in 2024, was vacated by the Eighth Circuit in July 2025 on procedural grounds before taking effect. Advocates read that as a defeat on process; critics as evidence that rules written at the level of interface mechanics are fragile.

Is there durable harm at all? The strongest industry position is not "dark patterns are fine" but "the harm is self-correcting": users who feel tricked leave, so a pattern surviving years cannot be doing much damage. The strongest rebuttal is Ritwika's third row — 19% of marginal saves revoked the mandate at the bank. The harm was real and the pattern survived anyway, because it was invisible on the operator's instruments. Whether that generalises is unsettled: no large-scale, multi-firm study links dark-pattern exposure to switching with credible causal identification, and until one exists both positions are held partly on faith.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has merely studied this can recite the thirteen and point at a screenshot. Someone who has internalised it differs in four observable ways. They ask for the holdout before the lift, and treat a business case built on blended averages as unfinished rather than wrong. They separate the two wrongs instinctively, asking of any remediation whether it addresses belief or effort, and rejecting a disclosure fix for a friction problem without arguing about ethics. They audit the objective function rather than the artefact, having watched removed patterns grow back. And they hold the question continuously rather than when a notice arrives — one standing metric, exit completion or its equivalent, in the same weekly review as growth, owned by someone whose promotion depends on growth. That arrangement is deliberately uncomfortable, and the only one that survives a quarter in which the number is bad.

12. Decisions, and Three Questions

Ritwika presented the break-even framing on 3 March 2026, and the committee approved removal of the typed confirmation, the survey and the pre-selected pause, retaining a single discount offer shown once. She argued that the pattern was a bet requiring belief that enforcement probability was below 24%, that the CCPA had already advised self-audits, that 214 helpline complaints were themselves evidence of raised probability, and that ₹22 crore was not worth the wager. She did not argue that it was wrong, and afterwards said that was the only reason it passed.

Adhiraj accepted the exit-parity clause for self-serve accounts and rejected it for enterprise contracts, on the grounds that negotiated notice periods are not interface friction. He moved seat reduction into the console for every account below ₹5 lakh ARR, covering all the sole proprietors, and kept the retention desk above it, where he argued a call is what the customer expects. His ARR at risk was ₹4.1 crore of the ₹11.4 crore the desk protected. His internal note recorded that he could not tell whether he had drawn a principled line or a convenient one.

Discussion questions. (1) Ritwika reframed an ethical question as a risk wager to get it approved. What does an organisation lose when that becomes the standard move, and what would the alternative framing have had to contain to succeed? (2) Adhiraj's line — parity below ₹5 lakh ARR, retention desk above it — tracks a legal boundary rather than a behavioural one. Is a sole proprietor on a ₹2,400 plan more susceptible than a procurement officer, or merely better protected? (3) Jaalika AI's confirm-shaming was learned, not authored. Who in that company is accountable, and what would a defensible audit of a non-deterministic exit path actually consist of?

13. Going Deeper

  1. Why dark patterns emerge without malice — the causal account behind the optimiser nuance; why removal fails without an objective-function change.
  2. Auditing your own product — turns the taxonomy into a standing practice rather than a response to a notification.
  3. The Hook model — the persuasion architecture these patterns are built from.
  4. Growth without dark patterns — which levers remain once the manipulative ones close, and what they cost.
  5. Consent flows and cookie UX — where the DPDP consent test and the interference test collide.
  6. Habit formation and attention — the welfare school at full strength, and where habit stops serving the user.
  7. External and internal triggers — the mechanism under Nagging; why frequency caps treat the symptom.
  8. Fogg behaviour model (B = MAT) — why reducing ability is as powerful as raising motivation: the theory of sludge.
  9. Variable rewards — Bhanwar Mobility's driver bonus in general form.
  10. Investment and stored value — why switching costs the user built herself function as obstruction.
  11. Applying the Hook to your product — where these judgements stop being theoretical.

Ethics, Persuasion & Trust · Dark Patterns Taxonomy

The Thirteen Named Patterns

What the Central Consumer Protection Authority actually wrote down, and how a real checkout looks once you know where to point.

1. A Notification on a Tuesday Morning

On 4 December 2023, Meher Vasudev, VP of Growth at Mrigtrishna Mart — a Bengaluru-based online furniture and home-décor marketplace with roughly ₹640 crore in annual order value — opened an email from Legal with the subject line "Gazette notification: please review before Friday." Four days earlier, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), the enforcement arm under India's Ministry of Consumer Affairs, had notified the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023, naming thirteen specific manipulative design practices and declaring each one an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

Meher's checkout flow used at least four of them, and she knew it because she had built two of them herself. A "Care & Convenience" charge of ₹1,150 appeared only on the payment screen, after the buyer had already entered an address and expected the price shown in the cart to be final. A banner above every sofa listing read "Only 2 left at this price," refreshed by a script that reset the count nightly regardless of actual stock. Legal's question was blunt: does any of this now carry personal and corporate liability, and if so, which version of the checkout survives contact with the law without gutting the number that had made her promotable — a payment-page conversion rate of 58%, contributing an estimated ₹11.3 crore a month from the furniture-and-décor category alone.

The stakes were not abstract. The guidelines gave the CCPA power to investigate on its own motion, to direct a platform to modify or withdraw an offending interface, and — because a dark pattern is treated as a false or misleading representation under Section 21 of the Act — to impose a penalty starting at ₹10 lakh for a first contravention and rising for repeat ones, alongside reputational damage that a public direction against a consumer brand invites. Meher had two weeks to decide what to change, what to defend, and what to quietly stop calling a "growth win" in her next review.

2. The Idea, Precisely

A dark pattern is a user-interface choice engineered so that the path the interface makes easiest is not the path that best serves the person using it, and the gap between the two exists because it benefits the business. The term was coined in 2010 by Harry Brignull, a British UX specialist who started a public gallery of offending screens because he noticed that the same handful of tricks kept recurring across unrelated products — evidence that they were being copied deliberately, not stumbled into by accident. For over a decade "dark pattern" remained a design-community term with no legal teeth in India; the CCPA guidelines changed that by taking Brignull's loose taxonomy, narrowing it to thirteen named practices with operational definitions, and attaching a statute to each one.

The single sentence Meher could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "A dark pattern is a designed asymmetry between what the screen makes easy and what it makes true." It is not simply persuasion — every checkout persuades — and it is not simply an ugly interface. It is a mismatch, engineered on purpose, between the effortless path and the honest one, and the CCPA's contribution was to stop treating that mismatch as a matter of taste and start treating it as a matter of law.

3. The Mechanics: Thirteen Patterns Against One Checkout

The guidelines' Annexure lists thirteen patterns, each with a short definition and at least one illustrative example. Read in isolation they sound like a UX glossary; read against Mrigtrishna Mart's five-step checkout — Browse, Cart, Address, Payment, Confirmation — four of them appear in sequence, which is itself the point practitioners tend to miss: dark patterns are rarely a single rogue screen, they are a funnel designed so that each step launders the deception created by the one before it.

The remaining nine patterns did not appear in this particular flow, but a growth team eventually meets all of them, so the full taxonomy is worth having in one place rather than discovered one CCPA notice at a time.

PatternOperational definition
False UrgencyA false sense of time pressure — fake countdowns, stock counts that do not reflect real inventory.
Basket SneakingAdding items, fees or donations to the cart without explicit consent.
Confirm ShamingPhrasing a decline option to guilt or embarrass the user into compliance.
Forced ActionRequiring an unrelated action (follow, share, sign up) to complete the intended task.
Subscription TrapEasy sign-up, deliberately hard cancellation, for a recurring charge.
Interface InterferenceVisual design that highlights one choice and buries or disguises another.
Bait and SwitchAdvertising one outcome while the actual result delivered is materially different.
Drip PricingWithholding part of the true price until a late stage in the transaction.
Disguised AdvertisementAn ad presented so it appears to be organic content, search results, or user reviews.
NaggingRepeated interruption for a request the user has already declined.
Trick WordingLanguage deliberately confusing or double-negatived to produce an unintended choice.
SaaS BillingComplicating cancellation or downgrade of a paid plan relative to how easy upgrading was made.
Rogue MalvertisingAds or pop-ups mimicking system or security alerts to induce a click.

4. The Arithmetic Legal Actually Wanted

Meher's team modelled a cohort of 10,000 checkout sessions a month in the sofa-and-dining category. The average cart before fees was ₹18,400. Under the pre-review flow, the ₹1,150 "Care & Convenience" charge appeared only at Payment, and the conversion rate from that screen to a completed order was 58% — 5,800 orders. At a fee-inclusive average order value of ₹19,550, that cohort generated 5,800 × ₹19,550 ≈ ₹11.34 crore a month. But 9% of those orders (522) triggered a dispute over the undisclosed fee, each costing roughly ₹380 in reverse-logistics and refund handling — about ₹1.98 lakh a month in pure friction cost, before counting the support headcount needed to resolve them.

Moving the fee to the Cart screen, disclosed as a separate line before Address, is the direct fix for Drip Pricing. Some buyers who would have proceeded out of momentum now abandon earlier: conversion from Payment to order fell to 55% — 5,500 orders — for revenue of 5,500 × ₹19,550 ≈ ₹10.75 crore, a drop of about ₹59 lakh a month. Against that, the fee-dispute rate fell to 1.5% (82 orders), cutting friction cost to roughly ₹31,000 a month, and — the number that mattered to Legal, not Growth — the exposure to a CCPA direction on Drip Pricing dropped from live to effectively closed.

Meher then ran a second pass, changing one input: instead of disclosing a forced ₹1,150 bundle, she unbundled it, making the ₹899 protection plan a genuine opt-in and disclosing only a flat ₹450 convenience fee upfront. That also resolves Basket Sneaking, not just Drip Pricing. Base revenue became 5,500 × ₹18,850 ≈ ₹10.37 crore; take-up of the now-optional plan by 22% of buyers at ₹700 added a further 5,500 × 0.22 × ₹700 ≈ ₹8.47 lakh, for a total of about ₹10.45 crore — roughly ₹30 lakh a month below the disclosed-bundle scenario, but with two named patterns closed instead of one. The decision was no longer "comply or don't"; it was which ₹30–59 lakh a month the company was willing to trade for how much legal exposure, and that framing — not a vague commitment to "ethical design" — is what got the redesign approved by Friday.

5. What a Learner Must Get Straight

Effect, not intent, is what the law tests.

Meher's engineers had genuinely forgotten the stock counter was decorative; the guidelines do not care. The CCPA framework asks whether the interface produced a false impression, not whether the product team meant it to. Good-faith accident and calculated manipulation are legally indistinguishable once the screen is live.

A dark pattern is not simply "aggressive marketing."

Discount banners, scarcity that is real, and reminder emails for an abandoned cart are ordinary persuasion; the line is whether the claim behind the persuasion is true. "3 people are viewing this room" is a dark pattern if the number is invented and ordinary information if it is a live count pulled from actual sessions.

The thirteen-item list is a floor, not a ceiling.

It captures 2023's most common tricks; it does not yet name patterns built around conversational AI interfaces, voice checkout, or recommendation systems that quietly narrow choice. A pattern that evades all thirteen definitions can still violate the Act's general prohibition on unfair trade practice.

Confirm Shaming has a genuinely fuzzy edge.

"No thanks, I'll pay full price" is shaming; "Skip" is not. Between those two sits a wide zone — "I don't need to save money" — where reasonable design teams disagree, and no CCPA order has yet drawn the exact line.

The taxonomy tells you what is prohibited, not what is optimal.

Removing a dark pattern is a compliance action; it says nothing about whether the resulting screen actually serves the user well. A checkout can be fully compliant with all thirteen definitions and still be confusing, slow, or badly designed.

Marketplace platforms answer for sellers too.

Under the guidelines and the Consumer Protection (E-commerce) Rules, 2020, a marketplace that hosts a seller's misleading listing carries its own due-diligence obligation — Mrigtrishna Mart cannot treat a seller-side false urgency banner as someone else's problem.

"We disclosed it somewhere" is not a defence to Interface Interference.

A fee mentioned once in an 800-word terms page is legally disclosed and practically invisible; the CCPA's own guidance language repeatedly ties compliance to what a reasonable user would actually notice, not what a document technically contains.

6. Consumer, B2B, and Marketplace Versions

Consumer apps are where the thirteen patterns concentrate, because the CCPA guidelines were written with retail, travel, and food-delivery checkouts explicitly in mind — Basket Sneaking and Confirm Shaming are almost entirely consumer phenomena. B2B software shows a narrower subset: SaaS Billing dominates, because enterprise buyers rarely encounter False Urgency banners but frequently encounter a self-serve upgrade button next to a downgrade path that requires a phone call to a retention specialist — a company Meher's counterpart at a Pune-based project-management SaaS, Andhkaar Cloud, cited in a joint industry call as its own open item. Marketplaces carry a second layer entirely: Mrigtrishna Mart must audit not only its own screens but every seller's listing template, since Disguised Advertisement and False Urgency are patterns individual sellers reach for on their own initiative.

Company stage changes the mix differently. An early-stage app under growth pressure tends toward Nagging and Forced Action — cheap to build, immediately visible in activation metrics — because a ten-person team optimises for the number the next funding round asks about. A large, established platform drifts toward Interface Interference and Drip Pricing instead, because those patterns survive quarter after quarter inside a settled checkout that no single team owns end to end, and because removing them requires cross-functional sign-off that a startup does not yet need.

7. Where Teams Go Wrong

Treating the thirteen-item list as a compliance checklist.

Symptom: a legal sign-off memo confirming "none of the thirteen patterns present," produced by scanning screenshots rather than actually completing a checkout. Underlying error: compliance is a legal floor, not evidence of trust. Cheapest diagnostic: have someone outside the product team attempt to cancel a subscription or complete checkout with a slow connection and report where they got confused, not just where they got blocked.

Fixing the pattern on the primary flow and leaving it in variants.

Symptom: complaint volume drops on the English-language desktop site but not on the Hindi-language app or the WhatsApp-based ordering flow. Underlying error: assuming one redesign propagates automatically. Cheapest diagnostic: run the same mystery-shop script across every surface the product ships on, not just the one engineering touched.

Assuming "we didn't mean to deceive anyone" is a defence.

Symptom: a team is genuinely surprised when a decorative stock counter draws a CCPA notice. Underlying error: conflating intent with effect, discussed above. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether a reasonable user, told the truth about the mechanism, would feel misled — if yes, intent is irrelevant.

8. What Good Looks Like

Three weeks after the notice, Mrigtrishna Mart shipped a checkout in which every charge appeared as a line item on the Cart screen before the buyer entered an address; the protection plan required an active tick rather than an active un-tick; the stock counter was either a real number pulled from the inventory system or removed entirely; and the cancellation flow for the loyalty subscription took exactly as many taps as sign-up had. Monthly revenue from the category fell by roughly the ₹30–59 lakh modelled above. Complaint volume fell by 71% within two months, refund-driven support cost fell by more than half, and — the detail Meher put in her own review — the redesign became the reference example Legal used with two other product teams instead of a warning.

9. The Decision, and Two Questions

Meher chose the unbundled version: flat fee disclosed at Cart, protection plan genuinely optional, stock counter either real or gone. She reasoned that ₹30 lakh a month was a known, bounded cost, while an open Drip Pricing and Basket Sneaking exposure was an unbounded one — a CCPA direction would have forced the same redesign anyway, on a public timeline, with a penalty attached. What she takes to next is why these thirteen patterns kept appearing in a team that never set out to deceive anyone — the module this one unlocks, on how dark patterns emerge from ordinary incentive structures without any villain in the room — and how to audit her own product on a standing basis rather than only when a gazette notification arrives.

Two questions worth sitting with: which of the thirteen patterns exists somewhere in a product you use every week, disguised as a feature you'd defend if asked? And if your own growth metrics improved the day a pattern like this shipped, what would have to be true for you to notice before the regulator did?
case40v1-ethics.accountability:
Pournami Technologies: ₹30 a Day

A savings app, a streak, and the question of what the product does to the people who use it.

Case for discussion · Chennai, October 2026

I. Sunday night

Rain had come early to Chennai, and on the night of Sunday 18 October 2026 it was loud on the window of the Guindy office. Bhuvaneswari Ilanthirayan was alone on the floor. In nineteen hours she would be on a board call — 7:30 pm India time on Monday the 19th, ten in the morning in New Jersey, four in the afternoon in Berlin — and she had to arrive with a recommendation about the mechanic that had built Pournami's business.

That mechanic was the streak. Save ₹10 and the day counted; miss a day and the count went to zero. One crore ninety-four lakh people had registered since 2017. In September 2026, 41.2 lakh put money in at least once, 12.6 lakh on an average day, and the company held ₹2,180 crore of gold for them — a mean holding of ₹5,291, a median of ₹1,840.

Six exhibits sat on her screen, assembled by four teams in three time zones. Two did not agree.

II. The company, and the decisions that are still running

Pournami Technologies Private Limited was founded in Chennai in 2017 by Bharanidharan Indraganti and two engineers from a payments firm, on an unfashionable thesis: that a dyeing-unit worker in Tiruppur would buy gold in ₹10 increments if the friction went away. The rails were UPI autopay mandates; metal and vaulting came from the category's usual suppliers.

Three decisions still bind. In March 2024 round-up went on by default for new users: a ₹183 grocery payment rounded to ₹190, and the ₹7 went to gold. On 1 October 2024 came the advance — ₹500 to ₹10,000 from a licensed non-banking lender in Mumbai, serviced by Pournami for a fee and underwritten on the lender's score, not the saver's gold. On 20 January 2025 it signed a white-label contract with Pravasi Pathway Services FZ-LLC of Dubai, whose payroll covers 2.3 lakh Emirates workers, 1.47 lakh of them Indian. Pravasi pays ₹21 crore a year; the contract names the engine by API version and requires sixty days' notice and joint testing for any change.

In November 2025 the mechanic was monetised directly. A shield — one missed day a month that would not break the streak — went into Pournami Plus, which had been selling at ₹149 a quarter since 2023. By September 2026 Plus was 10.6 lakh subscriptions and an annualised ₹63 crore (Exhibit 1).

III. The category

Digital gold is sold by almost everyone with an app — PhonePe, Paytm and Groww offer it — and micro-savings has its own cluster, with Jar and Gullak as comparables. The instrument sits in an empty regulatory space: neither a security nor a deposit, so no regulator supervises it, and SEBI in 2021 directed brokers to stop distributing it. Everything around it is regulated. The advance falls under the Reserve Bank's digital lending framework, which binds lender and app together. The interface falls under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 dark-pattern guidelines, which prohibit false urgency, nagging and confirm-shaming among thirteen practices. The data falls under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, notified in November 2025, whose children's provisions — verifiable parental consent, no behavioural monitoring — phase in on a timetable counsel calls vague.

Gold was the macro story: through 2026 the metal rose enough that a holding kept all year gained before the 3 per cent GST borne on purchase, which made the advance easy to sell. The calendar matters too — Akshaya Tritiya in April, Deepavali in November, whose creative was in production the week this case opens.

IV. What happened, and what was believed at the time

Figure 1 sets out the sequence. At each point the company had evidence, and the evidence is given with it.

Figure 1. Markers 1 to 4 are release-log dates; 5 is the Authority's letter as received by counsel; 6 is when the category went live.

Round-up, March 2024. The belief was that savers liked it. A survey that July reached 2,310 round-up users; 1,642 still had it switched on, and 1,166 of those 1,642 — 71.0 per cent — said they would not turn it off. The other 668 had turned it off already and answered a different question set.

The advance, October 2024. A pilot of 400 savers supported the belief that it would go on medical costs and school fees; the pilot asked them, before disbursal, what they intended. Exhibit 5 sets the advance's charges against the gold credited, by decile.

The shield, November 2025. The belief was that it relieved anxiety. Of 3.41 lakh shield activations in the twelve months to 30 September 2026, 1.19 lakh — 34.9 per cent — came within sixty minutes of the 9:12 pm “your streak is at risk” notification.

April 2026. A consumer-rights collective in Pune published a report on streak mechanics, naming no company. On 6 April the Central Consumer Protection Authority sought information under the 2023 guidelines; counsel replied in May. On Friday 9 October it sought more, reply due 31 October.

July 2026. Two things happened on 1 July. The grievance tool gained a category called pressure or coercive reminder; until then such complaints went under other (Exhibit 4). And growth ran a three-cell test over 21 days, 2.4 lakh savers a cell: cell one capped reminders at one a day and dropped the loss-framing copy, and daily saves per saver fell 4.1 per cent against control; cell two capped reminders only, and fell 1.6 per cent.

September 2026. Inampudi's team ran the survey that became Exhibit 3, from Monday 14 to Saturday 26 September. That month a vendor age model marked 1.4 per cent of monthly transacting savers — about 57,700 accounts — as probably under eighteen.

V. The people

Figure 2 shows where Monday's call sits.

Figure 2. Berlin moves to −4:30 on 25 October. A loaded engineer-month is ₹2.6 lakh in Pune and Bengaluru, ₹8.1 lakh in Berlin.

Bhuvaneswari Ilanthirayan — vice-president, product; Chennai
Owns the recommendation; wants to be able to say what the product does to a saver, not only for one. Her 2027 options vest on the Series C milestone. Has not said she approved the shield over a written objection.
Bharanidharan Indraganti — co-founder and chief executive; Chennai
Wants the worst reminders fixed and the streak kept; nobody else ever let a ₹30-a-day saver own gold. Has not said a term-sheet condition references the Authority's query.
Boothalingam Inukollu — principal data scientist; Toronto
Says nothing the company owns measures harm; wants a holdout with the streak off. Her July test is read two ways. Has not said a second memo, sent 14 October, never reached the pack.
Bishwajit Immadisetty — design lead; Berlin
Wants streak and shield removed together; wrote the November 2025 objection. Has an offer elsewhere. Has not said the loss-framing copy the shield monetises is his, from 2022.
Bhanumathi Inampudi — customer success lead; Singapore
Ran the survey; wants the pressure category backdated and the grievance flow rebuilt. Her team is nineteen agents short. Has not said she set the frame at thirty days expecting the effect there.
Bijendra Ipparthi — head of enterprise sales; New Jersey
Wants nothing changed before the Pravasi renewal and two North American deals close; his commission is weighted to it. Has not said Pravasi's compliance head has already written asking about Emirati consumer rules.
Bharathan Ilanchezhian — director of engineering; Pune
Can cap reminders in a fortnight; the real cost is forking the engine so India can change while Dubai cannot. Has lost eleven of thirty-four engineers in eighteen months. Has not said he thinks the affordability flag unbuildable, not costly.
