VII. Voices

“A third of our best savers told Bhanumathi's team they saved money they could not afford. On that frame it is close to five lakh people, and their alternative was owning nothing.” Indraganti, board pre-read, Thursday 15 October 2026
“The frame was 2,400 numbers and 638 answered. Exhibit 2 ranks savers by how much they already save. Nobody has let me switch the streak off, so I cannot tell you what it does.” Inukollu, chat to Ilanthirayan, 6:34 am IST Friday 16 October
“We charge ₹149 a quarter for the right not to be punished by a mechanic we built, and the notification that sells it goes out at 9:12 at night.” Immadisetty, design review, Friday 9 October
“Nothing has come from Dubai in writing and I would prefer it stayed that way until February. Change the engine now and we open the contract and the renewal at once.” Ipparthi, email to the leadership list, Tuesday 13 October
“The cap is a config change, in production by the 31st. The affordability flag is another animal: the bounce feed is the lender's, and clause 9.3 says credit decisions only.” Ilanchezhian, engineering channel, Wednesday 14 October
“I said I will pay on Monday, when the contractor pays me. She said the streak breaks on Sunday. So I took the ₹2,000 and paid the ₹30.” Grievance transcript, Coimbatore, 22 September 2026, translated from Tamil

VIII. The options as Ilanthirayan sees them

By Saturday she had four, costed in Exhibit 6 and ranked in an order she had changed twice.

A. Cap the reminders, make the pause free. One notification a day, the 9:12 pm message retired, two free pause days a month. It ships in a fortnight and touches no API Dubai consumes. It also gives away what Pournami Plus sells, a ₹63 crore line.

B. Remove the streak and the shield. A goal view takes their place: a target for Akshaya Tritiya and progress towards it. Immadisetty wants this; Inampudi would defend it to the Authority. It is also sixty days' notice to Pravasi and joint testing with a client whose compliance head is already asking.

C. Gate the streak on affordability. Keep the mechanic, suppress nudges for savers the system believes are stretched, make round-up opt-in. It needs 132 person-months against 118 uncommitted, a fork of the engine, and the bounce feed that clause 9.3 reserves for credit decisions.

D. Measure first. Define what harm would look like, instrument it, publish quarterly, submit it to an external panel, change nothing until the first reading. It changes no product, and it puts the ₹21 crore licence in play through the adverse-findings clause, ten business days from the announcement.

She had written a fifth line and crossed it out: ask the 57,700. She could not decide whether that was an option or another case.

IX. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board call is at 7:30 pm IST on Monday 19 October. The Deepavali creative freezes on Friday 23 October, running to 8 November. The Authority's reply is due 31 October. The Pravasi renewal window closes on 31 January 2027, and the Series C, expected in February, carries a milestone of 15 lakh daily active savers by 31 March 2027 against 12.6 lakh in September.

Money: ₹214 crore of cash on 30 September, net burn ₹9.4 crore a month in the September quarter. People: 95 engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, 118 uncommitted person-months before 31 March, a hiring freeze since July. Regulation: the dark-pattern reply, the lender's digital-lending obligations, which reach the sourcing app, and the Act's children's provisions over 57,700 accounts. Contract: sixty days' notice and joint testing on the licensed engine, service credits capped at ₹1.7 crore, adverse findings disclosable in ten business days, and clause 9.3, which permits the bounce feed for credit decisions only.

X. Questions for discussion

  1. Using only the figures on this page, describe what a year on Pournami did to a borrowing saver in the lowest holding decile, naming the denominator and window under each figure.
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 describe overlapping populations and point opposite ways. Which would you put before the board, and what does the other still oblige you to explain?
  3. Exhibit 4 is the only record of what savers themselves called pressure. Given how it was collected, what can be said about the six months it covers, and what cannot?
  4. Exhibit 6 prices every option in revenue at risk, person-months and contract exposure. Whose assumptions sit inside those prices, and what would an option cost that none of the three units can price?
  5. The one signal that would identify a stretched saver belongs to the lender, for credit decisions only. What is each option worth if it never arrives, and what do you do about the 57,700 accounts?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October. What does Ilanthirayan do before 7:30 pm, what does she say to the board, and what does she tell them she will not know until when?

XI. 11:40 pm

She opened the app on the test handset she kept in the drawer, registered to a number nobody at Pournami used. The counter read 114. At 9:12 that evening it had told her, in Tamil, that her streak was at risk; she had not acted, and the day was nearly over.

On the desk lay the Coimbatore transcript, the Toronto chart, Indraganti's pre-read and Immadisetty's objection from November. Bengaluru had asked whether the Deepavali creative could go ahead on the old copy, the freeze being Friday.

The rain had not stopped. Ilanthirayan picked up the transcript, read the last line again, and sat with the handset face down and the counter running.
exp40v2-ethics.accountability:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance · Ethics, Persuasion & Trust · Deep reading

Accountability for What Products Do to People

Own outcomes, not just outputs — and know precisely what you are claiming when you say so.

1. Two Rooms, Ten Days Apart

On 11 March 2026, Adithi Varadan, Head of Product at Saakshi Devices in Pune, was reading a spreadsheet her field engineer had built without being asked. Saakshi makes a driver-monitoring unit — infrared camera, inertial sensor and edge inference chip, bolted to a truck cab's A-pillar — that detects eye closure, phone use and prolonged gaze off the road, streaming scored events to a fleet dashboard. Thirty-eight fleets ran it across 42,000 vehicles for ₹19 crore of annual recurring revenue. The safety case was unusually strong: across the eleven fleets with clean baselines, reportable collisions per million kilometres had fallen from 1.9 to 1.3 in eighteen months.

The spreadsheet described what happened to events after they left Saakshi's dashboard. Eleven fleets had wired the event feed into payroll: each flagged event triggered an automatic deduction of ₹250 from the driver's monthly safety incentive. Saakshi had built that integration and sold it as a headline feature; two of the eleven had named it in their procurement decision. From raw inference logs, the field engineer had reconstructed the detector's precision in operating conditions: 0.41 overall against the manual review set, and 0.29 between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m., when the infrared path is noisiest and drivers wear the reflective glasses several fleets issue. Three in five deductions were being levied for events that had not happened.

Nothing in that sentence violated a contract, a regulation or a specification. AIS-140 says nothing about the labour economics of false positives, and the unit performed to its datasheet. Adithi's question, with a renewals forecast on the other screen, was whether Saakshi was accountable for a wage transfer it had engineered but did not collect.

Ten days later and 840 kilometres south, Zoya Mirza, VP of Product at Bayaan AI in Bengaluru, read a research deck before a Series B partner meeting. Bayaan's product, Sunwai, is a voice-first AI companion in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and Marathi: users talk to it about work, family, exams and loneliness, and it remembers. It had 2.4 million monthly actives, 187,000 subscribers at ₹149 a month, a ₹33.4 crore run rate, and 61 percent of users aged sixteen to twenty-four.

The deck reported a six-month panel of 2,900 users. In the middle deciles, self-reported loneliness had fallen by 0.2 points. In the top decile — 240,000 users averaging 68 minutes and nineteen sessions a day, contributing 31 percent of subscription revenue — loneliness had risen by 0.4, and 44 percent agreed that "Sunwai is the main thing I talk to about difficult things," against 9 percent in deciles one to five. The aggregate effect was faintly positive; the distribution was not.

Zoya's team had an intervention ready: an off-ramp that, after 45 minutes of continuous conversation or after 11 p.m., closes the session and suggests a human contact. Finance modelled a 7 percent hit to ARR, concentrated entirely in the cohort that was getting worse. The term sheet was expected in five weeks.

Both product leaders had built what they meant to build. Both had a growth number that was real. Both were looking at a second number that had no owner.

2. The Idea, Precisely Stated

Accountability for what products do to people is the claim that a product owner is answerable for the distribution of outcomes their product produces across everyone it touches — including people who never chose it — not merely for whether the artefact conforms to its specification. Three components are routinely collapsed into one word, and separating them is the expert's first move. Attributability: does the outcome trace to a choice you controlled? Answerability: do you owe an account to someone with standing to demand it? Remedy: must you bear a cost and change the thing? A team can be attributable without being answerable, answerable without holding remedy, or forced into remedy for something not attributable to it at all. Most dysfunction here is a mismatch between the three.

The idea was invented to solve a specific problem: the diffusion of responsibility inside organisations that H. L. A. Hart's taxonomy — role, causal, liability, capacity — made legible in the 1960s and that Dennis Thompson in 1980 named the "problem of many hands." When a hundred people each contribute a defensible increment to an indefensible whole, conventional responsibility finds nobody at fault. Helen Nissenbaum's 1996 account added the modern aggravations: software's many hands, the tolerance of bugs as normal, the computer as a scapegoat that absorbs blame no human need carry, and — the sharpest — ownership without liability, where a firm captures a system's upside while its terms disclaim the downside. Product-safety law approached the same terrain through foreseeability, duty of care and Judge Learned Hand's algebra: negligence where the burden of precaution is less than the probability of harm times its magnitude. The Markkula Center's lenses supplied the individual vocabulary; trust-and-safety and responsible-AI functions built after 2016 supplied the plumbing. India's scaffolding arrived later and unevenly — RBI digital lending guidelines, DPDP Act fiduciary duties, AIS-140 for telematics — and none of it speaks to either room above.

The schools that disagree are not caricatures, and each will sign a proposition the others will not. The table states them in operative form, because the difference shows up in what a practitioner is willing to write down.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Welfarist"A feature is acceptable if measured expected benefit across all affected parties exceeds measured expected harm.""Some harms are impermissible regardless of aggregate benefit."
Rights and dignity"No person may be made an instrument of growth without meaningful consent, whatever the aggregate."Any Hand-rule trade funding a benefit out of an unconsenting minority.
Procedural"Accountability is a property of structure — named owner, pre-registered threshold, audit trail — not of virtue.""A conscientious PM with good judgement is sufficient."
Contractarian"Informed adults with a real exit own their choices; the duty ends at non-deception.""A duty of care survives disclosure and consent."
Information-fiduciary"Asymmetry of information and power creates a duty of care that consent does not discharge.""Terms accepted at signup settle the question."
Table 1 — The five positions in signable form. Adithi's welfarist colleagues and her rights-oriented counsel were arguing not about facts but about which row they stood in; most deadlock here is a row mismatch nobody names aloud.

3. Mechanics, Worked Through

Expert practice begins by drawing the affected-person set, which is almost never the user list. For Saakshi it includes the monitored driver, his household, other road users and the insurer; for Bayaan, the subscriber, the people the subscriber is no longer talking to, and — 61 percent of users being under twenty-five — guardians who consented to nothing. The step left implicit is that the person bearing the harm is usually not the person choosing the product, and in B2B is almost never the person paying for it.

Fig. 1 — The chain from a design choice to a household's income, with the perimeter inside which Saakshi's conventional metrics live. The harm is attributable (remove the integration and it stops), foreseeable (precision was measurable before shipping) and unowned.

The second step is the harm ledger: not a list of concerns but a table with a column per property that changes the answer — incidence, severity in the currency the harm lands in, reversibility and exit cost. Reversibility is most often omitted and most often decisive. A wrongly deducted ₹250 is recoverable in principle; if the grievance process requires a written appeal to the supervisor who set the rule, practical reversibility is near zero.

The third step is the counterfactual baseline, where competent practitioners err in the generous direction. Harm is measured against the world without the feature, not against zero. Drivers were fatigued before Saakshi arrived; the honest question is marginal harm against marginal benefit. Sunwai's heaviest users were not a random slice and may have been lonelier on arrival, in which case a rising loneliness score is part selection and part effect — inseparable without a holdout.

The formal treatment is the arithmetic of classifier error, worth working rather than naming. Take 1,000 Saakshi-monitored driver-months of 190 driving hours each. At a genuine distraction-event base rate of one per 380 hours, the true event count is 500. At the shipped threshold the detector recalls 78 percent, giving 390 true positives; at precision 0.41, total flags are 390 ÷ 0.41 = 951, so false positives number 561. More than half of all flags are wrong, and at ₹250 a flag that is ₹1.40 lakh of wages per 1,000 driver-months removed for events that did not occur — roughly ₹6.7 crore a year across the 11,600 driver-months under deduction contracts.

The distribution is worse than the average. Night shifts are 22 percent of driving hours but, at precision 0.29, generate 44 percent of false positives: the drivers with least schedule choice absorb double their share of an error they cannot see, cannot appeal and did not cause. That is the quantitative core of the topic. A classifier's error rate is not a user-experience annoyance, it is a transfer, and the accountable question is who receives it.

Fig. 2 — At precision 0.41 the detector produces more wrong flags than right ones, and the night shift — 22 percent of hours — carries 44 percent of them. The aggregate error rate hides that entirely.

Two second-order effects follow. First, instrumentation creates evidence: the spreadsheet Adithi was reading is discoverable, and everyone in the room knew it, which is why "we never measured that" is so often an achievement rather than an oversight. Second, guardrails move demand rather than deleting it — if Bayaan closes a session at 11 p.m., some of the top decile opens a less careful competitor with no crisis routing at all. Neither effect argues against acting; both argue against claiming that acting has settled the matter.

4. When the Idea Applies, and When It Misleads

Stating the doctrine's conditions as testable claims prevents it from expanding until it means nothing. Claim one: a causal chain runs from a choice you control to a change in a person's condition — test it by asking whether reversing the choice would measurably change the outcome. Saakshi passes emphatically; remove the payroll integration and the transfer stops that week. Bayaan passes weakly; removing the streak and the 10:40 p.m. nudge changes session counts, but whether it changes loneliness is exactly what nobody knows. Claim two: the affected person cannot fully price or avoid the harm. A driver cannot read the precision curve of a camera pointed at his face; a nineteen-year-old cannot price swapping an always-agreeable listener for a difficult friend. Claim three: the harm was foreseeable at design time or is detectable now — Saakshi could have measured night-time precision before shipping and did not; Bayaan measured and found it. Claim four: you hold authority to change the thing. Adithi does, through the contract; Zoya does, if the board lets her.

Where the idea misleads deserves equal precision. It misleads when "harm" is a preference the product team disapproves of: a user who chooses two hours a night with an AI is not thereby harmed, and a PM who assumes otherwise has replaced accountability with taste. It misleads when accountability is claimed for outcomes outside the claimant's control, because a person held answerable for what they cannot change stops surfacing evidence — the first casualty of unbounded accountability is honest instrumentation. And it misleads applied to general-purpose infrastructure, since a database company is upstream of every harm any application causes and a doctrine reaching that far dilutes to a slogan.

5. Hard Edges

Harm is frequently a property of a combination rather than a product. Saakshi also sells a route-optimisation module; fleets running both push drivers into tighter turnarounds, raising fatigue, raising genuine event rates, raising deductions. No single owner authored that loop, and each roadmap is defensible alone. Multi-product firms handle this badly because ownership follows surfaces, not the user's experience of the combination. The seam is worse in B2B, where the harmful configuration is usually written by customer success rather than product. At Hazri Workforce Cloud, an attendance and shift-scheduling vendor, the field team's implementation playbook — not the product — recommended the geofence radius that made warehouse staff clock in on their own time; the product team had never read it. Mature companies say they solve this with an ethics review board. What works is narrower and less photogenic: a release gate a named person can hold shut without escalation, an acceptable-use clause with a revocation right, and a periodic audit of how the largest customers actually configured the thing.

Two-sided markets add a complication: the platform's ranking authors a distribution it does not directly control. Vachan Freight Exchange, a Chennai load-matching marketplace, found that a reliability score built to protect shippers concentrated 71 percent of return loads among 12 percent of owner-operators, pushing the rest into empty running they could not price. Vachan neither dispatched a truck nor set a rate; it set a rank. Regulated categories present the opposite failure. At Tasdeeq Money, a Mumbai payments firm, every consumer-facing decision passed compliance review, and the review's existence quietly ended the ethical conversation: the team asked whether a flow was permitted and stopped asking whether it was defensible. Regulatory sufficiency is the commonest anaesthetic for judgement in Indian fintech.

Hardware changes the reversibility column. A software guardrail ships in a week; Saakshi's threshold change reaches only the 82 percent of units on fleets permitting over-the-air updates, and the remaining 7,500 sit in cabs for four to six more years. AI-native products break stationarity: the harm profile belongs to a model version, so a routine update silently changes who gets hurt and a launch-time review has no purchase on it. The only instrument that survives an update is an eval suite with distributional slices and a release gate wired to it — which is why Bayaan's off-ramp argument was inseparable from whether the crisis-routing eval, passing at 84 percent, should block a release at all.

6. Eight Distinctions That Separate Expert from Competent

Accountability is answerability plus authority, not blame. The tell-tale sign is what an expert asks after an incident: not who was fired, but who now holds power to stop the thing without permission. A firm that answers harm with a dismissal and no change in decision rights has performed accountability and installed none — the price paid by a departing individual is exactly what lets the structure continue unchanged.

The harm lives in the tail, and the tail usually pays the bills. When harm is discussed in averages, an expert stops and asks for the worst decile. This is a structural regularity, not a statistical preference: the heaviest users of an engagement-optimised product are both the most valuable cohort and the most likely to be harmed, so the population ethics should protect is the one the revenue model depends on. Bayaan's top decile is 31 percent of revenue and 100 percent of the deterioration. A net-positive average settles nothing, because two morally opposite worlds produce the same average.

Consent does not discharge the duty where exit is costly. The phrase "they agreed to the terms," delivered as a closing argument, is the tell. Experts test consent by asking what refusing would cost: a driver who declines camera monitoring declines employment; a subscriber who cancels at month nine loses a memory of themselves that she cannot export. Consent under those conditions is real but thin, and thin consent shifts the burden of care back toward the party holding the information.

Measuring harm creates evidence, and the expert measures anyway — having had the conversation first. The sign of a competent-but-not-expert team is a data question deferred twice without anyone saying why. The expert takes counsel into the room before the query runs, agrees scope, retention and escalation, then runs it. Treating legal caution as cowardice is the wrong reading: the exposure is real, and pretending otherwise is how good instrumentation gets killed rather than scoped.

The right comparison is the realistic substitute, not a harm-free world. Before celebrating a guardrail an expert asks what the affected cohort does next, because guardrails displace demand more often than they delete it. If Saakshi withdraws from the eleven deduction fleets, they may install an unmonitored regime or a cheaper camera at precision 0.31; if Bayaan closes a session, the user may open a worse app. Instrument that migration before shipping the cap: a fall in your own harm metric is a fall in harm only about half the time.

Foreseeability is dated, and the date is the fact that matters. Once a firm knows, a clock starts, and both the moral and legal positions turn on what happened between knowing and acting. Experts date their knowledge deliberately — "we learned this on 11 March; remediation lands by 30 June" — because an undated finding can later be found to have sat for two years. The tell is a memo carrying a decision deadline rather than a recommendation.

A threshold set after seeing the number is not a threshold. Ask when the line was written down relative to when the data arrived. Pre-registration is the whole mechanism: it converts a judgement made under the pull of a quarter into one made before the pull existed. The function of the number is to bind a future self who will have excellent reasons.

Classifier error is a currency, not a nuisance. An expert converts every false positive and false negative into the unit it lands in for the person receiving it — rupees of wages, hours of unpaid appeal, a declined loan, a missed escalation — and only then compares. The tell is a team quoting precision and recall to three decimals that has never multiplied either by the consequence: the commonest signature of technical competence without accountability in AI work.

7. Where the Shape Genuinely Changes

In consumer products the chain is short and the harmed party is the chooser, making attribution easy and distribution hard: Bayaan sees everything a user does and still cannot see what the product displaced. In B2B the buyer is not the harmed party, so the lever is contractual rather than design-side — acceptable-use terms, configuration limits, revocation rights. That is why Adithi's real decision is commercial, and why B2B teams watching only customer satisfaction are blind one hop out. Platforms author a distribution indirectly through ranking, so their instrument is a fairness constraint on allocation, not a limit on any single interaction. Hardware moves the binding constraint to reversibility and unit lifetime; the decision that matters is made at design freeze, because afterwards a change means a truck rolling to a depot. AI-native products move it to non-stationarity: accountability attaches to an eval suite and a release gate, since nothing established at launch survives a model update.

Stage changes the answer more honestly than most ethics material admits. At seed a team cannot instrument everything, and the correct practice is not a programme but one written harm hypothesis with one metric attached. Growth is the dangerous stage, and both protagonists are in it: instrumentation exists, the harm is visible, and every incentive — a term sheet, a renewals forecast, a review cycle — points the other way. At public-company scale the incentive turns legally defensive, which changes not whether harm is measured but how findings are written and who may read them. What does not change is the arithmetic: harm ledger, counterfactual and error-cost conversion are identical for a twelve-person startup and a listed company. Only the levers and the excuses differ.

8. Three Worked Cases

Saakshi's decoupling, modelled. Of ₹19 crore ARR, the eleven deduction-integrated fleets contribute ₹4.7 crore. Prohibiting per-event pay deduction by contract, and offering an aggregated monthly coaching score with no automatic financial consequence instead, puts an estimated ₹1.9 crore at renewal risk — finance assumed four of the eleven would churn or renegotiate. The safety benefit survives intact, because detection and coaching remain; the harm removed is the ₹6.7 crore annual wrongful transfer. The asymmetry is the lesson: the ₹1.9 crore appears on Saakshi's P&L and the ₹6.7 crore appears on nobody's, which is precisely the accounting outcome accountability exists to correct.

Pramaan Learning's failure, and what recovery cost. The Noida skilling company sold ₹68,000 programmes to low-income households through counsellor-led calls with EMI financing, under an affordability guardrail: no EMI above 12 percent of declared monthly income. The guardrail was real, documented and audited — and passed 96 percent of applications, because income was self-declared and the counsellor, whose commission depended on enrolment, helped fill in the form. A later bureau check found declared incomes inflated by a median of 34 percent; ninety-day default reached 19 percent and grievances 2,100 a month. The failure was measuring the output — guardrail applied — rather than the outcome — affordable in fact — with the guardrail owned by the function it constrained. Recovery took four quarters: bureau income verification cut qualifying applications 28 percent and annualised revenue by ₹41 crore, ₹9.6 crore was refunded to 14,000 families, and the change that held was moving ownership from sales into finance and re-basing the sales incentive on 90-day non-default.

Bayaan's holdout, and the limits of a four-week read. Rather than argue the off-ramp on theory, Zoya's team ran it for four weeks against a control on 120,000 top-decile users; the results complicated both sides.

Measure (4 weeks, top-decile holdout)ControlOff-rampDelta
Median daily session minutes6847−31%
30-day subscription retention81%72%−9 pts
Conversion, deciles 4–7 (exposed to same build)7.6%9.0%+1.4 pts
Users reporting a human conversation after an off-ramp—23%—
Net modelled ARR impact——−4.1%
Table 2 — Measurement moved the estimate from finance's modelled −7 percent to −4.1, because the middle deciles converted better on a build that visibly did not fight to keep them. What four weeks cannot measure is the loneliness outcome the intervention exists to change. The decision has to be made on a proxy, and saying so aloud is the accountable move.

9. Failure Modes and Their Early Warnings

The failures below are not moral lapses; each is a reasonable-looking organisational arrangement that reliably produces an unowned harm. Each diagnostic question is one an experienced practitioner asks in a review meeting.

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching late
Review-board theatreThe board has never blocked a launch"Name the last decision this changed."A dated paper trail proving you knew
Proxy captureGuardrail pass rate above 95%"Who fails this, and why so few?"Pramaan's ₹41 crore and 14,000 refunds
Owner without authorityOutcome owner reports to growth owner"Can they stop a ship without escalating?"Findings that arrive after the launch
Threshold retrofittingLine set in the meeting the data landed"When was this written down?"Every future threshold discounted
Aggregate launderingNet-positive claim, no distribution shown"Show me the worst decile."Harm compounds in the paying cohort
Deliberate non-measurementSame query deferred twice, unexplained"What would we do if it were bad?"Regulator infers negligence from silence

Table 3 — Eight arrangements that produce unowned harm. Six of the eight are visible without new data — they are facts about reporting lines, meeting records and pass rates — which is why an experienced reviewer diagnoses most of this from an org chart and a launch calendar.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Individual ownership versus institutional design. The naming school argues that harm is caught only when a specific person's name sits on a specific number, citing the many-hands literature and incident reviews where the catch came from one accountable owner. The institutional school replies that named owners in growth-stage companies are routinely overridden, so naming without authority manufactures a fall guy and suppresses reporting from below. The naming school is wrong if override rates are as high as the institutionalists believe.

Common currency versus lexical priority. The welfarists insist that without a common unit you cannot choose, and that refusing to choose is a choice for a status quo with its own body count; Saakshi's crash reduction is real, and lives are the most consequential unit on the table. The rights school answers that aggregation licenses exactly what happened here — funding road safety out of the wages of drivers wrongly accused, who never agreed to pay — and that the minority made to pay is reliably the one with least exit. Welfarism fails if the harms it aggregates away fall systematically on the same group across products, making the arithmetic a redistribution rather than a trade; the rights position fails if a measured accounting shows its prohibitions costing more lives than they protect.

Measure everything versus measure narrowly. The first camp notes that you cannot fix what you cannot see, and that regulators increasingly read absent instrumentation as indifference. The second observes that the firms which looked hardest were punished with their own documents — a perverse selection against diligence. The disagreement would dissolve given credible safe harbours for good-faith internal audit; there are none.

Autonomy versus engineered preference. The autonomy camp asks who a product manager in Bengaluru is to decide what a nineteen-year-old in Warangal needs, and treats revealed preference as the only non-arbitrary signal. The protective camp answers that the Hook-model machinery — triggers, variable rewards, stored value — exists precisely to move behaviour independent of considered preference, so preference revealed inside such a system is not evidence of autonomous choice. Bayaan can partly settle it: offer the off-ramp with full disclosure and see whether the top decile keeps using anyway.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a values statement and an ethics review; someone who has internalised it produces a contract clause, a release gate and a dated memo. They ask for the distribution before the average, every time. They convert model error into the currency it lands in before comparing anything. They separate attributability, answerability and remedy out loud, because most disagreements dissolve once the three come apart. They name which school they are arguing from, so an opponent can say where the argument forks. They date knowledge and deadline the response. And the clearest marker: they will accept a harm explicitly — "we run at this precision until Q3, roughly 240 wrongful flags a month will occur, affected drivers are made whole by this mechanism, and here is what would make us stop" — rather than argue the harm is not real. Denial is the amateur's move; an owned, bounded, remediated, stated harm is the professional's.

12. What They Decided

Adithi Varadan kept the detector and killed the integration. Saakshi's contracts were amended to prohibit per-event pay deduction, with a revocation right; fleets were offered an aggregated monthly coaching score instead, and Adithi wrote the ₹1.9 crore renewal risk into her own plan rather than a footnote. She pre-registered a threshold — night-shift precision reaches 0.40 by 30 September or the night flagging path is disabled — with her name against it, circulated before calibration work began. Her reasoning was a rights argument, not a welfarist one: she would not fund a crash reduction out of misattributed wages. What she gave up was the cleanest commercial story she had.

Zoya Mirza shipped the off-ramp to the top two deciles only, kept the streak, which she judged load-bearing for the median user, and pre-registered a six-month loneliness readout on a maintained holdout. She took the ₹1.4 crore revenue risk to the Series B partners before the term sheet closed, on the view that a dependency finding disclosed by the founder is a governance asset and the same finding surfaced in diligence is a valuation event. Her reasoning was fiduciary: the asymmetry between a sixteen-year-old and a memory-keeping model creates a duty the subscription agreement does not discharge. What she gave up was the argument that the numbers were still uncertain — which was true, and which she decided was not a reason to wait.

  1. Saakshi's payroll integration was legal, contracted and sold as a feature. Where, if anywhere, does Saakshi's accountability for the wage transfer begin — at building the integration, selling it, learning the precision figure, or the moment a fleet configured it? Defend the boundary you draw.
  2. Bayaan's aggregate effect on loneliness was positive. Make the strongest case that shipping the off-ramp is wrong, then name the single piece of evidence that would defeat it.
  3. Design the arrangement that would have surfaced each harm eighteen months earlier, and state what it would have cost when nobody yet knew it was needed.

13. Going Deeper

Accountability for What Products Do to People

Am I accountable for what the product does to people, not just for them?

1. A Tuesday in February

Ritika Dave, VP of Product at Mohar Credit, a Bengaluru-based lending app for gig and contract workers, sat in a fourteenth-floor conference room on a Tuesday morning in February 2026, looking at a slide her data team had rebuilt twice because she had not believed the first version. Mohar Credit's flagship feature, SalaryLine Advance, let a driver, delivery rider or warehouse packer draw up to half of their earned-but-unpaid wages, days before payday, for a flat fee of ₹49 per ₹1,000 advanced. It had been the biggest growth driver in the company's history: monthly disbursals had risen from ₹14 crore to ₹61 crore in eighteen months, and the dashboard projected on the wall behind her showed that number in green. Ritika's own performance review, six weeks away, would cite it.

The second slide, the one she had asked for twice, showed something else. Of the 118,000 people who used SalaryLine Advance in January, 26,400 – about 22 percent – had taken a fourth or later consecutive advance inside the same ninety-day window, meaning they were drawing down next month's wages before this month's had even cleared. For that group, outstanding-advance-to-monthly-income had climbed from 8 percent in September to 34 percent in January. An overnight ticket audit found forty-one complaints in the past month alone from users who said they had taken an advance specifically to repay the fee on a previous one. Two used the word "trap."

Nothing about SalaryLine Advance was illegal. Its disclosures met the RBI's digital lending guidelines to the letter, and every fee was quoted upfront before a user tapped confirm. The feature had shipped exactly as specified eighteen months earlier: fast, transparent, within its brief. Ritika's team had built precisely what they set out to build. The question in front of her was not whether SalaryLine Advance worked as designed. It was whether "worked as designed" was the same thing as "acceptable" – and whose job it was to decide.

2. The Idea

Accountability for what products do to people means being answerable for the actual downstream consequences a product has on the humans who use it, not merely for whether the product does what its specification said it would do. The distinction matters because a feature can be a complete engineering and design success – built on time, meeting every acceptance criterion, moving every launch metric in the intended direction – while still leaving a meaningful share of its users measurably worse off. Output accountability asks: did we build the thing correctly? Outcome accountability asks: what happened to people because we built it? – and insists the second question belongs to the product owner, not to legal, not to "the algorithm," and not to the user's own choices alone.

The idea has no single inventor the way a pricing formula might; it crystallized across the late 2010s as two lessons landed together. The Markkula Center for Applied Ethics at Santa Clara University formalized "ethical lenses" – rights, justice, utility, common good, virtue – as tools an individual could apply to their own decisions, not just abstract policy. Around the same years, a string of visible product failures – engagement-optimized feeds, biased lending models, gig-platform designs maximizing hours worked over worker welfare – made clear a team could hit every internal metric and still cause harm nobody had been assigned to notice. Responsible-AI and trust-and-safety functions at large technology and financial firms formalized the practice soon after: know your ethical lenses, then apply them to your own product, on the record.

"I'm accountable for what happens to the people who use SalaryLine Advance – not only for whether we built what the spec said."

Fig. 1 – Output metrics stop at "fee collected"; the outcome – rising repeat borrowing and debt-to-income – happens two steps further down a chain nobody had instrumented on purpose.

3. How It Actually Works

Applying accountability mechanically starts with tracing the causal chain from a feature to a real person's life, not stopping at the metric the feature was designed to move, as Figure 1 shows for SalaryLine Advance. The dashboard had always tracked the first two links – advances issued, fees collected – because those move the P&L. Nobody had built a view for the third link, repeat-advance frequency, because it does not appear on a growth scorecard; it has to be asked for on purpose, usually by someone willing to look for evidence their own feature is causing harm.

The second step is separating who captures a decision's benefit from who bears its cost, because in a lending product these are often different people at different times. Mohar Credit's revenue team benefited immediately from every advance issued; the cost, if any, landed weeks later on a different line entirely – loan losses, or no company line at all, such as a missed rent payment. Accountability means pulling that deferred, often invisible cost onto the same table as the immediate benefit before deciding whether the feature is working.

Third, outcome signals need instrumentation before launch, not after a complaint spike forces the question. Fourth, someone with real authority to change or kill the feature has to be named, in writing, as owner of the outcome, not merely of the output; a chart that lists "product" as responsible for shipping and "risk" as responsible for compliance leaves outcome ownership sitting nowhere between the two. Fifth, that owner needs a threshold agreed before the data arrives – a number past which the feature changes regardless of what it is doing for growth that quarter. Practitioners routinely skip this step, setting thresholds only after a number already looks bad, which functions exactly like not having one.

4. A Worked Example

Take Mohar Credit's January cohort of 118,000 SalaryLine Advance users and work through what "outcome" means in numbers, not sentiment. The output view showed 118,000 users, ₹61 crore disbursed, average advance ₹5,170, fee revenue ₹2.99 crore, and activation among eligible workers up from 31 to 44 percent since October. Every one of those numbers had grown, and every one was true.

The outcome view splits the same 118,000 by how many advances each took inside a rolling ninety-day window: 61,400 users (52 percent) took one advance and repaid it in full with no repeat; 30,200 (26 percent) took two or three; 26,400 (22 percent) took four or more. For that last group, a fee of ₹49 per ₹1,000 taken four-plus times in ninety days works out to an effective annualized cost of roughly 71 percent, even though each individual transaction's fee looked trivial inside the app. For a rider earning ₹18,000 a month, four consecutive ₹4,000 advances at that fee structure meant close to ₹800 a month – 4.4 percent of income – spent purely on the cost of borrowing against wages already earned.

Under a 3-advance cap≈00%≤17%

Now change one input: cap consecutive advances at three within any ninety-day window, the way a peer lender, Naqsh Finance, had already done. Modelled on the same January cohort, that cap stops the 26,400 heaviest-repeat users at their third advance, cutting projected disbursal volume by roughly ₹9.6 crore for the month – about 16 percent of the ₹61 crore total – and fee revenue by a proportional ₹47 lakh. The number that never shows up on the P&L: an estimated 26,400 workers no longer sliding past a 34 percent debt-to-income ratio inside a single quarter. The arithmetic does not say which number should win; it only makes both numbers visible at the same time, which is the entire point of outcome accountability.

5. Nuances a Learner Must Get Straight

Outcomes are not intentions. Nobody at Mohar Credit designed SalaryLine Advance to trap anyone; the fee model and the repeat-borrowing pattern emerged from ordinary optimization toward activation and volume. Accountability for outcomes does not require, or even usually involve, bad intent – which is exactly why it has to be checked for on purpose rather than inferred from motives.

Accountability is broader than legal liability. SalaryLine Advance broke no law and violated no disclosure rule. A product can clear every regulatory bar and still be one where the owner should be answerable for what happened to real borrowers; treating "legal" as a synonym for "fine" is the most common way this gets waved away.

Not every bad outcome is a harm the product caused. Some repeat borrowers might have faced the same cash-flow gap with or without SalaryLine Advance, using a moneylender at far worse terms instead. Genuine accountability requires a counterfactual – what would have happened to this person absent the feature – and skipping that question inflates blame just as skipping measurement understates it.

It is easily confused with paternalism. "You are accountable for what happens to users" can slide into "you should decide for users what is good for them," a different and more contested claim. Accountability obliges you to see and own the consequence; it does not by itself tell you to remove the choice that produced it.

It cannot tell you where to draw the line. Knowing that 22 percent of borrowers are repeat-cycling does not tell Ritika whether 22, 10 or 2 percent is the acceptable ceiling. The concept forces the trade-off onto the table; it does not resolve it, since that is a values and business-model question, not a measurement one.

Responsibility diffuses across functions by default. Growth built the activation flow, risk built the credit model, design built the reminders, and each team could reasonably say the pattern was not entirely theirs. Without one named owner of the outcome, that diffusion is the default state accountability has to be deliberately imposed against.

Scale changes the moral weight of a small percentage. "Only 22 percent" sounds containable until converted into 26,400 people, each with a debt-to-income ratio that quadrupled in four months. Any percentage discussed without its absolute headcount understates what is actually being decided.

It depends on what gets measured. Ritika saw the repeat-borrowing pattern only because Farheen built the cohort view. A team cannot be accountable, in any meaningful sense, for an outcome it has no instrument to observe – making the decision to build that instrument itself part of the accountability question.

6. Consumer, B2B, Marketplace – and Company Stage

In a consumer product like SalaryLine Advance, the person harmed and the person who tapped "confirm" are the same individual, and the chain from feature to consequence is short. In a B2B product the chain runs longer: a firm such as Hastakshar, an e-signature and contract-workflow company selling to employers, is not itself harmed or helped by its own product; the people affected are the employer's employees, whose contracts get signed through Hastakshar's flow. If a customer configures that flow to rush signatures past employees without a real chance to read the terms, Hastakshar's product did exactly what it was built to do, and the harm still traces back through it. B2B accountability requires looking one hop past the paying customer to that customer's employee or counterparty – a hop many B2B teams never take, because their own dashboard ends at customer satisfaction.

A marketplace complicates this further because there are two sides to weigh against each other. Mohar Credit sits partly in this position: fee revenue is a cost imposed on the borrower and a benefit captured by the platform, but the platform also depends on lenders willing to fund advances, whose risk appetite shapes how it is priced. Marketplace accountability means refusing to treat either side's metric as the whole picture – borrower welfare and lender sustainability have to be read together, not traded off silently inside one blended growth number.

Stage matters as much as product type. At an early-stage startup, accountability for outcomes usually sits informally with the founder or the one PM close enough to the data to notice a pattern like Ritika's, because no dedicated trust function exists yet; the risk is that growth pressure crowds the question out. At a large company, a trust-and-safety or responsible-AI team typically exists – but the risk inverts: line product teams treat outcome accountability as "that team's job," reporting a metric to them rather than owning the decision. Both failure modes end the same way: an outcome nobody with power to change the product actually owns.

Fig. 2 – The harmed person sits at different distances from the decision-maker depending on product type; each extra hop is a place accountability can quietly stop.

7. Common Mistakes

"We built what the spec said." The symptom: a team treats a post-launch harm finding as someone else's problem because the ticket is closed. The misunderstanding equates accountability with authorship rather than ongoing ownership of consequences. The cheapest diagnostic: ask who gets paged this week if the feature is quietly hurting users right now; if the answer is nobody, there is no owner, regardless of who wrote the code.

Outcome metrics that live in a deck nobody acts on. The symptom: a monthly slide on complaint rates that has appeared, unchanged, for a year. The misunderstanding treats outcome tracking as reporting rather than a decision input. The diagnostic: find one past instance where the metric actually changed a roadmap call; if there is none, it is decorative.

"The algorithm decided." The symptom: language that describes a model's output as if no person chose the objective it optimized. The misunderstanding treats automation as removing accountability rather than relocating it upstream to whoever set the target. The diagnostic: ask who can override or pause the model this week, by name.

Calling harm an "edge case." The symptom: a harm rate discussed only as a percentage – "just 22 percent" – never a headcount. The misunderstanding is that small shares of large numbers still feel small. The diagnostic, used every time: convert the percentage into actual people before the conversation continues.

8. What Good Looks Like

Naqsh Finance, a smaller Pune-based competitor in the same salary-advance category, had faced the identical growth-versus-harm tension roughly a year earlier. Its head of product asked the data team, before launch rather than after a complaint spike, to build the same cohort view Farheen improvised for Ritika: repeat-advance frequency and debt-to-income drift, tracked from day one alongside disbursal volume. When the pattern appeared – smaller, because it was caught earlier – the team set a hard cap of three consecutive advances per ninety days, named the head of product accountable for the debt-to-income number in the same review where growth was discussed, and absorbed an eleven percent hit to disbursal growth for two quarters. Naqsh's default rate in that segment came in roughly a third below the category average the following year, and the cap became a selling point with the lenders funding its book, who priced the portfolio more cheaply because it carried less tail risk. Nothing about this required Naqsh to abandon growth as a goal; it required treating the outcome metric as load-bearing rather than decorative, before the number got large enough to be a crisis.

9. What Ritika Decides

Ritika recommended a three-advance cap per ninety-day window, effective the following cycle, alongside a redefined north-star metric that paired disbursal growth with debt-to-income drift on the same slide, reviewed by the same people, every month. She named herself, in writing, as accountable for the second number, not just the first, and told the board to expect roughly a sixteen percent disbursal hit for one or two quarters while the lending model recalibrated around a healthier base of borrowers. She did not claim the change eliminated every risk, and she did not claim the feature had been wrong to build. What she owned was narrower and more defensible: that a product built exactly to spec had produced a measurable harm nobody had been assigned to watch for, and that fixing it belonged to the person who ran the product – not to compliance, not to the algorithm, and not to the borrowers who had simply used the feature as designed.

From here, the natural next step is dark patterns: understanding how features like SalaryLine Advance drift toward harm through ordinary incentives and small design choices, with no one ever deciding to cause it – the mechanism that makes accountability necessary in the first place, rather than optional. Two questions worth sitting with: what outcome metric does your own product currently have zero instrumentation for, and if it started climbing tomorrow, who, by name, would be the person expected to notice?
case20v1-ethics.accountability:
Nilgiri Pay and the Festive Boost

A decision case on accountability for what a product does to people

The evening of 20 October

At 8:30 on the evening of Tuesday, 20 October 2026, Abirami Harikrishnan closed the door of a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of Nilgiri Pay's Bengaluru office and opened a spreadsheet that had reached her from Toronto the night before. As Head of Product she owned Festive Boost, a one-tap offer that raised a borrower's spending limit by half in the weeks before Diwali, which fell on Sunday, 8 November. Leadership would meet at 6 p.m. on Friday, 23 October to decide whether Boost went to every eligible borrower on Monday, 26 October. Marketing had already booked the push notifications. The pilot numbers were excellent for the business. She was no longer sure they were excellent for the people using it.

Company background

Nilgiri Pay was founded in 2019 by Ambarish Hariprasad and two classmates from NIT Trichy. Its "Pay Later" product is a credit line issued by a regulated NBFC partner and distributed through Nilgiri's app. Salaried staff and gig workers use it at partner merchants, settling in thirty days without interest or converting the bill into EMIs. Limits run from ₹3,000 to ₹25,000. At 30 September 2026 the app had 8,00,000 active borrowers, of whom 6,00,000 had at least three clean repayment cycles and counted as eligible for a higher limit. Revenue ran at roughly ₹110 crore a year, from merchant fees, EMI interest and late fees, and the company employed 640 people, with engineering in Bengaluru and Pune.

Growth had come from merchants rather than advertising. The first partners were electronics and appliance retailers in Chennai and Hyderabad, whose shoppers wanted EMIs without a credit card. Quick-commerce and food-delivery merchants followed, and with them smaller, more frequent purchases. Nilgiri raised its last round in 2024 on the strength of its repayment record, and the leadership still describes that record as the company's real asset.

It competes with Simpl, LazyPay and Paytm Postpaid, with the pay-later options inside Flipkart and Amazon, and increasingly with credit lines on UPI. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending rules shape the product: a key fact statement must precede each loan, and a credit limit may not be raised without the borrower's explicit consent.

The situation

Until September, a borrower wanting more headroom had to find a "Request increase" button in settings. Boost put the offer on the home screen with the higher limit pre-filled and a single Accept button. Between 1 and 7 September, the team showed it to a random 40,000 eligible borrowers and left another random 40,000 with the old button. The offer was the only designed difference. Exhibit 1 gives the results. Priced across all 6,00,000 eligible borrowers, the pilot's difference in net contribution came to ₹1.68 crore a month, or about ₹20 crore a year.

The costs sat in the lower rows. Late payment, meaning unpaid seven days after the due date, rose from 6.0 to 8.5 per cent, which at full roll-out implies about 15,000 more late borrowers every cycle. Amaresh Haranath's cut by declared income, in Exhibit 2, showed where the lateness sat: takers earning under ₹20,000 a month were late 18.0 per cent of the time and carried month-end balances equal to 65 per cent of a month's income. Nilgiri's standing dashboards track default at ninety days, a horizon at which none of this had yet appeared. Exhibit 3 shows the calendar that remained.

Uptake was not even. Because the pilot arm mirrored the eligible mix, the takers in Exhibit 2 imply 40 per cent uptake in the lowest band, 35 per cent in the middle and 28 per cent in the highest. Contacts to support about a due date also rose, from 410 to 640 borrowers, or 1.0 to 1.6 per cent of each arm. Abirami also knew that the pilot covered a single cycle, and that borrowers who stumble in a first cycle on a higher limit may recover or may not.

The people

Ambarish Hariprasad, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru, wants Boost live on the 26th. A funding round is planned for January, and festive-quarter growth will anchor it. "Late fees are not part of our plan," he told Abirami. "Boost gives good customers room." He is not wrong that most takers pay on time, and he is not indifferent to harm; he wants evidence of it that is larger than one cycle, and he points out that the company's ninety-day default rate has stayed low through every earlier festive season.

Amaresh Haranath, senior data scientist, Toronto, built both exhibits. On a call that evening, at 11 a.m. his time and nine and a half hours behind Bengaluru until 1 November, he told Abirami he would not put his name to a roll-out without a stopping rule, and that he would rather be asked to rerun the numbers than to defend them later.

Annapurna Harivel, customer-success lead, Singapore, runs the Tamil, Hindi and English support desks. Her agents were the first to hear borrowers asking for more time, and she wants an affordability screen before any offer reaches a low-income borrower. Singapore is two and a half hours ahead of Bengaluru, so her team usually reads the day's complaints before product has started.

Anbuselvi Hemaraj, product designer, Berlin, three and a half hours behind Bengaluru until 25 October, drew the Accept screen. She attributes the sevenfold rise in uptake to the pre-filled limit rather than to need, and wants the monthly cost shown above the button.

The options

Option A: launch to all 6,00,000 eligible borrowers on 26 October, as piloted. The upside is the full ₹1.68 crore a month, no rework and a clean festive story for investors. The cost is more late borrowers every cycle, concentrated in the lowest income band, and a consent design that rests on a single pre-filled tap.

Option B: pause Boost, keep the old "Request increase" button, and revisit in January. This adds no new harm and buys time for a longer read than one cycle. It forgoes ₹1.68 crore a month, weakens the January story, and leaves unexamined whatever the existing button is doing.

Option C: launch to the two upper bands only, 3,90,000 borrowers, with the monthly cost shown above Accept, no pre-filled limit and a published pause rule. The upper bands hold 65 per cent of eligible borrowers but only 60 per cent of pilot takers, so the upside is some 60 to 65 per cent of the total, depending on whether contribution follows eligible borrowers or takers. Lower-band borrowers would be excluded from credit some may genuinely need, uptake may fall once cost is visible, and Pune estimates the pause-rule dashboard cannot be ready before mid-November.

Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 show that Boost does to a borrower's spending and to Nilgiri's revenue, and where does the incremental money come from?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows who is late. What would you need to know before attributing that lateness to Boost rather than to who chose to accept it?
  3. For which of these outcomes is Abirami accountable, and to whom, when an NBFC holds the loan, the borrower pressed Accept and the RBI rule asks for consent?
  4. Which option would you take to Friday's meeting, and what evidence would change your mind?

A note for the learner

Accountability moves the question from what Abirami shipped to what the shipment did to the person who tapped it. Nobody here intended harm and the rule may well be satisfied, so neither intent nor compliance settles the matter. The test is whether she could show the borrower's family the numbers and stand behind the decision. A well-reasoned answer identifies who carries the cost, prices each option in rupees and in borrowers, and fixes in advance a measurable condition under which the product stops.

One defensible path is Option C. It keeps roughly 60 to 65 per cent of the upside, withdraws the offer from the band where revenue and strain are most tangled, and turns accountability into a number: pause Boost if its late rate exceeds the control rate by more than one percentage point after the first full cycle. She would tell Ambarish that the lowest band is not being denied revenue but exempted from a risk the pilot cannot yet price, and that the exemption can be lifted when evidence arrives. Option B is defensible for a reader who distrusts one cycle of data; Option A is hard to defend.
exp20v2-ethics.habit:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance · Ethics, Persuasion & Trust

Habit Formation and Attention

1. The Monday Deck

On the morning of Monday, 14 September 2026, Meera Kulkarni, Head of Product at Dincharya Wellness, a Bengaluru habit-and-meditation app with 1.1 million registered users, opened a retention dashboard she had been avoiding for a week. Dincharya's core loop was deliberately plain: open the app, complete a five-minute breathing or journaling routine, close the app until tomorrow. The company had built its brand around the Sanskrit word for daily routine, and its seed investors had underwritten that promise on the belief that a product people return to on their own is worth more than one that chases them. Eighteen months in, the numbers were less comfortable than the pitch deck. Of the 120,000 users who had installed the app the previous quarter, 42 percent opened it again the next day, 18 percent were still active after a week, and only 6 percent remained active after thirty days.

Her growth lead, Arvind, had a fix ready before she had finished her coffee: add visible daily streaks, replace the single fixed morning reminder with three notifications spread through the day, and randomise the evening nudge between an affirmation, a mini quiz, and a "your streak is at risk" warning, so users could never predict what the app would show them next. He had numbers to back it: a rival wellness app's thirty-day retention had climbed from single digits into the mid-teens within two quarters after a similar change. The board met in five days, and the term sheet for Dincharya's next funding round, worth ₹18 crore, assumed a thirty-day retention figure the current product was not delivering. Meera's problem was not whether Arvind's tactics would move the number — she suspected they would — but whether they would build something she could still call a habit, or something that only resembled one on a dashboard until users noticed how it had been built.

Figure 1. Of 120,000 new installs, only 6 percent — about 7,200 users — were still active by day thirty. The board's growth model needs a materially higher number.

2. The Idea

To decide well, Meera needed a definition sharper than "something users do a lot." A habit, in the sense product teams use the word, is a behaviour a person performs automatically, triggered by a cue in their environment or their internal state, with little or no deliberate decision-making at the moment it happens. Frequent behaviour that still requires a conscious choice each time — deciding whether to open a shopping app because a discount email just arrived — is not yet a habit; it is a repeated decision.

The idea has a long lineage that predates any product team. The psychologist William James described habit in 1890 as the mechanism that lets the nervous system act without "the effort of a fresh deliberation," calling it society's most precious conservative agent. B. F. Skinner's mid-century work on operant conditioning showed that rewards delivered on an unpredictable schedule strengthen a learned behaviour more durably than rewards delivered every single time. Journalist Charles Duhigg popularised a three-part "habit loop" — cue, routine, reward — in his 2012 book The Power of Habit, and in 2014 Nir Eyal's Hooked translated that loop explicitly into a product-design sequence, adding a fourth step, investment, and a filter for which behaviours are even candidates for automation. All of it converges on one sentence Meera could say in a boardroom without sounding glib:

A habit is a behaviour that fires from a cue before the user chooses it, and the products that win are the ones that install themselves into that automatic layer of a person's day, rather than competing for deliberate attention every time.

Figure 2. A century of research feeding one product-design vocabulary.

3. How the Loop Actually Works

The mechanics practitioners rely on have four moving parts, and skipping any one of them is usually where a hook goes wrong. First is the trigger, which comes in two forms: external triggers are information in the world telling the user what to do next — a push notification, an app icon, a friend's message — while internal triggers are an emotion or state the user is trying to resolve, such as the low hum of stress that made someone download Dincharya in the first place. Second is the routine: the behaviour itself, simple enough to perform with little friction once the trigger fires. Third is the reward, and this is where Skinner's variable schedule matters most — a reward that varies in kind or intensity keeps the brain's reward-prediction system engaged in a way an identical, fixed reward does not, because it introduces the same uncertainty that makes a slot machine hard to put down. Fourth is investment: a small piece of effort the user puts in — a streak, a journal entry, a customised routine — that raises the value of returning and loads the next trigger.

The step teams most often skip is checking, before any of this design work, whether the target behaviour clears two prerequisites Eyal calls frequency and perceived utility: it must occur often enough, and matter enough relative to alternatives, to be worth automating at all. A once-a-year tax filing cannot become a habit no matter how well the loop around it is designed; a five-minute breathing exercise plausibly can.

Figure 3. The loop only compounds if each stage feeds the next; a variable reward without a real routine, or a trigger without a genuine internal cue, breaks the cycle.

4. The Arithmetic Arvind Brought

Meera ran the numbers Arvind had promised. Among a cohort of 10,000 new users given a single fixed evening reminder with an identical affirmation every night, thirty-day retention held at 6.1 percent — 610 users still opening the app on day thirty. A matched cohort of 10,000 users received the same reminder timing but a randomised reward, alternating an affirmation, a short breathing tip, and a streak badge. Thirty-day retention in that cohort rose to 9.4 percent, or 940 users: a gain of 330 retained users from reward variability alone, with trigger frequency held constant. At Dincharya's ₹450 monthly price and roughly 60 percent gross margin on retained subscribers, that gain was worth close to ₹89,000 in monthly gross margin from this one cohort — the number in Arvind's deck.

Meera then reran the comparison changing one input: notification frequency. A third cohort received the same variable reward but three notifications a day instead of one. Thirty-day retention there was 9.6 percent — barely above the once-daily variable-reward cohort — but the rate of uninstalls accompanied by a negative public review was 4.2 percent, against 1.1 percent in the once-daily cohort.

Cohort (n = 10,000)TriggerRewardD30 retainedNegative-review uninstalls
A1 notification/dayFixed message610 (6.1%)1.0%
B1 notification/dayVariable message940 (9.4%)1.1%
C3 notifications/dayVariable message960 (9.6%)4.2%

Tripling notification volume bought two-tenths of a retention point and nearly quadrupled visible reputational damage, while introducing reward variability alone had already captured almost all of the usable gain. The arithmetic said something specific: variability of reward, not volume of trigger, was doing the useful work, and pushing volume past what the underlying five-minute routine could bear was buying retention with trust Meera could not recover later by simply toning a notification down.

5. Nuances a Learner Must Hold Onto

Habit versus addiction. These are often used as synonyms in criticism of the industry, but the working distinction matters to a builder: a habit serves the goals the person would endorse if asked calmly, while addiction persists despite the person's own stated wish to stop and against their own interest. A meditation habit that helps someone sleep is not automatically suspect merely because it is automatic; a mechanic that keeps someone checking a screen at 2 a.m. against their own regret is a different thing wearing the same loop.

Habit versus engagement. High daily-active-user counts are routinely read as evidence of habit formation, but engagement can be produced by anxiety, social obligation, or plain novelty without ever becoming automatic. The honest test is what happens when the trigger is removed: if usage collapses immediately, the behaviour was prompted, not habitual.

External triggers as an immaturity signal. A product still leaning on notifications to bring users back has not yet built a habit; it has built a reminder system. The mark of a mature habit is that the internal trigger — the boredom, the stress, the specific itch — now reliably calls the user back on its own, and the notification becomes optional scaffolding rather than the mechanism itself.

The frequency-and-utility filter is a gate, not a formality. Not every behaviour a product wants repeated is a legitimate habit candidate. A behaviour that occurs rarely and matters little relative to alternatives cannot be turned into a habit through better hook design — only into an annoyance that a well-timed reward schedule cannot fix.

Habits are context-bound, not portable. Research on habit and context by Wendy Wood and David Neal shows a habit is cued as much by the surrounding environment — the same phone, the same time of day, the same physical posture — as by the behaviour itself. Move the context through a redesign or a new onboarding flow, and a habit that looked durable can collapse, which is why retention often dips after a redesign for reasons unrelated to the new design's quality.

What the mechanics cannot tell you. The loop says nothing about whether the automatic behaviour serves the user's actual interest; a well-executed hook and an exploitative one look identical on a retention chart. That judgment sits one layer up, in the ethics of persuasion, which is why this topic lives inside a module on trust rather than only inside growth.

Confusing habit with lock-in. Some retained usage is not habit at all but structural — a student who opens a school's assignment portal daily has no real choice, an employee gets paid to check a tool they cannot uninstall. Reading such lock-in as evidence of a well-designed loop leads teams to over-credit their own design work.

6. Consumer, B2B, Marketplace, and Stage

In consumer products, habit design usually chases an internal trigger the product did not create — loneliness, boredom, curiosity — and competes for the same idle moments every other app on the phone is also chasing, which is why variable reward and social validation loom largest here. In B2B products the habit that matters is workflow, not entertainment: a sales manager checking a pipeline dashboard every morning is a habit in the strict sense, automatic and cued by the start of the workday, but it forms around getting paid to do a job well, so the design lever is embedding the tool into an existing routine — the Monday stand-up, the weekly forecast call — rather than manufacturing a reward schedule. In marketplace products the two sides often need different strategies entirely: buyers form habits around browsing and discovery and respond to the consumer playbook, while sellers form habits around operational routines — checking orders, updating stock, reading a payout — and respond to the B2B playbook of workflow embedding.

SettingDominant triggerDesign lever
ConsumerInternal (boredom, loneliness)Variable reward, social validation
B2BExternal, tied to job routineEmbed in existing workflow ritual
MarketplaceSplits by sideConsumer lever for buyers, B2B lever for sellers

Stage matters too. An early-stage team like Dincharya reads habit strength from a handful of qualitative signals and a few hundred users; a large platform runs the exact cohort experiment Meera ran, at a scale where half a retention point is worth crores and a trust misstep is read by regulators as closely as by reviewers.

7. Common Mistakes

MistakeSymptomCheapest diagnostic
Mistaking notification volume for habit strengthOpens rise; unprompted, organic returns stay flatNotification-off holdout for one full habit cycle
Skipping the frequency-and-utility filterEngagement plateaus despite more gamificationAsk plainly how often, and how much, the behaviour matters
Treating variable reward as a free leverRetention looks healthy; ratings and uninstall reasons do notTrack sentiment on the same cadence as retention
Ignoring context-dependency in a redesignRetention dips right after a well-tested new interface shipsA/B test the new context itself, not just the feature

Each of these shares a root cause: a team measuring the metric its own mechanic was built to move, rather than the behaviour the metric was meant to stand in for. The fix is almost always the same — hold out a group that never sees the mechanic, and compare what happens in its absence.

8. What Good Looks Like

The version of this decision handled well starts with an honest check that the target behaviour clears the frequency-and-utility filter — Dincharya's five-minute routine plausibly helps with sleep and stress often enough to be worth automating, which a once-a-year reminder would not. It designs the trigger to anchor on an existing routine already in the user's day — right after the phone alarm, not whenever the team decides to ping — so the notification's job is to become unnecessary over time. It uses reward variability sparingly, tested against the specific harm it might cause and not only the retention it might buy. And it tracks organic, unprompted return as its primary metric, so a rising number always means more people found the product genuinely worth returning to.

Figure 4. Organic return should climb over time as the internal trigger takes hold; prompted return can stay flat without being a failure.

9. Meera's Decision

Meera went into Monday's meeting with a modified version of Arvind's plan. She kept the reward variability — the affirmation, the tip, the badge, rotated — because the arithmetic showed it did most of the useful work at the least reputational cost. She rejected tripling notification frequency, kept the single reminder anchored to the moment right after most users' phone alarms fired, and added the one metric the original deck had not tracked: organic, unprompted day-thirty return, measured against a small notification-off holdout the team would run every quarter. Her reasoning to the board was plain: Dincharya's business depended on being the kind of habit a user would defend if a friend asked why they still used it, not the kind that survived only because the phone kept ringing.

The natural next stop for a reader who has followed this argument is the Hook model itself — the fuller design vocabulary of trigger, action, variable reward, and investment that Eyal built on exactly this foundation, and the place where the ethical judgment this page has deliberately deferred becomes unavoidable.

Two questions worth sitting with:

If every notification your product sends were switched off for a month, which of your users would still come back on their own?

Is there a behaviour in your own product that your team keeps improving with better hooks, when the honest answer is that it should never have been made into a habit at all?
exp40v2-ethics.habit:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance · Ethics, Persuasion & Trust · Deep reading

Habit Formation and Attention

What a habit actually is, how it is measured, why the products that win hold attention without asking for it — and the places where the whole frame quietly stops being true.

This page assumes the vocabulary of cue, routine, reward and investment is familiar. It is concerned with what practitioners get wrong once they have it: what automaticity means formally, how it is measured rather than asserted, and why two competent product leaders can read the same retention chart and disagree about whether a habit exists at all.

1. Two decisions, one week

At 7:40 on the evening of Thursday, 11 June 2026, Devayani Raghunathan, VP of Product at Pagdandi Learning, was reading a table her machine-learning lead in Berlin, Kabir Menon, had sent forty minutes earlier. Pagdandi taught spoken English and interview readiness in nine Indian languages to 4.2 million monthly users, 62 percent of them outside the eight largest cities. Three weeks earlier the team had replaced its hand-written notification rules with a reinforcement-learning scheduler that chose, per user, the hour and the copy of the single daily nudge, optimising one objective: the probability of a session within twenty-four hours. Against a 200,000-user holdout, day-7 reopens were up 14 percent and day-30 retention up 2.6 points.

Kabir's table was a sample of what the model had learned to send. For a cluster of users aged eighteen to twenty-four in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, the highest-scoring message was a social-comparison line — a named classmate had overtaken them on the weekly board — delivered at 11:20 pm. Nobody had written that rule; the scheduler had found it, and it worked. Pagdandi's Series B, ₹40 crore at a valuation underwritten by day-30 retention, was to be signed in September. Devayani had until Monday to ship the scheduler as trained, ship it inside constraints, or turn it off.

In Pune that same week, Ananth Vaidyanathan, Chief Product Officer of Lakeer Field Cloud, was looking at a different number. Lakeer ran field maintenance for electricity distribution companies and telecom tower operators: 38,000 technicians across nine states, each closing four to seven jobs a day, each required to log the job with a photograph and a meter reading before leaving site. Only 61 percent of jobs were logged on site; the rest were entered in a batch on Saturday from memory, which made the photographs useless and the timestamps fiction. A client had just turned data quality into a contractual clause, and the renewal was worth ₹6.2 crore of annual recurring revenue. Ananth's growth lead wanted points, badges and a leaderboard. Ananth's objection was harder to articulate: his users could not uninstall the app, so whatever he built would not be competing for their attention. He suspected that made every habit playbook he had read inapplicable, and could not yet say why.
