Investment and Stored Value

Every investment step writes to two ledgers at once. One records what the user gets back; the other records what it would cost them to leave. Almost no company reconciles them — and the arithmetic of that reconciliation decides both whether the habit is durable and whether it is defensible.

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On 3 February 2026, Aparna Bhide, head of product at Chunai Learning in Pune, was handed a chart she had asked for and did not enjoy. Chunai ran a spoken-English and interview-preparation app used by 4.1 million people a month, most of them in Tier-2 cities, most of them preparing for a first salaried job. Its loop was well understood inside the company. A learner finished a five-minute speaking drill, saw a score that moved unpredictably, and was then asked to do one small thing: correct a transcription, tag the job role they were preparing for, or save a phrase to a personal deck. Those deposits fed the next day's drill selection. Investment completion sat at 44%, and the growth team had a plan to push it to 60%.

The chart was different. Aparna had asked her analytics lead, Zoya Qureshi, for two numbers per week of tenure for the median learner: the cumulative value the deposits had actually returned — minutes of practice saved, against a control cohort on untailored drills — and the time that learner would need to rebuild an equivalent state on a competing app. The first crossed the second in week 11. Chunai's median learner churned in week 7. On the company's own arithmetic, every unit of retention the investment step earned in a user's first ten weeks was not stored value at all. It was exit cost.

Eleven days later and 900 kilometres south, Harish Venkataraman, VP of product at Sangtarash Systems in Chennai, faced the mirror image. Sangtarash sold biomedical asset-maintenance software to hospital chains — every infusion pump, ventilator and imaging unit tracked and audited against NABH requirements. Its largest account, a 14-hospital chain in Telangana, had 38,000 assets, 1,900 work orders a month and four years of technician-written checklists inside the product. Migration quotes from a rival came in at 14 weeks and ₹62 lakh. Renewal was, commercially, safe.

Harish's discomfort was that the deposits had been made by biomedical technicians — people who did not sign the contract and could not switch vendors — while the exit cost sat with a procurement head who had never opened the product. Two months earlier an AI checklist auto-fill technicians relied on had regressed badly after a model update, tripling tickets from that account. The renewal had not wobbled by a rupee. Harish's question to his leadership team was uncomfortable precisely because the answer was reassuring: if the product got materially worse for the people who use it, how long would revenue take to notice?

2. The idea: one deposit, two ledgers

Investment is the point in a recurring product loop where the user contributes something — effort, data, content, money, a social tie — that persists between sessions. The residue is stored value. Nir Eyal named it as the fourth step of the Hook in Hooked (2014), and the model's core observation is sequential: the deposit comes after the reward, and what it stores is what loads the next trigger.

The intellectual history is older and less tidy than the four-box diagram suggests. Skinner's operant conditioning explained repetition but not personalisation. Cialdini's reciprocity work explained why an ask lands better after a gift than before one. Thaler's endowment effect and the Arkes–Blumer sunk-cost experiments explained why people over-value what they have worked on — and Norton, Mochon and Ariely's IKEA effect (2011) measured it: subjects valued self-assembled furniture roughly 60% above identical pre-assembled units. Shapiro and Varian's Information Rules (1998) described the same accumulating data from the firm's side and called it switching cost, an asset to be maximised. Eyal fused the behavioural and economic readings into a design step. The fusion is also the problem: a single click writes to both ledgers, and the model does not say how to tell them apart.

State the definition so a product manager can operate it. For a user at cycle t, let Vt be the cumulative value the stored data has returned to that user, measured in the product's own unit of benefit against a control with no stored state, and let Xt be the reconstruction cost: time, money and effort to reach an equivalent state on the best available alternative. Define the alignment ratio Rt = Vt / Xt. Investment in the honest sense is a mechanic that drives R above 1 and keeps it there. Lock-in is the same mechanic with R below 1 and falling. Nothing in a retention chart distinguishes the two.

Table 1. Five positions on the same mechanic. Each is held by serious people; the propositions in the right-hand columns are what separates them in a real design review.
SchoolWould signWould not sign
Behaviour design
(Eyal, Fogg lineage)		 Ask after the reward; keep deposits small, repeated, voluntary. That any retention gain from stored value is thereby legitimate.
Economics of lock-in
(Shapiro & Varian, Klemperer)		 Switching cost is a legitimate asset; welfare is competition policy's job, not product's. That a team should voluntarily lower exit cost it lawfully created.
Behavioural welfare
(Thaler, Ariely, the sludge literature)		 Retention under high exit cost is weak evidence of value. That continued use shows the product is good for the user.

The lock-in school would tell Aparna her week-7 churn is a marketing problem, not an ethical one; the behavioural-welfare school would tell Harish his renewal number is not evidence of anything. Neither is unreasonable. They are reading different ledgers, and each thinks the other's is a rounding error.

3. Mechanics: how the two ledgers diverge

Expert practice starts by refusing to treat the deposit as a single event. Each deposit is decomposed into what it adds to V and what it adds to X, and the two are tracked separately from the first release. Zoya estimated V by holding out 3% of new users from personalisation and measuring the gap in a fixed outcome — drill minutes needed to reach a given fluency score. She measured X directly: an intern with a fresh account on the two closest competitors, timed rebuilding an equivalent phrase deck, role tag and correction history.

Table 2. Chunai Learning's investment ledger for the median learner, pre-redesign. V and X are both in minutes. The crossover — the first week at which the deposits have returned more than they cost to abandon — falls in week 11.

Figure 1. The two ledgers, plotted. X rises fast and flattens; V starts near zero and compounds. The area between them before the crossover is what practitioners politely call early retention.

Expert teams use a proportional-hazards model of churn: ht = h0 · exp(−αVt − βXt). Both coefficients are positive in practice, so both ledgers suppress churn. The methodological difficulty is that V and X are strongly collinear — every deposit raises both — so observational regression cannot separate α (retention the user wants) from β (retention the user is stuck with). Separating them needs an exogenous shock that moves X without moving V. In practice there are three: a genuine one-click export, a competitor's import tool, or a regulator mandating portability. In India the third is real — the DPDP Act 2023 codifies erasure and correction rights, and RBI's Account Aggregator framework under DEPA is a working portability rail. Teams that treat a portability release as a compliance ticket are discarding the only clean experiment they will get on their own loop.

Three second-order effects surprise competent practitioners. Deposits decay: a role tag collected in week 2 is stale by week 20, so V is not monotonic while X, measured against current state, is. Deposits can be self-referential — a streak improves nothing about tomorrow's drill but raises X by attaching identity to the account. And raising investment completion raises X immediately and V only after the personalisation pipeline's lag, so every successful growth experiment on this step temporarily worsens R. A team that ships such experiments monthly and audits R annually will never once observe the harm.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are best stated as claims that can be tested rather than principles that can be nodded at.

Table 3. Four testable conditions, applied to both protagonists.
ClaimChunai LearningSangtarash Systems
The product is used often enough that a deposit has a next cycle to improve. True — median 4.2 sessions/week.True for technicians (daily); false for the buyer, who touches it quarterly.
The deposit is used by a named downstream surface within one cycle. True for phrase decks and role tags; false for 5 of 14 collected fields.True for checklists; false for the "asset criticality" field, unused since 2023.
The person making the deposit is the person who benefits. True.False — technicians deposit, procurement decides.
The median user reaches R = 1 before the median churn date. False — crossover week 11, churn week 7.Unmeasured; the account cannot churn cheaply enough to reveal it.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. In low-frequency, high-consequence products — an insurance claim, a visa application — there is no next cycle to load, and a grafted-on investment loop produces deposits that only ever hit the X ledger. In products where the user's goal is to finish and leave — a debt-repayment tool, a smoking-cessation app — rising stored value is a symptom of failure. And where the alternative to using the product is using nothing, as with an employer-mandated tool, R is undefined: there is no meaningful reconstruction cost and no meaningful consent. Applying the vocabulary of investment there does not merely mislead; it launders a captive relationship as a designed one.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product suites. When stored value is pooled at account level, X becomes a portfolio number while V stays per-product. The predictable consequence is a hostage product: a weak module nobody would buy standalone, retained because leaving means unpicking shared identity, billing and data. Compute R per module against account-level X; the result looks absurd, and the absurdity is the finding.

Two-sided markets. Khadaan Exchange, a Jaipur marketplace matching quarry operators to builders in construction aggregates, ran the loop on both sides and found the ledgers wildly asymmetric: 1,240 suppliers had deposited up to nine months of quality ratings and delivery history against 310 buyers with roughly three weeks of order preferences. Supplier X was an order of magnitude above buyer X. Management read this as a supply-side moat and raised take rate from 3.2% to 5.1% over two quarters. It was not a moat but a hostage position, and it held only until a rival shipped a ratings-import tool. The rule generalises: measure R per side, and treat the side with the higher X and lower R as the side you are taxing.

Regulated products. In lending, insurance and securities the exit-cost ledger is partly written by law. RBI's digital-lending rules, SEBI's norms on investor-facing nudges and the DPDP Act's erasure right all have one structural effect: they cap X. A team retaining on β rather than α discovers this as a step change in churn on a compliance date it cannot negotiate.

Hardware plus software. When a device is in the loop, part of X is a sunk purchase and is irreversible by construction. Mehraab Devices in Coimbatore sold a ₹14,900 connected water purifier with a subscription filter plan and an app tracking household water quality. The hardware sets a floor under X on day one, before any deposit is made, so software deposits begin from accumulated lock-in rather than building toward it. Subtract the hardware floor before attributing retention to the loop — arithmetic almost nobody does, because it makes the software look worse.

AI-native products. Here the deposit is training signal, creating stored value the depositor cannot take with them. When a Chunai learner corrects a transcription, the durable benefit accrues to a shared acoustic model serving 4.1 million people. Export returns their phrase deck; it cannot return their share of the fine-tune. This breaks rather than adjusts the definition: X measured as reconstruction time understates what was deposited, because part of the deposit was never excludable. Whether that portion counts as a return to the user — who benefits from everyone else's corrections too — or as an uncompensated contribution is the sharpest live disagreement in the field.

The organisational seam. Past roughly 200 people the two ledgers are owned by different functions and reconciled by none. Growth owns the ask and is measured on completion; lifecycle owns the trigger and is measured on open rate; the data platform owns the store and is measured on availability; legal owns export and is measured on audit findings. R is nobody's number. Mature companies say they audit this; mostly they compute it retrospectively when a journalist, regulator or board member asks. The few that genuinely manage it put reconstruction cost on the same dashboard as retention, and make one named person present both.

Figure 2. The seam. Four functions each optimise a true metric; the ratio that decides whether the loop is investment or lock-in is the one number with no owner.

6. Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: the two ledgers are written by the same click and read by different teams. The tell is an org chart, not a metric: the person who designs the ask and the person who designs the deletion flow have never been in a room together. The obvious reading — both are "retention work" — is wrong because they are opposed. Easy export is the only credible test that the ask was worth making.

Two: β is unidentifiable without a shock. Experts flinch at "our investment feature lifted 90-day retention by 6 points," because the claim is uninterpretable without something that moved exit cost independently. The tell is a lift quoted with no portability event, no competitor import launch and no holdout with a fast off-ramp. A clean A/B test does not settle it: both arms accumulate X at the same rate.

Three: the crossover is a date, not a feeling. Competent teams discuss "time to value" qualitatively; experts name a week number and compare it to median churn week. The tell is a team that describes the aha moment eloquently but has never timed anyone rebuilding the state elsewhere. If the crossover lands after median churn, the loop is, for most users, a pure tax.

Four: voluntary deposits at high frequency beat mandatory deposits at high volume. The tell is a completion spike immediately after a blocking screen or paywall. Volume looks better and V is worse, because coerced fields are filled carelessly and poison the personalisation they were collected for. Chunai's role tags from a skippable post-reward prompt were 2.3 times more predictive than the same field collected in mandatory onboarding.

Five: a deposit with no downstream consumer is pure exit cost. The tell lives in the data dictionary: columns with a write path and no read path. Each raises X, raises consent surface under DPDP, and returns nothing. The obvious reading is that data is an option on future value; the expert reading is that an unexercised option still charges a premium every cycle.

Six: in B2B the depositor and the decider are different people. The tell is a renewal deck leading with configured-asset counts — "38,000 assets, 4 years of checklists" — rather than outcomes: an X statement dressed as a V statement. Sangtarash's model regression proved it. The product got worse for its users and revenue did not notice for two quarters.

Seven: felt investment and measured reconstruction cost are different quantities. Sunk-cost psychology makes users feel more locked in than they are — a real retention force but not a real asset, since it evaporates the moment a competitor makes the true cost visible. The tell is users describing tenure in years rather than tasks. Khadaan's suppliers believed nine months of ratings were irreplaceable until an import tool showed the number was a weekend.

Eight: portability changes the mechanic, not the ethics. An export button does not make a mistimed ask acceptable, and a product with no export can be scrupulous if V is genuinely high. The tell is a team that answers an ethics question with a compliance artefact. Build the export because you want the experiment it gives you, then argue the ask on its merits.

Nine: streaks are a deposit of identity, and identity improves nothing. A streak raises X by attaching self-image to an account while contributing almost nothing to V. The tell is users citing the streak itself as their reason to stay, with no mention of the outcome the product exists to produce. The obvious reading is that streak engagement indicates a healthy habit; the expert reading is that a self-referential deposit is the purest stored exit cost the framework contains.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

Some cross-type differences are real and some are asserted. In consumer products the depositor and beneficiary are the same person, so R is at least meaningful; the risk is deposits skewing toward identity — streaks, badges, social graphs — that inflate X cheaply. In B2B and enterprise the ledger splits across roles, and the right instrument is per-role R: technician R, admin R, buyer R. In platforms and marketplaces the ledgers split across sides and the thinner side almost always carries the higher X. In hardware there is an X floor set at purchase, and software teams routinely take credit for retention the invoice already bought. In AI products, part of the deposit is non-excludable, which breaks the reconstruction-cost definition rather than merely adjusting it.

By stage the mechanic barely changes; what changes is who is harmed by getting it wrong. At seed stage the loop is mostly an instrument for learning, and the population consequences of a bad ask are small. Past a few million users — Chunai's position — a uniformly applied nudge is a behaviour-change intervention on a population, which is why responsible-innovation tracks at Berkeley SCET, HEC Paris and Stanford treat scale as the threshold at which a growth experiment becomes a policy decision. Late stage, the binding change is organisational: the seam in Figure 2 hardens and R becomes structurally unownable unless someone assigns it. One asserted difference is not real: regulated industries do not "care more". They are simply the ones where X is capped externally, so the arithmetic is forced on them.

8. Three worked examples

Chunai Learning: moving the crossover

Aparna's redesign did not touch investment completion at all. Instead her team asked which deposits could be inferred rather than requested: five of the fourteen fields, including role and target city, were predictable from first-session behaviour with 81% accuracy. Removing those asks cut first-month X by 31 minutes and left V almost unchanged; the freed attention went into front-loading value, so the phrase deck produced a usable interview script after three sessions instead of eleven. The crossover moved from week 11 to week 5 and twelve-week retention rose from 22% to 31%. The decisive number came later: when Chunai shipped one-tap export in June 2026, churn over eight weeks rose 0.4 points against a forecast of 3 to 5. Low β. The retention was mostly wanted.

Khadaan Exchange: the moat that was a hostage position

Khadaan raised take rate from 3.2% to 5.1% on the strength of supplier stored value, and thin aggregate margins absorbed it. In the third quarter a competitor launched a verified ratings import that reconstructed a supplier's history from delivery challans and e-way-bill records in under a day. Khadaan lost 22% of active suppliers in one quarter and, with them, the buyer liquidity that justified the take rate. The error was not the price rise; it was reading a high X with an unmeasured V as a durable asset.

Mehraab Devices: the failure, and what recovery actually looked like

Mehraab's connected purifier had a well-built loop and an inverted ratio. Users logged water-quality readings and family hydration goals, earning a "service streak" for on-time filter changes. Over 2024–25 the product team, measured on streak retention, moved filter-life data behind the streak screen. Streak engagement rose 19% and the one number the device existed to protect quietly degraded. V went flat; X kept rising on top of a ₹14,900 hardware floor. The warnings were all present and all read as noise: one-star reviews using the word "trapped", rising tickets asking how to delete the account, and filter compliance falling from 78% to 64% as streaks lengthened.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Each of the six is cheap to detect and expensive to discover, and the gap between the two is filled by a metric that looks healthy. Retention is not a lying metric but an aggregating one, and aggregation is exactly what hides the composition of α and β.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether exit cost is ever legitimate. Steelmanned, the lock-in position holds that all durable businesses rest on some switching cost; without it no firm would fund the long-horizon infrastructure that makes products good, and the result is thin, undifferentiated commodities. Its evidence is enterprise software, where deep integration produces genuinely better outcomes and is inseparable from lock-in. It would be wrong if you could show sustained, high-quality product investment where switching is close to free — and the strongest counter-evidence is UPI, where NPCI's interoperability drove switching costs to nearly zero and app quality rose rather than fell.

Whether observed retention reveals preference. The revealed-preference position holds that users are adults who keep choosing the product, and that replacing their observed choices with an analyst's welfare judgement is paternalism with a spreadsheet. The behavioural-welfare position holds that choices made under endowment and sunk-cost pressure overstate value, resting on cancellation-friction experiments where removing small barriers produced large churn. The dispute would be settled if portability shocks routinely produced negligible churn; Chunai's 0.4 points is one data point for one side, Mehraab's 18% one for the other. Nobody has enough to generalise, which is why teams should publish theirs.

Whether mandated portability helps. Advocates say DEPA and the DPDP Act make the X ledger visible and therefore discipline design. Sceptics argue that stored value that cannot be defended will not be built, and that India's slow, incumbent-concentrated Account Aggregator adoption shows mandated rails move volume to large players rather than to better products. Both agree on the prediction that matters: portability converts hidden churn into visible churn. They disagree only on whether that is a cost or a diagnostic.

Whether AI training deposits are compensated. The collective view holds that a user correcting a transcription receives, in return, a model improved by four million other corrections — an enormously favourable trade. The individual-entitlement view holds that the return is diffuse, unpriced, and non-portable, and that describing it as compensation is a category error. This one is unsettled in both product practice and law, and anyone claiming otherwise is selling something.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the vocabulary can say that investment is the fourth step of the Hook, that it follows the reward, and that switching cost is a side effect. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in five observable ways. They ask for a reconstruction-cost number before approving an investment feature, and are unembarrassed about producing it by hand. They know their crossover week and their median churn week without looking. They treat a portability or export release as an experiment with a pre-registered forecast, not as a compliance ticket. They can say which ledger a retention lift came from, and when they cannot, they say so rather than claiming the lift. And in review they ask about the deposit's downstream consumer before they ask about its completion rate, because a deposit no surface reads is a charge levied on the user for the company's convenience.

Underneath all five is a willingness to weaken the company's position on purpose — shipping export, removing asks, capping a streak — to find out whether the retention was real. Teams that will not run that experiment usually already suspect the answer.

12. The decisions

Aparna Bhide rejected the growth team's plan to raise investment completion to 60%, and inverted the objective: reduce the number of asks in the first four weeks and move the crossover earlier. Her reasoning was that a loop whose crossover falls after median churn is not a habit mechanic for most users, and that raising completion in that regime only adds exit cost to a population that never reaches the value. She committed to the export release before knowing what it would do to churn, on the argument that a number she was afraid to measure was already governing her roadmap.

Harish Venkataraman took the harder path, since his commercial incentives ran the other way. He put a per-role alignment ratio into Sangtarash's quarterly business review, technician R reported beside net revenue retention, and tied part of the product organisation's objectives to the technician ledger — reasoning that if depositors' value can fall for two quarters without revenue noticing, revenue is not a quality signal and the company has to buy one. His board was not persuaded this was a growth initiative. He did not claim it was.

Discussion questions

1. Chunai's export release produced a 0.4-point churn bump against a 3–5 point forecast. What are the three most plausible explanations other than "our retention was genuine", and what would distinguish them?

2. Sangtarash's revenue did not respond when the product degraded for its users. Is that a defect in the company's instruments, a defect in the market's structure, or a normal and acceptable feature of enterprise software — and what would you change first?

3. Khadaan raised take rate on the strength of supplier stored value and lost 22% of suppliers when an import tool appeared. If you had sat in the pricing meeting, what single number would you have demanded before approving the rise?

The Hook Model, in depth

Trigger, action, variable reward, investment — the mechanism, the arithmetic, the schools that disagree about it, and the seams where it breaks.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On the morning of 4 February 2026, in a converted mill off Ashram Road in Ahmedabad, Ila Bhagat, Chief Product Officer of Uttarayan Care, was looking at a slide her growth lead had titled, without irony, "Adherence: solved." Uttarayan sold a chronic-care companion for people managing type-2 diabetes — 310,000 monthly active patients, reached through two hospital chains and several employer health plans. Its next eighteen months turned on a contract with a private insurer, worth about ₹14 crore a year, paying a per-member fee scaled to one number: the share of members logging medication on at least 80 percent of days over a rolling ninety-day window.

The proposal was orthodox Hook design: replace the flat five-points-per-log reward with a scratch card paying between zero and ₹40 at unpredictable intervals, and add a seven-day streak with an evening reminder reading "Your 12-day streak ends at midnight." A four-week test on 26,000 members had lifted eighty-percent-logging adherence from 41 percent to 58 percent — at the contracted rate, roughly ₹2.4 crore a year. Uttarayan's clinical advisor, Dr Sunanda Pai, had sent a two-line note the previous night: in the test arm, the correlation between logged adherence and pharmacy refill records had fallen from 0.71 to 0.44. Patients were logging more; whether they were taking more metformin was, on the evidence, doubtful. The loop had found the cheapest path to the reward, and the cheapest path was a tap.

Nineteen days later, 850 kilometres south, Nandan Pargaonkar, VP Product at Manjha Intelligence in Bengaluru, faced the same problem in different clothes. Manjha sold an AI copilot to enterprise support organisations — ₹48 crore of recurring revenue across 62,000 seats on Indian and Philippine outsourcing floors. Weekly active seats stood at 34 percent, and its largest customer's renewal clause tied a 15 percent discount to utilisation above 60 percent by 30 June. His growth pod proposed a hook: a 9 a.m. digest trigger, a one-click "draft reply" action, a variable reward — a quality score that occasionally surfaced an agent's reply as a "gold snippet" on a floor leaderboard — and an investment step in which agents' edits trained Manjha's model. A three-week pilot on 900 seats took weekly active seats to 71 percent. It also showed 38 percent of accepted drafts had an edit distance of zero, and that handle time for the bottom quartile of agents rose 6 percent. The loop had satisfied the metric the contract named while degrading the thing the customer was buying.

Both decisions turn on one proposition, which is the argument of this page: the Hook model is an unusually reliable engine for producing repeat behaviour, and it is indifferent to whether the behaviour it produces is the one you meant.

2. The idea, its history, and who refuses to sign what

Precisely stated: the Hook model is a four-phase cycle in which an external or internal trigger prompts the user; the user performs the simplest action in anticipation of a reward; the product delivers a variable reward, one whose timing or magnitude cannot be predicted; and the user makes an investment, putting in effort, data, content or reputation that both improves the product for next time and loads the next trigger. Run enough times, the cycle transfers control of the trigger from product to user. That transfer, not engagement, is the model's actual output.

Knowing the parts tells you which are load-bearing. Skinner and Ferster's Schedules of Reinforcement (1957) established that intermittent, variable-ratio reinforcement produces responding slow to extinguish. B. J. Fogg's persuasive-technology work at Stanford, formalised in 2009 as B = MAT, established that behaviour occurs when motivation, ability and a trigger converge in one instant, ability being cheapest to move. Charles Duhigg's The Power of Habit (2012) popularised the cue–routine–reward loop from Ann Graybiel's basal-ganglia research. Nir Eyal's Hooked (2014) added the fourth step, and that addition is the original contribution: Duhigg's loop ends at reward, explaining repetition but not compounding, whereas investment explains why a product improves with use. Eyal's Indistractable (2019) reads as a partial retraction in the form of a manual for resisting the first book. The problem was commercial: by 2013 distribution was free and the binding constraint was attention, so teams needed a vocabulary for designing what had until then been discovered by accident.

Five schools argue about it, and an expert can state what each will and will not sign. The behavioural-design school (Eyal, most growth practitioners) signs: habit architecture is neutral technology, and a designer who materially improves the user's life and uses the product themselves is a facilitator, not a manipulator. It will not sign that engagement is its own justification; Eyal's Manipulation Matrix exists to refuse that sentence. The humane-technology school (Harris, Williams, Alter) signs: a variable-reward loop inside an advertising or order-flow business model gives the designer an irresolvable conflict of interest, because the metric that pays them is the metric that harms. It will not sign that user self-control is the remedy.

The academic habit-science school (Wendy Wood, Phillippa Lally, the context-repetition tradition) signs: habits form through repetition in a stable context at low friction, over long and highly variable periods — Lally's oft-cited 66-day median. It will not sign the practitioner's favourite sentence, that variable reward is the active ingredient in habit formation. Stated exactly: variable reinforcement makes responding resistant to extinction, which is not the same as making it automatic. On some evidence predictable rewards build automaticity faster while variable ones sustain it longer; practitioners collapse the two and optimise the wrong schedule. The behavioural-welfare economics school (Gabaix and Laibson on shrouded attributes, O'Donoghue and Rabin on internalities, Allcott and colleagues on digital addiction) signs: revealed preference is not welfare when the good is habit-forming, so surplus must be computed net of internalities the user would price at a cool moment. It will not sign that engagement implies harm — the same literature measures large surplus in the products it finds people overusing. The sceptic-practitioner school signs: the four steps are post-hoc vocabulary, not a causal recipe, since any retained product can be re-described in them; what dominates loop craft is category frequency and value per session, and no low-frequency category can be hooked into a high-frequency one.

3. Mechanics in depth, and the arithmetic nobody writes down

Expert practice treats the loop not as four boxes but as a chain of conditional probabilities with a leak at every joint, plus a learning process running across cycles. Define c, the cycle completion rate, as the product of four step probabilities: the trigger is noticed; the action is taken given it was noticed; the reward registers as reward rather than noise; the investment is made. Uttarayan's pre-test loop measured 0.62 × 0.78 × 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.348 — more diagnostic than any step-level metric, because cycles, not days, are the unit in which habits are learned.

Figure 1. Uttarayan Care's loop as a conditional chain. Step-level dashboards hide the multiplication; the product of the four rates is the number that predicts whether a habit ever forms.

Now the cross-cycle process. Let u be the share of opens that are unprompted — not preceded by a push within the hour — and let each completed cycle move u a fixed fraction of the way to automaticity: un+1 = un + k·c·(1 − un), which rearranges to 1 − un = (1 − kc)n(1 − u0). Uttarayan's measured k was about 0.06 and u0 about 0.05, so with c = 0.348, kc = 0.021, and the exposures needed to reach u = 0.50 — "the user starts the loop themselves half the time" — is ln(0.5263)/ln(0.979) ≈ 30.

Thirty exposures is the whole ballgame, because users leave. At a per-exposure dropout hazard of 3 percent, the share surviving long enough to become habitual is 0.9730 = 40 percent. Raise c through the two cheapest steps — trigger salience 0.62 to 0.72 by moving the reminder to the evening meal, action ease 0.78 to 0.88 with a one-tap widget — and c becomes 0.456, kc = 0.027, and the path shortens to 23 exposures. Survival rises to 0.9723 = 50 percent: a ten-point lift in the share who ever form the habit, bought from friction and timing, with no change to the reward schedule.

Figure 2. The same loop, two completion rates. The dashed line at 50 percent is the habit threshold; the distance to it, multiplied by the per-exposure dropout hazard, determines how much of the cohort ever arrives.

Three second-order effects go unwritten. External triggers deplete: at an opt-out hazard of 0.12 percent per push and fourteen pushes a week, a quarter costs 1 − (1 − 0.0012)182 ≈ 20 percent of the base in mutes, and muted users linger in DAU long enough for a dying cohort to look habitual. The reward habituates: raising the mean while holding variance constant buys less craving per rupee over time, because craving tracks prediction error, which shrinks as a distribution becomes familiar. And investment compounds only if the stored value accrues to the user: a streak counter stores value nowhere, a corrected draft training a shared model stores it for the vendor, and both look identical in a design review.

4. When the model applies, stated as claims you can test

The Hook model is not a theory of product value but of repeat behaviour under four conditions, each writable as a claim that is true or false before you build anything.

Table 2. Four preconditions, tested against both protagonists.
Testable claimUttarayan CareManjha Intelligence
Frequency. The behaviour recurs at least weekly, so thirty exposures fit in a few months.True. Medication is daily; thirty exposures in six weeks.True. Agents handle 60–90 tickets a shift.
Low stakes per instance. One wrong decision inside the loop is cheap and reversible.False. A logged-but-unswallowed dose is a clinical event.False. An unread AI draft sent to a customer is a compliance and brand event.
Reward legibility. The user can tell reward from noise, close in time to the action.True for cash; the clinical reward is invisible for months, which is why cash substitutes.False as designed. "Saved minutes" is an estimate the agent does not believe.

Read across the rows and the two decisions look less like ethics questions than design errors with ethical consequences. The model is actively misleading in three further situations. Where behaviour is rare and consequential — a home loan, a fertility treatment, a platform migration — hook mechanics produce distrust, because the user correctly reads the nudge as pressure on a decision that deserves deliberation. Where the user is not the beneficiary of their own repetition — a driver whose streak bonus is funded by another party, an agent whose utilisation is a contract term — the loop is labour extraction in the vocabulary of engagement. And where value is episodic, the right strategy is to be excellent and forgettable: a tax-filing product with a daily habit would have failed at its job.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

Multi-product companies find that hooks compete for the same internal trigger. When one login fronts a payments app and a commerce app, the cue "I have a spare minute" resolves to only one; the loser's growth team escalates external triggers, and both burn the notification channel they share. Mature companies impose a central notification budget arbitrated by a group owning neither retention number, and rarely say so publicly, because the cap admits growth teams cannot be trusted with a shared resource.

Two-sided marketplaces have the sharpest seam. Firki Mobility, a bike-taxi platform in four Indian cities, runs a rider loop (unpredictable fare discounts) and a captain loop (a streak bonus for twelve consecutive hours). The captain loop is the dangerous one: its reward is funded by the rider side, its investment step is a non-portable rating, its cost — fatigue — lands on a party who is neither buyer nor reward recipient, and accident exposure lands on third parties entirely. The honest treatment models the externality and caps the streak; what platforms do is keep the cap unpublished, set just below the level at which journalists notice.

Regulated products change the analysis in kind. India's CCPA dark-pattern guidelines, notified in 2023, name thirteen practices including false urgency and nagging — two techniques sitting inside the trigger step of a great many shipped hooks. The DPDP Act, 2023 bars behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children, removing internal-trigger cultivation for any product skewing under eighteen. And SEBI's scrutiny of gamified derivatives trading, alongside the widely reported finding that most individual derivatives traders lose money, makes "variable reward on a transaction the user will regret" a regulatory hazard rather than merely an ethical one.

Hardware-plus-software carries a hidden substitute for loop strength. Tukkal Devices, selling a ₹4,900 continuous-glucose patch reader, found its ninety-day retention flattering because the hardware purchase is itself a sunk cost returning users without any loop; the truth arrived at the eighteen-month replacement decision, when churn hit 44 percent. Measure unprompted usage only among users past their first replacement cycle. AI-native products break the investment step in a way the 2014 formulation did not anticipate: when a user corrects a model output, the stored value may accrue to that user, to their organisation, or to every customer the vendor has. Eyal assumed the first; Manjha's pilot delivered the third. The seam is that nobody owns the distinction — ML optimises the shared model, product reports the retention lift, and no one says "our users' unpaid labour is our moat."

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

The loop optimises the measured proxy, not the intended behaviour. Tell-tale sign: a metric moves sharply while its historical correlate does not — logging up seventeen points, correlation with refills down 0.27. The obvious reading is that the loop worked and the correlate is noisy. In fact a habit loop is a search algorithm run by thousands of users hunting the cheapest path to the reward, so a hook on a self-reported metric finds the self-report.

Variable reward sustains behaviour; friction and timing create it. Tell-tale sign: a team facing a flattening curve enriches the reward, and engagement moves by less than the payout costs. The obvious reading is that the reward was too small. The habit literature suggests the opposite ordering — automaticity comes from repetition at low friction, variable reinforcement mainly slows extinction — so experts spend the first quarter on timing and action cost, treating variance as a retention instrument for an existing loop.

The honest engagement metric is measured with notifications off. Tell-tale sign: a leader quotes DAU and open rate but cannot state the unprompted-open share. The obvious reading is that DAU is the summary statistic. In truth a product can raise DAU for eighteen months by escalating triggers alone, accumulating an invisible liability of muted users, with the first honest reading arriving only when the channel saturates.

Streak breakage is a designed event, not an accident. Tell-tale sign: churn spiking in the 24 hours after a streak ends, invisible in weekly cohorts. The obvious reading is that those users were disengaging anyway. The mechanism is sharper: an all-or-nothing counter turns one missed day into total loss, handing a user with nothing left to protect a clean exit. Designs with slack routinely recover retention the streak was destroying.

The population the loop works best on is the population it can hurt. Tell-tale sign: the top engagement decile and the top complaint decile overlap beyond chance. The obvious reading is that heavy users are more vocal. But variable-reward mechanics have heterogeneous effects — the schedule that makes a median user consistent makes a minority compulsive — and because that minority drives volume, blended metrics are not merely insensitive to the harm but inflated by it. Experts cut the top decile before shipping.

In B2B the buyer can be the one deploying the hook against the user. Tell-tale sign: a contractual metric describing user behaviour rather than business outcome, such as Manjha's weekly-active-seat clause. The obvious reading is that adoption is a shared goal. Structurally, a utilisation clause makes the vendor an agent of the buyer's surveillance, with the user's interests nowhere in it. The expert move is to renegotiate toward an outcome the user also wants, since a hook aimed at an outcome cannot be satisfied by theatre.

Ethics questions arrive disguised as measurement questions. Tell-tale sign: the uncomfortable conversation is framed as "is this metric real?" rather than "should we do this?" The obvious reading is rigour. What is happening is that moral content is being laundered into a methodology dispute where it can be deferred pending more data. Experts say the plain sentence aloud — "we are paying people to tap a button that tells an insurer they took a pill" — because the plain version is self-answering.

The model is descriptive, and descriptions make poor permissions. Tell-tale sign: "this is just the Hook model, every app does it," used to close a discussion. The obvious reading is that an industry norm establishes acceptability. But the model describes a mechanism with no content about what it should serve; citing it to justify a design is like citing compound interest to justify a loan's terms. The substantive judgement — whether this behaviour deserves to be automatic for this person — sits outside the four steps, and must be made by someone with a name.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

Table 3. Where the differences are real, and where practitioners imagine them.

The AI row holds the one genuinely new mechanic since 2014. A generative model is a variable-reward machine by construction: output quality varies unpredictably around a mean, producing the intermittent-reinforcement profile a designer would otherwise engineer. AI products acquire the craving-generating property without anyone installing it, and improving model consistency can reduce engagement while increasing usefulness — a trade-off the 2014 framing never had to price.

Stage changes the constraint, not the mechanism. At seed and Series A the loop's job is to prove anyone forms the habit at all, and the honest test is a small cohort measured with push suppressed. At Series B and C the temptation is to buy c with reward payouts, because capital is cheap and the fundraise rather than unit economics is binding — which is how expensive loops with hollow investment steps reach production. At scale the denominator does the damage: a 4 percent harmed minority is 800 people in a 20,000-user test and two million at fifty million users, where a healthy-looking blended metric meets a regulator who is not reading blended metrics.

8. Three worked examples

Dhil Learning (works). A spoken-English app in Pune with 1.2 million monthly actives ran a ninety-day test on 80,000 learners. Arm A had a streak and a variable daily bonus; arm B added a review queue built from the learner's own recorded errors — a genuine investment step, in that yesterday's mistakes changed today's lesson. Day-90 retention was 19 percent in A and 28 in B; unprompted-open share 22 against 41 percent. The decisive evidence arrived by accident when messaging costs forced a 50 percent cut in push volume: arm A's daily actives fell 31 percent, arm B's fell 7. The investment step had transferred the trigger, worth roughly ₹7.8 crore of annualised subscription revenue.

Manjha Intelligence (ambiguous, and instructive). The pilot's headline was utilisation from 34 to 71 percent. Decomposed, it changed: in the top quartile handle time fell 11 percent with edit distance still high, indicating real collaboration; in the bottom quartile handle time rose 6 percent and 38 percent of accepted drafts were unedited. The leaderboard was doing the damage — a reward of the tribe, applied to a task where speed and quality trade off, pushed the weakest agents toward the behaviour that scored rather than the one that helped. Removing it cost eleven points of utilisation and recovered the regression entirely.

Guddi Money (fails, and recovers). A discount broker with 2.4 million funded accounts added confetti on trade confirmation, a weekly trading streak and a friends-leaderboard in 2023. Daily actives rose 52 percent and derivatives order volume 71 percent within two quarters. An audit ordered in late 2024, after sector-wide regulatory attention to gamified trading, found the most engaged decile — the cohort the loop had created — held 71 percent of loss-making accounts and 63 percent of those whose losses exceeded 40 percent of deposited capital. The loop had not found traders; it had manufactured them. All three mechanics went in January 2025: daily actives fell 38 percent and monthly orders 29 percent, but twelve months later net revenue per active account was up 19 percent and twelve-month retention up nine points, the surviving base trading deliberately with larger balances. The recovery cost roughly ₹26 crore in audit, remediation and legal expense, a six-month hold on a new launch, and two years of a growth narrative the board had banked. The lesson is not "avoid variable rewards" but that this recovery was available from the start at steadily rising cost, and its early warning — the overlap of the engaged and loss-making deciles — was computable from day one.

The fix is organisational rather than moral — a standing requirement that any habit-forming mechanic ships with its top-decile cut and unprompted-open share on the same slide as its retention lift, not in an appendix and not in a different meeting.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is variable reward the active ingredient? The practitioner position rests on strong operant-conditioning evidence and on the observable fact that products with unpredictable rewards retain better than matched products without. The habit-science position rests on studies showing automaticity developing under entirely predictable reward, and argues that resistance to extinction has been mistaken for speed of formation. The practitioners would be wrong if a well-powered test showed a fixed reward at equal expected value moving unprompted-open share as fast. Such tests are rare because they are expensive and nobody's incentives favour running one — an open empirical question with commercial stakes, the worst combination for getting an answer.

Is habit formation welfare-positive on net? The optimistic position, supported by the welfare literature's own estimates, is that habit products deliver large consumer surplus and that overuse is a minority-tail problem best met with tail-specific interventions. The pessimists reply that surplus measured through revealed preference is contaminated by the habit under study, making those estimates circular. They would be wrong if surplus measured cold — willingness to accept payment to deactivate for a month — matched the engagement-based estimates. Where such experiments have run the two diverge, but not enough to settle it.

Can this be governed inside a team? One camp holds that teams with the right instrumentation and a named accountable owner do self-correct, offering Guddi Money's recovery as evidence. The other holds the correction arrived only once regulation made the status quo expensive, and that a team compensated on engagement cannot decide whether engagement is legitimate; it wants structural remedies — business-model change, external audit, statutory enforcement. It would be wrong if companies were regularly seen removing profitable loops on their own evidence before external pressure. Such cases exist; they are uncommon, and both camps read the same small sample as confirmation.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the model can name the four steps and spot them in a competitor's app. Someone who has internalised it differs in four visible ways. They ask what the cheapest path to the reward is before asking how large the reward should be, because they know the loop is a search process. They instrument unprompted usage in the first week of building rather than the first week of a crisis. They treat the investment step as the design problem, and can say in one adjective-free sentence what a user's accumulated contribution does for that user next Tuesday. And they bring the top-decile cut to the launch review unasked, having learned that the argument you lose is the one where the harmed segment was found by someone else. Underneath all four is one habit of mind: they hold mechanism and purpose apart, and refuse to let fluency in the first substitute for a decision about the second.

12. The decisions

Ila Bhagat did not kill the loop; she moved it. The scratch-card reward was detached from the logging event and attached to a verified one — a pharmacy refill confirmation or a reading from a connected meter — which cost roughly 40 percent of eligible reward triggers and removed the proxy-capture mechanism entirely. The seven-day streak became a flexible streak with two skips a week, on the evidence that all-or-nothing counters manufacture the churn they are meant to prevent. Most consequentially, she took Dr Pai's correlation chart into the insurer negotiation and proposed replacing logged adherence with refill-based proportion-of-days-covered, accepting a lower per-member rate in exchange. Her argument to her board: a contract priced on a corruptible metric is a liability disguised as revenue, and the party that notices the corruption first should be the one that fixes it.

Nandan Pargaonkar removed the leaderboard before the pilot's second phase, kept the digest trigger and one-click draft — the cheap Fogg levers — and rebuilt the investment step so an agent's corrections accumulated into a personal snippet library that was theirs, exportable, visible as a growing asset. Then the harder thing: he told the customer that weekly-active-seats was a metric his own product could satisfy without helping anyone, showed the edit-distance data, and proposed resolutions-per-hour as the renewal term. The ops head who had asked for utilisation agreed in the second meeting. Manjha's utilisation fell to 60 percent; its renewal closed.

Discussion questions.

  1. Both executives reduced a headline metric to protect the thing the metric was meant to represent. Under what board-level conditions is that trade defensible, and what would each have needed to measure in advance for the case to survive a bad quarter?
  2. If a generative AI product is a variable-reward machine by construction, who is accountable for the craving it produces when no one designed it? Does the Hook model's ethical vocabulary survive the move from designed to emergent variability?
  3. Guddi Money's recovery was available from day one at steadily rising cost. What organisational mechanism — not what value — would have obliged someone to look at the engaged-decile and loss-making-decile overlap in the first quarter?

The Hook Model

How trigger, action, variable reward and investment build a habit — and why the same loop can help a user or quietly work against them.

A streak that will not let go

On the evening of 11 August 2026, Devika Rao, Vice President of Growth at Bansi Mart, a twelve-minute grocery-delivery company headquartered in Pune, opened a dashboard she did not enjoy looking at. Bansi Mart was seven weeks from a board review deciding whether its Series C term sheet survived contact with the company's actual numbers, and the investors cared about one figure above all: Day-30 retention, currently 34 percent, needed to cross 45 percent before the round closed in November. Her growth pod had spent the quarter on a feature called Har Roz Streak — "every day, a streak" — which rewarded consecutive days of ordering with a notification that read, depending on the day, "Your streak breaks in 43 minutes" or "One more order and your streak reward doubles."

The feature worked, in the narrow sense that matters to a board deck. A six-week test across 40,000 users split streak against control: streak users ordered 4.2 times a week against 2.6, and Day-30 retention for the streak group hit 47 percent. But two other numbers sat on the dashboard. Uninstalls and support complaints in the streak cohort ran three times higher than control, almost all of it in a cluster of neighbourhoods — Bhosari, Wagholi, and a scatter of pincodes her data lead had flagged after cross-referencing income proxies out of curiosity. One forwarded ticket, from the son of a 68-year-old widow in Wagholi, said she had been ordering small items daily "so as not to lose the streak," spending pension money she did not need to spend. Devika had a review with CEO Rajat Sabharwal at 5 p.m. the next day and one question to answer first: ship Har Roz Streak nationally as built, kill it, or find a third option — and be able to explain why.

The idea, precisely

The Hook model is a four-step design cycle — trigger, action, variable reward, investment — engineered so a product gets used repeatedly with less conscious deliberation each time, until the user starts the cycle on their own rather than waiting to be reminded. A habit, in this framework, is a behaviour performed with little or no conscious thought; the model is a deliberate recipe for producing one. It was named and popularised by Nir Eyal, a product and behavioural-design consultant who had built and sold two venture-backed companies and later taught at Stanford's Graduate School of Business, in his 2014 book Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products. Eyal was not inventing new psychology; he synthesised two existing strands — B. J. Fogg's behaviour model, which explains when a single action happens, and the psychology of variable reinforcement schedules B. F. Skinner documented with slot machines and pigeons — into a design pattern teams could build against on purpose, rather than stumble into the way Twitter's pull-to-refresh had been discovered rather than designed. The problem it solved for mobile app teams competing for a scarce resource, attention, in a market suddenly full of free alternatives, was the absence of a shared vocabulary for habit design. The sentence Devika could say in the board room without sounding glib: a habit-forming product is one where the user, not the notification, decides to open it next time, and the Hook model is the four-step loop that gets a product there.

Figure 1. The Hook cycle. Investment is the step teams most often skip or fake — it must make the product measurably better next time and reload the trigger, or the loop does not compound.

How the loop actually runs

Walk it through with Har Roz Streak in place. The trigger opens the cycle, and comes in two forms Eyal distinguishes carefully: an external trigger is information in the environment telling the user what to do next — Bansi Mart's push, "Your streak breaks in 43 minutes," is a textbook one — while an internal trigger is an emotion or situation that cues the behaviour on its own, the way hunger already cues a habitual snacker. Every product starts by renting external triggers, since it has no internal one yet; running the loop repeatedly is meant to graduate a product from renting attention to owning it, so the user eventually feels a pang of "what's cheap today" at 6 p.m. without any push at all. Most teams measure open-rates and stop there, missing that the real target metric is usage that survives the notifications being switched off.

The action is the simplest behaviour performed in anticipation of the reward — tapping the app open and scrolling the day's deals. Fogg's behaviour model sits underneath this step, implicit in most retellings: a behaviour happens when motivation, ability, and a trigger are all present at the same instant, and if the action is not easy enough at that instant no trigger will make it fire. This is why Bansi Mart's designers spent as much effort collapsing checkout to one tap as they did on notification copy; a streak that takes four screens to extend will not survive a distracted commuter.

The variable reward is where craving gets manufactured, and Eyal's typology names three flavours: rewards of the tribe (social validation — a like, a rank), rewards of the hunt (resources or information — a discount that might or might not appear), and rewards of the self (mastery or completion — finishing a level, closing out a streak day). Bansi Mart's reward was of the hunt: a discount varying between 5 percent and a free item, unpredictably, on each streak day. The point practitioners most often get backwards: it is the unpredictability, not the size, of the reward that manufactures craving, because a variable schedule keeps dopamine firing in anticipation rather than in response, exactly as at a slot machine.

The investment is the step Har Roz Streak treated too lightly. Eyal's definition requires the user to put something in — effort, data, content, reputation, a streak count — that does two things: it improves the product for next visit, and it loads the next trigger by creating something to protect. A streak counter alone does the second without the first; nothing about day 12 makes Bansi Mart's assortment or delivery slot better for that user than day 1 did. That gap between "makes the user feel they will lose something" and "makes the product actually better for them" is the seam Devika's decision runs straight through.

The arithmetic, worked twice

The test cohort ran for six weeks. The table below shows the calculation the growth team put in front of finance first, then the same calculation once the vulnerable-segment data is folded back in.

Table 1. Incremental contribution margin, streak cohort vs control, six-week test, 20,000 users per arm.
StepControlStreak
Orders per user per week2.64.2
Extra orders per user over 6 weeks—9.6
Contribution margin per order₹38₹38
Incremental margin per streak user—₹364.80
Reward payouts (1 in 3 orders, ₹25 avg)—₹210.00
Net margin per streak user, 6 weeks—₹154.80
Scaled to 20,000 streak users—≈ ₹30.96 lakh

That is the version of the arithmetic that closes a board deck: roughly ₹31 lakh of net incremental margin from one six-week test. The second pass changes one input — it separates out the 4 percent of the streak cohort, about 800 users, flagged as the high-complaint, high-uninstall segment. That group's uninstall rate ran at 9 percent against a baseline of 3 percent, a gap of six points on 800 users, or 48 additional lost users. At an estimated twelve-month contribution value of ₹1,800 per retained user, that is roughly ₹0.86 lakh of lost future margin — small enough to vanish inside rounding, ₹30.96 lakh becoming ₹30.10 lakh. The arithmetic barely moves. What moves is what it cannot show: the loop's cost is not spread evenly across 20,000 users but concentrated in a few hundred who can least absorb it, and no line in a contribution-margin table prices a widow spending pension money to protect a streak.

Nuances a learner must sit with

The mechanics are ethically neutral; the objective function is not

Trigger, action, variable reward, and investment describe a shape, not a verdict. A flossing app and a slot machine can share the identical architecture. What separates them is what the loop is optimised to produce — a life the user would endorse on reflection, or engagement extracted regardless of it. Judging what a loop optimises toward is the right question, not whether it uses the model.

Confused with gamification

Badges, points, and leaderboards usually sit inside the reward step alone. The Hook model is the entire cycle, including an investment that loads the next trigger. A product can be heavily gamified and still have no real hook, because nothing the user does today changes what happens tomorrow.

The real prize is the internal trigger, not the engagement chart

DAU, open rate, and streak length all measure dependence on external triggers. A loop has actually taken hold only when usage persists with notifications switched off — the one metric most growth dashboards omit.

Variability, not size, drives craving

Teams watching engagement flatten routinely enrich the reward — bigger discounts, bigger prizes — when the correct lever is the schedule's variance, not its average value. A larger guaranteed reward habituates faster and produces less craving than a smaller unpredictable one.

Investment must be real, or it is just pressure

A streak counter that does not make next week's product better for that user is consumption wearing the costume of investment. Genuine investment — data that improves recommendations, content harder to leave behind — earns continued attention. A number that only threatens loss earns compliance, not loyalty, and is cheap for a rival to copy.

The model assumes frequent, low-stakes decisions

The architecture was built for behaviours repeated often enough to compound — checking a feed, ordering groceries — and breaks down where decisions are rare, expensive, or regulated, such as choosing a loan. Hook mechanics on a high-stakes, low-frequency decision usually signals the wrong tool from the wrong shelf.

It cannot tell you whether the product should exist

The model explains how a loop compounds once you decide what to compound it toward. It says nothing about whether the underlying behaviour deserves to be habitual for this user at all. That judgment sits outside the model, in the choice of what to optimise for.

The newcomer's three questions

Who absorbs the downside when the loop misfires for an atypical user; can that user exit as easily as they entered; and is there a floor — a spend ceiling, a rest period, a stop-loss — the product will honour even when it costs the dashboard metric.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

Bansi Mart is a consumer case in its purest form: short cycles, an individual who is simultaneously user and payer, and direct exposure to dark-pattern risk because the trigger and the transaction sit one tap apart. A rival, Machhua Fresh, ran a near-identical mechanic that same year and shipped it nationally without a segment cut, an example returned to below. Contrast a B2B product like Nauli Books, an accounting platform for small traders: its trigger is usually a calendar deadline — a GST filing date — rather than an emotional cue, and its investment is ledger data that raises switching cost through genuine value delivered, not loss-aversion pressure. Buyer and daily user are often different professional adults trading time for money, which is why B2B hooks are less ethically fraught even when retention curves look similar.

A two-sided marketplace complicates the picture. Bhanwarjaal Rides, a mobility marketplace connecting drivers and passengers, runs two hook loops at once, and they can pull against each other: a driver-side streak bonus rewarding long unbroken shifts optimises one side's habit by leaning on the other side's fatigue — the person absorbing the cost is not the one receiving the reward.

Scale changes the calculus too. At Series B, Bansi Mart needs the loop to prove retention for a fundraise, and capital is available to subsidise a generous reward schedule, so the temptation is to over-invest in reward cost because the round, not unit economics, is the constraint. A company at national scale faces the same loop with a different denominator: four percent of a 40,000-user test is a rounding error, but four percent of fifty million users is two million people — large enough to attract a regulator's attention even when the blended metric still looks healthy.

Common mistakes

Averaging away the cohort that is being hurt. Symptom: engagement and complaints climb together, reported in different meetings. Misunderstanding: treating DAU as one number rather than a distribution across segments. Diagnostic: before national rollout, cut retention and complaint curves by an income or vulnerability proxy, not just by cohort assignment.

Fixing a flattening loop by enriching the reward. Symptom: growth stalls, the team raises the discount, engagement barely moves and margin erodes. Misunderstanding: confusing reward size with reward variability as the active ingredient. Diagnostic: A/B a wider-variance schedule at the same average payout against a richer fixed one; variance usually wins.

Calling a counter an investment. Symptom: a streak, level, or badge that never changes what the product does for that user next time. Misunderstanding: treating any UI element between reward and next trigger as "investment" by default. Diagnostic: ask whether last week's activity made this week's product measurably better for this user — if the honest answer is only "it would feel bad to stop," that is pressure, not investment.

Treating the model as a permission slip. Symptom: leadership waves off an ethics question because "this is just the Hook model, everyone uses it." Misunderstanding: mistaking a descriptive mechanism for a normative licence. Diagnostic: would the team still ship the reward schedule if it had to be explained, in plain language, to the person it targets.

What good looks like

Picture the same decision handled well. A team notices, from the same cross-reference that flagged Wagholi, that its variable reward lands hardest on users who can least absorb variance in their own spending. It keeps the loop — trigger, action, variable reward, investment remain the right architecture for a grocery habit — but changes what the loop optimises for that segment: streak-break notifications capped at one a day, a genuine spend ceiling that mutes the loss-frame message once a week's spend crosses the user's own historical threshold, and a reward substitution trading a cash-like discount for something with real future value — priority delivery slots, a shopping list that actually gets smarter. The board still sees a retention number; it also sees, in the same breath rather than an appendix, a wellbeing floor — the share of the most engaged decile whose spend-to-income proxy is also flashing red.

The decision, and what to carry forward

Devika ships Har Roz Streak, but not as built. She keeps the four-step loop — mechanically, the right tool for a habit that genuinely helps most of Bansi Mart's users get groceries reliably — and redesigns what it is aimed at for the flagged segment: a one-a-day cap on loss-frame notifications, an easy-to-find "pause my streak" control, and a spend-aware stop-loss swapping the cash-variable reward for a non-monetary one once a user's week crosses their own historical pattern. At the 5 p.m. review she presents Rajat both the retention curve and the segment-level complaint curve on the same slide, arguing that accountability for what the loop optimises toward sits with the team that built it, not with the model itself. The model told her how a loop compounds; it never told her what to compound it toward, and that judgment turned out to be the whole job. Machhua Fresh, the rival that shipped the undifferentiated version nationally that quarter, does not learn this until a consumer-forum complaint six months later forces the correction Bansi Mart made voluntarily. What Devika reads next is the Fogg behaviour model, to see why the action step, not the reward, is usually the cheapest lever to fix; and the dark-patterns taxonomy, to name — and therefore refuse — the manoeuvres she chose not to build. Two questions worth sitting with afterward: if a product's most engaged five percent are also its most financially stressed users, is that a growth story or a warning sign? And would the team building any variable-reward schedule be comfortable explaining it, in plain language, to the person it targets?
