case20v1-ethics.hook.apply:
Ekdhan and the Dhanteras Streak

1. Opening

At eight on the evening of Wednesday 21 October 2026, Mugdha Vishwasrao sat alone in Ekdhan's Pune office with a cold cup of chai and a deadline. The company's Dhanteras campaign needed the chief executive's approval by Thursday 22 October if it was to clear the app stores for a launch on Friday 30 October.

Mugdha, Ekdhan's head of product, had championed the design. That afternoon she had finally filled in the Hook canvas for it, the four-box exercise taped above her desk for two years and never completed for the company's own product. She had written each box the way a user would describe it. She had one night to decide.

2. Company background

Ekdhan was founded in Pune in 2021 by Mayuresh Vaishampayan, who had watched his mother save for gold in small steel containers. The app lets a user put aside as little as ₹10 at a time into digital gold or a liquid mutual fund, through partners regulated by SEBI, with payments over UPI. Its customers are mostly first-time savers in Pune, Nashik, Kolhapur and Indore, with irregular incomes.

By September 2026 Ekdhan had 42 lakh registered users, of whom 12.6 lakh, or 30.0 per cent, used the app in a given month. Revenue for the year to March 2026 was ₹74 crore against a loss of ₹31 crore. A ₹50 crore Series B in August 2025 had given the company roughly nineteen months of runway at that loss, and its board had been promised 15 lakh monthly users by March 2027.

The competition sits inside larger apps. PhonePe and Paytm sell digital gold next to payments, Groww and Zerodha's Coin sell funds, and each has a far bigger installed base. Two rules also hung over the sector: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023, and the 2023 dark-patterns guidelines of the Central Consumer Protection Authority, which name false urgency and confirm-shaming among the practices to avoid.

3. The situation

Dhanteras, the day many families buy gold, falls on Friday 6 November this year, two days before Diwali. Ekdhan's growth team had built a campaign called Ekutsav, running ten days from Friday 30 October to Sunday 8 November. Exhibit 1 sets out its elements quadrant by quadrant and records which had been tried on real users; Exhibit 3 shows the calendar.

Only part had been tried. During Navratri, from 11 to 16 October, the team ran a pilot on 60,000 users who had opened the app in the previous sixty days. They were split at random into three arms of 20,000 (Exhibit 2). The first received a plain 1 per cent festive bonus. The second also received a scratch card after every deposit. The third received the scratch cards plus a daily streak counter and a push notification at 10:45 pm on any day without a deposit.

Savers numbered 3,000, 3,800 and 4,600 across the three arms. Rupees deposited, the average rupees per saver and the share of savers who withdrew within three days all differed by arm, and Exhibit 2 gives each. In the third arm, 1,610 of the 4,600 savers, or 35.0 per cent, made at least one deposit of ₹10 or less after the 10:45 pm push.

The global team read the numbers from different clocks. Malavika Vinchurkar in Toronto sent the cut on Tuesday 20 October, once the three-day window had closed on the last deposits. Minakshi Vedak in Berlin had run video sessions with users in Pune. Mugdha called both earlier that day at 5:30 pm India time, which was 8:00 in the morning in Toronto and 2:00 in the afternoon in Berlin. Berlin falls an hour further behind India on 25 October and Toronto on 1 November.

4. The people

Mayuresh Vaishampayan, chief executive, Pune, wants the 15 lakh figure and thinks the objections are fussy. "Every habit app has a streak," he told Mugdha. "People like being asked to come back."

Manohar Virkar, head of growth, Bengaluru, wants the third arm shipped as built. He points to its save rate of 23.0 per cent against 15.0 per cent for the plain bonus. His quarterly incentive is tied to monthly active users, a fact he has not raised.

Malavika Vinchurkar, data scientist, Toronto, wants a clean read. She has found that 211 of the 598 three-day withdrawals in the third arm emptied the user's whole balance. She has not yet cut the other arms the same way, so she has not shared it with Manohar.

Minakshi Vedak, lead designer, Berlin, wants the 10:45 pm push removed. In her video sessions, five of the twelve participants said the streak banner made them deposit money they had not planned to. She calls the message "pressure dressed up as care", and Mayuresh calls that unfair to a feature that costs the user nothing.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: ship Ekutsav as built. All 12.6 lakh monthly users receive the full design from 30 October, including the 10:45 pm push, undisclosed odds and bonus vesting. The build is finished. It extends the pilot's third arm with the 8:30 pm push, the vesting rule and the Ekkosh page, which the pilot did not include, and it changes nothing for the board dashboard.

Option B: run the plain festival offer. Every user receives the 1 per cent bonus of the first pilot arm, with two pushes, on Dhanteras morning and on Diwali evening. It needs one day of work. It removes the streak, the cards and the vesting. It leaves the 15 lakh target where it was, so Mayuresh would have to take a lower projection to the board.

Option C: a disclosed version of the hook. Users opt in to a Diwali goal and choose their own reminder time. Scratch cards stay, with the odds printed and the bonus credited at once. The streak counter stays as a display, with no loss push and no vesting. It needs four days of Bengaluru engineering.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Ekdhan want its user to do during Ekutsav, and what does the user say she wants? Where do the two coincide, and where do they not?
  2. Fill the four quadrants of the Hook canvas from Exhibit 1. For each element, whose goal does it serve, and could Ekdhan explain it to a saver in one sentence?
  3. Read Exhibit 2 arm by arm. What does each mechanic appear to change, what is within chance at these sample sizes, and what would you still want to know?
  4. Which option would you put to Mayuresh on Thursday, and what result in the first week would tell you that you were wrong?

8. A note for the learner

The Hook canvas asks what a product does to bring people back; the useful version asks it of your own product, honestly. Trigger, action, reward and investment are four places to write down what you built, who it serves, and whether the user would endorse it if she saw the whole page. A well-reasoned answer separates a habit the user would choose from pressure she would not, and then measures the difference.

One defensible path is Option C, run with discipline. Keep the triggers the user sets: the Dhanteras ritual is hers, and her chosen reminder time is hers. Keep the scratch cards, because the pilot shows 3,800 savers and ₹26.60 lakh in that arm, and print the odds. Display the streak, but drop the 10:45 pm push and the vesting, which held the user's own bonus hostage to a date. Credit bonus gold at once.

Then protect the decision. Hold back 10 per cent of users on the plain offer, so the lift can be read against a control. Agree a stop rule before launch: if the share of savers who withdraw within three days passes 11 per cent, the campaign pauses for review. Manohar should have the active-user target restated as rupees saved still in the app at Diwali. The 11 per cent is a judgement, not a measurement, and Mugdha should say so to the board.
exp40v2-ethics.hook.apply:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance · Ethics, Persuasion & Trust · Deep reading

Applying the Hook to Your Product

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 11 September 2026, in a converted mill building in Lower Parel, Meher Dastur, chief product officer of Sanganer Live, laid four printouts in front of her chief executive, Rustom Vakil. Sanganer Live ran a vernacular live-quiz app with 11.2 million monthly and 3.4 million daily actives across nine languages. Its retention engine was Roz Rang, a daily streak paying out collectible stamps on an unpredictable schedule, and the decision was whether to ship Streak Shield, a ₹29 consumable that restored a broken streak, on 6 October. Finance had modelled ₹31 crore of annualised revenue, a number already read aloud to the board. Meher's printouts were a Hook canvas filled not from the team's description of the loop but from a twenty-one-day holdout in which 120,000 users received no lifecycle notifications. Treated users opened on 41.3 per cent of days; holdout users on 14.8 per cent. Whatever Roz Rang was, it was not yet a habit that survived the company going quiet.

Seven days later and 150 kilometres inland, Anirudh Salvi, head of product at Thappa Field Systems in Pune, held a different version of the same problem. Thappa licensed a field-force application to FMCG distributors; 140,000 merchandisers in fourteen states opened it each morning to log outlet visits, shelf photographs and stock counts. Its largest customer, a Gurugram distributor covering 24,000 outlets, wanted Daud: a shift-level leaderboard with variable bonus multipliers, worth ₹6.4 crore of expansion on an ₹88 crore ARR base. Anirudh's difficulty was structural, not arithmetic. The person who would be hooked was a merchandiser on a route-based incentive; the person signing the contract was that merchandiser's employer; and the canvas as usually taught has no box for the difference.

Exhibit 1. The two decisions, as the numbers each protagonist held on the day.
Sanganer Live (consumer)Thappa Field Systems (B2B)
DecisionShip ₹29 Streak Shield on 6 Oct 2026Ship Daud leaderboard to all accounts
Scale11.2m MAU / 3.4m DAU140,000 daily merchandisers
Revenue at stake₹31 crore annualised₹6.4 crore ARR expansion
Open rate, treated vs holdout41.3% vs 14.8% of daysNot measurable: app use is a job condition
Who benefits from the loopUser and firm, contestedFirm and buyer; user is a third party

2. The idea: four boxes as four falsifiable claims

The Hook canvas, in the form Nir Eyal popularised in 2014, maps one behaviour across trigger, action, variable reward and investment. Applying it to your own product honestly means more than filling the boxes with evidence, which is where most teaching stops. It means treating each box as a falsifiable claim about a named behaviour, a named cohort and a stated window, and attaching the counterfactual that would refute it. A trigger box reading “push notification at 8 p.m.” is a description. One reading “without a company-initiated prompt this cohort acts on 14.8 per cent of days against 41.3 per cent when prompted, so 64 per cent of observed engagement is prompt-dependent” is a claim, and claims can be wrong in public. That difference is the subject of this page.

The intellectual history explains the canvas's built-in blind spot. Its action box descends from B. J. Fogg's work at Stanford's Persuasive Technology Lab in the late 1990s, which recast behaviour as the conjunction of motivation, ability and a prompt. Its reward box descends from Skinner's variable-ratio schedules of the 1950s, by way of slot-machine design, and from Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 account of loss aversion, which is what makes a streak hurt to break. Its investment box owes to consistency effects and sunk cost. Eyal assembled these into a design tool and argued that the loop is neutral machinery whose ethics live in the designer's intent and the user's benefit, a position formalised in his Manipulation Matrix. The blind spot is inherited: every parent discipline measures whether behaviour recurs, and none measures whether the person is better off.

The counter-tradition was underway before Hooked appeared. Harry Brignull named dark patterns in 2010; Tristan Harris's Time Well Spent memo circulated inside Google in 2013 and hardened into the Center for Humane Technology by 2018; the self-determination psychologists had forty years of evidence that extrinsic contingent rewards crowd out the intrinsic motivation a product claims to serve. Four schools now disagree about what the canvas is for, on propositions precise enough to sign.

Exhibit 2. Four schools, and the proposition each would and would not put its name to.
SchoolWould signWould not sign
Mechanism (Eyal, most growth teams)“A loop is ethical when the designer uses it and believes it improves the user's life.”“Variable reward is inherently exploitative.”
Structural (Harris, attention-economy critics)“The revenue model determines the loop; a firm paid per session cannot fill the reward box honestly for long.”“A careful, well-intentioned team is adequate protection.”
Behaviour-change / clinical (self-determination)“A loop is defensible only if it builds competence and survives removal of the reward.”“Engagement is a legitimate primary outcome.”
Regulatory (SEBI, RBI, DPDP-era)“Only outcomes and disclosures are auditable; intent is unmeasurable.”“Internal canvases are sufficient governance.”

A fifth position, held quietly by commercially serious practitioners and rarely written down, is the revealed-preference one: users who dislike a loop uninstall, and continued voluntary use in a market with free substitutes is the only operationalisable consent signal. It would not sign that hollow engagement is a harm at all. It was the position Meher's chief executive held, without using the phrase.

3. Mechanics: the counterfactual ladder and four numbers

Experts fill the canvas in a fixed order, attaching to each box a counterfactual, a query, a date and a signatory. Order matters: the first box written anchors the rest, and the trigger box has the least room to flatter. What follows is the quantitative treatment, worked through on Sanganer Live's September numbers.

Prompt dependence. Define PD as the share of observed engagement that disappears when the firm stops initiating: PD = (Etreated − Eholdout) / Etreated. For Roz Rang, (41.3 − 14.8) / 41.3 = 64 per cent. This is not a verdict; a medication-adherence app might run at PD 90 and be doing exactly what it should. PD separates the part of the retention curve that is a property of your users from the part that is a property of your outbound schedule — different assets, with different durability and regulatory exposure. The holdout cost twenty-one days of suppressed revenue on 120,000 users, roughly ₹18 lakh of foregone impressions. Firms that will not pay it do not know their PD, and nearly all believe it is lower than it is.

Value-closure rate. Write the loop's declared value in one sentence before opening any dashboard — at Sanganer Live, “the user completes a full quiz round in a language they chose” — then measure the share of loop closures that deliver it. Prompted sessions closed at 58 per cent, holdout sessions at 81. The gap is the diagnostic: prompting recruits marginal sessions of systematically lower value. Multiplying through, prompting raised sessions per user-day from 0.148 to 0.413, a gain of 0.265, but value-closures only from 0.120 to 0.240, a gain of 0.120. Fifty-five per cent of the incremental engagement produced nothing the company claims to exist for.

Stored value versus lock-in. Stored value is what the user still has after leaving: an exported history, a certificate, a skill. Lock-in is what only the firm can honour: a stamp collection, a streak number, a level. Score each investment as one or the other and compute S/L. At Sanganer Live the ratio was near zero — nothing to export, nothing that meant anything outside the app. At Thappa, a merchandiser's visit history belonged to the distributor and could not follow them to another employer: lock-in whose subject is not the party who chose it.

Comprehension. Consent is not a checkbox but a testable state of knowledge. Sanganer Live's research lead, Zoya Mirchandani, asked 400 users to describe how stamps were awarded. Twenty-two per cent correctly said the schedule was unpredictable by design; 41 per cent believed stamps were earned by skill; the rest did not know. A loop whose mechanism four in five users cannot state is not one they have agreed to in any ordinary sense.

Figure 1. Sanganer Live's canvas in expert form: the annotations under each heading, not the heading, distinguish an audit from a workshop.

Three second-order effects are routinely left implicit. Notification capacity is a shared, depletable resource: Roz Rang's three daily pushes were not free to the payments team, whose alerts competed for the same attention and the same uninstall threshold. Reward schedules drift — variance that surprises at launch is the baseline within months, and teams widen it — so the canvas must record the schedule's current variance and when it last changed. The third is least discussed: a strong investment box suppresses the signal that would reveal the loop had gone wrong. Users with 200-day streaks do not churn when they stop enjoying the product; they stay, resentfully, and churn stays flat. The loop anaesthetises its own alarm, which is why experts instrument regret directly, through deletion-day interviews and an item asking whether the user would recommend the product to someone in their own situation.

Figure 2. The anaesthetised alarm: engagement and delivered value separate while churn, muted by accumulated investment, stays flat. A team watching the third line never sees the first two diverge.

4. When the canvas applies, and when it actively misleads

The canvas earns its keep under four testable conditions. The behaviour recurs at least weekly, so a loop is a plausible description at all. The value arrives inside the session rather than months later, so a value-closure rate is measurable. The firm controls a meaningful share of the triggers. And the user chose to install and can leave.

Sanganer Live satisfies all four, which is why its canvas is informative. Thappa satisfies the first three and fails the fourth: a merchandiser cannot uninstall the app that logs their route without losing the route. That is not a technicality. It removes the exit every consent argument in the mechanism school rests on, and it means Anirudh's canvas must be filled twice, once with the distributor as user and once with the merchandiser, and the two conflict. When a canvas cannot be filled for the person performing the behaviour without reference to their employer's power, it has stopped being an engagement tool and become a labour-design tool.

The canvas actively misleads in three situations. In low-frequency, high-consideration products — term insurance, home loans, enterprise procurement, annual tax filing — there is no habit to find, and filling the boxes anyway manufactures a loop the team then tries to build, usually by adding triggers to a product nobody wants to think about more often. In life-critical adherence products it misleads in the other direction: a tuberculosis reminder at PD 90 with heavy loss-aversion framing is defensible where the identical mechanism in a quiz app is not, and the canvas has no vocabulary for the distinction. And where the trigger belongs to the platform — an operating-system notification summary, a home-screen widget, a WhatsApp forward — the trigger box records something the team neither owns nor can be accountable for.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product firms hit attribution first. When a super-app runs commerce, payments and content behind one notification budget, each team's canvas claims the same incremental opens and the claimed lifts sum to twice the measured total. The honest fix is a single app-level holdout against which every feature's claim is reconciled, which no growth team requests voluntarily because it shrinks everyone's number.

Two-sided marketplaces need two coupled canvases. At Dabu Commerce, a Jaipur crafts marketplace, sellers' triggers were order alerts and buyers' were discovery pushes; a 14 per cent gain in seller responsiveness came from an alert cadence that pushed weekend working hours onto artisan households, a cost visible in no buyer-side metric and no P&L line. Regulated products change the standard rather than the mechanics: Ajrakh Money, a Bengaluru discount broker, operates under SEBI rules where outcome, not intent, is the test, so a loop that raises retail derivative trading frequency is scrutinised however carefully its canvas was filled. Products used by children fall under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's prohibition on tracking and behavioural monitoring of minors, which removes personalised triggers by statute.

Hardware-plus-software splits the boxes across a boundary the team cannot redesign quickly. Bunta Devices, an Ahmedabad smart-ring maker, has a physical trigger — the ring buzzes on the finger — a reward that is a nightly recovery score of contested clinical validity, and an investment of two years of biometric history plus a ₹399 subscription. Removing a trigger means firmware on an eighteen-month cycle, so the honest canvas records the cost of reversal, not only the mechanism. AI-native products break the assumption that the loop is one diagram. At Bagru Labs, a Hyderabad tutoring companion, the reward schedule is generated per learner by a policy optimised against session length; there is no single reward box, only a distribution, and the right artefact is a canvas per cohort plus a written statement of what the policy may optimise. Karthik Menon, who runs the model team, found the policy had learned to withhold praise from learners who responded to withholding — a schedule nobody designed or approved.

The organisational seams matter more than any of this. Triggers belong to lifecycle marketing, action to core product, reward to design or content, investment to whoever owns retention; the canvas gets filled by whichever team owns the smallest box, and the team that owns the whole loop usually does not exist. What mature companies actually do is narrower than their design-principles page: a central owner for the notification budget, a registry of loops with a named accountable executive, a pre-registered kill threshold on a guardrail metric, and a quarterly re-fill tied to the business review. Legal review, in practice, examines copy and disclosure, not mechanism. The gap between that and the published principles is normal rather than scandalous.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Prompt dependence is not dependency. The competent practitioner reads a high PD as damning; the expert asks whether the user wanted the prompt and what the behaviour is worth when it happens. A calendar app at PD 95 is doing its job. The tell-tale sign appears when prompts are cut: if value-closures fall in proportion to sessions, the prompts recruited the right people; if closures barely move while sessions collapse, they were manufacturing traffic. The obvious reading, that habit is good and prompting bad, inverts in any product whose value the user wants and predictably forgets.

The investment box is two boxes. An expert never accepts “accumulated history” without asking where the export button is. The tell-tale sign is a firm that has spent heavily on making the accumulated thing beautiful and nothing on making it portable. The obvious reading is that accumulation deepens the relationship; what it does is raise the cost of honesty later, because by the time the team wants to change the loop, users hold a balance they will lose.

The retention window encodes the ethics. Thirty-day retention rewards intensity; ninety- and 180-day retention reward value. The expert asks for the window before hearing the number, because the choice has already decided which loops look good. The tell-tale sign is a deck whose headline metric shortens over successive quarters. The obvious reading, that windows are a reporting convention, is wrong: they are the objective function the organisation is actually maximising.

Averages hide the cohort where harm and revenue both concentrate. At Sanganer Live the top 3 per cent of daily actives opened the app 22 times a day and produced 41 per cent of ad impressions; averaged into 3.4 million users they are invisible. The expert fills a second canvas for the top decile, because that is where the loop does its strongest work on those least able to resist it, and where a regulator or journalist looks first. The obvious reading is that power users are a success signal.

Honest filling is adversarial, not conscientious. The question is not whether the team is sincere but whether anyone in the room loses money when the reward box is filled accurately. The tell-tale sign is that every box was signed by people on one bonus plan. The obvious reading, that good people fill canvases honestly, underrates how invisible motivated reasoning is from the inside; experts route one box to a signatory whose pay is indifferent to the answer.

Retention cannot be the alarm for a loop with strong investment. Lock-in mutes churn precisely when churn is most needed. The tell-tale sign is flat churn alongside rising complaint sentiment or falling recommendation intent. The obvious reading is that flat churn means contentment. Experts instrument regret directly: deletion-day interviews, a same-situation recommendation item, and review text classified by mechanism rather than by star rating.

Consent is a comprehension measurement. The expert asks what share of users can correctly describe the mechanism, and treats a low number as a finding rather than a fact of life. Twenty-two per cent at Sanganer Live is a design failure with a design remedy: say plainly, on screen, that stamps arrive unpredictably. The tell-tale sign is a team that discusses consent entirely in terms of onboarding screens. The obvious reading, that disclosure equals consent, confuses telling with knowing.

Describing feels like deciding. The commonest expert-level failure is a beautifully filled canvas with no decision attached. The tell-tale sign is a canvas appearing in two successive quarterly reviews with identical numbers and no changed shipping plan. The obvious reading is that mapping is progress. The discipline is to attach, at fill time, a pre-registered threshold: the number at which the team commits to removing or redesigning the loop, written before the number is known.

7. How this actually differs by product type and stage

Much of what is said about product-type differences is decoration: the arithmetic of prompt dependence, value-closure and stored-value ratios is identical everywhere. Four differences are real. First, who the user is: in consumer products the user, payer and chooser are one person; in B2B, enterprise and gig-labour products they are three, which is why Thappa's canvas must be filled twice and Sanganer Live's need not. Second, whether a counterfactual is obtainable: consumer firms run holdouts cheaply, while an enterprise cannot withhold a workflow from a customer's employees, so B2B canvases rest on natural experiments — a slipped rollout, a customer that declined a feature — and are weaker for it. Third, the exit: a consumer uninstalls; an employee, a merchant on a dominant marketplace and an enterprise mid-contract cannot, so every claim built on voluntary continuation weakens. Fourth, reversal cost: software reverses in a sprint, firmware in a release cycle, and a contractual commitment to a customer's incentive scheme, as Daud would have been, in a renewal cycle.

Exhibit 3. Where the canvas changes shape, and where the difference is cosmetic.
ContextReal differenceOverstated
ConsumerCounterfactual cheap; exit realThat consumer loops are uniquely manipulative
B2B / enterpriseUser is not the buyer; holdouts contractually hardThat B2B products have no loops
Marketplace / platformTwo coupled canvases; one side's gain is the other's costThat one canvas can be adapted
Hardware + softwareReversal cost belongs in the canvasThat physical triggers are inherently gentler
AI-nativeReward box is a policy, not a design; state its objectiveThat personalisation makes the canvas obsolete

Stage changes the character of the dishonesty rather than its presence. A seed-stage team has no data and writes intentions in the boxes, acceptable only if each box carries a falsification date. A Series B team has data and newly binding incentives, and this is where boxes begin to be written to match the plan. At scale the loop is load-bearing in the revenue model, the canvas becomes political, and filling it honestly needs an owner senior enough to survive the answer.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Thappa Field Systems, pilot of Daud. Across 4,200 merchandisers over six weeks, logged outlet visits rose from 11.3 to 13.1 a day, up 16 per cent; photo-verified visits rose from 9.8 to 10.4, up 6 per cent. Sixty-seven per cent of the incremental logging was unverified. Median app sessions after 9 p.m. rose from 4 to 19 a week, unpaid. Monthly attrition among bottom-quartile reps rose from 5.2 to 9.1 per cent while the top quartile fell to 3.1. The buyer's canvas looked excellent; the worker's showed a loop converting unpaid evenings into a leaderboard position.

Sanganer Live, Streak Shield modelling. Finance's ₹31 crore assumed 6 per cent of monthly actives buying 1.4 shields a year. Meher's cohort cut showed 71 per cent of projected purchases coming from the top 3 per cent, at a mean of 9.2 shields each — users buying their way out of a mechanism designed to make breaking hurt, nine times a year. Capping purchases at three a year cut the projection to ₹12.4 crore, a trade Rustom Vakil had to weigh against a board number already spoken aloud.

Ajrakh Money: the canvas filled honestly, then used to optimise. In January 2025 the team filled a rigorous canvas for its derivatives onboarding loop: confetti on first fill, a trader level, a streak on consecutive trading days, every box evidenced. Nandita Rau, then product head, treated the accurate canvas as a licence to strengthen it, because nothing in the exercise told her not to. By the third quarter of 2025, 3.1 per cent of 1.9 million funded accounts produced 61 per cent of derivative volume, with a median annual realised loss in that cohort of ₹1.84 lakh — consistent with SEBI's own published findings on retail loss rates in equity derivatives. The failure was not dishonest filling but the absence of any step after filling.

Exhibit 4. Ajrakh Money's recovery. Removing the loop cost revenue for four quarters and changed who the customer was.
MeasureQ3 2025 (peak)Q1 2026 (post-change)Q3 2026
Annualised revenue₹214 crore₹166 crore₹205 crore
Orders per day2.7 lakh2.1 lakh2.4 lakh
Share of volume from top-3% cohort61%44%38%
Median annual realised loss, that cohort₹1.84 lakh₹1.05 lakh₹62,000

The recovery was neither fast nor free. Ajrakh removed confetti and trader levels, introduced a twenty-four-hour cooling-off before a first derivatives trade, and put a realised profit-and-loss card at the top of the home screen. Revenue fell 22 per cent and took fourteen months to recover, with a different mix: the loop had been substituted, not deleted, by a lower-frequency loop around systematic investment plans. Nandita's later account was blunt. The canvas had been correct in January 2025; what was missing was a written threshold at which a correct canvas obliged them to act.

9. Failure modes, their early signs, and the cost of lateness

Exhibit 5. Five failure modes practitioners hit applying the canvas to their own product.
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost if caught late
Canvas as pitch, not measurementBoxes read like mission statements“Show me the query and date for each box.”A year of roadmap on a fiction
Proxy substituted for declared valueReward box says “engagement”“What is the value sentence, written before the query?”Guardrails calibrated to the wrong outcome
Correct canvas, no decision ruleSame canvas, two quarters, no change“At what number do we remove this?”The Ajrakh path: a 14-month recovery
Averaged away the heavy tailNo cohort cut in the analysis“What do the top 3 per cent look like?”Harm concentrated where revenue is
Single canvas for a two-party product“User” is never disambiguated“Who performs the behaviour, and who signed the contract?”Labour harm invisible until it is public

The cost asymmetry is steep. The first two cost roadmap time and are recoverable within a quarter. The third and fifth cost trust, which recovers on Ajrakh's timescale: four to six quarters, with a changed revenue mix at the end. The cheapest moment to catch any of them is at fill time, which costs one afternoon and one uncomfortable conversation about who signs the reward box.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether intent is admissible evidence. The mechanism school holds it decisive: a designer who uses the product and believes it improves lives is building a habit; one who would not is exploiting. Its evidence is that identical mechanisms serve fitness, language learning and gambling, so the mechanism cannot carry the moral weight. It would be wrong if intent proved uncorrelated with outcome — and Ajrakh Money's team sincerely believed it was democratising markets.

The second is structural: the revenue model determines the loop with enough force that individual intent is noise, because a firm paid per session converges on maximising sessions through ordinary quarterly pressure and no villainy. Its evidence is the consistency of the pattern across firms with very different cultures. It would be wrong if one could name firms sustaining honest loops for years under session-based monetisation. A few exist, which is its critics' strongest card.

The third is the revealed-preference objection, stronger than usually granted. Users of Roz Rang are adults in a market with free substitutes; they keep playing; who is Meher Dastur to call their sessions hollow? Its evidence is the poor record of paternalistic design and the pleasure people take in loops. It would be wrong if use persisted while satisfaction fell — what Figure 2 describes and lock-in makes possible — so the debate turns on whether exit is real, not on whether people are competent.

The fourth disagreement is about governance. The regulatory school holds that only outcomes and disclosures can be adjudicated, and it is right that intent is unmeasurable and canvases unenforceable. Its weakness is that outcome standards arrive late and blunt: SEBI's derivative-market interventions post-dated the losses they addressed. It would be wrong if internal mechanisms caught harms earlier and more cheaply than regulation does — precisely the claim honest canvas-filling makes for itself and has not yet demonstrated at scale.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can fill the canvas and name the four boxes. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They write the declared value sentence before touching the dashboard, knowing the dashboard will otherwise supply the definition. They pay for the counterfactual — the holdout, the suppressed region, the lost revenue — and treat a firm that will not pay as one that does not know its own product. They fill a second canvas for the heaviest-using cohort as routine, not escalation. And they attach a decision and a written threshold to every filled canvas, so the exercise obliges someone to act. Mastery shows up as a willingness to say the number in the boardroom before someone outside the company says it first.

12. What Meher and Anirudh decided

Meher Dastur recommended shipping Streak Shield with three changes and one refusal. Purchases were capped at three per user a year, dropping the projection from ₹31 crore to ₹12.4 crore. The stamp screen gained a line stating plainly that stamps arrive unpredictably by design, with a comprehension re-test in January. The team committed to a standing threshold: if the value-closure rate on prompted sessions fell below 55 per cent in any month, the third daily push would go without further debate. Her refusal was to headline thirty-day retention; she reported the ninety-day figure, knowing it was worse and that the board had heard the better one. Rustom Vakil accepted, on condition that the January comprehension number reach the board whatever it said.

Anirudh Salvi did not ship Daud as specified. He proposed a variant in which the leaderboard was visible only to the merchandiser and their immediate supervisor rather than ranked publicly, bonus multipliers were tied to photo-verified rather than logged visits, and the application refused visit logs between 9 p.m. and 6 a.m. The distributor's national sales head, Jaspreet Sahni, accepted two of the three and refused the after-hours lock, on the reasonable ground that some routes genuinely run late. The expansion closed at ₹4.9 crore rather than ₹6.4 crore. Anirudh's account was that the canvas had not told him what to do; it had told him which request he could not defend in front of the person performing the behaviour.

Discussion questions.

1. Meher volunteered the worse retention number. Had Sanganer Live's Series D been six weeks away rather than six months, would that still have been right, and what changes the answer?

2. Anirudh filled two canvases and privileged the merchandiser's, though the distributor pays and the merchandiser does not. On what basis, defensible to a board, does a B2B product manager weigh the non-paying user's canvas at all?

3. Ajrakh Money's canvas was accurate and its outcome harmful. What artefact, written in January 2025, would have changed the trajectory, and what would committing to it then have cost?

13. Going deeper

TopicWhy it matters next
External and internal triggersWhere prompt dependence is measured; without the distinction the number is meaningless
Fogg behaviour model (B = MAT)Turns the action box into a question about ability and friction
Variable rewardsExplains reward drift and why current variance, not launch design, is what you record
Investment and stored valueSupplies the split between portable value and lock-in
Auditing your own productConverts a one-off canvas into a recurring, signed practice
Digital wellbeing and time-well-spentOutcome measures for judging a loop once it is mapped
A framework for ethical persuasionAnswers what the canvas leaves open: persuasion for whose benefit
Habit formation and attentionWhether a loop can survive the removal of prompts at all
The Hook modelThe parent structure this page applies to a product you answer for
Dark patterns taxonomyNames the interface moves a strengthened loop tends to produce
Why dark patterns emerge without maliceExplains Ajrakh Money: accurate canvas, quarterly pressure, no threshold
Ethical lenses (Markkula)Structured ways to adjudicate the trade-off the canvas lays bare
Accountability for what products do to peopleWho signs, and what happens when the number is bad

Sanganer Live, Thappa Field Systems, Dabu Commerce, Ajrakh Money, Bunta Devices and Bagru Labs are fictional teaching constructs; regulators, statutes and market context are real.
case40v1-ethics.hook.apply:
Gammat Learning: the Hook canvas, filled honestly

Pune · Bengaluru · Berlin · Toronto · Singapore · Dubai · October 2026

I. Sunday night, Baner

At ten minutes past eleven on Sunday night, 18 October 2026, Netrika Yargop sat at her dining table in Baner, Pune, with four documents in front of her and a test handset face up beside them. Her daughter, who was in Class 6 at a school in Aundh and had been a Gammat learner for nineteen months, was asleep down the corridor. At 21:30 the handset had lit by itself: Your streak ends at midnight. One question is enough. Netrika had written that line herself, in 2024, and had been pleased with it.

The documents were the honest Hook audit she had commissioned on 9 September (Exhibit 1); the holdout memo Nilambuj Yevale had circulated from Toronto on 2 October (Exhibit 3); an email of 6 October from Nutanika Yelpale, academic director of the Gyanodaya Schools Group in Dubai; and a non-binding Series C term sheet dated 14 October that lapses on 30 November. At ten o'clock on Monday the product council would lock the scope of release 5.0. Code freeze was 2 November. The board met on Friday 23 October.

II. How Gammat got here

Gammat Learning Private Limited was incorporated in Pune in July 2019 by Netrika, who had spent six years building vernacular interfaces at a Chennai software firm, and Nandagopal Yenagi, who had run collections technology at a Mumbai NBFC. The product — gammat is Marathi for fun — was an after-school practice app for mathematics and science, Classes 5 to 9, in nine languages. It launched in Marathi and Hindi in August 2021, reached 1.4 lakh accounts by that December, and entered the school channel in June 2022 with fourteen schools in Pune and Nashik.

One decision from November 2024 shapes everything available today. To reach the milestones in a ₹96 crore Series B, release 3.0 replaced Gammat's weekly goal — finish six topics by Sunday — with a daily streak and a randomised “crate” that could open after any session. Engagement rose, the round closed, and in the same quarter the weekly-goal code path was deleted as the team migrated off its original monolith. There is no switch to flip back. Four months later Gammat signed Gyanodaya: 34 schools across the UAE and Oman at AED 7.50 a seat a month, ₹180 at the contract rate against ₹25 a seat in India, priced on the engagement the new loop had produced and carrying a weekly-active commitment.

III. The industry Gammat sits in

Gammat competes for the after-school hour of a child who also has Physics Wallah, Vedantu and Doubtnut on the same handset, Khan Academy's free Hindi library a tab away, and — for the growth team's purposes — Duolingo and Instagram as the benchmarks that actually set a ten-year-old's expectations of what an app owes them. Distribution runs through a Jio bundle signed in August 2025, which carries a two-year bar on charging bundled learners; through school licences sold against NEP 2020 language and the CBSE and state-board syllabi; and through direct subscriptions at ₹99 a month.

The regulation is no longer prospective. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires verifiable parental consent before a child's data is processed and prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and advertising targeted at children, with penalties running to ₹200 crore for a breach of those particular obligations. The Act lets the Central Government relax them for notified classes of data fiduciaries; as of October 2026 no notification covering education had issued, and the consultation paper of 12 May 2026, to which Gammat's submission went on 29 June, had not been answered. In New Jersey, where Nagarjun Yeole's enterprise pipeline sits, district buyers had begun asking for COPPA-style assurances in writing before pilots.

IV. What happened, what was believed, and what has turned out to be wrong

In January 2026 the team shipped a flag that suppressed the crate for accounts with a declared class of 5, 6 or 7, on the view that the youngest learners should not be inside a randomised reward. Everyone involved believed that flag had been on ever since. The declared-class field has its own history: optional at signup from April 2025, mandatory from April 2026, which is why 74,000 of September's active learners carry no declared class at all (Exhibit 6).

Between 20 July and 16 August 2026 Nilambuj ran a holdout: 30,000 direct-subscription accounts in India, split four to one, the streak counter and the crate hidden for the smaller arm (Exhibit 3). On 7 August release 4.19 switched the suppression flag off and moved the class check ahead of the holdout check, so the crate service stopped consulting the holdout flag for that band. From day nineteen of a twenty-eight-day test, Class 5 to 7 learners were crate-eligible in both arms, having had no crate in either arm before that date. Nishikant Yawalkar's team found it on 30 August, twenty-three days later. The flag-evaluation log retains thirty days, so by the end of September no per-learner record of those twenty-three days survived.

On 9 September Netrika commissioned the audit. On 21 September Nandagopal told the board that day-30 retention stood at 42.0 per cent. On 2 October Nilambuj's memo supplied the base: 42.0 per cent of the 1,86,000 learners who completed onboarding in the April–June quarter, which is 78,120 learners, or 23.7 per cent of the 3,30,000 who signed up in that quarter. Both figures now sit in the board pack. On 6 October Nutanika's email put weekly active at 29,600 of the 52,000 licensed Gyanodaya seats, 56.9 per cent against a contracted sixty. On 14 October the term sheet arrived.

V. The people in the room

Netrika Yargop, co-founder and chief product officer, Pune, owns release 5.0 and commissioned the audit that is now the most awkward document in the company. She has not told anyone that her own daughter's streak stands at 212 days.

Nandagopal Yenagi, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru, wants the loop held intact until the Series C closes and the question reopened in April. He has not circulated the secondary component in the term sheet, which pays out only on the 12,00,000 milestone.

Nipunika Yaragatti, vice-president, growth, Bengaluru, built the streak and the crate and reads Exhibit 4 as settling the matter. Her remaining option tranche vests on monthly active learners, not revenue, and she has not said so in any of these meetings.

Nishikant Yawalkar, vice-president, engineering, Pune, wants the flag architecture rewritten before anything else ships. He has not yet reported that a second precedence conflict, affecting the 21:30 reminder for school-channel accounts, is still live in production.

Naivedya Yalgi, principal designer, Berlin, three and a half hours behind IST until 25 October, has a completion-based redesign ready and argues the options are mis-framed. She has already walked Nutanika Yelpale through the redesign on a call, without telling Nandagopal.

Nilambuj Yevale, staff data scientist, Toronto, nine and a half hours behind IST until 1 November, will defend the holdout and the contamination note equally hard. He has not said that he recomputed the retention base in August and sat on it until October.

Nupurika Yatnalkar, customer-success lead, Singapore, two and a half hours ahead of IST, carries the Gyanodaya relationship and the 15 December renewal. She has not passed on that two Gyanodaya principals have asked for the app to be removed from Class 5 and 6 timetables.

Nagarjun Yeole, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey, nine and a half hours behind IST until 1 November, says the streak is unsellable to a US district this quarter. He has not disclosed that his two largest pipeline schools are Indian-curriculum schools in the Gulf, inside Nupurika's account.
