Nandagopal Yenagi, call with Netrika, 15 October

VIII. The options on Netrika's whiteboard

A. Ship release 5.0 as scoped. The streak, the crate and the 21:30 reminder stay for every learner in every channel. Legal has quoted ₹18 lakh to prepare a representation seeking a notification under the Act's relaxation power and to sit with the industry body on the children's-data submission. No engineering plan changes, the 15 December renewal is measured on the mechanics that produced 56.9 per cent, and the 74,000 undeclared accounts stay undeclared.

B. Age-gate the loop. Suppress the crate, the streak counter and the break reminder for declared Classes 5 to 7, for Class 8 to 9 learners whose only consent is a tick-box, and for all undeclared accounts: 5,18,000 of September's 9,12,000 active learners, or 56.8 per cent. Nishikant costs it at five weeks for two squads starting this week, which places it in release 5.1 on Monday 23 November rather than 5.0. Classes 10 to 12 keep the consumer loop. It reaches the Gyanodaya learners in Classes 5 to 7, who sit inside the weekly-active commitment.

C. Rebuild the weekly goal for everyone. Eleven weeks for two of the four squads, so the first week of January at the earliest, three weeks after the Gyanodaya renewal date. The streak and the crate leave the product entirely and the 21:30 reminder becomes a Sunday summary. The DPDP consent-manager integration, which those same two squads own, moves by the same eleven weeks.

D. Split the build. A schools build with the loop switched off, where consent is routed through the licensing school, which means collecting it afresh for 80,000 of the 3,18,000 school-channel learners, whose consent is not school-mediated today, and a consumer build unchanged. Three weeks to split the release train and about ₹9 lakh a month in added QA and release overhead thereafter. The Gyanodaya commitment would then be measured on a build with no streak in it, and the 2,68,000 India school learners move with it.

IX. The deadline and the hard edges

Gammat held ₹38.4 crore of cash on 30 September against net burn of ₹2.6 crore a month: 14.8 months. September revenue of ₹266.58 lakh annualises to ₹31.99 crore, of which the Gyanodaya contract is ₹93.60 lakh a month, or 35.1 per cent. Missing the sixty per cent weekly-active commitment in two consecutive quarters triggers a twelve per cent fee rebate — ₹1.35 crore against the contract's ₹11.23 crore a year — and the renewal signature is due 15 December. The term sheet lapses on 30 November and carries the 12,00,000 milestone for 31 March 2027. Code freeze for release 5.0 is 2 November, with schools shut for Diwali in early November. Two of four squads are already committed to the consent-manager work. The Jio agreement bars charging bundled learners until August 2027.

X. Late, in Baner

At midnight Netrika turned the test handset over and tapped through to the crate screen. Five tiers, a half-second pause, the sound a colleague in Pune had recorded on a borrowed tabla. On the audit, open at its last page, someone had pencilled 86 items. Down the corridor her daughter's streak had stood at 212 days when she went to bed, and the 21:30 notification had gone to her as it goes every night. The rain started again. Netrika put the pencil down and read Nutanika's email a third time.

Questions for discussion

  1. Fill the Hook canvas for Gammat from Exhibits 1 to 6. For each quadrant, name the figure on this page that measures it, and the population it was measured over.
  2. Exhibit 2 reports 52,000 licensed Gyanodaya seats and 50,000 active learners; Exhibit 6 counts those 50,000 inside its total while the group's own registry lists 47,100. Which number goes to the board on Friday, and what would you check first?
  3. Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 4 are both offered as the effect of the loop. What does each one measure? What measurement would let you choose between them, and could Gammat still make it?
  4. The audit was commissioned to measure grip, and it did. What would an equally honest measurement of the loop's effect on learning look like, what would it cost, and who in section V should own it?
  5. The Gyanodaya commitment, the Series C milestone and the Act's children's provisions all pull on the same mechanic. Which of the three is negotiable, on what evidence, and with whom?
  6. What should Netrika do at ten o'clock on Monday 19 October, and what exactly should she say to the board on Friday 23 October about release 5.0, the renewal, and the twenty-three days in August?
exp20v2-ethics.hook.apply:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance · Ethics, Persuasion & Trust

Applying the Hook to Your Product

1. A canvas due on a Tuesday

On the second Monday of March 2026, Ananya Deshpande, VP of Product at Chaakriya, a Pune-based fitness-habit app, sat with eleven days left before a board meeting that would decide whether the company raised its Series C at the valuation its term sheet implied. Her CEO, Rohit Sabharwal, had asked for one slide: a Hook Canvas for Chaakriya's flagship streak feature, filled in and defended in front of Kavita Iyer, the lead partner from the fund pushing for the round. Kavita's diligence memo used the phrase "engagement uplift of fifteen percent" three times. Rohit wanted Ananya to show the mechanics behind the number and commit to hitting it within two quarters.

Chaakriya had 640,000 monthly active users, a thirty-eight percent thirty-day retention rate, and a streak feature that forty-six percent of those users had opened at least once. The streak was the product's best number and, Ananya suspected, its most fragile one. She had spent the previous week pulling logs rather than opinions, and what she found troubled her enough that she called Farhan Qureshi, the team's data scientist, in twice on a Sunday. The canvas Rohit wanted filled by Tuesday was not a fundraising exhibit to Ananya; it was the only honest way she knew to find out whether Chaakriya's most profitable loop was helping people exercise or merely training them to open an app.

Chaakriya, March 2026Value
Monthly active users640,000
30-day retention38%
Users who have opened the streak screen46%
Board's requested retention uplift+15% in two quarters
Premium upsell tied to unbroken streaks (12-month projection)+₹4.2 crore ARR

2. The idea

The Hook Canvas is a one-page worksheet, popularised by Nir Eyal alongside his 2014 book Hooked and now taught in variations at Stanford, HEC, and Berkeley's SCET, that maps a single user behaviour across four boxes: the trigger that starts it, the action it asks for, the reward that follows, and the investment the user makes that primes the next cycle. On its own the canvas is neutral; it is a diagram of a mechanism, the same one an engineer might draw for a pump. Applying it to your own product, honestly, is a different exercise from drawing it in a workshop. It means filling each box with evidence pulled from your own logs and interviews rather than with the aspiration you wrote in the product brief, and being willing to leave a box blank, or ugly, when the evidence says so.

Eyal built the canvas to solve a specific problem: teams could describe their product's habit loop in a sentence but could not point to where, in their own data, that loop actually lived, which made it impossible to test or improve deliberately. The sentence Ananya could now say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: the canvas is only as honest as the evidence in each box, and the discipline is admitting when a box is empty, borrowed from a textbook, or propped up by a number that does not mean what the team wants it to mean.

Figure 1. The canvas as handed out in a workshop: a diagram, not yet a fact about your product.

3. Filling the canvas without flattering it

Ananya's team worked the canvas in a fixed order, because filling the boxes out of order tends to let the most flattering box get written first and the others get shaped to match it. They began with the trigger, because it is the box with the least room to lie: a trigger either fired in the logs or it did not. Farhan pulled the split between external triggers, mostly push notifications, and internal triggers, the boredom or guilt that made a user open the app without being prompted. Chaakriya was sending three streak-reminder pushes a day, and those pushes accounted for thirty-one percent of daily opens, against a baseline of nine percent for users who had every notification turned off. That gap told them the external trigger, not habit, was doing most of the work.

The action box came next, and here Ananya insisted on the smallest unit of behaviour, not the outcome the team wanted: tapping the streak-flame icon, not "staying fit." The reward box was where the team's own language started doing the lying, because "streak saved" is a description of a mechanism, not a measurement. Farhan had to go back to the event logs to find out what fraction of streak-triggered opens ended in an actual logged workout, because a saved streak and a completed workout are not the same event, and the canvas is worthless if the team writes down the one it wishes were true. The investment box, last and hardest, asked what a user was building for next time: a longer streak, yes, but also, Ananya realised uncomfortably, a growing cost of quitting that had nothing to do with fitness.

Figure 2. The same canvas after a week of pulling logs instead of assuming.

4. The arithmetic Ananya could not unsee

The number that changed the meeting was not the retention rate; it was what happened inside the thirty-one percent of daily opens that notifications caused. Of Chaakriya's 640,000 monthly active users, thirty-one percent of daily opens attributable to push notifications works out to roughly 198,400 opens a day. Farhan's log pull showed that only fifty-two percent of those notification-triggered opens ended in a logged workout, meaning about 103,168 opens produced the real-world action the app existed to encourage. The remainder, roughly 95,232 opens a day, closed the loop in the technical sense — the app opened, the streak flame stayed lit, the retention dashboard ticked up — without a workout ever happening. Ananya called these "hollow opens," and they were, by her arithmetic, the single largest component of the retention number the board found so attractive.

She ran a second pass changing one input: cut the push schedule from three reminders a day to one, sent only in a user's own historical workout window rather than a fixed studio-wide time. The projected effect, based on a two-week pilot with 40,000 users, was a fall in notification-triggered opens to about eighteen percent of DAU, or 115,200 opens a day, but a rise in the completion rate of those opens to seventy-four percent, because the remaining pushes were arriving when a user was actually likely to train. That yields about 85,248 real workouts from push-triggered opens, a drop of only seventeen percent in genuine value, against a drop of sixty-eight percent in hollow opens, from 95,232 down to roughly 29,952. Thirty-day retention slipped two points, from thirty-eight to thirty-six percent, and the near-term premium-upsell projection fell from ₹4.2 crore to about ₹1.1 crore in incremental ARR. Ninety-day retention, which the fixed-schedule pushes had never been measured against, rose from twenty-one to twenty-seven percent, and the monthly rate of app-store reviews citing "too many notifications" fell from 4.1 percent to 1.3 percent.

Metric3 pushes/day (current)1 targeted push/day (pilot)
Opens caused by push, per day198,400115,200
Of those, ending in a logged workout103,168 (52%)85,248 (74%)
"Hollow" opens (no workout logged)95,23229,952
30-day retention38%36%
90-day retention21%27%
Complaints citing notification volume4.1%/month1.3%/month
12-month incremental ARR+₹4.2 crore+₹1.1 crore

The canvas had not told Ananya what to do; it had told her, in arithmetic she could defend line by line, exactly what she would be trading and against what.

5. What a learner has to notice

The canvas rewards the box that is easiest to measure, not the one that matters most

Triggers show up cleanly in event logs, so teams over-invest in describing them and under-invest in the reward box, which requires deciding what the "real" reward is, separate from the proxy metric the dashboard already shows.

Filling the canvas is a mechanics exercise; judging it is a separate, ethical one

A canvas can be filled with complete honesty and still describe a loop that is bad for the user. Honesty in the filling tells you the mechanism is accurately drawn; it says nothing yet about whether the mechanism should exist in this form.

"Engagement" and "value delivered" are not the same number, and the canvas will hide the gap unless you go looking for it

Chaakriya's dashboard called both events an "open." Only the workout-completion field, three tables deeper in the data warehouse, separated a real behaviour from a loop closing on itself.

A canvas filled from analytics alone differs from one grounded in interviews, and the two disagree more often than teams expect

Farhan's numbers said the reward was working; five customer calls Ananya sat in on that same week said users felt "nagged," a word that never appears in an events table.

The canvas cannot tell you whether the underlying habit is healthy

It can tell you that a loop is efficient at recurring. Whether daily exercise driven by loss-aversion over a streak number is a healthier habit than exercise driven by how a person feels afterward is a question the canvas has no box for.

Team incentives corrupt the filling before anyone notices

When a product manager's quarterly bonus is tied to the same retention number the canvas is meant to interrogate, the reward and investment boxes tend to get filled generously and the trigger box gets filled last, if at all.

A generic canvas copied from a competitor's teardown is not "your own product's" canvas

The instruction to fill it honestly presumes your own evidence. A canvas assembled from a rival's public case study describes their mechanism, possibly convincingly, but tells you nothing certain about yours.

The canvas has no box for consent or disclosure, so a team has to add one itself

Whether users understand that a streak is engineered to exploit loss-aversion, and would consent to that if asked plainly, is the question a thoughtful newcomer should carry into every filled-in canvas, because the four boxes will happily stay silent on it.

6. Where the canvas changes shape

In a consumer product like Chaakriya, the trigger is usually a notification the company controls directly, the reward is emotional and immediate, and the investment accumulates as personal data and social proof, a streak, a badge, a follower count, that the user alone holds. In a B2B product, the trigger is more often a colleague or a workflow deadline than anything the vendor sends, the reward is typically the relief of a task cleared rather than a dopamine spike, and the investment accumulates as organisational memory, templates, configured dashboards, integrations, that the company, not the individual, would lose on churn. A marketplace product complicates the canvas further because it has to be filled twice, once for each side: a driver's trigger might be a low-earnings notification while a rider's trigger is hunger or a missed bus, and the two reward loops can pull against each other in ways a single canvas, drawn for only one side, will never surface.

Company stage changes what "honest" filling can even look like. An early-stage team, as Chaakriya was three years earlier, usually has too little data to fill any box with confidence and is tempted to write down intentions instead, which is a forgivable but dangerous habit if it hardens into belief once the company scales. A large company, with years of event logs, has the opposite failure mode: enough data to fill every box impressively while nobody asks whether the underlying loop should still exist in its current form, because the dashboard has made the mechanism feel inevitable rather than chosen.

7. Where teams go wrong filling their own canvas

SymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Every box reads like a mission statementTreating the canvas as a pitch document rather than a measurement exerciseAsk for the query that produced each number; if there isn't one, the box is fiction
Reward box cites "engagement," never a completed real-world actionConflating the proxy metric with the value the product was built to deliverDefine the real action in one sentence before opening the dashboard, then measure against that sentence
Investment box only ever grows, never gets re-examinedAssuming stored value is always healthy, when it can just as easily be sunk-cost coercionAsk what a user loses by quitting, and whether they know it
Canvas gets filled once, at launch, and never againTreating the canvas as a design artifact instead of a living auditPut a re-fill date on the calendar tied to the next major metric review

8. What good looks like

Sunil Bhatt, product lead at Mrinmaya Money, a Bengaluru budgeting app, filled the same exercise a year before Ananya did, for a feature that nudged users to log every expense within an hour of spending. His team's trigger box cited an actual push-open rate, not an aspiration; his reward box distinguished a completed expense log from a mere app open, the same distinction Farhan later had to dig for at Chaakriya; and his investment box flagged, in writing, that a user's growing transaction history was valuable to the user's own budgeting insight, not only to Mrinmaya's retention curve. When his own numbers showed that a fourth daily reminder produced mostly hollow opens, he cut it before any board asked him to, and said so in his own product review, numbers attached, rather than waiting to be caught.

Canvas boxMrinmaya Money's honesty rating
TriggerEvidenced: real open rates by channel
ActionEvidenced: friction measured, not assumed
RewardEvidenced: real action distinguished from proxy metric
InvestmentEvidenced, and re-examined for whose benefit it accrues

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya walked into the board meeting with the filled canvas, both passes of the arithmetic, and a recommendation to move Chaakriya to the targeted, once-a-day notification design before the retention metric the fund had anchored on, not after. She told Kavita Iyer directly that the fifteen-percent uplift the diligence memo assumed had been manufactured largely from hollow opens, and that chasing it as written would mean shipping more of the same mechanism, only harder. Rohit backed her, and the board approved a revised target: ninety-day retention, not thirty-day, as the headline metric for the next two quarters, with the honesty-filled canvas re-run each quarter rather than filled once and framed on a slide.

What she would need next is not a better canvas but a way to audit the whole product this way as a standing habit, not a one-off exercise before a board meeting, and a clearer framework for deciding, once a loop is accurately mapped, whose interests it is actually allowed to serve. Two questions are worth sitting with before you fill your own canvas: which box in your product's loop would embarrass you most if a user read exactly what you wrote in it, and what number would have to move, and by how much, before you would recommend removing a feature that your own bonus depends on.

Unlocks nextWhy
Auditing your own productTurns the one-time canvas into a recurring, defensible practice
Digital wellbeing and time-well-spentGives you a vocabulary for judging a loop once it is accurately mapped
A framework for ethical persuasionAnswers the question the canvas deliberately leaves open: for whose benefit?
exp40v2-ethics.variable.reward:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance · Ethics, Persuasion & Trust

Variable Rewards

Tribe, hunt, self — and the harder question of what a person has already learned about your reward schedule by the fortieth time they meet it.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On 14 January 2026, Meera Bhagat, head of product at Sargam Riyaaz, sat in the company's Pune office with a research deck she did not like. Sargam Riyaaz taught Hindustani vocal and film-song singing to 2.9 million monthly users; 186,000 paid ₹399 a quarter. Its practice loop was honest and dull: a learner sang a phrase, an on-device pitch model scored it, and a fixed star appeared if accuracy crossed 80%. Median session, eleven minutes; share of installs still practising on day 30, 22%.

Her growth team proposed the Guru's Nod. After a take, a learner would sometimes — not always — receive a twelve-second recorded appraisal from one of nine working ustads, the panel Sargam Riyaaz had paid ₹28 lakh to record: 2,400 clips, from a curt "theek hai" to a genuinely warm reading of a specific phrase. The clip would be unpredictable in arrival and in warmth. Simulations put paid conversion at 8.1% against a 6.1% baseline. Meera's discomfort was precise rather than squeamish: a schedule tuned for persistence is tuned for persistence whether or not the learner is getting better at singing, and the ustads' warmth, once randomised, stops being feedback and becomes payout.

Eight days later and 1,400 kilometres away, Rohit Sathe, chief product officer of Munshi Fieldforce in Gurugram, took a call he had been dreading. Munshi sold sales-force automation to 1,100 FMCG distributors; 78,000 field representatives logged orders on its Android app every working day. The company's largest customer, a foods distributor with a ₹14 crore renewal due in March, wanted scratch cards: every tenth order line a rep logged would reveal a prize of between ₹0 and ₹200. The distributor's own analysts had modelled a 9% lift in order lines. Rohit's problem was structural rather than psychological. Munshi's user was the rep; its buyer was the distributor who paid the rep; and a variable reward attached to a person's earnings is not engagement design but a change in the volatility of a working household's income. One mechanism, two entirely different ethical surfaces — and the same body of theory, which answers neither decision.

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

A variable reward is reinforcement delivered on a schedule whose next payoff the subject cannot predict from the last one. The precise vocabulary matters and is routinely lost: Charles Ferster and B. F. Skinner's Schedules of Reinforcement (1957) distinguishes ratio schedules, where payout depends on the count of responses, from interval schedules, where it depends on elapsed time, and crosses each with fixed and variable. Those four cells produce four different behaviours, and most product arguments about "variable rewards" are arguments about which cell a feature sits in.

The problem the schedule literature was invented to solve was not engagement but extinction: why does behaviour persist when the payoff stops? Lloyd Humphreys had shown in 1939 that partially reinforced behaviour survives longer without reward than continuously reinforced behaviour — the partial reinforcement extinction effect. Skinner's 1948 "superstition" paper added the uncomfortable corollary that pigeons will invent rituals when reinforcement is merely coincident with behaviour rather than caused by it. Modern practice inherits both: variability buys persistence, whether or not the user's behaviour caused the reward.

Four camps now disagree, and an experienced product leader should be able to state what each will and will not sign.

CampWill signWill not sign
Schedule engineers
(Ferster–Skinner lineage; most growth teams)		Persistence is a property of the schedule. Choose the cell, choose the rate, measure the behaviour.That the user's beliefs about the schedule matter. They treat the learner as a rate, not as someone forming a theory.
Prediction-error modellers
(Rescorla–Wagner 1972; Schultz 1997; Fiorillo, Tobler & Schultz 2003)		What drives anticipation is the error between expectation and outcome, not randomness as such. Surprise is computable.That any randomisation works. A distribution the user has fully learned yields predictable error and loses most of its force.
Self-determination theorists
(Deci 1971; Lepper 1973; Deci & Ryan)		Extrinsic rewards attached to an already-intrinsic behaviour crowd it out; removal leaves behaviour below the original baseline.That a retention lift measured while the reward is running is evidence the reward was a good idea.
Structural-harm researchers
(gambling studies; Schüll's Addiction by Design, 2012)		A commercial VR schedule with a hidden rate, a near-miss animation and no stopping cue is a slot machine irrespective of intent.That disclosure and good intentions neutralise the mechanism. They locate harm in the structure, not the motive.

Nir Eyal's Hooked (2014) sits deliberately across these camps, naming the three reward families — Tribe, Hunt and Self — and adding a manipulation matrix that asks whether the designer would use the product and whether it materially improves lives. Critics read that matrix as a conscience clause bolted onto an engineering manual; defenders read it as the only honest position available, since the mechanism exists and will be used.

3. Mechanics: what actually decays, and how fast

The competent practitioner picks a probability. The expert models a belief. Rescorla and Wagner's 1972 learning rule is the smallest formal object that captures the difference, and it is worth working rather than naming. Let V be the user's expectation that this action pays off, r the outcome (1 or 0), α a learning rate. After each trial, δ = r − V is the prediction error, and V moves a fraction of the way toward the outcome: V ← V + αδ.

Take a Sargam Riyaaz learner who arrives believing, from onboarding copy that promised feedback from real ustads, that V = 0.50. The true rate is 0.30. With α = 0.3:

TakeNod?V beforeδ (surprise)V after
1no0.50−0.500.35
2yes0.35+0.650.55
3no0.55−0.550.38
4no0.38−0.380.27
5yes0.27+0.730.49
6no0.49−0.490.34
7no0.34−0.340.24
8yes0.24+0.760.47

Two things happen here that a probability-only view misses. First, V oscillates around the true rate but never settles, because a Bernoulli outcome is never equal to its own mean. At the stationary point where V = p, the expected absolute prediction error is E|δ| = 2p(1−p): 0.50 at p = 0.5, 0.42 at p = 0.3, and 0.147 at p = 0.08. Surprise does not go to zero as the user learns the rate — a genuinely important result, and the reason a well-set variable reward outlives the novelty period while a fixed one does not. Second, the first four takes are dominated by disappointment, because onboarding oversold the rate. A learner who quits on take four did not find the schedule boring; she found it worse than advertised. Expectation-setting copy is part of reward design, and is almost never owned by the same person.

The second-order effect the expert watches for is the decay of the distribution, not of the rate. Once a user has met all nine ustads and roughly learned the warmth distribution, the residual uncertainty is only the Bernoulli coin, not the content. Sargam's own instrumentation could see this: the lift from the Guru's Nod in a six-week pilot ran at +34% practice-days in week one, +21% in week three, +11% in week six, on an unchanged p. Nothing about the schedule changed; the user's posterior did.

The third piece of formal machinery is Richard Herrnstein's matching law (1961): given two concurrent options, subjects allocate responses in proportion to the relative rate of reinforcement, B1/(B1+B2) ≈ r1/(r1+r2). Sargam Riyaaz had two surfaces: the practice room and the Sangat social feed. Salient rewarding events ran at roughly 2.4 per minute in the feed and 0.35 per minute in practice. Matching predicts a feed time-share of 2.4/2.75 = 87%; the observed share was 83%, the mild undermatching the literature usually finds. This is the most under-used tool in the topic: a variable reward added to one surface does not create engagement out of nothing, it reallocates it from whatever else the user would have done inside the same product. Meera's real risk was not that the Guru's Nod would fail, but that a strong reward in practice would pull time out of Sangat, where her ad revenue sat — and that whichever surface won would look like a triumph in its own dashboard.

4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

Four conditions can be written so that a team can falsify them with data it already has, rather than argued about in a review.

Claim one: the action is frequent and low-stakes — at least weekly, ideally daily, with a per-instance cost to the user of minutes and no irreversible consequence. Sargam passes easily (median 4.1 sessions a week among actives). Munshi passes on frequency and fails on stakes: an order line is a commercial commitment with a real customer, and randomising its reward puts variance on the wrong side of the transaction.

Claim two: the variability is about the payoff, not about the product's reliability. A user must be able to say "the reward is uncertain" without saying "the product is unreliable". Sargam passes if the pitch score stays deterministic and only the ustad's appraisal varies; it fails the moment the score itself is randomised. Munshi fails structurally — reps cannot separate "my scratch card was unlucky" from "Munshi's app lost my order", and the app already dropped 0.7% of orders on weak rural networks.

Claim three: the reward is causally attributable to the user's own action. Where it is not, users build folk theories — Skinner's superstition — and the product acquires a mythology it cannot correct. Sargam passes only if better singing genuinely raises the odds of a Nod; if the draw is a pure coin, learners will decide that time of day matters and practise at the wrong hour for the wrong reason.

Claim four: no party's income or health depends on the outcome. Munshi fails this outright, and it is where the idea turns actively misleading: the literature offers a rate, the rate produces a lift, and nothing in the framework flags that the lift was bought with somebody's household budget volatility.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In two-sided marketplaces, variable rewards run on the supply side as quests and surge multipliers, and the supply side is usually the party least able to absorb variance. India's gig-mobility and delivery platforms have lived this publicly: a quest structure raises hours worked without raising hourly earnings, which is exactly what a VR schedule is supposed to do, and exactly what a labour regulator reads as something else.

In regulated categories the mechanism can be flatly illegal rather than merely distasteful. India's Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 removed real-money online gaming from the table entirely; the Ministry of Consumer Affairs' 2023 dark-pattern guidelines name several adjacent practices; and in insurance, Section 41 of the Insurance Act has long prohibited inducements to buy cover, which is why a wellness app's "spin to win a premium discount" is a compliance question before it is a growth question. Tashan Live, a Hyderabad trivia app, rebuilt its economy around non-cash, non-transferable rewards for exactly this reason: engagement fell by a third, then recovered to within 8% of the old level over five months — evidence that the cash was carrying less of the effect than its finance team believed.

In hardware-plus-software, variance is constrained by the returns window and by the fact that the device is a sunk purchase. Vyayam Wearables found its randomised "bonus ring" demotivated exactly the users it needed — new owners in weeks two to four who had not yet formed the habit and read a missed bonus as the ₹6,499 band not working. Hardware buyers have already paid; they experience a withheld reward as a defect.

In AI-native products the mechanism arrives whether or not anyone designs it. A generative model is a stochastic oracle: regenerate is a pull of the lever, and the variance is free. Worse, a system optimised on engagement signals can discover variable reinforcement endogenously — learning that intermittent flattery retains better than consistent flattery — with no line of code anyone would recognise as a reward schedule. That is the bridge to sycophancy, and the reason AI teams need a reward-schedule review even when they have built no rewards.

What mature companies actually do, as distinct from what their blogs say: freeze p at quarter-end so nobody raises it under pressure; log every change to the rate, because a regulator's first request is the change log; and build the kill-switch before the feature, because a reward economy unwound over a weekend is the most expensive item on this list.

6. Eight things that separate the expert from the competent

Randomness is not the lever; the user's posterior is. The tell is a team defending a decaying lift as "novelty wearing off". Novelty is a label, not a mechanism: the user has learned the distribution, and the fix is not more randomness but another dimension of uncertainty — a reward whose kind, not just whose timing, is unresolved. Experts ask what a user can predict after forty exposures, and design against that answer.

Variable ratio and variable interval are different products. A team complaining that users open the app too rarely, and proposing a scratch card, has confused them: VR raises actions per session, VI raises sessions. The tell is a roadmap where the metric problem is frequency and the solution is per-action randomisation. Experts diagnose which cell the deficit sits in before choosing a mechanism.

An extinction burst looks exactly like success. When a reward is reduced or removed, reinforced behaviour first increases sharply before collapsing — pigeons peck harder, users refresh more. The tell is a metric spike in the 72 hours after a takeaway, celebrated in a standup. Experts refuse to read a takeaway experiment before day fourteen, and say so before the test starts.

The near-miss is a separate, and more dangerous, lever. Slot-machine research finds that outcomes falling just short of a win recruit reward circuitry almost as strongly as wins, and drive continued play harder. In product terms this is the animation that stops one slot from the prize. The tell is designers tuning the reveal animation rather than the odds. The obvious reading — that this is a polish decision — is precisely wrong; it is the most regulatorily exposed choice in the whole feature.

Your measured lift is selected on survivors. Variable rewards drive out the users least tolerant of variance, and retention metrics are computed on those who remain. The tell is a healthy cohort-retention chart alongside a quietly worsening install-to-day-7 rate. Experts insist on measuring the effect on the entry cohort, not the retained one, and treat any lift that appears only in the retained cohort as evidence of selection rather than causation.

Rewarding a behaviour people already did for free can leave it below baseline. Deci's and Lepper's overjustification results are the single most commercially relevant finding in the whole literature, and the one growth teams most reliably have not read. The tell is a reward attached to a behaviour that had strong unrewarded engagement. The diagnostic is a holdout that removes the reward after twelve weeks and compares against never-rewarded users — not against the pre-launch baseline, which is contaminated by seasonality.

The reward pool is an economy and economies inflate. The tell is users describing yesterday's prize as "nothing", or a secondary market appearing on Telegram. Because expectation adapts to the distribution, a reward held constant in rupees falls in psychological value; teams raise it, which raises the baseline again. Experts design the sink before the faucet: expiry, caps and non-transferability keep the economy from eating the P&L.

Harm concentrates in a tail that the mean cannot see. Mean session time can be flat while the 99th percentile doubles. The tell is a support queue whose tone changes before any dashboard moves — three families writing in the same week. Experts instrument the p99 and the complaint text from the first day of the pilot, because the cost of learning this from a journalist eighteen months later is a category of cost that does not appear in any experiment readout.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the mechanism is strongest and most legitimate, because frequency is high and the stakes are minutes. In B2B and enterprise engineered variability almost never works, for a reason usually stated wrongly: not that professionals are immune, but that the buyer is not the user, and a mechanism that makes the user work more without earning more is one the buyer can be sold and the user will resent. The legitimate analogue is uncertainty that already exists — an anomaly alert, an unexpected match — surfaced rather than manufactured.

In platforms and marketplaces variable reward arrives free on the demand side (not every search is a great result) and arrives as income volatility on the supply side, which is a different ethical object entirely. In hardware, as Vyayam found, the sunk purchase converts a withheld reward into a perceived fault. In AI products the variance is endogenous and must be governed rather than designed.

Stage changes three things and not more. Early-stage teams lack the volume to estimate p per cohort and should not try; one rate and honest disclosure beats a badly estimated segmentation. Growth-stage teams have volume and metric pressure at once, the most dangerous combination in this topic. Late-stage companies have volume, lawyers and brand exposure, and their binding constraint becomes reversibility: at 40 million users a reward economy cannot be switched off without a communications plan.

8. Three worked examples

CaseDesignResult
Sargam Riyaaz
Guru's Nod pilot, 6 weeks, n = 240,000		p = 0.30, gated on a real pitch-accuracy improvement over the learner's own trailing median, so the reward was causally earnedPractice-days +34% wk 1 → +11% wk 6. Paid conversion 7.4% vs 6.1%. Sangat feed time −9% (matching-law reallocation, as predicted)
Munshi Fieldforce
Scratch-card pilot, 9 distributors, 4,100 reps		One card per 10 order lines, prize ₹0–₹200, EV ₹9, undisclosed distributionOrder lines +9.2% in wk 1, +2.1% by wk 7, −1.4% by wk 11. Rep attrition 4.8% → 7.1%. Cost to distributors ≈ ₹673 per rep per month
Bharosa Health
Step lottery, national, 11 months — the failure		Daily 8,000-step target entered users into a draw for premium discounts; odds never publishedWithdrawn. Fraud (phone-on-fan step spoofing) reached 14% of entries; the insurance-inducement question under Section 41 arrived from the compliance side, not the product side

Bharosa Health is the instructive one, and it failed for three compounding reasons. The reward was not causally attributable — a spoofed step counted as much as a walked one — so the schedule reinforced fraud at the same rate as health. The odds were hidden, so the company had no defensible answer about what it had promised. And the prize was a discount on a regulated financial product, which put the mechanism inside a statute the product team had not read.

The recovery was not a retreat. Bharosa replaced the lottery with a fixed, published, capped benefit — a ₹500 premium credit at 150 active days — and moved the variability somewhere it cost nothing and broke no rule: the content. A short, genuinely useful message from a named physiotherapist, arriving on some days and not others, on a variable-interval schedule. Day-90 active rate landed at 31%, against the lottery's 34% and the pre-lottery 19%, at a fifth of the cost and none of the exposure. Variability survived; the gambling structure did not.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Rate ratchet under quarterly pressureTwo increases to p in one quarter, neither reviewedWho is allowed to change the rate, and where is the log?An unfundable reward economy and a change log you must hand a regulator
Novelty decay mistaken for a broken featureWeek-6 readout well below week-1What is the half-life, and did we forecast it before launch?Rebuilding a working feature, or raising p to chase a number that was never sustainable
Overjustification of free behaviourReward attached to already-high unrewarded engagementWhat happens to this behaviour if we remove the reward for twelve weeks?Permanent loss of intrinsic engagement; the baseline never returns
Tail harm invisible in the meanSupport tone changes before dashboards doWhat is p99 session time, by age cohort?Press, regulator, and an unwind under deadline
Reward decoupled from real valueMetric holds while NPS and review sentiment fallIf the reward budget were cut to zero on Monday, what would remain?Retention collapses the day finance reallocates the budget

The pattern across all five is latency: each is cheap to catch in week three and structurally expensive in month twelve, and every diagnostic above can be run by one analyst in an afternoon. They go unrun not through ignorance but because the team that would run them is measured on the number the failure mode flatters.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position one: the mechanism is neutral and the ethics live in the application. Its strongest form is Eyal's: unpredictability is a property of every worthwhile thing — teaching, research, love — and a rule against it is a rule against surprise. The evidence is that products people are glad to use — a good feed, a good recommender — are variable, and removing the variability makes them worse. It would be wrong if harm scaled with the mechanism's strength irrespective of content, that is, if a well-intentioned variable reward produced the same compulsive tail as a slot machine.

Position two: the structure is the harm. Natasha Schüll's account of machine gambling holds that rate, feedback latency and the absence of stopping cues produce the same state — the "machine zone" — regardless of what the payout is. The evidence is the striking convergence of design choices across slot machines, loot boxes and infinite feeds, arrived at independently. It would be wrong if products with matched schedules but different content showed materially different tail behaviour, which is a study nobody has properly run at scale.

Position three: the schedule literature transfers badly to humans. This is the least-known and most serious challenge. Human subjects, unlike pigeons, form verbal rules about contingencies, and a literature running from C. F. Lowe's work in the late 1970s shows that rule-governed behaviour often overrides the schedule: tell a person the rate and their behaviour tracks the instruction, not the reinforcement history. On this view most product "variable reward" effects are small, confounded with novelty and better explained by content quality — and the modest, decaying effect sizes seen whenever the features are tested properly are the evidence, Sargam's +11% at week six well within the predicted range. It would be wrong if disclosed-odds designs showed the same persistence as hidden-odds designs at the tail; the gacha markets of Japan and China, where odds disclosure is mandatory and spending remained high, are the strongest evidence against it, and it is genuinely unresolved.

Position four: it is commercially self-defeating. The self-determination camp holds that variable extrinsic rewards buy short-run frequency at the cost of the intrinsic motivation behind long-run retention and willingness to pay; Bharosa's recovery — higher day-90 activity after the lottery was removed than before it existed — is the shape of evidence it points to. It would be wrong if the crowding-out effect proved to be small outside laboratory tasks with clear intrinsic appeal, which several replications suggest it might be.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic proposes a probability. Someone who has internalised it asks four questions before proposing anything: what will the user believe about this schedule after forty exposures; which of the four cells does our actual deficit sit in; what does this reward pull time away from inside our own product; and who in this building is allowed to change the rate. They forecast the decay curve before launch rather than explaining it afterwards. They design the removal at the same time as the launch. They read the support queue's language, not only its volume. And they hold a distinction that the framework itself does not supply — between a habit the user would endorse on reflection and one they would not — and they know that no value of p will ever tell them which one they have built.

12. What each decides

Meera Bhagat shipped the Guru's Nod, with four changes. The draw is gated on a real improvement over the learner's own trailing median, so the reward is earned rather than drawn; onboarding copy states the rough frequency, ending the disappointment run in the first four takes; the panel expands quarterly, adding a genuine new dimension of uncertainty rather than a higher rate; and the six-week decay curve, not the week-one lift, is what the board sees. She kept the right to cut the feature if the p99 practice time among under-18s moved at all.

Rohit Sathe declined. He offered the distributor a different build: real-time visibility of a rep's own progress against a published, fixed incentive schedule, with the variability left where it already lives — in which shops reorder. He put the ₹14 crore renewal at risk to do it, and wrote a one-page memo stating why, which is the artefact that will matter if Munshi is ever asked how it decides these things.

For discussion. (1) Meera's gating on real improvement makes the reward partly contingent on skill — does that make the Nod a better teaching tool, or simply a more defensible one? (2) Rohit's refusal protects reps from variance they did not choose; is a product company the right party to make that call on a distributor's behalf, and what changes if the reps themselves prefer the scratch cards? (3) If the rule-governed-behaviour camp is right and these effects are small and decaying, what is the strongest remaining argument for regulating them at all?

13. Going deeper

  1. The Hook model — the frame this reward step sits inside; without trigger and investment, a reward schedule has nothing to compound.
  2. Applying the Hook to your product — turns the analysis above into a specification your team can actually build and instrument.
  3. Gamification and its limits — most of gamification is fixed-ratio and fixed-interval, which is why so much of it flattens in three weeks.
  4. Engagement-optimised AI and sycophancy — where variable reinforcement emerges without being designed, and the review process that catches it.
  5. Habit formation and attention — the account of why persistence becomes automaticity, and where the schedule stops mattering.
  6. External and internal triggers — the internal trigger is what a successful reward schedule eventually builds, and the real measure of whether it worked.
  7. Fogg behaviour model (B = MAT) — motivation is only one of three terms; many reward problems are ability problems in disguise.
  8. Investment and stored value — the durable alternative to reinforcement, and the reason some products retain with no reward at all.
  9. Dark patterns taxonomy — the named categories a regulator will use, including the three that a badly built reward draw falls into.
  10. Why dark patterns emerge without malice — the organisational seam in section 5, explained as a system rather than a failure of character.

The argument has been a single one: variability works because prediction error does not converge to zero, and it stops working when the user's beliefs converge instead. Everything an expert does differently follows from taking that learning seriously — as something that happens, that can be forecast, and that the person doing the learning did not consent to be the object of.

Swarnim Labs: The Potli Ladder

A reward engine has moved the numbers it was built to move, and some it was not. On the night before a board meeting, its founder has four options on four sheets of paper and four days of other people's arithmetic that will not agree.

1. Sunday night, Bengaluru

At twenty past eleven on Sunday 22 February 2026, Devashree Kavlekar was sitting on the floor of her flat off 12th Main in Indiranagar with four printed sheets fanned out in front of her and the board pack face down on the sofa. The board met at half past ten the next morning, nine floors above Lavelle Road, and the second item was hers: a slide titled Potli 2.0 — holding at 100 per cent.

Her co-founder had already sent that slide to the lead investor. Her chief financial officer had sent a different number for the same thing. Her designer in Berlin had sent four lines asking to be taken off the feature, and her customer-success lead in Singapore a survey with 312 responses and the subject line please read before Monday. Devashree had built Swarnim since 2019 on a proposition her mother understood in one sentence: ten rupees a day becomes gold. She was now fairly sure the thing that made ten rupees a day happen was not the gold.

2. Six and a half years, and one clause

Swarnim Labs Private Limited was registered in Bengaluru in August 2019 by Devashree Kavlekar, then twenty-nine and four years out of a payments team, and Devbrat Kshirsagar, who had run growth at a listed ticketing company. The product was deliberately small: a UPI autopay mandate, a ten-rupee minimum, digital gold with a licensed refiner. Revenue came from a margin inside the buy and sell quotes, a partner small finance bank's commission, a ninety-nine-rupee membership and placement fees from brands in the reward catalogue.

The decision that constrains February 2026 was taken in June 2023. Short of growth capital, Swarnim licensed its consumer stack to Shurfa Financial Group of Dubai for a three-year term with automatic renewal. The agreement carries a feature-parity clause: any engagement mechanic Swarnim operates in India must reach Shurfa within ninety days, on the same specification. It bought eighteen months of runway and the Gulf market. It also means that what Devashree decides for Bengaluru, she decides for Dubai.

3. The market Swarnim sits in

Indian daily-savings apps grew up in a gap. Digital gold is not a regulated security: SEBI's 2021 direction stopped registered intermediaries distributing it, and the RBI's perimeter covers the payment rails and the partner bank's deposits, not the gold. There is no single regulator to ask. What there is instead is GST at three per cent on every gram, NPCI's rules on UPI autopay, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 dark-pattern guidelines, which name nagging among thirteen prohibited practices.

Swarnim competes for the same ten rupees as Jar and Jupiter, against PhonePe, Paytm and Google Pay for the mandate itself, against Groww and Zerodha for the next spare rupee, and against Tanishq and the refiners' apps at Dhanteras and Akshaya Tritiya, when gold volumes triple in a fortnight. Its gold sits with MMTC-PAMP. Roughly nine per cent of group deposit value comes through Shurfa's Gulf deployment, and the Series C model assumes that share doubles.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Until October 2025 every Swarnim deposit earned a Potli card worth a flat two rupees in gold, credited on the spot. Growth was 4 to 7 per cent a month and flat per user. In September Devbrat proposed a prize ladder instead: most cards worth a rupee, some worth nothing, a thin tail worth up to five hundred. Dnyanada Kalelkar built the reveal in Berlin, including an animation in which the five-hundred tile slides past the window and stops one position short.

Version 6.2, released on Friday 3 October 2025, added the app-open event in its current form. Everything Swarnim knows about app opens begins there; the comparison Devbrat wanted against Diwali 2024 does not exist. A three-cell test ran from Friday 14 November to Thursday 11 December on 5,40,000 users who had deposited at least once in the fortnight to 13 November (Exhibit 2). On 12 December the snapshot was read, in Devbrat's summary, as an unambiguous win. The ramp began on Monday 15 December at 5 per cent of deposits, reached 20 per cent on 29 December, 50 per cent on 12 January and 100 per cent on Republic Day (Exhibit 3, Figure 1).

Three things surfaced in February. Users opening the app ten or more times a day had gone from 38,600 in October to 1,18,400 in the fortnight to 31 January, over which exposure to the new ladder averaged 71.4 per cent against 8.2 per cent in the fortnight to 31 December (Exhibits 1 and 3). The log retains ninety days, so from 22 February the first ten days of the test window cannot be re-cut. And Dwijen Kodolikar's response model, which decides who sees the richest reveal, draws its strongest feature from the account-aggregator balance feed users consented to for the recurring-deposit product.

5. The people

Devashree Kavlekar — co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Wants a decision she can defend in five years, not five quarters. Her Series C secondary is worth roughly eleven times her salary to date. She has not told the board that she asked Dnyanada for the near-miss animation herself.
Devbrat Kshirsagar — co-founder, president of growth, Bengaluru. Position: hold at 100 per cent, then take the ladder to Shurfa and the pipeline. His carry rests on the Series C closing at the current mark. He is not saying the 12 December snapshot was the only read he commissioned.
Deepika Kothavale — chief financial officer, Bengaluru. Position: keep the variable schedule, cut the ladder to the matched variant. Her incentive is the 31 March term sheet and a burn line the lead investor reads monthly. She has not circulated the catalogue commitments.
Dattatray Khandeparkar — principal engineer, Pune. Owns the reward ledger and the exposure hash. Position: whatever is decided, decide it once. He has not said in writing that the ledger has no reversal path, so a rollback leaves the unredeemed balance standing.
Dnyanada Kalelkar — product designer, Berlin, on contract to 30 April. Position: remove the near-miss reveal, keep the ladder. She ran an unlogged session with nine Berlin savers in January; the transcripts sit in a thread no exhibit draws on.
Dwijen Kodolikar — data scientist, Toronto. Built the response model and the snapshot. Position: the test answers a narrower question than the slide claims. He has not told anyone the model's top feature is days since the user's linked balance last fell below five hundred rupees.
Devesh Kenjale — customer success lead, Singapore. Position: roll it back. He says his tickets per thousand users have doubled since December; his headcount request is in the same board pack. He wrote the survey items himself and did not pilot them.
Dhairyasheel Katdare — head of licensing, New Jersey. Position: do not touch the specification before the Shurfa notice date. Two-thirds of his variable pay is on licence bookings. He has not forwarded a US prospect's request for a dark-pattern attestation.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 holds the four months the board has seen, Exhibit 2 the December snapshot, Exhibit 3 the ramp Dattatray's team ran, Exhibit 4 the revenue build under Exhibit 1's last column, Exhibit 5 the two ladders, Exhibit 6 Devesh's survey. Figure 1 puts the dates on one scale, Figure 2 the working day the eight of them do not share.

7. Voices

“Round it however you like — the engine is 4.06 crore a month, against 3.99 of revenue. That is what 7 per cent a month costs instead of 4.”

Devbrat Kshirsagar, board pre-read, Friday 20 February

“A third of our users are telling us they open the app more than they want to. A third.”

Devesh Kenjale, #potli-2 channel, Saturday, 06.12 IST

“Cell B is two changes in one coat. Cell C answers the question anybody is actually asking, and it got 60,000 users because growth needed the traffic.”

Dwijen Kodolikar, Toronto, reply to the pre-read

“Two thirds of the lift at seventy paise in the rupee. I am not asking you to switch the ladder off, Devbrat. I am asking you to stop paying 85 paise a card for the part we cannot attribute.”

Deepika Kothavale, finance review, Thursday 19 February

“I built the near-miss. It tested better than anything I have made. I would like it removed, I would like that minuted, and I know those two sentences read strangely together.”

Dnyanada Kalelkar, Berlin, 19.14 IST Sunday

“If the India specification changes before 31 March they can reopen the term. Also, one of the US accounts has started using the word attestation.”

Dhairyasheel Katdare, New Jersey, Friday

“Your deck has four options and every one of them is about the card.”

The lead investor's partner, on a call Sunday afternoon

8. The four sheets on the floor

Devashree wrote these on Saturday night, one to a page, in the order they occurred to her.

Option 1 — Hold exposure at 100 per cent on the current ladder

Potli 2.0 stays at 100 per cent exposure on the Exhibit 5 ladder, at ₹2.85 a card on Exhibit 1's volume. The Shurfa specification is unchanged. The response model, the near-miss reveal and the account-aggregator feature stay as they are; the catalogue commitments are met.

Option 2 — Hold exposure, move to the matched ladder

Exposure stays at 100 per cent and the prize table becomes Exhibit 5's second ladder, at ₹2.00 a card — ₹285.20 lakh a month at January's volume. Nothing already paid out is reversed. The reveal, the animation, the response model, the account-aggregator feature and the Junior population are untouched.

Option 3 — Keep the ladder, drop the targeting, cap the cards

The response model is switched off, so every user sees the same reveal; the near-miss animation goes; cards are capped at one per user per day. Dattatray's replay of January's deposit log puts the cards above that cap at 18.40 lakh of the month's 142.60 lakh, 12.9 per cent, worth ₹52.44 lakh at the fully-ramped ₹2.85. The cap cuts impressions against the catalogue commitments. Expected value and schedule are unchanged.

Option 4 — Flat credit in India, ladder for licensees

India returns to the flat ₹2.00 credit, ₹285.20 lakh a month at January's volume; October's actual, on 120.90 lakh cards, was ₹241.80 lakh. Potli 2.0 goes only through licensing. The flat credit has no prize inventory, so Exhibit 4's catalogue line ends while its commitments stand. The rollback runs eleven working days and leaves outstanding the ₹2.94 crore of Potli credits the ledger showed unconverted to gold on 20 February. Whether a licensee-only mechanic satisfies the parity clause is for counsel.

9. The deadline and what cannot move

The board sits at 10.30 IST on Monday 23 February 2026. The Series C term sheet, ₹310 crore from the existing lead, lapses on Tuesday 31 March. Swarnim holds ₹128 crore against net burn of ₹9.40 crore a month, which is 13.6 months. Shurfa's notice window closes on 31 March and the parity clause runs to the end of the term. Catalogue placement is ₹0.57 crore a month with minimum-impression commitments to 30 June: ₹2.28 crore from March to June. Dnyanada's contract ends 30 April and Dwijen alone can retrain the response model. Swarnim Junior has 2,14,000 guardian-linked accounts; the linkage table was migrated over the weekend of 3 and 4 January and pre-migration linkage was not preserved, so the overlap with Exhibit 1's trailing-14-day row cannot be computed.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 reports three cells against one control. What can the Cell A to Cell C comparison establish about the schedule, what can it not, and what is Cell B's margin over control evidence of?
  2. Devbrat tells the board the engine costs ₹4.06 crore a month; Exhibit 3 reports ₹344.63 lakh for January. Say what each figure measures, and which the Series C model should carry.
  3. Exhibit 6's percentages all have 312 in the denominator. Which population do they describe, and what would you measure, over which base, before any of them reaches the board?
  4. Using only this page's figures, work out what January's round trips cost the people who made them and how that cost divides. What does the division change about who ought to be in the room on Monday?
  5. The response model ranks users on a feed consented to for a different product, and the Junior overlap cannot be computed. What does the DPDP Act, 2023 oblige Devashree to establish before the next release ships, and what could discharge it by Monday?
  6. The lead investor's partner says every one of the four options is about the card. Construct the fifth, price it on this page's own numbers, say whose incentives it cuts against — then say what Devashree should do on Monday morning and what, in six sentences, she should say to the board.

11. A quarter past midnight

The four sheets went back into the folder in the order she had written them, which was not the order she would present them in, and she did not yet know what that order was. On the sofa the board pack was still face down. Devashree opened Swarnim on her own phone, made a ten-rupee deposit, and watched the five-hundred tile slide past the window and stop one position short. The water pump started up below the window. It was a quarter past midnight, which made it Monday.
