case20v1-ethics.variable.reward:
The Scratch Card Question

Ravaani, Pune · a decision case on variable rewards

1. A decision by Monday

At 8:30 pm on Wednesday 21 October 2026, Chiranshu Jorvekar closed his laptop on a half-eaten dinner and opened it again. As Head of Product at Ravaani, a bill-payment app in Pune, he had until Monday 26 October to settle a question that looked small. The Diwali build, due to reach customers before Dhanteras on Friday 6 November, would freeze on that Monday, and it had to say what a customer receives for paying an electricity bill: the flat ₹4 cashback Ravaani had given since 2022, or a scratch card whose prize might be ₹1 or ₹200.

A four-week test had ended on 4 October and was read out on 14 October (Figure 1). In half an hour he would join a call with colleagues for whom it would then be 11:30 am in Toronto, 5:30 pm in Berlin and 11:30 pm in Singapore.

2. Company background

Ravaani was founded in Pune in 2019 by Chetas Jawadekar, a former telecom engineer, to make household bills a two-tap task. Through Bharat BillPay, the NPCI-run bill network, customers pay electricity, mobile, DTH, gas and FASTag bills. By September 2026 it had 38 lakh monthly active payers, mostly in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Gujarat, 410 employees, and engineering teams in Pune and Bengaluru. It earns a commission from the biller on each payment. In 2024 it added Udhaar, a pay-later line issued by an RBI-regulated NBFC partner: a customer may pay a bill from Udhaar, repay within 30 days at no cost, and pay a fee of 2.5 per cent on any amount unpaid after that.

The market was crowded. PhonePe, Paytm and Google Pay all took bill payments, and scratch cards had made the reveal-a-prize reward familiar to millions of Indians. Since 2022 Ravaani had stood on a plain promise: ₹4 back on every bill of ₹100 or more, credited the moment the payment cleared. Customers trusted it. The board had begun to call it dull, and a Series C round was planned for March 2027.

3. The situation

In July Chetas asked whether the cashback could be made more exciting at the same cost. Charmaine Jambotkar, a data scientist in Toronto, designed the test. From users who had paid at least one qualifying bill in August she drew two random cells of 50,000. From 7 September to 4 October one cell kept the flat ₹4. The other received a scratch card after every qualifying payment, with a prize table whose expected value was also ₹4 (Exhibit 1). The only difference between the cells was the reward schedule.

The readout gave Chetas his headline. Payments per user rose from 3.10 to 3.41, and contribution after rewards rose with them (Exhibit 1). Scaled to 38 lakh payers over thirteen 28-day periods, the extra contribution came to about ₹3.2 crore a year. Charmaine had also grouped users by how often they paid (Exhibit 2) and profiled the heaviest group, those making eleven or more payments in four weeks (Exhibit 3).

Chiranshu had read all three exhibits more than once. Nobody disputed the arithmetic. The disagreement was about what it meant, and it ran along time zones: the founders in Pune saw an opportunity with a date on it, while those further away had been looking at the same rows and drawn quieter conclusions.

4. The people

Chetas Jawadekar, chief executive, Pune. He wants the card live for Diwali. A ten per cent rise in payments per user is the story investors will pay for in March, he says, and the big apps' festival offers will be everywhere on 6 November. He is not indifferent to harm. He asks only that it be shown to him in rupees.

Charmaine Jambotkar, data scientist, Toronto. She ran the test and stands behind its arithmetic. She does not trust any single number to summarise it, and wants a longer run through a festival fortnight, with a group left on the flat cashback.

Caetano Janorkar, product designer, Berlin. He drew the card and its reveal. He believes it is honest if the odds are on the screen, as in “one in two hundred for ₹200”, and is uneasy at a button that can be tapped fifteen times in a day.

Chakor Jedhe, customer-success lead, Singapore. She leads 22 agents. She read forty chats from the heaviest users in the card cell: nine mentioned paying a bill in parts for the sake of the cards, and several asked how to clear an Udhaar balance before the fee fell due. She wants a limit.

5. The options

Option A: ship the scratch card to every payer for Diwali and keep it. The test measured ₹0.65 more contribution per user per 28 days, about ₹3.22 crore a year across 38 lakh payers (₹0.651 × 38,00,000 × 13). The card applies to every qualifying payment. The figure assumes the test cells represent all 38 lakh payers.

Option B: keep the flat ₹4 through Diwali and revisit in January. Customers see nothing change, the build is untouched. Ravaani forgoes the measured gain and has no scratch card of its own beside its rivals' festival offers.

Option C: ship the scratch card with rules. One card per bill per cycle, none on payments funded by Udhaar, and no more than 10 cards per customer per 28 days. The Bengaluru engineers estimate eight working days. The card stays for payments under the cap and goes from those above it, so Ravaani gives up part of Option A’s gain.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the test measure, and what does each of Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 add to the headline that payments rose by a tenth?
  2. The two cells cost Ravaani the same expected ₹4 a payment. Using the idea of a variable reward, why might the card cell behave differently?
  3. Who gains, and who bears the cost, when a user in the eleven-plus group makes an extra payment? How would you weigh them against ₹3.2 crore a year?
  4. Which option would you take to Monday’s meeting, what would you change in it, and what would make you reverse it in the first fortnight of Diwali?

7. A note for the learner

In the Hook model, reward is the third step after trigger and action, and a variable reward is the version that pays out unpredictably: this payment might be the ₹200 one. Its pull belongs to what the module calls the hunt, alongside the tribe and the self. Exhibit 1 shows the pull working at an identical expected cost. The topic then asks a second question: does the changed behaviour serve what the customer came to do? Here the customer came to pay a bill on time. A strong answer keeps the two questions apart and does not let an average stand in for a population.

One defensible path is Option C, with three additions. Show the prize odds on the card, as Caetano proposed. Leave 5 per cent of payers on the flat ₹4 through Diwali, which gives the first festival-season comparison. And fix a stop rule now: revert to flat if split payments exceed 10 per cent of the eleven-plus group’s payments, a line between the 5.0 and 19.0 per cent of Exhibit 3.

The reasoning: of the extra 15,500 payments, 15,000 came from the eleven-plus group (Exhibit 2), and the card cell's group paid smaller sums, split bills and held Udhaar balances more often (Exhibit 3). The metric moved where the customer’s interest and Ravaani’s parted. Option C keeps the card for the 96 per cent of users below eleven payments, apart from Udhaar-funded and repeat-bill payments, costs eight days, and can be reversed. It probably gives up much of the ₹3.2 crore, because almost all the extra payments came from that group.
exp20v2-ethics.variable.reward:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance · Ethics, Persuasion & Trust

Variable Rewards

Tribe, hunt, self — and why a reward a user can predict stops being a reason to come back.

On the morning of 3 March 2026, Ananya Rao, VP of Product at the Bengaluru short-video app Anhad Play, had four days to send the board a recommendation she had been putting off for a week. Anhad Play carried 38 million monthly users across Hindi, Tamil and Telugu feeds, and a growth-stage investor negotiating the Series C term sheet had made one number the centrepiece of due diligence: DAU/MAU, the share of monthly users who open the app on a given day, needed to cross 45% before the round closed in June. It stood at 34%. Ananya's growth lead, Dev Kulkarni, had a fix ready: a "Mystery Coin Drop" — after a video finished, a spinning wheel would give an 8% chance of coins redeemable for mobile recharge. His simulation showed double-digit gains in 30-day retention. The same week, Anhad Play's support-ops team had logged 340 complaints, mostly from parents, about the app's existing daily-streak badges and teenagers spending four-plus hours chasing them. Whatever probability Ananya chose would run against 38 million people, a large share of them on their first smartphone, under India's 2023 guidelines against dark patterns and a data-protection law about to gain teeth. She needed to understand exactly what a variable reward does before she could decide how much of it to ship.

1. The idea

A variable reward is reinforcement delivered on a schedule the user cannot predict — not whether an action will pay off every time, or never, but whether it will pay off this time, and if so, how much. The problem it solves is habituation: once a person is certain a behaviour will always be rewarded, or certain it never will, the anticipation collapses and the behaviour stops compounding into a habit. This is why unpredictability, not generosity, is what keeps a product being checked.

The underlying mechanism was formalised by B. F. Skinner, working with Charles Ferster and publishing Schedules of Reinforcement in 1957: pigeons and rats pressed a lever far more persistently, and kept pressing long after rewards stopped ("extinction" took longer to set in), when reinforcement arrived on a variable schedule rather than a fixed one. Nir Eyal carried the idea into product design in Hooked (2014), naming it the third step of his Hook Model — Trigger, Action, Variable Reward, Investment — and split the rewards themselves into three families borrowed from evolutionary psychology: rewards of the Tribe (social validation — likes, replies, being seen by others), rewards of the Hunt (resources or information — a good deal, an unexpectedly good video), and rewards of the Self (mastery or completion — a streak, a level, a finished task). The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "A reward a user can predict stops being a reason to come back; one they can't is what keeps them checking."

2. How it actually works

Walking the loop through Anhad Play: the Trigger is a push notification or, once the habit forms, simply boredom. The Action is opening the app and watching. The Variable Reward is delivered by a probabilistic draw the user cannot see or predict — this video might unlock coins, the next might not. The Investment is whatever the user does that raises the odds of a future reward or pulls them back later: following a creator, saving a video, building a streak — which itself becomes the next Trigger. Practitioners describe those four steps easily; what they usually leave implicit is harder and matters more: choosing the reward rate (the probability), choosing which reward family — Tribe, Hunt or Self — actually matches what the product is for, and capping the variance so the reward is neither so rare that most users quit before ever being reinforced ("extinction") nor so frequent that it becomes predictable and boring ("habituation").

Underneath the design choice is a neuroscience finding worth naming precisely, because it is usually misquoted. Christopher Fiorillo, Philippe Tobler and Wolfram Schultz, recording dopamine neurons directly in monkeys (Science, 2003), found that firing did not track reward size — it tracked reward uncertainty, peaking when the probability of a reward sat near 50%, and falling away toward both 0% and 100%. Anticipation itself, not the payoff, is what the dopamine system is built to respond to. That is the whole mechanical case for variability: a reward given every time teaches nothing new after the first time; a reward given with genuine uncertainty keeps the anticipatory system engaged on every single check.

3. A worked example

Dev's 8% coin-drop can be checked with arithmetic Anhad Play's data science team already had on hand. If a reward arrives with probability p on any given session, the number of sessions until the first reward follows a geometric distribution: expected wait = 1/p, and the uncertainty that drives anticipation, per Fiorillo and Schultz, is the Bernoulli variance p(1−p), which is mathematically maximised at p = 0.5.

p (reward chance)Uncertainty p(1−p)Expected wait (1/p)SD of waitP(20+ sessions unrewarded)
1.00 (fixed)0.001.00.00%
0.500.25 (max)2.01.4~0%
0.150.1286.76.13.9%
0.08 (Dev's pitch)0.07412.512.018.9%

The last column matters most and is the one Dev's pitch deck skipped: at p = 0.08, the probability a user opens the app more than 20 times without ever being rewarded is (0.92)20 ≈ 18.9% — nearly one user in five. For an established user with a year of habit behind them, that is tolerable. For a new user in week one, still deciding whether Anhad Play is worth keeping on the phone, an 18.9% chance of total extinction before the mechanism ever pays off is a retention problem disguised as a growth feature.

Run the same table at p = 0.15 instead, and the tail risk falls to 3.9% while uncertainty (0.15 × 0.85 = 0.128) stays well above the near-zero uncertainty of a very rare reward — most of the anticipatory effect, far less extinction risk. Ananya's real decision variable was never "variable versus fixed," which was already settled by the arithmetic; it was which probability, for which cohort, since new and established users need different answers to the same equation.

Note what the table does not settle: p = 0.5, the neurologically ideal setting, was never a live option. At 50% of sessions paying a coin, Anhad Play's redemption cost would run many multiples of what a 15% or 8% rate would cost, since the reward economy has to be funded out of ad revenue per user, not out of dopamine research. Every variable-reward design in practice is this same trade against a cost curve — the probability that maximises anticipation and the probability the business can afford are rarely the same number, and the gap between them is exactly what a product leader is paid to close.

4. Nuances a learner must hold onto

Not the same as gamification

Gamification is a broad toolkit — points, leaderboards, fixed badges — and much of it runs on entirely different psychology (status, the goal-gradient effect of a visibly near finish line) with no probabilistic step at all. Treating "gamified" and "variable reward" as synonyms leads teams to expect anticipation effects from features, like a fixed streak counter, that structurally cannot produce them.

The reward family must match the value proposition

A video app's actual value is content, so a Hunt reward — an unpredictably good recommendation — reinforces the real product. A bolted-on coin drop is a Self/token subsidy for attention that can vanish the day the reward budget is cut, taking the retention gain with it.

Where it applies, and where it doesn't

Variable reward works on frequent, low-stakes, repeatable actions. It does nothing for a one-time, high-consideration decision — a mortgage, an enterprise contract — where uncertainty reads as risk, not anticipation, and erodes trust instead of building a habit.

What it is routinely confused with

"Engagement" in general, and manipulation specifically. Variable reward tips into a dark pattern through three separable design choices, not through variability itself: hiding the true odds, targeting cohorts known to be vulnerable (minors, compulsive users), or attaching the reward to no genuine value at all.

What it cannot tell you

It is a mechanism for behavioural frequency, indifferent to welfare. The same well-tuned probability produces a habit people are glad to have and one they regret in equal measure; the arithmetic in Section 3 cannot distinguish the two, and no amount of tuning will make it.

Rewards decay too, just more slowly

Once users learn the range of possible outcomes, even a variable reward loses potency — the surprise was never in the randomness alone but in not yet knowing the boundaries. Reward pools need periodic refreshing or the anticipation effect flattens over months.

Questions before relying on it

Are the odds disclosed where a curious user can find them in two taps? Has the mechanism been tested against identified vulnerable cohorts, not just averaged across everyone? And is anything besides engagement — complaints, satisfaction, session-time outliers — being measured alongside it?

5. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

Consumer apps are where deliberate variable reward is most legitimate: usage is frequent and low-stakes, and Tribe and Self rewards (likes, streaks) match how people already relate to social and gaming products. In B2B software, engineered randomness usually backfires — an admin accountable for a tool at work reads a spinning wheel as unserious, sometimes as a reason to distrust the vendor. The B2B analogue of a Hunt reward instead comes from the real world: an anomaly a monitoring dashboard surfaces unprompted, where the uncertainty is genuine, not manufactured. Marketplaces get a milder version for free — not every search yields a great price or a fast driver, so an intermittently great match functions as a Hunt reward on its own, before any coupon or spin-wheel is layered on top, as Swiggy and Ola's naturally variable outcomes show.

Stage changes the calculus too. Early-stage teams rarely have the volume to calibrate p correctly and tend to either extinguish new users or overspend the reward budget; large platforms can run cohort-specific probabilities, as Section 3 suggests Anhad Play should, but a probability chosen at 38-million-user scale also carries proportionally larger regulatory and reputational exposure the moment it harms even a small percentage of a very large base.

6. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptomCheapest diagnostic
Calling fixed badges/streaks "gamification" and expecting anticipation effectsEngagement flattens after 2–3 weeks' noveltyAsk if a user who's seen the reward twice can predict its timing — if yes, it isn't variable
One global probability for every cohortNew-user D7 retention lags while mature-user metrics look fineSegment first-reward latency by account age
Optimising DAU aloneDAU rises while one-star reviews mention "addictive" and tickets climbTrack a fortnightly satisfaction pulse and the 95th-percentile daily session time, not just the mean
Treating disclosure as a launch afterthoughtRegulatory or press scrutiny appears with no warning in the metricsAsk whether true odds are findable within two taps before build starts, not after

7. What good looks like

Anhad Play's shipped design split the mechanism by cohort: new users in their first 30 days get p = 0.15, keeping extinction risk under 4% while the habit is still forming; mature users move to p = 0.08, but the payoff is reweighted toward a Hunt reward — a personalised, unpredictable content recommendation — with only a small coin element attached. Odds are shown on tap. A daily coin cap and a break-nudge after 90 minutes of continuous use are built in. Product and legal review the mechanic jointly against MeitY's dark-pattern categories before anything ships, and success is tracked not only by D30 retention but by a satisfaction pulse-survey and the support-ticket rate, reported to the board alongside the growth number.

Closing

Ananya recommends the cohort-split, Hunt-weighted, disclosed design over Dev's flat 8%, telling the board that a mechanism this effective earns its place only if it can survive a regulator's or a journalist's look eighteen months out — the same variance that makes it work on a neural level is exactly what she would have to defend in that room. What to learn next, and why: Applying the Hook to Your Product, because a reward step does nothing without the trigger and investment steps around it; and Gamification and Its Limits, because knowing where the mechanism doesn't apply — B2B, one-time decisions — stops it being reached for by reflex. Further out, Engagement-Optimised AI and Sycophancy matters because a system that tunes its own responses for stickiness can apply this same uncertainty mechanism to language itself, faster than any human review cycle.

Sit with these: if your product's core reward is entirely engineered rather than earned from real value delivered, what happens to retention the day the reward budget is cut? And who in your organisation owns the welfare metric — not the growth metric — before a variable reward ships?
case40v1-ethics.triggers:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance · Ethics, Persuasion and Trust

Mehfooz Technologies: The 22:50 Send

A savings app in Pune has found something that works. Its product head has until Monday morning to decide what it is that works, and whether he will ship it.

1. Sunday night, Baner

At 22:50 IST on Sunday 18 October 2026, Yatiraj Ganpule sat at the dining table of his flat in Baner, Pune, with three slides open and a cold cup of tea beside them. They were for 11:00 the next morning, when the board of Mehfooz Technologies Private Limited would ask what the company intended to do with Nudge 2.0.

The call had been the only hour that worked: 18:00 in Berlin, noon in Toronto, midnight in Singapore. Yashoda Gothankar had joined from Singapore anyway, apologising for the hour. Nobody had raised their voice, and that was part of what worried him.

Between 18 August and 28 September, Mehfooz had run a notification experiment across 4,10,000 of its savers. One cell had lifted deposits by 26.9 per cent against the control; another by 36.5 per cent. The same two cells carried the pilot's two highest uninstall rates, and a September support queue that Gothankar's team was still clearing on Sunday night.

Ganpule had been a product manager for nine years, two at Mehfooz, and had learned to distrust the feeling he had now, that the numbers had already decided. He opened the fourth slide, the one he had kept out of the deck, and read the second line of Yadnika Gaunekar's memo again: we did not build a reminder. We built something that waits for a feeling.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2024

Mehfooz was founded in March 2024 by Yachana Ghugare, formerly a payments product lead, on a then-unfashionable premise: that India's next hundred million savers would not open a demat account, and would save ₹20 and ₹50 at a time if something asked them to. The app rounded up UPI spends, bought digital gold vaulted through MMTC-PAMP, and ran micro-SIPs into Mirasa Asset Managers' schemes as an AMFI-registered distributor. By 30 September 2026 Mehfooz had 2.4 crore registered users, 41 lakh monthly transacting savers and ₹1,840 crore of customer savings under management — ₹1,140 crore in digital gold, ₹700 crore in micro-SIP assets. FY26 closed at ₹34 crore of revenue against a loss of ₹104 crore.

The decision that constrained Monday was taken in November 2024, when the company was eleven people and chasing its first enterprise contract. To ship a white-label build in nine weeks, the engineers collapsed consent into a single boolean on the user record, msg_consent, covering transactional alerts, promotional pushes and, when it was added in 2025, personalisation. A saver who turned off the 22:50 campaign therefore turned off the alert that her autopay mandate had failed.

3. The industry

By 2026 the micro-savings shelf in India was crowded. Jar had taken daily gold savings to the mass market, Groww and Zerodha had carried direct mutual funds into tier-2 cities, PhonePe and Paytm distributed gold at the scale of their payment bases, and Navi and Angel One bought installs at prices Mehfooz could not match. Nobody competed on returns, which the gold price and scheme performance set. Everybody competed on how often a saver came back.

Three regulators shaped the product. UPI autopay mandates, on NPCI's rails, made the ₹50 deposit collectable at all. The Reserve Bank's Account Aggregator framework let Mehfooz read a consenting saver's bank narration, which is how it knew a salary had landed. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 required consent that was specific, informed and revocable for each purpose — and Mehfooz held one flag. Overseas, Mishkat Exchange Holdings of Dubai ran Mehfooz's white-label product for Gulf remitters, leaving the second-largest revenue line on a contract signed in January 2026.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Figure A sets out the sequence. The Mishkat contract was signed on 9 January 2026 and carried a feature-parity clause. On 12 February the Series B closed: ₹310 crore at ₹2,050 crore post-money, against a plan promising ₹3,600 crore of savings under management by 31 March 2027.

On 21 May the internal-trigger score first ran on live users. Yuvashree Godinho's model in Toronto scored each saver hourly on app telemetry and Account Aggregator narration: late-night sessions, balance checks without a deposit, a salary credit, a broken streak. It was built to answer one question — when is this saver most likely to act — and the product organisation read it as a scheduling input.

The pilot opened on Tuesday 18 August and closed on Monday 28 September: 42 days, five cells of 82,000 savers each, randomised within declared bands from the 41 lakh transacting base. Exhibit 1 reports it. On 30 September the growth team circulated a memo headed Nudge 2.0: ship it, putting the deposit lift at 26.9 per cent and first-year contribution at ₹4.65 crore.

Two things have since changed. The dashboard behind that memo showed cell B at a 14.2 per cent lift; a join on a stale copy of the send log was found on 8 October, and the corrected figure is 7.1 per cent, as Exhibit 1 now carries. On 6 October Godinho circulated the income-band split, Exhibit 2, which nobody had asked for and which did not exist when the memo went out. Gothankar's team had meanwhile been running a manual suppression list for savers who complained; 1,840 of those names sit inside the pilot cells, and the analysis does not know which.

5. The people

Figure B shows where the reporting lines run.

Yatiraj Ganpule, Chief Product Officer, Pune. Owns the decision and the slide. Says the pilot answered a narrower question than the memo claims. His variable pay is tied to monthly transacting savers, not deposits. He has not told the board that splitting msg_consent sat on his own 2025 roadmap, deprioritised twice.

Yachana Ghugare, co-founder and Chief Executive, Pune. Wants a decision she can defend publicly and to the Series B investors. Told the lead investor the March 2027 number was "ahead of plan" and has not corrected it since the September quarter closed.

Yagnika Girvalkar, Vice-President, Growth, Bengaluru. Wrote the 30 September memo and wants cell E shipped to the whole base before Diwali, when deposits peak. Forty per cent of her variable pay is on incremental deposits. She has already walked Mishkat's product team through the engine.

Yallappa Gaydhani, Chief Financial Officer, Pune. Built Exhibit 5 and calls the engine "a rounding error with a reputational tail". The ₹2.4 crore build was capitalised in March 2026; shelving it means a ₹2.10 crore write-down this quarter, which he has not put to the board.

Yuvashree Godinho, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Built the internal-trigger score, reports to Girvalkar, ran the survey in Exhibit 6, and circulated Exhibit 2 on her own initiative. She now believes the 2025 label set she trained on is partly a proxy for income, and has put that in no document.

Yashoda Gothankar, Director, Customer Success, Singapore. Owns the queue in Exhibit 4 and the twenty-nine escalations. Her suppression list has reached 14,000 savers, 1,840 inside the pilot; she has not told Godinho, because the list is what keeps her escalation count down.

Yadnika Gaunekar, Principal Designer, Berlin. Argues that Mehfooz has paid, earned, relationship and owned triggers available and has spent two years investing in the owned one. Her 9 October memo proposes a saver-set goal instead. An unlogged test of her prototype moved deposits less than the control; she has not mentioned it.

Yogaditya Gorhe, Data Protection Officer and General Counsel, Mumbai. Holds that the Account Aggregator consent artefact covers personal finance management and not marketing triggers. His draft opinion, which names the two features shipped in 2025 that it would also catch, is unsent.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 restates the figures on which the 30 September memo rests. Cell D moved both the wording and the hour; cells B and C each moved one; cell E moved three things, one being how many messages a saver received. Exhibit 3 shows send-hour outcomes inside cell E, where the model chose the hours.

Exhibit 2 arrived at 02:10 Toronto time with a one-line covering note. It is the same 82,000 savers as cell D above, and the same ₹262.2 lakh.

7. Voices

"Twenty-six point nine per cent, and the copy is doing it. People respond to what they stand to lose; that is not a trick, it is how saving works. The memo puts ₹4.65 crore a year on it, after the ₹68 lakh run cost, on cell D's lift per saver across all 2.4 crore registered users, a full year of trail, and the pod already funded."

Yagnika Girvalkar, growth memo, 30 September

"I can tell you the send log. I cannot tell you which of our savers your team was muting. And please stop saying my score detects anxiety. It detects a pattern that correlates with something, and I am no longer sure what."

Yuvashree Godinho, pilot review call, 7 October, 23:40 IST

"Eleven escalations in September. One is a gentleman in Nashik who says we messaged him nine times in a week about a streak, after his father's hospital bill. He is right about the nine. He is on the mute list now, one of 14,000."

Yashoda Gothankar, email to Ganpule and Ghugare, 9 October

"One flag. If a saver revokes, she loses her mandate-failure alert, and then she loses money. The Account Aggregator artefact says personal finance management. I do not read that as covering a 22:50 push built around a broken streak, and the Act asks for consent specific to a purpose."

Yogaditya Gorhe, note to the board's risk committee, 13 October

"Four kinds of trigger are open to us. Paid, which we cannot afford at Navi's prices. Earned, which we have not tried since 2024. Relationship, which is a saver telling her sister. Owned, which is this engine. We have spent two years making the owned one louder, because it is the only one we can schedule."

Yadnika Gaunekar, memo, 9 October, Berlin

8. The options as Ganpule has them on the slide

Four options are on the slide for 11:00. Gaunekar's 9 October memo, which proposes a fifth, is not on it.

Option 1: ship cell D to the whole transacting base on Monday. It takes the tested configuration — loss-framed copy at 22:50 — to 41 lakh savers before Diwali, carries Exhibit 5's ₹68 lakh a year of engine running cost, and leaves msg_consent as it is, so a saver who mutes the campaign also mutes her mandate-failure alert.

Option 2: ship cell E with a curfew. The model chooses copy, hour and volume, but nothing sends between 22:00 and 07:00 and no saver gets more than three a day. It takes two weeks of engineering and removes the two late hours carrying Exhibit 3's tallest bars. It leaves the model, its 2025 label set and the single consent flag untouched.

Option 3: hold the engine and split the consent flag first. Eleven weeks of six engineers — the six committed to the UPI autopay mandate work Mehfooz owes its payments partner — would land in the first week of January and give every saver separate, revocable choices for transactional, promotional and personalised messages. Nudge 2.0 would be re-tested after that, and the capitalised ₹2.10 crore goes for write-down review this quarter.

Option 4: ship to the two highest declared bands only. Cell D's configuration goes to savers who declared more than ₹30,000 a month, 28 per cent of each pilot cell, and Mishkat is offered the pre-engine build. It leaves msg_consent as it is, and every other saver on the 09:40 reminder.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 11:00 IST on Monday 19 October in Baner and has asked for a recommendation, not a discussion. Mishkat served its parity notice on Wednesday 14 October: the engine, or written notice that it will not be supplied, within ninety days, which falls on 12 January 2027. Gorhe's compliance calendar puts Mehfooz's own deadline for granular, revocable consent at 1 January 2027. ₹310 crore came in eight months ago against an FY26 loss of ₹104 crore. The six engineers who can split the consent column are the six who owe the autopay work, and a replacement data scientist in Toronto costs ₹1.42 crore fully loaded against ₹38 lakh in Bengaluru, so Godinho's hours are rationed. Against all of it sits the number in the Series B plan: ₹3,600 crore of savings under management by 31 March 2027, from ₹1,840 crore on 30 September. Gaydhani's own projection, at the September quarter's ₹61 crore a month of net additions over the six months to March, reaches ₹2,206 crore.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Nudge 2.0 did not change what Mehfooz offers a saver, only when and how it asks. What does Exhibit 1 establish about the asking, and what does it leave open?
  2. Exhibit 2 splits cell D by declared income band. What does it not show that you would want before shipping, and could you get that by Monday?
  3. Exhibit 5 and the 30 September memo each put a first-year figure on Nudge 2.0, and they land more than ₹5 crore apart. What has to be true for either to be the right one for a board?
  4. Exhibit 6 reports two questions answered by the same respondents. What would you have to believe about who answered in order to act on either answer?
  5. The November 2024 decision to hold one consent flag for transactional and promotional messages constrains every option on the slide. What should the product organisation have asked then, and at what cost?
  6. It is 11:00 on Monday 19 October in the Baner boardroom. What does Ganpule do about Nudge 2.0, what does he say about the 31 March 2027 commitment, and what does he tell Mishkat that evening?

11. Sunday, 23:40

The call had ended at 22:40. Gothankar had gone to bed in Singapore; Berlin had logged off without a goodbye. Ganpule opened the admin console, as he did most nights, and looked at the queue for Monday: 41,02,418 savers, one message each, scheduled 09:40 IST, copy unchanged since 2024.

In the other tab the model's hourly scores were rewriting themselves for the same savers: the top decile, 4.1 lakh of them, recomputed as he watched at 23:40 on a Sunday. He read the second line of Gaunekar's memo once more, closed the laptop, and left the fourth slide where it was.
exp20v2-ethics.triggers:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance — Ethics, Persuasion & Trust

External and Internal Triggers

What prompts a user to act — and which negative emotions become internal triggers

1. A Thursday-night decision at Nindiya

On the evening of 14 March 2024, Ananya Rao, VP of Product at Nindiya, a Bangalore-based sleep and mindfulness app with 2.4 million registered users, was looking at a dashboard she had asked her data team to stop refreshing until she had eaten dinner. It refreshed anyway. Thirty-day retention had slid from 34% to 27% over two quarters, and the board had given her until Friday's review to present a fix. Her growth lead, Rohan Mehta, had one ready: Nindiya's evening journaling feature already asked users to tag how they felt before bed, and a meaningful share tagged "anxious," "lonely," or "can't switch off." Rohan's proposal was to route users who tagged those feelings three nights running into a separate push-notification track — worded to reference the feeling directly — because his early tests showed it worked. Ananya did not doubt that it would work. She doubted whether "it works" was the only question a product leader was supposed to ask before she used a user's own disclosed loneliness as the lever that pulled them back into the app. The decision in front of her was not abstract. It was due in three days, it involved a specific data field, and getting it wrong in either direction — dismissing a legitimate growth lever out of squeamishness, or shipping something that quietly weaponised vulnerability — would show up in Friday's numbers and, eventually, in Nindiya's reputation.

2. The idea

A trigger, in the vocabulary product teams borrow from behavioural design, is anything that cues a user to take the next action in a product. Nir Eyal formalised the concept in 2013–2014, first in a series of essays and then in the book Hooked, while studying why some consumer products became daily habits and others, built with comparable features, did not. His answer was that habit-forming products are not simply useful; they are triggered repeatedly until the behaviour needs no prompt at all. Eyal split triggers into two families. An external trigger is information planted in the user's environment that tells them what to do next — a push notification, an email, an app icon with a red badge, a friend's recommendation. An internal trigger is an emotion, usually an uncomfortable one, that the user has learned to soothe by opening the product without being told to — boredom reaching for a feed, loneliness reaching for a messaging app, anxiety reaching for a search bar. The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: every product starts by pushing external triggers at users, but a product only becomes a habit once it has attached itself to an internal trigger the user already carries around — and that attachment is where the ethical weight of the whole design sits.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in a sequence practitioners usually compress, which is exactly where the implicit steps get lost. First, a product must earn the right to send external triggers at all — through a permission the user granted (a notification opt-in, an email address) or a channel the product does not own but can reach (a paid ad, a press mention, a friend's share). Second, each external trigger has to be specific enough to prompt one action, not a vague "come back" — Nindiya's early notifications said "We miss you," named no action, and produced a 1.4% open rate. Third, and this is the step teams skip, the team has to identify which internal state the trigger is meant to interrupt: "Your streak ends tonight" aims at loss aversion, "4 minutes to quiet your mind" aims at anxiety. Fourth, the product delivers an action so easy and reliably satisfying that the discomfort actually resolves — if it doesn't, the user learns the product doesn't work and the loop breaks. Fifth, over repeated cycles the user stops needing the external trigger at all: opening the app becomes the automatic response to the feeling itself, at which point Eyal's model calls the product "habit-forming" and Rohan's team calls it "healthy retention." The ethical fork sits precisely at step three, because naming the internal state a trigger targets is a choice a team can make thoughtlessly or deliberately, and it is invisible in every metric except which emotions a company has decided it is willing to design around.

4. A worked example, run twice

On 20 January 2024, Rohan's team ran an A/B test on 50,000 lapsed Nindiya users — people who had not opened the app in nine or more days. The control group received a generic external trigger with no reference to an emotional state: "Time for Nindiya," sent at 9:00 pm. Of 25,000 recipients, 525 opened it — a 2.1% open rate — and of those, 18%, or 95 users, completed a full session. That is the arithmetic of an external trigger with no internal-trigger match: 95 completions from 25,000 sends, a 0.38% yield.

The treatment group of 25,000 was drawn from users who had tagged "anxious" or "can't switch off" in their last three journal entries before lapsing. They received a personalised trigger referencing that disclosed state: "You mentioned trouble sleeping last night — 4 minutes could help." Open rate jumped to 6.4%, or 1,600 opens; completion rate among openers rose to 31%, or 496 completions. Yield: 496 from 25,000, or 1.98% — more than five times the control. That gap is the entire commercial case for internal-trigger targeting in one number, and it is also exactly the number that should make a product leader pause, because the 5.2x lift was produced by using information the user had disclosed in a moment of vulnerability, inside a wellness product, as targeting criteria for a re-engagement campaign — a use the user had not consented to when they typed the word "anxious" into a journal at 11 pm.

Changing one input sharpens the point. When Rohan's team re-ran the treatment using the same emotional data but removed the reference to the specific feeling — "4 minutes could help you sleep better tonight," no mention of anxiety or the prior entry — open rate fell to 4.1% and completions to 342, a yield of 1.37%. Still nearly four times the generic control, but a third weaker than naming the emotion outright. That 0.61-point gap is the price the emotional specificity was buying, and the number Ananya needed the board to see: it isolates how much lift comes from touching the internal trigger directly rather than merely being well-timed.

5. The nuances

External and internal triggers are not interchangeable

An external trigger can launch a session with no internal trigger present — a friend's share, a well-placed ad — but that session will not repeat unless it eventually attaches to a feeling the user already has. Teams that only optimise external triggers (better copy, better timing) hit a retention ceiling no notification tuning fixes, because the thing doing the real work in a habit is the internal trigger, not the message that reminded the user of it.

Four kinds of external trigger behave differently

Eyal's typology — paid, earned, relationship, owned — matters because each has a different cost curve and a different half-life, and confusing them leads teams to over-invest in the wrong one, as the table below shows.

Internal triggers are discovered, not invented

A product cannot manufacture an internal trigger from nothing; it can only identify one that already exists in its users' emotional lives and position itself as the response. Nindiya did not create anxiety about sleep — it found a population that already felt it and built a fast, satisfying response to that feeling. This is precisely why the ethical question is not "did we create a bad feeling to exploit," which is rare, but "did we use disclosed, sensitive information about an existing feeling without the consent the sensitivity deserved," which is common and easy to miss.

Not every negative emotion is fair game at equal cost

Boredom and mild frustration are internal triggers nearly every consumer product can ethically court — they are diffuse, low-stakes, and not typically disclosed in confidence. Loneliness, grief, financial anxiety, and health fear sit in a different category: acting on them without consent, especially when the data came from a context of trust such as journaling or therapy notes, is where regulators, journalists, and eventually users themselves draw a hard line.

Frequency erodes an internal trigger's power

Because an internal trigger works by resolving discomfort, over-triggering teaches the brain that the discomfort resolves itself without the product, which weakens the association. Nindiya's data showed exactly this: users triggered on the same emotional tag more than four times in three weeks had a lower subsequent completion rate than users triggered once — a pattern easy to miss if a team only looks at aggregate open rates.

A high lift number tells you the mechanism worked, not that it was earned

The 5.2x figure in Section 4 is a measurement of leverage, not of legitimacy. Two triggers can produce identical arithmetic while one draws on a habit the user is glad to have and the other draws on a disclosure the user would be upset to learn was reused — the metric cannot distinguish them, and a team that reports only the metric will not either.

What triggers cannot tell you

Trigger design explains what gets a user to open an app in a given moment; it says nothing about whether the underlying product is good for the user over months, and nothing about whether the relief a session provides is real or merely a distraction from the feeling that prompted it. A well-designed trigger can make a mediocre product look sticky for a quarter before the underlying weakness catches up.

Questions a newcomer should ask before relying on this

Where did the data behind this internal-trigger match come from, and did the user know it could be used this way? Is the emotion diffuse (boredom) or disclosed-in-trust (grief, anxiety)? What happens to retention if this specific trigger is switched off — is the product still worth using, or does the trigger do the product's job for it?

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

In consumer products like Nindiya, internal triggers are usually personal — boredom, loneliness, anxiety — and owned triggers (push, badge) are cheap enough that the temptation to over-target is constant. In B2B products, the internal trigger is more often organisational anxiety than personal feeling: an admin worried about a compliance deadline, a manager worried about a report before Monday's meeting. External triggers there tend to be email and in-app alerts tied to calendar events, which lowers the ethical stakes without removing them — a tool that manufactures false urgency about an audit deadline is exploiting anxiety just as surely as a wellness app is. In marketplace products, the trigger question splits by side: supply-side triggers (a driver, a seller) tie to income anxiety and respond well to owned channels; demand-side triggers behave more like consumer triggers, and a marketplace that treats both sides identically usually over-triggers one and under-triggers the other. On the stage axis, an early-stage company like Nindiya at Series B has thin trust reserves and a small, watchful user base — one visible misuse of a disclosed emotion can define the brand for years, exactly Ananya's situation. A large incumbent has more reputational buffer but far more scale, so the same yield gap translates into millions of messages, and regulatory attention arrives faster and hits harder.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: treating "engagement went up" as the whole verdict. Symptom: a team ships an internal-trigger campaign, retention improves, and no one revisits it. Underlying error: conflating a lift metric with a legitimacy judgment. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether the team can explain, in one sentence, why the specific user would be glad to know this trigger exists — if the sentence is hard to write, the trigger is probably wrong.

Mistake two: confusing an external trigger with an internal one. Symptom: a team calls a notification "the trigger" and stops there, never asking what feeling it is meant to interrupt. Underlying error: the model has two triggers, and only naming the visible one hides the ethically loaded half of the design. Cheapest diagnostic: for every notification in the send calendar, write down the internal state it targets; a blank row is a warning sign, not a neutral one.

Mistake three: over-triggering because the first result was strong. Symptom: send frequency on a given emotional tag climbs from once to four times a week because the initial lift looked good. Underlying error: mistaking a one-time measurement for a durable rate. Cheapest diagnostic: track completion rate by trigger count per user per fortnight — a downward slope is the association wearing out, well before churn shows up in the top-line number.

Mistake four: assuming consent to collect data implies consent to target with it. Symptom: a feature built for one purpose (self-reflective journaling) quietly becomes an input to another (re-engagement targeting) with no new disclosure to the user. Underlying error: treating "we have the data" as equivalent to "we may use the data this way." Cheapest diagnostic: read the original consent language the feature shipped with, out loud, in the room where the new use is being proposed.

8. What good looks like

Six months earlier, Nindiya's competitor Shanti Mind, a Mumbai-based sleep app, had faced a similar dashboard slump and a similar proposal from its growth team. Its product lead approved internal-trigger targeting only on tags the user had separately and explicitly opted to share for "personalised reminders" — a second consent step distinct from the original journaling prompt — and capped any single emotional tag at two triggers per week regardless of measured lift. The resulting campaign delivered a smaller uplift than an uncapped design would have, roughly 3.1x instead of 5.2x, but its opt-in rate for the reminder feature climbed for four straight months as word spread that the app "actually listened," with no complaints tying journal data to marketing. The lesson is not that ethical design is free — Shanti Mind left real short-term lift on the table — but that the lift it kept was durable, and durability, not the peak of a single test, is what a habit-forming product is actually trying to build.

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya took Rohan's data to Friday's review alongside the Shanti Mind comparison and a redesigned proposal: internal-trigger campaigns could proceed, but only on emotional tags covered by a distinct, explicit opt-in separate from the journaling consent, capped at two sends per tag per week, and reviewed quarterly against completion-rate decay. The board approved it, at a projected 3x lift rather than Rohan's 5.2x — a trade she described to the room as buying four months of goodwill with one afternoon's foregone growth. What she asked her team to learn next was the companion topic this one unlocks: how to apply the full Hook model, trigger through investment, without letting any single step run ahead of what users have actually agreed to. Two questions worth sitting with: when a user discloses something painful inside your product, who besides them gets to decide what that disclosure is worth to your growth numbers — and if your product's retention chart depends on a feeling you did not create but do profit from, what do you owe the people who feel it?
case20v1-ethics.triggers:
Lokshala: The Nine-Thirty Push

A decision case on notifications, aspirants and the emotions a product chooses to use

1. Opening

On Tuesday, 20 October 2026, at half past six in the evening, Vanshika Edake sat in a small meeting room in Lokshala's Pune office, in Kothrud, with two documents open. Edake was the company's chief product officer. The first document was a growth plan from Vyomesh Ekavade, her head of growth in Bengaluru, proposing a nightly notification for the company's Diwali Sprint. The second was a short note from Vedprakash Edlabadkar, a data scientist in Toronto, asking her to read three tables before she approved anything.

Diwali fell on Sunday, 8 November. The notification schedule had to be locked with the messaging vendor by Friday, 23 October, so that the sprint could begin on Monday, 26 October (Figure 1). Edake could back the plan, replace it with an alternative, or ask for something new, and each choice cost a different thing.

Figure 1. The three weeks before Diwali. Scale: 30 pixels per day, with 20 October at the left-hand marker.

2. Company background

Lokshala was founded in 2019 by two former schoolteachers, and it sold daily practice to people preparing for government and bank recruitment: the SSC, IBPS and Railway exams and state public service commissions. Its twenty-question daily sets, timed mock tests and worked explanations came in Marathi, Hindi and English. Its users were mostly in Nashik, Kolhapur, Latur, Nagpur, Indore and similar towns, where a year at a coaching centre could consume a family's savings.

By September 2026 the app had 6,20,000 monthly active users, of whom 48,000 paid ₹1,500 a year: an annual run rate of ₹7.20 crore before GST. The company had raised ₹22 crore, employed 140 people, and wanted 60,000 paying users by 31 March 2027. It competed for the same evening hour as Testbook, Adda247, Unacademy and PhysicsWallah, and for the same thumb as Instagram Reels and YouTube.

Regulation sat quietly behind every messaging decision. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 required recorded consent for communications, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns named practices such as false urgency and confirm-shaming. Lokshala's outside counsel had not been asked whether the current plan touched either.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 shows where September's 1.2 crore session starts came from. Users opening the app unprompted accounted for 48,00,000, or 40.0 per cent. The 42,00,000 starts that followed a push notification, WhatsApp message or email from Lokshala itself were the next largest group, and they cost the least per start of anything the company bought.

Ekavade's test ran from 7 to 13 September on 1,00,000 of the roughly 4,10,000 users who had notifications enabled, split evenly (Exhibit 2). Arm A received "Today's 20 questions are ready" at 9:00 a.m. Arm B received, at 9:30 p.m., "Your rank fell 412 places today. Aspirants who practised overtook you." Exhibit 2 gives the results.

Edlabadkar had also asked 400 randomly chosen users, active in the week to 20 September, what they felt just before they last opened the app (Exhibit 3). He reported the answers without comment.
