The review call that afternoon had been set for 4:30 p.m. in Pune, 1:00 p.m. in Berlin and 7:00 a.m. in Toronto, and it had ended without agreement.

The three views differed with the city. From Bengaluru, Ekavade saw ads at ₹3,000 per thousand starts and messages at ₹143. From Berlin, Eksarkar read the 6,500 switch-offs in Arm B as that many people who had asked Lokshala to be quiet. From Toronto, Edlabadkar saw two arms that differed in the hour as well as the wording, and said so.

4. The people

Vanshika Edake, 41, chief product officer, Pune. She owned the notification roadmap and the January numbers. She wanted a sprint that Lokshala would not have to explain to its users, its investors or a regulator.

Vyomesh Ekavade, head of growth, Bengaluru. He wanted the nightly message approved. "We did not put the fear there," he told the call. "The exam did. Every aspirant already lies awake over their rank, and we are the one app that tells them something useful about it."

Veronika Eksarkar, designer, Berlin. In August she had interviewed fourteen aspirants in Kolhapur and Latur, and several described a ritual she called "the nine o'clock dread". She wanted users to control when and whether Lokshala spoke to them. "A true sentence can still be a push on a bruise," she said.

Vedprakash Edlabadkar, data scientist, Toronto. He had built all three exhibits, and he wanted the decision made with their limits understood. Lokshala measured payment and activity; it did not measure whether practice after midnight improved anyone's mock-test scores.

5. The options

Option 1: Scale the rank-drop message. Send Arm B's 9:30 p.m. message nightly to all 4,10,000 notification-enabled users through the sprint. Per 50,000 users the test showed 150 extra paying users, worth ₹2.25 lakh at ₹1,500, along with 3,500 more switch-offs and 1,750 more uninstalls. It is ready on 26 October and leaves users' settings as they are.

Option 2: Send only the neutral reminder. Send Arm A's 9:00 a.m. message to everyone. It needs no new work, gives up the 150 extra paying users per 50,000 that Arm B produced, avoids its extra switch-offs and uninstalls, and leaves the rank feature unused in the notification channel.

Option 3: Let each user set the trigger. Ship a "study plan" screen on the first open after an update. Users pick days and a time, rank messages appear only if chosen, nothing is sent between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m., and no one gets more than four a week. Berlin and Pune estimate three weeks of work, so it would go live on Monday, 16 November, with Option 2's message running until then. Its effect on payment has not been tested.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Sort the four groups in Exhibit 1 into paid, earned, relationship and owned triggers. Which kind is the 9:30 p.m. message, and what internal trigger is it working on?
  2. Read Exhibits 2 and 3 together. What is the message doing to the user, and which measures in Exhibit 2 point in which direction?
  3. For each option, whose interests does it serve, and what would Lokshala have to believe for it to be right?
  4. Which option would you take to Friday's lock, with what limits, and what measure in a month would tell you that you were wrong?

7. A note for the learner

The topic frames the decision through the first step of the Hook. A trigger is whatever prompts an action. External triggers are paid (install ads), earned (creator mentions and referrals), relationship (Lokshala's own push, WhatsApp and email) and owned (the icon on the home screen). Internal triggers are feelings. The aspirant's worry about falling behind is one, and the 9:30 p.m. message is a relationship trigger that presses on it.

A well-reasoned answer separates attaching to an emotion from manufacturing one, and asks whether the user would endorse the trigger on reflection, whether they can control it, and how vulnerable they are. It names the trigger types before judging them, uses every exhibit, and states what the chosen path forgoes. Here the audience is young, anxious and spending family savings.

One defensible path is Option 3, with Option 2 running until it ships. The relationship channel supplies 35.0 per cent of session starts at the lowest cost, so 7.0 points more switch-offs (13.0 per cent against 6.0) spend the asset that Option 1 is trying to harvest. The study plan lets an aspirant who finds rank messages motivating keep them. The path gives up some of the 150, and the whole Diwali week runs on the neutral message, and it should be judged at day 30 on switch-offs, uninstalls, late-night sessions and conversion together, with a rule agreed beforehand for stopping.
exp40v2-ethics.triggers:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance — Ethics, Persuasion & Trust

External and Internal Triggers

What actually prompts a user to act, what happens to the emotion you keep reaching for, and where the best practitioners still disagree.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 7 August 2025, Meera Kulkarni, chief product officer of Kifayat Money, a Pune-based savings-and-credit app with 9.1 million registered users, sat with a proposal her growth team had labelled "Spend Shock." Kifayat's core loop read a user's UPI and card transaction feed and produced a weekly spending summary. Growth had found that users whose discretionary spend exceeded their trailing four-week average by more than 40% opened the app within two hours of a notification at 11.3%, against 2.6% for the generic Sunday summary. The winning copy did not describe the amount neutrally. It said: "You spent ₹4,180 more than usual this week. See where it went." Internally it was called "the wince." Meera's problem was not that it worked; the arithmetic was unambiguous. It was that Kifayat earned 62% of revenue from personal-loan referrals, and the same anxiety that drove a user to open the app drove a measurable uplift in loan-offer acceptance within eleven minutes.

Eight days later and 550 kilometres away, Vikram Iyer, head of product at Mustaid Field Cloud, a Hyderabad company selling shift-safety software to 240 industrial sites across India and South-East Asia, faced a structurally similar decision with the opposite sign. Mustaid's supervisors were meant to complete a pre-shift hazard walk on the app; completion had stalled at 58%. The proposal was to send the supervisor, four minutes before shift start, a notification naming the one open hazard on their line and the date of the last incident at that site. Early tests moved completion to 81%. The mechanism was identical to Meera's — reach for an uncomfortable feeling the person already has, here accountability dread, and offer a two-minute action that relieves it. Vikram's discomfort was that the supervisors were not his customers; the plant's EHS director was. He was designing emotional pressure on one group at the request of another, and nobody knew what the supervisors would say if asked.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A trigger is the cue that initiates a behaviour. An external trigger is information placed in the user's environment specifying what to do next: a push notification, an SMS, a badge, a friend's forward. An internal trigger is an internal state — usually an uncomfortable emotion — associated with the product so reliably that it prompts the behaviour with no environmental cue. The claim binding the two is developmental: external triggers buy the repetitions during which an internal trigger can form, and a product that never makes the transition keeps paying for every session it gets.

The intellectual history runs through three lineages practitioners blend without noticing. The oldest is behaviourist: Skinner's discriminative stimulus, the cue signalling that reinforcement is available. The second is the habit psychology of Wendy Wood and David Neal, whose mid-2000s field studies found everyday habits cued far more reliably by stable context — time, place, preceding action — than by mood, and persisting after the reward stopped mattering. The third is persuasive technology: B. J. Fogg's behaviour model, in which behaviour occurs when motivation, ability and a prompt converge — which is why experts treat trigger timing as an ability problem, not a copy problem. Eyal's Hooked (2014) sits downstream of all three and added what the industry adopted: the external/internal distinction and the paid–earned–relationship–owned taxonomy, itself borrowed from media planning.

The problem it was invented to solve was commercial. Consumer software of the 2008–2014 era acquired users cheaply and lost them almost as fast; the question was why a handful escaped the re-acquisition treadmill. "They attached to an internal trigger" was the answer, and a good one. It is also where the ethical charge sits, because the internal triggers with the highest commercial value are negative: boredom, loneliness, financial anxiety, status insecurity, professional dread.

Four schools disagree about what follows, and each will sign a different sentence.

The habit-design school (Eyal, the Fogg lineage, most growth practice).
Signs: internal triggers pre-exist the product; the designer's job is to become the fastest reliable response to one; a product that delivers real relief has made the user better off. Will not sign: that designers manufacture the emotion, or that engagement is self-justifying. Eyal's own test — would the designer use it themselves, and does it materially improve the user's life — is a virtue test, not a metric.
The attention-critique school (Tristan Harris, James Williams, and the humane-technology tradition).
Signs: the asymmetry between a designer with a thousand experiments and a user with one unexamined reflex makes "the feeling was already there" an insufficient defence; triggers should be judged against what users say they want, not what they do. Will not sign: that the technique is inherently wrong. Their objection is aimed at business models that reward volume of attention; they would approve Vikram's hazard notification without hesitation.
The behavioural-welfare school (the nudge and internalities literature).
Signs: cue-based habit design is welfare-improving when the habit is one the user endorses on reflection, and endorsement is measurable by asking. Will not sign: that continued use demonstrates endorsement. Their claim is that present bias makes revealed preference unreliable precisely in the moments triggers exploit.
The revealed-preference school (most economists, and most boards).
Signs: switching costs in Indian consumer mobile are near zero, uninstalling takes four seconds, and sustained voluntary use across millions is the strongest available evidence of value. Will not sign: that a designer's intuition about what users "really" want should override what they repeatedly choose. Unfashionable, and stronger than its critics allow.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice differs from competent practice in four places, three of which are measurement.

The first is the trigger inventory. Before any copy is written, an expert team lists every cue the product can send and, for each, the internal state it is meant to interrupt. Blank rows are defects. Meera's team found 34 active templates at Kifayat: 9 targeted financial anxiety, 4 social comparison, 2 curiosity, and 19 named no internal state at all — meaning, in practice, whatever the copywriter's instinct reached for, unaudited.

The second is trigger independence. Define an organic session as one beginning more than 60 minutes after the last external trigger of any kind reached the user, deduplicated across push, SMS, email and badge. The trigger-independence ratio is organic sessions over total sessions. It is the operational measure of whether an internal trigger is forming, and it can move in the opposite direction from everything growth teams usually report. Figure 1 shows two Kifayat cohorts with almost identical week-12 session counts.

Cohort B's shape is the diagnostic one. Organic share rises for four weeks, peaks, then falls — not because users leave, but because the external trigger does progressively more of the work while the unprompted reflex atrophies underneath. This is trigger dependency: invisible in DAU and in retention, and the reason a channel-policy change becomes an existential event.

The third is marginal send economics. The naive question is whether a notification produces incremental sessions. The expert question is whether the nth weekly send produces more value than it destroys, given that opt-outs are effectively irreversible. Table 1 works this through per 1,000 anxiety-targeted Kifayat users.

Two things about this table matter more than the numbers. First, none of it is computable without a permanent holdout — a randomly assigned 2–5% of users who receive no external triggers, ever. Kifayat's naive attribution credited the anxiety campaign with 1,600 incremental sessions a week; the holdout showed 1,150 of those users would have arrived anyway, so true incrementality was 450 — an overstatement of 3.6×. Cannibalisation is the single largest source of self-deception in trigger work. Second, the cost side is denominated in lost future organic sessions, which requires the organic baseline, which requires the holdout again. Teams without one are not measuring badly; they are not measuring.

The fourth difference is a second-order effect the textbook understates. The standard claim is that internal triggers are discovered, not created — Kifayat did not invent money anxiety. That is true of the emotion's existence and false of its frequency. Repeatedly pairing a cue with an emotional state is the classical recipe for raising that state's salience; cue-reactivity research finds the cue itself begins to evoke the feeling. Figure 2 sets the textbook loop against the observed one.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions can be stated as testable claims.

Claim one: an internal trigger sustains usage only at or below the frequency at which the emotion naturally recurs. Test it by measuring the emotion's base rate independently of the product. Kifayat's money anxiety is cyclical — spiking around salary credit, EMI debits and month-end — giving four to six genuine episodes a month. The daily-active ambition was therefore unavailable no matter how good the copy; anything above the base rate had to be manufactured, which is what Cohort B's declining curve records. Mustaid passes easily: shift-start dread recurs every shift, which is the frequency the product wants.

Claim two: the action must resolve the discomfort inside one session, reliably. Where it does not, the trigger teaches the user that the product does not work, and repetition accelerates churn rather than habit. Kifayat fails awkwardly: seeing that you overspent by ₹4,180 does not reduce money anxiety, it raises it, and the only in-app action that reduces it quickly is accepting a loan offer. Mustaid passes: the hazard walk genuinely discharges the supervisor's exposure, in under two minutes.

Claim three: the channel must be durable enough to amortise acquiring the habit. Android's runtime notification permission and TRAI's commercial-communication rules have made owned channels materially less owned; Kifayat's push opt-in on new installs fell from 78% to 41% in three years. A strategy premised on many external repetitions before independence emerges is premised on a resource that will not be there.

The frame actively misleads in three situations. For low-frequency, high-consideration products — home loans, term insurance, enterprise procurement — habit is the wrong model; availability at the moment of need is the right one, and machinery aimed at manufacturing frequency destroys trust for no gain. Where use is mandated, as much of Mustaid's is, trigger metrics measure compliance pressure rather than habit. And for any product whose purpose is to reduce the emotion it triggers on — debt counselling, sleep, sobriety, screen-time management — success means the internal trigger fires less often, which the retention chart records as failure.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product and super-app estates. When six teams share one notification permission, the channel is a common-pool resource and the failure is a tragedy of the commons: each team's sends are positive-ROI against its own metric and collectively drive the opt-out that destroys the channel. Mature companies say they solve this with a centrally allocated per-user weekly send budget plus an exception queue. What they have, if you read the queue, is a budget that holds for ten weeks of the quarter and an exception approval rate above 80% in the final two.

Two-sided markets. Supply-side triggers reach people whose income depends on responding — a delivery partner, a seller — so what is cued is closer to economic compulsion than preference, and the ethical, increasingly regulatory, standard is higher. Demand-side triggers behave like ordinary consumer triggers, and platforms running one policy across both sides are almost always over-triggering supply.

Regulated domains. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 makes purpose limitation the operative constraint: data collected to render a service may not be silently repurposed for engagement targeting. Kifayat's transaction feed was collected to produce a spending summary; using it to time loan offers is a different purpose, and a defensible reading requires fresh notice. RBI's digital lending guidance constrains unsolicited credit pushes and TRAI's rules constrain SMS independently. Here compliance and ethics point the same way, which is fortunate and not typical.

Hardware plus software. When the device is the trigger surface — a haptic pulse, an always-on display, an LED — the cue reaches the user pre-attentively and cannot be dismissed the way a notification can. Iteration is slow and partly irreversible: firmware ships quarterly, and a haptic pattern that proves anxiogenic cannot be hot-fixed on Tuesday.

AI-native products. This is where governance breaks. When a model composes the trigger at inference time, personalised to a user's history, there is no fixed copy to review, and emotional targeting emerges without a human having written the sentence: a system optimised on open-rate will discover the wince by itself. Governance must shift from copy approval to policy plus evaluation — a written list of internal states the system may and may not appeal to, and an eval suite that samples generated triggers and classifies them against it. Few companies have this; most have a prompt saying "be helpful and not manipulative," which is not a control.

The seam. Growth owns sends, CRM owns the calendar, legal owns consent, support owns complaints — and nobody owns cumulative emotional pressure on a single user. The tell is that "how many anxiety-themed messages did our median user get last month, across all channels?" cannot be answered in under a week.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. Context, not emotion, is doing most of the cueing. The tell is usage clustering tightly by time of day, location or preceding action rather than by anything users report feeling. The obvious reading — "our users open the app when they feel anxious" — is usually a story told over a pattern that is really "our users open the app on the train at 9:10." Context cues are cheap, stable and ethically inert, and a team that mislabels one as an emotional trigger builds emotional machinery it did not need.

2. "We didn't create the emotion" defends less than it seems. The tell is a rise in unprompted opens in the minutes after unrelated notifications arrive, or users saying they check "to make sure nothing's wrong." The obvious reading is that the internal trigger has formed. The expert reading is that cue salience has risen — the product now generates some of the demand it serves, making discovery-not-invention a claim about origins that says nothing about ongoing effects.

3. Organic does not mean internal. The tell is that organic opens collapse when the icon badge is suppressed for a week. A red dot is an external trigger sitting permanently on the home screen, and much of what teams classify as unprompted use is badge-driven. Experts run a badge-suppression holdout because it separates a habit from a persistent visual cue.

4. Most measured lift is reallocation. The tell is attributed sessions climbing while total sessions stay flat. Triggers are very good at moving a session from Thursday evening to Thursday morning and much worse at creating one that would not have happened. Without a never-triggered holdout the two are indistinguishable, and the reported number is wrong by a multiple rather than a margin.

5. Frequency caps are enforced on the wrong unit. The tell is a compliance report showing every channel within cap while one user received two pushes, three in-app cards and an email all about money worry in seven days. Users do not experience channels; they experience themes. The expert cap is per theme per user per period — which almost no marketing-automation platform supports natively, which is why almost no one does it.

6. Negative-emotion habits decay differently, and break loudly. The tell is the language of one-star reviews: functional complaints ("slow," "buggy") indicate a product problem; moral complaints ("guilt-trip," "manipulative," "preys on you") indicate a trigger problem, and arrive after the association has broken. Relief-driven habits are more fragile than reward-driven ones, because one session that fails to deliver relief disconfirms the whole association.

7. Consent language is simultaneously the weakest design element and the strongest defence. The tell is a decision memo citing the privacy policy rather than a sentence the user actually read. Experts apply a harder test: can you say, in one sentence a user would recognise, what you are using and why — and would they be unsurprised? Under a purpose-limitation regime that is also the legal test, which is why the ethical and legal shortcuts fail together.

8. The best internal triggers are often the least fraught. The tell is a growth roadmap listing six emotional states, none neutral. Curiosity, the urge to close an open loop, and dead time in a queue are internal triggers with high frequency, low disclosure sensitivity and no reputational tail. Experts exhaust these before touching anything disclosed in confidence — not because anxiety works less well, but because it works well for four months.

9. In B2B the internal trigger belongs to a role, not a person. The tell is cohort retention tracking individual tenure rather than account age: usage decays on a cycle matching supervisor turnover, not contract age. A habit built in one supervisor's head walks out of the plant. Experts anchor B2B triggers to ritual and artefact — the shift handover, the Monday review — because those survive the person.

7. How this changes across product types and stages

In consumer products the internal trigger is personal, owned channels are cheap, and the temptation to over-trigger is permanent; the binding constraint is the opt-out economics of Table 1. In B2B and enterprise the internal trigger is organisational anxiety wearing a personal face — the audit, the review, the incident — and the distinctive feature is that the buyer and the triggered party are different people, as at Mustaid. Manufactured urgency about a compliance deadline that is not real is Kifayat's wince performed in a suit.

Platforms and marketplaces differ mainly in the supply-side compulsion point already made. Hardware differs in cue modality and iteration speed. AI products differ genuinely: generated triggers move the control point from copy to policy and evaluation. Beyond those, the differences most frameworks assert are not real — mechanism, measurement and failure modes are the same throughout, and treating each vertical as special is how teams rebuild the same holdout methodology five times.

Stage matters, but symmetrically. An early-stage company has thin trust reserves and no reputational buffer, so one visible misuse defines it; it also has a real excuse for lacking a holdout, since 3% of a small base is statistically useless, and experts there substitute interviews about why users opened the app. A scaled company can afford perfect measurement, but the same policy across 90 million users draws regulatory and press attention no buffer absorbs. Small companies over-trigger because they cannot measure the damage; large ones because the damage is diffused across too many teams to attribute.

8. Three worked examples

Bhorbela Learning, Kolkata, 2024. An after-school tutoring app for classes 6–10, triggering parents rather than students. The first design cued parental guilt: "Aarav has not practised in 4 days." Weekly parent opens rose 3.1×, but against a 4% holdout incremental student practice sessions rose only 6% — opening the app is the parent's action, practising is the child's. Recut to parental curiosity — "Aarav's fractions score moved from 61 to 74" — and sent only on a real change, volume fell from five sends a week to 1.4, parent opens to 2.2×, while incremental practice rose 23% and 12-month parent retention ran 14 points higher. Triggering the wrong person's emotion produces a real metric attached to no real outcome.

Mustaid Field Cloud, 2025. Vikram shipped the pre-shift notification with three constraints: it fired only when the site actually had an open hazard, never referenced the individual's past misses, and carried a one-tap "this hazard is already closed" that fed back into the record. Completion went from 58% to 79% and held at 76% after nine months — unusual durability, attributable to the trigger tracking a genuine state of the world rather than a schedule. The revealing number was the exception: at four sites where hazards were logged sloppily, notifications fired on stale data, and completion fell below the pre-launch baseline within eleven weeks. A trigger that cries wolf does not decay to neutral; it decays below where you started.

Qissagoi Audio, Mumbai, 2023–2025 — the failure. An audio-storytelling app with 6.4 million users, Qissagoi found that listeners who used the in-app "mood" tag after 11 pm responded powerfully to loneliness-referencing triggers. Late-night sessions rose 2.8× over five months. Then three things happened in sequence. Play Store rating fell from 4.4 to 3.6 over nine months; internal review found 31% of one-star reviews used moral rather than functional language; and a consumer-press story in early 2025 quoted three users' notification screenshots verbatim. Installs fell 38% quarter-on-quarter. Recovery took longer than the damage: the company withdrew all mood-derived targeting, put a plain-language "why am I seeing this" line on every notification, capped each theme at two sends a week, and rebuilt on serialised release at a user-chosen time — a curiosity trigger with a user-set clock. Organic share recovered from 28% to 54% over nine months; daily actives took fourteen months to regain the prior peak, and roughly ₹11 crore of incremental paid acquisition covered the install shortfall. The failure was not that the trigger was too aggressive. It was that the company had no measurement that could tell a habit from a dependency until the press did.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Attribution without a holdout.
Warning sign: attributed sessions grow faster than total sessions. Diagnostic: what is our never-triggered holdout's session rate? Cost of catching late: a multi-year growth strategy built on a number inflated three-fold.
Trigger dependency.
Warning sign: organic share falling while DAU is flat. Diagnostic: if push permission dropped 20 points tomorrow, what happens to next month's actives? Cost: a platform policy change becomes an existential event.
Purpose drift.
Warning sign: a data field built for one feature appears in a targeting query for another. Diagnostic: read aloud the consent text the field shipped under. Cost: a regulatory finding plus the trust loss, which outlasts the fine.
Optimising the proxy person.
Warning sign: the triggered metric improves while the outcome metric does not. Diagnostic: whose behaviour do we need, and is that the person we are messaging? Cost: quarters of work on a metric with no downstream effect, as at Bhorbela.
Cry-wolf triggers.
Warning sign: a rising share of sends fire on stale or inferred state. Diagnostic: what fraction of triggers referenced something still true on arrival? Cost: response settles below the pre-trigger baseline, not at it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position one: sustained voluntary use is sufficient evidence of value. Its strongest form rests on real evidence: Indian consumer switching costs are near zero, uninstall is trivial, competition is intense, and the same population critics say is being manipulated abandons products at enormous rates when they stop delivering. If manipulation were the mechanism, it should also work on the products people abandon, and it does not. This is wrong if a substantial share of use comes from a minority experiencing compulsive patterns they disendorse; research on problematic use suggests that share is real but small, and the disagreement is really about whether a small disendorsing minority should govern design for the majority.

Position two: declared intention, not behaviour, is the standard. Its strongest form notes that the relevant comparison is not use versus non-use but use versus what the user wanted when not in the grip of the cue; people using time-limit tools repeatedly set limits well below their actual use and then exceed them. That is an observation of preference reversal, not an inference. It is wrong if stated intentions are cheap talk — aspirations people never meant to act on — and the honest position is that we cannot cleanly separate a second-order preference from a socially desirable answer.

Position three: the technique is neutral and the business model is the variable. Its strongest form observes that Vikram's hazard notification and Meera's wince are mechanically identical and morally different, and the difference lies in whether the party paying for the trigger profits from the user's action or from the user's wellbeing. It is wrong if trigger design in a subscription business proves just as harmful as in an attention business — and the evidence is thin in both directions, mostly because nobody has measured it.

These three do not reconcile. Practitioners who claim a synthesis usually hold position one's decision rule and position three's vocabulary.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can name the four external-trigger types and explain the Hook loop. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four visible ways. They ask what the holdout says before asking what the lift was, and treat a team without a holdout as making an unfalsifiable claim rather than an optimistic one. They write the internal state down before the copy, and refuse blank rows. They read complaint language for moral vocabulary as an early indicator rather than reading churn as a late one. And when a trigger works spectacularly they get more cautious, not less, because the size of a lift measures leverage over someone, and leverage is what needs justifying.

12. What Meera and Vikram decided

Meera killed the wince variant and kept the campaign. Kifayat's spending alert now fires at most weekly, describes the overspend without the second-person framing, and — the change her growth lead fought hardest — suppresses all loan-offer surfaces for sixty minutes after an anxiety-themed trigger, cutting projected annual referral revenue by about ₹6.4 crore. Her argument to the board was structural rather than ethical: a company whose credit revenue sits causally downstream of anxiety it generates will be read, correctly, as predatory the first time anyone reconstructs the sequence, and the suppression window was the cheapest available proof that the sequence did not exist.

Vikram shipped with the three constraints and added a fourth his EHS customers disliked: supervisors could see every notification the system had sent about them, and could dispute the underlying hazard record. Adoption at two pilot sites slowed by three weeks. He argued that a trigger aimed at someone who cannot see or contest its basis is surveillance rather than safety, and that the distinction would matter to a labour inspector long before it mattered to him.

  1. Meera's sixty-minute suppression costs ₹6.4 crore and prevents a harm no one has yet demonstrated. Is that a defensible use of shareholder money, and what would change your answer?
  2. Mustaid's supervisors never consented to being triggered; their employer did. Under what conditions, if any, does a buyer's consent legitimately stand in for a user's?
  3. Qissagoi's recovery restored organic share faster than daily actives. Which number should its board have written into the CEO's incentive plan?

13. Going deeper

The Hook model supplies the frame this page sits inside; without it, triggers look like a messaging tactic rather than step one of a loop. Applying the Hook to your product is where holdouts, trigger inventories and independence ratios become an operating routine rather than an audit. Habit formation and attention supplies the evidence base, including the context-cue findings that undercut naive emotional targeting. The Fogg behaviour model (B = MAT) explains why well-timed triggers fail when ability is low, converting trigger tuning into a friction problem. Variable rewards decides whether the relief a trigger promises actually lands — the condition claim two rests on. Investment and stored value explains why some products survive losing their notification channel. Dark patterns taxonomy gives vocabulary to classify the wince precisely rather than argue in the abstract. Why dark patterns emerge without malice is this page's necessary companion: almost every practitioner here was well-intentioned, and how good people ship the wince deserves its own study.
case20v1-ethics.wellbeing:
Tilmil and the Diwali Streak Fortnight

A decision case on digital wellbeing and time-well-spent

Opening

At 8:30 p.m. on Thursday 22 October 2026, Ezra Lagwankar, head of product at Tilmil, ended a video call with Berlin and Toronto and sat alone in the Pune office with a deadline. The Android release train would be cut at noon on Tuesday 27 October so that the Diwali Streak Fortnight could launch on Wednesday 28 October. The campaign promised a free month of Tilmil Plus to anyone who played fourteen days running. Whatever wellbeing control Tilmil shipped beside it had to be specified by six o'clock on Friday evening.

Two documents were open on his screen: a design brief for a daily time limit, and the Diwali plan, which asked users to do the opposite.

Company background

Tilmil began in 2019 as a daily Marathi crossword, built in Pune by Ekavir Lakhe and a college friend. It now offers word, number and picture puzzles and serialised audio stories in six languages, to 1.8 crore monthly users, most on Android phones costing ₹8,000 to ₹15,000 and connected through Jio or Airtel. Revenue comes from rewarded video advertising and from Tilmil Plus, an ad-free tier at ₹99 a month billed through UPI AutoPay, with 6 lakh subscribers. Monthly revenue is about ₹28.3 crore, or ₹340 crore annualised.

Tilmil competes for the same minutes as ShareChat's Moj, Josh, Pratilipi and the casual games on Google Play. Two rules frame its choices. The DPDP Act, 2023 requires verifiable parental consent for users under eighteen, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns name nagging and false urgency as practices to avoid. Tilmil plans to raise a round in January 2027, and its investors read time spent as the headline metric.

The situation

Tilmil's engagement rests on three devices: a streak counter that shows the number of consecutive days played, a 7:45 p.m. push notification reading "Your 212-day streak ends at midnight", and an "ek aur" button that starts the next puzzle automatically. In September, product research invited 15,000 users to a survey and 2,400 replied. Of these, 912 (38 per cent) agreed that they spent more time on Tilmil than they intended to. Tilmil's customer-success lead in Singapore adds that the few complaints using the word "addiction" mostly come from parents.

The call had begun at 7 p.m. in Pune, 3:30 p.m. in Berlin and 9:30 a.m. in Toronto, and it had not ended in agreement. The Diwali Streak Fortnight would make all three devices louder: the 7:45 p.m. push would run daily, and a ladder of badges would celebrate each extra day. A winner on the free tier sees no advertisements for the month, so the prize costs Tilmil that user's ad revenue. Exhibit 1 sets out users and advertising revenue by daily play time.

Exhibit 2 prices a loss of advertising revenue under a share of users with a limit in force and a fall in their revenue.

Exhibit 3 reports a prototype test. Edhitha Lalingkar, the data scientist in Toronto, gave 600 new installs a one-time card and a settings control for a daily limit, and left another 600 alone. The arms were assigned at random and differed in nothing else; both were enrolled between 7 and 13 September.

Ekavir has begun calling the result proof that limits do not hurt retention. Edhitha has declined to put it in the board deck.

The people

Ezra Lagwankar, head of product in Pune, owns the decision and reports to Ekavir. He wants a control he can defend to users, to the board and to his own family.

Ekavir Lakhe, co-founder and chief executive, also in Pune, wants the Diwali campaign and the January round to go ahead. "Our users are adults," he told the call. "If they want a limit, they will set one; if we set it for them, we are telling a Pune bus driver how to spend his evening."

Elvira Lonarkar, product designer in Berlin, drew the streak flame in 2022. "A control nobody finds is theatre," she said. "It has to appear at the moment a person is playing, not in a menu they open once a year."

Edhitha Lalingkar, data scientist in Toronto, wants whatever ships to teach Tilmil something by January, and will not endorse a number the data cannot carry.

The options

Option A: a default limit. Every user receives a 90-minute daily limit, switched on at install and changeable in two taps. At the limit, play ends with a "see you tomorrow" screen, and a limit day keeps the streak alive. If 40 per cent of heavy users keep a limit and their revenue falls 30 to 50 per cent, Exhibit 2 puts the cost at ₹132 lakh to ₹220 lakh a month, or ₹15.8 crore to ₹26.4 crore a year. The Diwali plan is unchanged.

Option B: a reminder only. After 60 minutes in a day, a dismissible card says so. The limit control stays in settings, three taps deep. It takes one engineer one week and leaves the streak, the push notifications and the autoplay as they are. At 10 per cent with a limit, the cost is ₹33 lakh to ₹55 lakh a month, or ₹4.0 crore to ₹6.6 crore a year.

Option C: an offer at the moment of play. The first time a user passes 60 minutes in a day, a card offers a limit in one tap. Limit-setters keep their streak on limit days and stop receiving loss-framed streak pushes, and 5 per cent of users, chosen at random, never see the card. The team reviews take-up and retention on Friday 8 January 2027, ahead of the January round. At 25 per cent with a limit, the cost is ₹82 lakh to ₹137 lakh a month, or ₹9.9 crore to ₹16.5 crore a year.

Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which users matter most to Tilmil's advertising revenue, and whom would a daily limit actually affect?
  2. Exhibit 2 offers nine possible costs and Exhibit 3 offers one experiment. Which numbers would you show the board as evidence, and which as assumptions?
  3. Elvira and Ekavir disagree about whether users will protect themselves. What would you need to know to say who is right, and could you learn it before Friday?
  4. Which option do you choose, what do you tell the board it costs, and what result in January would make you change course?

A note for the learner

The lens here is the question Tilmil's own hooks pose: can a user win against them? A streak, a loss-framed push and an auto-start button each work best on someone tired, and a control that sits three taps deep asks that person to out-think the design. Wellbeing here means a user's ability to stop, measured against what the product does to prevent it. A well-reasoned answer separates what the page knows (Exhibit 1) from what it only assumes (Exhibit 2), and prices the decision as a range.

One defensible path is Option C. It puts the control where the hook operates, and it spends the revenue sensibly: the middle of its range is about 4.9 per cent of monthly advertising revenue, set beside a user base in which 38 per cent of survey respondents already say they overplay. It also withdraws the loss-framed push from limit-setters, which is the practice closest to the false urgency the CCPA guidelines name. Exhibit 3 cannot say whether a limit helps or hurts retention, so the 5 per cent holdout is what will answer it, although it compares the whole offer, card, streak protection and push change together, with no card at all, and cannot say which part did the work. Ezra should tell the board that the range is wide, that January will narrow it, and that he has fixed in advance the take-up and retention results that would send him to Option A or to Option B.
exp40v2-ethics.wellbeing:
Digital Wellbeing and Time Well Spent: The Arithmetic of the Tail

1. Two decisions, a day apart

On Monday 12 October 2026, Gauresh Menon, vice-president of product at Veekshan Interactive, a Bengaluru studio whose single free-to-play puzzle title had 50 lakh monthly players, read a one-page memo from Gurupriya Mampilly, his staff data scientist, and understood that he had spent two years asking the wrong question. Veekshan carries no advertising; all of its ₹165.72 crore of annual revenue is in-app purchase. The memo said that 58,000 players — 1.16 per cent of the base — supplied 45.1 per cent of that revenue while accounting for 11.2 per cent of playing minutes. A twelve-week pilot of four wellbeing controls, run on a fifth of those heaviest players from Monday 1 June to Sunday 23 August, had cut their spending by 13.3 per cent. Gurnoor Mulackal, who runs live operations, had already done the multiplication: extending the controls to everyone would forgo about ₹13.59 crore a year, against a board plan built on 11 per cent growth. Gauresh had to decide by Monday 9 November, when the event calendar locked.

On Tuesday 13 October, Gandhali Marar, co-founder of Vyaayam Labs in Pune, held a harder version of the same problem. Vyaayam sells a ₹7,999 wrist band and a ₹499-a-month subscription to 4.1 lakh people — ₹245.51 crore a year — and its entire proposition is that it helps them sleep better. Gowsalya Moothedath's eight-week study had found what Gandhali did not want found: the daily readiness score was also what subscribers reached for before getting out of bed, five or six times before breakfast. A weekly summary, shipped alongside a cap on the coach's notifications, reduced that checking. It also raised monthly churn from 3.4 per cent to 4.6 per cent, where the cap on its own lowered it to 2.9 per cent. Gandhali's company would lose money by becoming less compelling in exactly the way its marketing claimed to care about.

These two decisions differ in one measurable respect, and the respect is arithmetic rather than ethical: whether the users whose usage is hardest to endorse are also the users who pay.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Digital wellbeing is the practice of designing a product so that the attention it takes is attention its users would, on reflection, agree to give. Time well spent is the standard of judgement: not duration but endorsement. An engagement metric rises whenever attention is captured, irrespective of whether it was wanted, so a team compensated on that metric is compensated for capture.

The lineage runs through B. F. Skinner's demonstration that unpredictably timed rewards sustain behaviour more stubbornly than scheduled ones; B. J. Fogg's Stanford work formalising behaviour as the coincidence of motivation, ability and a trigger; Nir Eyal's Hooked (2014), which turned the finding into a design method; and Tristan Harris's 2013 memo at Google, which became the Time Well Spent campaign in 2016 and the Center for Humane Technology in 2018.

The humane-design school holds that the metric itself is the defect. It will sign “a firm should forgo revenue it earns from attention its users would not endorse.” It will not sign “disclosure plus an opt-out discharges the duty.” The autonomy school holds that habit-forming design is morally neutral and the duty is a cheap, honest exit. It will sign “a product may build habits in service of a use the user endorses.” It will not sign “engagement metrics are inherently illegitimate.” The internalities school, descended from O'Donoghue and Rabin on self-control and sharpened by the 2020 Facebook deactivation study of Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer and Gentzkow — in which participants had to be paid roughly a hundred dollars to give the product up for a month — holds that the problem is the measurable gap between what users choose and what they would pay not to have to choose. It will sign “estimate the gap, do not assert it.” It will not sign “self-reported regret is sufficient evidence.” The structural school holds that voluntary controls cannot survive a bad quarter and must therefore be rules. It will sign “a threshold must be enforceable by someone who does not carry the revenue target.” It will not sign “firms can be trusted to set their own thresholds.”

3. Mechanics: six steps, three of them usually skipped

Expert practice begins not with a feature but with a census. Veekshan's, for May 2026, is Exhibit 1: players ranked by playing time, cut into ten equal deciles of 5,00,000.

Three readings follow immediately. The heaviest decile takes 42.6 per cent of the minutes and 77.5 per cent of the money, and the population mean of ₹27.62 across 50,00,000 players is ₹13.81 crore a month, or the ₹165.72 crore a year Gauresh was reading about. Figure 1 plots both cumulative curves and the sub-group Gurupriya named the deep tail: the 58,000 players above 3,000 minutes a month, averaging 4,210 minutes and ₹1,075 before any control was applied.

Figure 1. Both curves are cumulative sums of Exhibit 1, plotted at decile ends and joined by straight segments; the deep-tail dots sit inside decile 1 and so lie above the revenue segment, not on it.

Step two is to choose a threshold rather than a feature. Each of Veekshan's four controls carries a number: streak forgiveness (one missed day in seven does not reset), a default monthly spend ceiling of ₹2,000 raisable by the player after a 24-hour delay, a pause on event timers between 00:30 and 06:00, and a session prompt at 90 minutes. Step three tests where the control binds, in the tail, measuring behaviour, money and endorsement together. Every gap clears noise, and the gap that decides the business is still not on the table. Step four writes the firm's exposure as the sum, across groups, of each group's revenue share times the control's proportional effect inside it. The deep tail holds 45.1 per cent of revenue and responded at −13.30 per cent, which is 6.0 per cent of total revenue; the unrounded chain, 58,000 × ₹143 × 12, gives ₹9.95 crore a year. The pilot never touched the other 54.9 per cent; Gurupriya's central assumption, that the body responds at −4.0 per cent because the ceiling and the night-time pause rarely bind there, gives 0.451 × 13.30 + 0.549 × 4.00 = 8.2 per cent, the ₹13.59 crore Gurnoor quoted. Step five publishes a range on one basis, annual revenue forgone at today's 50 lakh players: ₹9.95 crore if the controls fire only in the tail, ₹22.04 crore if the whole base responded as the tail did. Step six, almost always skipped, puts each threshold in a versioned register owned outside the revenue line.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions can be stated as tests. First: the users whose usage is hardest to endorse are also the users who pay. At Veekshan the top 1.16 per cent by time supply 45.1 per cent of revenue, so it passes. At Vyaayam, on a flat ₹499 subscription, the heaviest 1.16 per cent of subscribers supply 1.16 per cent of revenue by construction; the test fails, and with it the whole concentration argument. Second: the control binds on the paying users. Veekshan's ceiling fires for 14,500 of the 58,000 deep-tail players, 25.0 per cent, and its 90-minute prompt for 57,000 of the 58,000, 98.3 per cent; Vyaayam's notification cap binds on everyone equally and costs nothing. Third: the metric the team is paid on rises when the user loses. True of in-app purchase per daily player at Veekshan; partly true of churn at Vyaayam, since the weekly score raised it; and true of the daily-score open rate its growth team had adopted as north star.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. Where time in product is the value delivered — a lecture, a consultation, a tutor — falling minutes may be abandonment rather than liberation. Where usage is the user's livelihood, as in a delivery partner's app, a control that reduces hours reduces income, and the welfare claim inverts unless the control targets the incentive rather than the time. And where minutes fall because the product got worse, a wellbeing dashboard will report the decay as a win; the only defence is to read minutes beside return rate and endorsement, never alone.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product. A group-level daily cap is the right unit for the user and the wrong unit for the organisation, because each app carries its own profit line and no general manager funds a cap whose benefit accrues to a sibling. The workable version holds group-level thresholds in one register and reconciles at the group's revenue line, not each app's.

Two-sided. Veekshan's clan leaders are unpaid supply: a streak that protects a player can punish the leader whose clan loses its bonus. Controls that cover only the demand side relocate the compulsion rather than removing it.

Regulated. The Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 dark-pattern guidelines name nagging and false urgency as specified practices, which makes a Veekshan event countdown a compliance object as well as a design one. Where minors are plausibly present, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 makes “we did not know their age” an expensive position.

Hardware plus software. Vyaayam's band vibrates on firmware. Removing a nudge needs an over-the-air release, a retail channel compensated on subscription attach rate, and a returns window; the product decision is coupled to a logistics decision in a way a pure app decision never is.

AI-native. A language-model coach generates its own triggers, so capping message templates caps nothing. The control has to sit on the policy — a hard budget of two outbound messages a day, enforced outside the model — and the evaluation set has to ask whether the model invented a reason to make contact. Mature companies mostly do this one badly and compensate with a human review queue they do not describe publicly.

6. Seven nuances that separate expert from competent

Reach and cost are concentrated differently

The tell is a wellbeing memo reporting reach in users and cost in rupees without ever crossing the two. One per cent of users looks like a one per cent problem; at Veekshan it is a 45 per cent problem.

Thresholds, not features, are the unit of governance

The tell is a release note that moves a number with no feature name attached — a ceiling from ₹2,000 to ₹5,000, a prompt from 90 minutes to 150. The obvious reading is that the control still exists. It does; it has simply stopped binding, and nothing in the changelog records that.

Elasticity in the tail is not elasticity in the mean

The tell is a team quoting one engagement elasticity for a control. Veekshan's measured tail response was −13.3 per cent against an assumed −4.0 per cent in the body, over three times as large.

A default that is on is not a default that binds

The tell is a control with near-total coverage and almost no firings. Veekshan's ceiling binds on a quarter of the deep tail and on almost nobody in the body. The diagnostic is not adoption but the share of covered users for whom the control actually fired.

Reversibility is asymmetric by design

The tell is a control whose introduction required a council and whose removal requires a flag flip. Practitioners read “we can always turn it off” as prudence. It is the mechanism by which the control dies.

Self-report moves with the framing, not only the behaviour

At Veekshan the endorsement item improved 13.0 points on a 57.0 base, a relative fall of 22.8 per cent, against 15.2 per cent off minutes. The expert reads the excess as partly the control reframing the session rather than shortening it, and refuses to treat a survey gap as a behaviour gap.

“Users can choose” is a claim about the price of choosing

The tell is a bypass costing one tap for everyone, including the person for whom one tap is the problem. Veekshan's 24-hour delay on raising the ceiling is the honest form: it preserves the choice and prices it in time.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the user is the revenue source, so the divergence is priced directly and concentration does the damage. In B2B and enterprise software the buyer is the employer, time in product is frequently the wrong metric altogether — an expense tool succeeds when it is closed quickly — and the question becomes notification load on salaried staff, where firm and user largely align. On platforms and marketplaces the controls must cover supply as well as demand, because the hooks aimed at earners are stronger and less examined. In hardware the device adds release latency and a channel with its own incentives. In AI products the trigger is generated rather than authored, so governance moves from content review to policy limits.

Stage changes the binding constraint rather than the idea. A twenty-person company can read three hundred endorsement answers by hand, has no metric orthodoxy to defend, and can set binding defaults in an afternoon. A company of Veekshan's size has the data and also the machinery: quarterly targets, a bonus plan, an event calendar sold to partners. There the decisive work is organisational, and the honest claim is that the design question was settled years ago while the governance question was never opened.

8. Three worked examples

Veekshan's pilot (worked). Priced honestly, the twelve-week pilot costs ₹9.95 crore a year in the tail alone and ₹13.59 crore at Gurupriya's central assumption. There is no offset to subtract: the ₹143 net spending gap is measured over all treated players, so the 1.2 points more still active in week 12 are already inside it. The firm loses money. That is the answer, not a problem to be modelled away.

Vyaayam's notification cap (worked, and free). From Monday 13 July to Sunday 6 September 2026, Vyaayam cut the coach's daily cap from nine messages to two for a quarter of subscribers, and tested a weekly score together with that two-message cap on another quarter. Exhibit 3 gives the cells.

Churn covers the last four weeks of the window, so the denominator is the cell: 6,970 of 2,05,000 is 3.4 per cent and 4,715 of 1,02,500 is 4.6 per cent. Survival compounds the monthly rate twelve times: 0.966 to the twelfth is 66.0 per cent, 0.971 to the twelfth 70.2 per cent, 0.954 to the twelfth 56.8 per cent. Cell A is the free move. Where the hook was not load-bearing for revenue, removing it was costless and slightly profitable, which is exactly why it had survived nine notifications a day for two years — nobody had tested it. Cell B costs, and which comparison you take decides how much. Against the status quo, the combined arm of cap plus weekly score gives a 9.2-point survival gap: 37,720 subscribers, ₹1.88 crore a month, ₹22.59 crore of annual run-rate, or 9.2 per cent. But Gandhali had already adopted the cap, so her live choice is B against A, which isolates the score at the same cap: 13.4 points of survival, 54,940 subscribers, ₹32.90 crore of run-rate, 13.4 per cent of ₹245.51 crore. The weekly score alone, without the cap, was never run. Both arms shrink; the gap is what the score costs.

Veekshan's first attempt (failed). On Monday 2 February 2026 the studio shipped a playtime dashboard and an opt-in daily limit, both inside settings. Over ninety days, 1,84,000 of 50,00,000 players opened the page, 3.7 per cent; 42,000 of 50,00,000, or 0.84 per cent, set a limit; and 25,620 of the 42,000, 61 per cent, came from deciles 6 to 10 — half the player base, 0.4 per cent of revenue. The programme cost the company nothing, which is precisely what was wrong with it. The recovery was the threshold register, a default that fires on measured behaviour rather than on intention, and a published elasticity that made the cost arguable.

9. Four failure modes and their early warnings

The free control. Early sign: the programme has no cost line. Diagnostic: what did this cost us in rupees last quarter? Caught late, an outsider prices it for you, and the answer is worse because you did not have one.

Threshold drift. Early sign: a changelog entry containing a number and no owner. Diagnostic: show me the register's diff for the last two quarters. Caught late, six quarters of erosion with no decision to point at.

Averaging the tail away. Early sign: one engagement elasticity quoted for the whole base. Diagnostic: the control's effect by revenue decile. Caught late, a rollout priced at a fraction of its true cost.

Endorsement without behaviour. Early sign: the survey improves and minutes do not. Diagnostic: report both, in the same review, to the same people. Caught late, a programme that has learnt to move a questionnaire.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Fix the metric, not the feature. The strongest case: feature-level controls have shipped for eight years while engagement targets survived every redesign, and the deactivation literature suggests the welfare gap is large enough to swamp any prompt. This is wrong if a firm can be shown to hold engagement targets and still ship binding defaults for years — that is, if governance substitutes for incentives.

The tail is not the harmed. The strongest case: heavy use is often the most endorsed use, and a deep tail holds devoted hobbyists alongside anyone whose use has become compulsive. It rests on a claim this page cannot settle: that endorsement and time are not reliably monotonic. It is wrong if the tail's endorsement gap is materially worse than the body's — 57.0 per cent against a base rate Veekshan has never measured outside the tail. That hole in the evidence is itself the finding.

Only a rule works. The strongest case: thresholds are soft numbers inside a hard incentive system, and the voluntary programmes its proponents cite have all eroded. It is wrong if a register with an external owner survives three consecutive down quarters. Nobody has published that test.

Pricing the control is itself the mistake. The least comfortable position, and seriously held: once ₹9.95 crore is written down it becomes a budget line to be argued down annually, and firms that never measured the cost have sometimes kept their controls longer. It is wrong if priced controls demonstrably outlive unpriced ones.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this ships a control and reports its adoption. Someone who has internalised it asks three questions first: who pays, where does the control bind, and who can move the number. They price the control before shipping it and publish the range rather than the flattering end. They expect the honest answer sometimes to be that the firm loses money, and say so in the room rather than discovering a model in which everyone wins. And they spend most of their effort on the register and the holdout, because that is what is still standing in eighteen months.

12. The two decisions

On Friday 16 October Gauresh committed all four controls to the whole base from Monday 9 November, on by default, the ceiling raisable after 24 hours, with a 2 per cent permanent holdout and the range ₹9.95 to ₹22.04 crore in the board paper rather than Gurnoor's single point. His reasoning was that the controls bind on the users who pay, which is both what makes them real and what makes them expensive. Gandhali decided three days later not to move the score to weekly. She kept it daily, suppressed it until 8 a.m., capped the coach at two messages, removed the streak badge outright, and recorded in writing that the 13.4 per cent the score would cost on top of the cap she was keeping was more than she could yet carry — a judgement about her firm's survival, not a finding that the score was harmless.

Three questions. First, had Veekshan's week-12 retention gain been a loss of 1.2 points instead, what cost would you still accept for a 13.0-point endorsement gain, and who should have authority to accept it? Second, Gandhali kept a control she believes is doing harm because removing it costs 13.4 per cent of run-rate: what would have to change — evidence, scale, financing, regulation — for that answer to become indefensible? Third, which number in your own product is a wellbeing threshold that no register records and any growth team could move next quarter?

13. Going deeper

Applying the Hook to your product names the loop these controls counter, step by step; read it to see which step your thresholds leave unopposed. Push and notification strategy governs the trigger, where most loops begin and the cheapest wins sit. Managing the consumer trust ledger asks what a firm owes users whose time it has already taken. Habit formation and attention supplies the evidence on how fast a loop becomes automatic. The Hook model is the canonical four-step frame; external and internal triggers explains why removing a notification does not remove a trigger. Fogg behaviour model (B = MAT) gives the ability lever — most controls here are ability taxes. Variable rewards is the mechanism a 90-minute prompt interrupts. Investment and stored value explains why a streak holds a player who has stopped enjoying the game.
exp20v2-ethics.wellbeing:
Digital Wellbeing and Time Well Spent

1. The decision

On Thursday 8 October 2026, Sarita Chacko, head of product for the feed at Jambu, a Kochi-founded short-video and messaging app with 40 lakh daily active users, faced two numbers she could not reconcile. The first came from Suma Chowta, the data scientist who had run a 28-day experiment. A bundle of wellbeing controls (a break prompt after 45 minutes, quiet hours from 11 pm, and autoplay that pauses after three videos) cut average daily use by 5.0 per cent. The second came from Sathya Chalil, who runs growth. At ₹0.10 of advertising revenue per minute, that cut was worth ₹45.26 crore a year against a base of ₹905.2 crore. The controls were due for every user on Monday 2 November. Growth wanted them opt-in, inside settings, where few users ever go. Sarita's choice was between controls that let users win against Jambu's own hooks and controls that existed so Jambu could say it had them. Choosing the second would keep the revenue and lose the only reason a user might believe any control Jambu ever offered.

2. The idea

Digital wellbeing is the practice of designing a product so that the time and attention it takes are time and attention its users would, on reflection, agree to give. Time well spent is the standard that practice is judged by: not how long people stayed, but whether they are glad afterwards that they did. It was invented to answer a problem in how products are measured. An engagement metric (minutes, sessions, return visits) rises whenever a product captures attention, whether or not the user wanted to give it, so a team rewarded on that metric is paid to capture.

The mechanism being resisted has a long pedigree. B. F. Skinner's mid-century experiments showed that rewards arriving unpredictably sustain repetitive behaviour more stubbornly than rewards that arrive on schedule. Nir Eyal's Hooked (2014) turned that finding into a design method, the hook: a loop of trigger, action, variable reward and investment that makes a behaviour habitual. Tristan Harris, then a Google design ethicist, circulated a 2013 deck urging designers to respect users' attention and in 2016 began campaigning under the name Time Well Spent; the Center for Humane Technology followed in 2018, the year Google and Apple shipped Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time on their phones.

The sentence Sarita could repeat in a meeting: “We count a minute as ours only if the user would give it to us again.”

3. How it actually works

The page's argument is that a wellbeing control is a counter-move to a specific step of the hook, and that each step must be matched. Figure 1 sets Jambu's loop beside the control aimed at it.

Figure 1. Jambu's hook loop (clockwise, numbers 1 to 4) and the control matched to each step.

Walk the loop with a Jambu user. The trigger is a notification that a friend has posted; a weekly budget on notifications attacks it at any hour, and quiet hours silence it after 11 pm. The action is opening the app, and autoplay lowers its cost to nothing, since the next video starts without a decision; the pause restores a decision. The variable reward is the unpredictable quality of the next clip, which is why a stopping point must interrupt it. The investment is the follows, posts and daily streak the user has built, which make leaving feel like loss.

Practitioners leave four steps implicit. A control's default matters more than its existence, because most users keep defaults. Its bypass must be cheap, or it patronises. Success must be measured as regret (how often users wish they had spent less time) rather than minutes alone. And someone other than the team paid on minutes must own the thresholds. Without that fourth step, the first three are quietly reversed the first time a quarter looks tight, because each threshold is a number the growth team can nudge by a few points without any announcement.

4. A worked example

Suma randomised 2,00,000 users into each arm of a 28-day test starting Monday 7 September. Table 1 shows what she found; “surveyed sessions” are sessions that ended with a one-question prompt, “Did you want to spend that time?”, and a regretted session is one answered “no”.

Before calling any gap a finding, compute its standard error. For minutes, 48 × √(2 ÷ 2,00,000) is 0.15, so a 3.1-minute gap is about 20 standard errors. For regret, √(0.31 × 0.69 ÷ 4,000 + 0.25 × 0.75 ÷ 4,000) is 1.0 point, so 6.0 points is six. Now the money. Sathya priced every minute at ₹0.10.
