The ₹905.2 crore in section 1 is the flat-rate base; at Pass 2 prices it is ₹826.4 crore. The cost falls by about 70 per cent (₹45.26 crore to ₹13.72 crore) because the controls remove the cheapest minutes. The lesson is not that the controls are nearly free; it is that a minute total alone cannot price them. Neither pass prices the 1,000 extra treatment users still active on day 28 (83,000 against 82,000): that omission is conservative if they stay, and 28 days cannot say whether they do.

5. Nuances a learner must know

Minutes are not harm, and regret is not harm either

A student watching three hours of lectures has spent time well. Regret is a better signal than duration, but it is self-reported, and it measures what users say about a session, not whether their lives improved.

Hooks and dark patterns are different things

A dark pattern deceives a user at a single decision point, such as a hidden unsubscribe link. A hook works across weeks and deceives no one. Fixing consent screens will not touch it.

Opt-in controls serve the already motivated

A control buried in settings is used mostly by people who needed it least. Defaults decide outcomes; that is why the quiet-hours rule must be on.

An average hides who is exposed

The 31 per cent regret share is a mean. Late-night users, and anyone for whom the app has crowded out sleep or work, may sit far above it. Cut the data by time band before concluding anything.

Device-level tools are not product-level answers

Android's Digital Wellbeing and Apple's Screen Time report time by app and cannot tell a lecture from a loop inside it. Only the product knows which of its own minutes are which, so the device layer is a floor, never a substitute for the product's own controls.

A 28-day test cannot speak to a year

Novelty fades. A prompt that works in week two may be dismissed by reflex in month six, and a retention gain at day 28 may not hold. This is why Jambu needs a long holdout.

A control can be a decoy

A company can ship a dashboard that reports usage and changes nothing, then cite it when criticised. The test is whether the control is on by default, whether it costs the company something, and whether anyone would notice if it were removed.

Ask who the control is for before relying on it

A thoughtful newcomer should ask whether the control serves the user, the regulator or the press release; whether the people it protects are the people who see it; and what number would make the team remove it. If no number would, it is a principle. If any would, the number matters.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

In consumer products, as at Jambu, the user is also the revenue source, so incentive and interest diverge most sharply: every minute removed is priced. In B2B software the buyer is the employer and the user a salaried employee, and time in product is often the wrong metric altogether; an expense tool succeeds when it is closed quickly, and the wellbeing risk is notification load on staff. In a marketplace there are two audiences: a delivery partner shown a streak bonus for another hour online is being hooked too, and the controls must cover supply as well as demand.

Stage matters as well. An early-stage team can read a few hundred regret answers by hand and has no metric orthodoxy to defend, so it can set defaults early. A large company has the data but also the incentive machinery: bonuses, quarterly targets and an advertising team that has promised a figure. There the decisive work is organisational, not design.

7. Common mistakes

Burying the control. From outside you would see a wellbeing page in settings that only a small fraction of users ever open. The misunderstanding is that availability equals help. The cheapest diagnostic is to count taps from the home screen and the share of eligible users who have ever seen it.

Celebrating lower minutes. The symptom is a dashboard that cheers a falling average. The misunderstanding is that less is automatically better, when a fall may reflect a worse product. Pair minutes with regret share and day-28 return in the same view.

A nudge that becomes a hook. The symptom is a break prompt that nearly everyone dismisses, with a bright “keep watching” button and a faint “stop”. The misunderstanding is that showing the prompt discharges the duty. Diagnose by reading the dismissal rate and giving both buttons equal weight.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Sarita's decision ships the controls on by default, with a one-tap way to continue. It publishes its cost under both price assumptions rather than the flattering one. It keeps a 2 per cent holdout for six months to learn what the 28-day window cannot. It reports regret share beside minutes to the same executives. And it gives a person outside growth the authority to veto a threshold change, so the rules cannot quietly erode when a quarter looks tight.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Sarita decided that the controls would reach everyone on Monday 2 November, on by default, with a 2 per cent holdout, and told Sathya plainly that the likely cost was ₹13.72 crore a year on Suma's late-night price assumption, against the ₹45.26 crore flat-rate figure Sathya used, which is not an upper bound. Her reasoning was that a control the user can turn off at any time is only trusted if it is real, and the 6.0-point fall in regret was the only evidence in the room about what users valued. She did not claim the cost was zero, and did not ask growth to pretend the interests align. Where they diverge, she chose the user.

Read next on push and notification strategy, since the trigger is where most of these loops begin, and then on managing the consumer trust ledger, which asks what a company owes users it has already taken time from.

Two questions to sit with. If the retention gain at day 28 had been a loss of 0.5 points, how much revenue loss would you accept for the regret reduction, and who should decide? And which of your own product's metrics would you stop reporting if it only ever went up when users were worse off?
case40v1-ethics.wellbeing:
Indian School of Business · Case 40 · Ethics, Persuasion & Trust

Veethi TechnologiesNinety-seven minutes, and a covenant measured in minutes

The company is fictional; the market and institutions around it are real.

1. Koramangala, Sunday night

At twenty past eleven on Sunday 29 November 2026, Gitanjali Mavlankar sat on the floor of her flat in Bengaluru, two laptops open and her phone face up between them. The Sunday digest her team had shipped in August had told her that morning, in its polite grey type, that she had spent ninety-seven minutes on Veethi the day before. She had not noticed ninety-seven minutes passing.

By six on Monday evening the board pack had to close. On Friday 4 December the board of Veethi Technologies Private Limited would ask what the company proposed to do about the time its users spent inside it, and whether the answer would survive a regulator, a school board or a newspaper reading it. Earlier, by Wednesday 2 December, Veethi had to give or withhold notice on a Dubai contract worth ₹31.0 crore a year.

Four options sat on the second laptop, drafted by a working group over nine days and read eleven times. Each was defensible in one sentence, she had decided, and none in two. What a pause costs a company whose investors measure it in minutes was the question Monday turned on.

2. How Veethi got here

Veethi began in 2019 in Lower Parel, Mumbai, as a Marathi-language video app built by Gurudas Mundkur, a former television distributor, and Gyandev Mhapsekar. By September 2026 it carried 48.0 million monthly active users across Hindi, Marathi, Bhojpuri, Telugu, Kannada and Bengali feeds, with product in Bengaluru, engineering in Pune and a head office in Mumbai. Revenue came from brand advertising, commission on live-commerce orders, and Veethi Live Studio, a white-label live-shopping stack sold to retailers (Exhibit 1).

The decision that constrains Monday was taken in March 2023, seven months before the Series C. The growth team removed the date-of-birth field from signup, replaced it with a single I am 13 or older checkbox, and completion rose 6.4 percentage points. The same release shipped Jaagte Raho, a streak reward that pays out only on a watch between 21:00 and 01:00. Minutes per daily active user climbed from the low thirties to the middle forties; both changes were credited in the Series C deck.

That round closed in October 2023. A second tranche of ₹220 crore was left undrawn, conditional on trailing-ninety-day minutes per daily active user holding at or above 38.0 at each quarter end to 31 March 2027 (Exhibit 5). Veethi therefore has no age data on the 33.12 million accounts created since March 2023, and a financing condition denominated in the quantity a wellbeing control is designed to reduce.

3. The industry

Short video in India in 2026 is fought over by Moj and Josh on one side and Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts on the other, and nobody in it has lost money by holding attention longer. Veethi's wedge is vernacular live commerce: a creator in Nanded sells to a viewer in Nanded, payment over UPI, the order fulfilled by a seller on ONDC rails. That has pulled it into the regulatory frame of the larger platforms. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 and its Rules, notified in November 2025, require verifiable parental consent before a child's data is processed and bar behavioural advertising directed at children, the main obligations biting from the middle of 2027; MeitY is expected to notify Veethi a Significant Data Fiduciary. ASCI's norms bind its creators.

In September 2026 a Maharashtra state school board wrote about night-time use by students sitting examinations, and a parents' collective in Pune published its own screen-time survey. Abroad, Live Studio sells in the Gulf, Singapore and the United States — the stack, not the feed. Its largest customer is Vrindavan Mart, a forty-one-store grocery chain in Dubai running a nightly live-shopping show for Indian expatriate households.

4. What happened, and what was believed

Saans shipped on Friday 14 August 2026: three opt-in controls — a nudge at sixty minutes, a Sunday digest, and Lights Out, a blackout window the user sets herself. The forecast was fifteen per cent adoption by the end of September. By 30 September 19,68,000 accounts, 4.1 per cent of monthly actives, had switched on at least one control, and 7,51,776 of them — 38.2 per cent — still had one on thirty days later.

Asked in September for the share of users under eighteen, the data team returned 2.3 per cent. On Monday 5 October Gitanjali commissioned a hand audit of 1,200 accounts from Nagpur installs, checked against signals independent of what the user typed (Exhibit 4).

Then the experiment. From Monday 19 October to Sunday 1 November four cells ran over 140,000 accounts in the Hindi and Marathi feeds (Exhibit 3, Panel A). Three were pre-registered; a fourth was added mid-flight. The headline that travelled was Cell C's: a pause costs 7.4 minutes a day. On Monday 16 November a two-line note came from Toronto.

There is also a collision nobody designed. Option 1 moves the Jaagte Raho payout out of the 21:00–24:00 band — the band Veethi sells hardest (Exhibit 2), and the band in which the Vrindavan Mart contract guarantees promotion of the client's live show, 21:00 to 23:30 IST, 19:30 to 22:00 in Dubai. On Tuesday 24 November Granthika Mithbaokar learned how the client reads that clause. Underneath sits a trend nobody can explain: minutes per daily active user have fallen for three consecutive quarters (Exhibit 5, Panel A).

5. The people

Gitanjali Mavlankar, 41, chief product officer, Bengaluru. A control nobody switches on is theatre: Saans 2.0 must be default-on. Her 2027 bonus vests on the tranche. Unsaid: she promised the Pune collective, in a room with no minutes taken, that defaults would change in January.

Gurudas Mundkur, 47, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai. He wants one page he can read aloud to the board and to a reporter unchanged. Unsaid: an investor has sounded him out about a secondary purchase and asked for the monthly minutes series.

Gyandev Mhapsekar, 44, co-founder, growth, Bengaluru. He quotes 7.4 minutes; a default cap spends headroom the company has not got. His targets are minutes and commission. Unsaid: forty-five was chosen because a 400-user pre-test at ninety moved nothing, and that pre-test is uncirculated.

Gulnaaz Malushte, 38, general counsel, New Delhi. Age assurance is unavoidable, and better before MeitY asks. Unsaid: outside counsel came back split and she forwarded only the half that agrees with her.

Gursimran Mahabal, 35, principal data scientist, Toronto. The October test cannot price what Option 1 proposes, she says; her standing rests on the measurement. Unsaid: she has an offer from a Canadian insurer and will not be there for the next one.

Gaurisha Murdeshwar, 36, design director, Berlin. The controls are the wrong unit of analysis; the ranking objective is the product. Unsaid: the 2025 Telugu re-rank in Exhibit 3, Panel B was her project, and she decided when it stopped.

Gaganpreet Mirashi, 48, head of global sales, New Jersey. He wants nothing shipped until three Studio deals close in the first quarter. Unsaid: two of them have already asked, in vendor review, about Veethi's under-eighteen policy.

Granthika Mithbaokar, 33, head of customer success, Singapore. Vrindavan Mart will accept a change if told early and in person; her variable pay turns on the renewal. Unsaid: the category head told her the nightly slot is why the contract exists.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Seven point four minutes. That is what a pause costs. Our floor is 38.0 and we are standing at 41.6. I am not signing a memo that spends 7.4 out of 3.6.”

Gyandev Mhapsekar, #growth, Tuesday 17 November, 11:20 IST

“Cell C removed autoplay as well as adding the pause. Cell B is autoplay alone. Cell D is the pause alone, over seven days, not fourteen. And we tested forty-five minutes. Option 1 proposes ninety.”

Gursimran Mahabal, replying, Wednesday 18 November, 02:10 IST — 15:40 Tuesday, Toronto

“We keep designing exits from a room we are still building. The ranking objective is the product. Not one of the four options touches it, and the one time we did, in the Telugu feed, we got a number nobody has repeated.”

Gaurisha Murdeshwar, email from Berlin, Thursday 19 November, 19:05 IST — 14:35 CET

“To protect a child you must first find the child. Verifiable parental consent is not optional for a user we know to be under eighteen. Nobody has put in writing what we must collect about forty-eight million to find the ones who are fourteen.”

Gulnaaz Malushte, note to the chief executive, Friday 20 November

“I asked their category head what happens if the nine o'clock slot moves. He said the slot is the contract. I have put nothing in writing and neither has he.”

Granthika Mithbaokar, chat, Tuesday 24 November, 12:10 SGT — 09:40 IST

“Give me one page. I do not need the right answer on Friday. I need to know which number you are betting the tranche on, and to be able to say it aloud.”

Gurudas Mundkur, by telephone, Sunday 29 November, 22:50 IST

8. The options as Gitanjali sees them

The working group's memo, drafted on the growth team's template, puts four options to the board, costed in Exhibit 6.

Option 1 — Saans 2.0, default-on. A ninety-minute daily limit by default, with a full-screen pause the user dismisses; Lights Out on by default from 00:00 to 06:00; the Jaagte Raho payout moved out of the 21:00–24:00 band. It applies to every account, and does not require Veethi to know anybody's age.

Option 2 — Minors-first, with age assurance. An age-assurance step at signup and on next launch for existing accounts, using DigiLocker-based verification where the user consents and a parental consent flow where the assessment returns a minor. Hard caps and a 22:00 blackout then apply only to accounts assessed under eighteen. Adults see what they see today.

Option 3 — Publish and tell. A weekly time report in the app, a quarterly public disclosure of minutes by hour band, and the Saans controls promoted but still opt-in. The ranking, the defaults and the Jaagte Raho window stay as they are.

Option 4 — Creator-side controls. A session-health dashboard for the top 40,000 creators, and a payout formula reweighted from watch duration to completed views and returning viewers. No user is shown a wall. The ranking objective, the defaults and the age question are untouched.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The pack closes at 18:00 IST on Monday 30 November; the board sits on Friday 4 December. Notice on the Vrindavan Mart contract, sixty days before the 31 January renewal, falls due on Wednesday 2 December — two days before the board can bless anything. The covenant is tested on the trailing ninety days at 31 December 2026, a window that opened on 3 October, and again at 31 March 2027. Cash stood at ₹188 crore on 30 September against a net outflow of ₹41 crore in the half year after capital expenditure and working capital, a little under ₹7 crore a month.

People are tighter than money. The identity squad in Pune is six engineers; the age-assurance build in Option 2 and the defaults work in Option 1 both need it, and it has one quarter. A ₹3.0 crore creator fund is already announced for the Makar Sankranti season, and the client's UAE subscriber data cannot be moved to Bengaluru.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 6 leaves the move of the Jaagte Raho payout out of the 21:00–24:00 band unpriced. Using Exhibit 2, what is the largest annual revenue that move could place at risk, and what does your figure assume?
  2. Exhibit 6 prices Option 2 from two shares of accounts. Rebuild that range from a share of minutes: what would you have to know, and which end would you take to the board?
  3. Exhibit 3, Panel A is the only circulated measurement of what a pause costs. What single figure would you carry into the pack as the minute cost of Option 1, and what have you assumed in choosing it?
  4. Gulnaaz Malushte argues that Option 2 cannot protect children without identifying them, and cannot identify them without processing more data about everyone. State that trade-off in the terms the DPDP Act uses, and say which way you would resolve it.
  5. Gaurisha Murdeshwar argues the controls are the wrong unit of analysis. If she is right, what is the decision really in front of the board, and whose targets must change for it to be taken?
  6. It is Monday morning, 30 November. What does Gitanjali Mavlankar do before 18:00, whom must she tell before 2 December, and what does she say to the board on Friday about the number she does not have?

11. A little after midnight

She opened the test build on her spare handset and triggered the forty-five-minute pause, to see what the dismissal looked like. It looked like a grey card with a soft round button. She dismissed it, and the feed returned a woman in Kolhapur selling copper vessels to four hundred people at half past midnight. The phone went face down. On the second laptop the board template was still open at the slide headed What we propose to do, and the slide was still empty, and in six hours the stand-up in Pune would want to know which of the builds to start.
exp40v2-ethics.trust.safety:
Trust and safety: the capacity you have against the arrival rate they choose

Abuse is not primarily a classification problem. It is the management of a scarce response capacity against an adversary who sets the arrival rate — and the quantity that matters is not accuracy but exposure.

1. Two decisions, five days apart

On Tuesday 13 October 2026, in Bengaluru, Esther Lonappan opened the capacity sheet she presents on Fridays. Lonappan directs trust and safety at Tevara, a short-video community with 1.8 crore monthly active users. Tevara takes 7,40,000 uploads a day, of which 46,100 of 7,40,000 (6.2 per cent) enter a review queue. Against that she has 120 reviewers, one shift each per day, 6.5 productive hours a shift: 780 reviewer-hours. Reviewing every queued item at current handling times would take 1,840. On Monday 2 November Tevara's creator payout programme goes live. A fourteen-day pilot in the Malayalam-language cohort took impersonation reports from 400 a day to 1,160 — 2.90 times. Extended platform-wide that is 8,700 items a day, 435 reviewer-hours, when the two categories she refuses to automate already hold 429 of the 780. She had until Friday to tell the growth team what she wanted, and had decided not to ask for headcount.

Five days earlier, on Thursday 8 October, Emil Lukose had a different problem in Mangaluru. Lukose runs product at Tappal, which sells 41,000 small businesses an assistant that drafts and sends customer messages over SMS and WhatsApp: 2.76 crore messages in September. A September audit found 246 accounts using it for loan-recovery intimidation, fake-invoice scams and brand impersonation — 0.6 per cent of the 41,000, sending 23,12,400 of the month's 2,75,79,880 messages (8.4 per cent). The people being harmed had never heard of Tappal — no account, no report button, no reason to look for one. All 198 complaints that reached Lukose in September arrived through the Department of Telecommunications' Chakshu facility and two operators' spam desks. His risk lead, Ebin Leelakrishnan, wanted to cap new accounts at 500 messages a day for their first fourteen days. Lukose's revenue lead called that a tax on every honest business in a hurry.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Trust and safety is the design and operation of the systems by which a product bounds, detects and responds to the harms its own affordances enable, inside a budget it does not control. Four harm families recur: fraud against the platform, scams against users, harassment between users, and content harm to third parties and the public. The discipline was invented because customer service could not absorb it. In the late 1990s eBay and PayPal found that fraud arrived faster than agents could be hired and had to be answered in the product — in pricing, limits and holds — rather than in a queue. In India, safe harbour under section 79 of the Information Technology Act 2000, narrowed by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal (2015) and conditioned by the 2021 Intermediary Guidelines, makes an intermediary's protection depend on the quality of its own response machinery.

Three schools disagree substantively. The risk-engineering school, descended from fraud analytics, would sign the proposition that every enforcement decision should carry a measurable expected cost; it would not sign that some categories must be actioned regardless of what measurement says. The governance school, descended from policy and law, would sign that power over speech and livelihood requires notice, reasons and a route back; it would not sign that a stated false-action rate is acceptable because the expected total is minimised. The architectural school, descended from security, would sign that an affordance which cannot be policed should not ship; it would not sign that review capacity can be scaled to meet demand. Lonappan was trained in the first, is held to account by the second, and on 13 October acted like the third.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic of a queue you cannot staff

Expert practice begins with a taxonomy that assigns each harm class a severity tier, an action and a handling time. Handling time is the step usually left implicit, and it is the one that decides everything. Table 1 is Lonappan's September sheet.

Harm classTierItems/dayMin/itemHours needed Hours givenHuman capacity/dayTo automation/day
Credible threat to a person11,4009210.02311,5400
Child safety190012180.01989900
Targeted harassment26,0004400.02203,3002,700
Scam promotion24,8005400.0901,0803,720
Impersonation33,0003150.0255002,500
Spam / engagement manipulation430,0001500.01696029,040
Total / average—46,1002.391,840.07808,37037,960

Table 1. Tevara's review demand and allocation, mean day in September 2026. Hours needed = items × minutes ÷ 60, the staffing at which service equals arrivals. Human capacity = hours given × 60 ÷ minutes. The Min/item average is pooled (1,10,400 minutes ÷ 46,100 items = 2.39), not a mean of rates. Capacity exceeds arrivals in the two Tier-1 rows by design, so capacity and automation sum to 230 a day more than arrivals — deliberate Tier-1 headroom, not a double count.

Write the queue formally and the conclusion is forced. For a class with arrival rate λ items a day and human service rate μ items a day, utilisation is ρ = λ/μ. Little's Law, L = λW, relates mean queue length to mean wait; a steady state exists only when ρ < 1. Harassment runs at ρ = 6,000/3,300 = 1.82, scam at 4,800/1,080 = 4.44, spam at 30,000/960 = 31.25. Above one there is no mean wait to improve: the backlog grows at λ − μ a day, 29,040 a day for spam, and any service-level promise attached to it is arithmetic fiction. Figure 2 is simply that line drawn.

The first mechanic is allocation; the second is choosing what not to look at. Tier 1 takes 2,300 of 46,100 items (5.0 per cent) and 429 of the 780 hours; humans dispose 8,140 of 46,100 items (17.7 per cent) in total. The second-order effect teams discover late: reviewers' decisions are the training labels, so the categories you staff thinly produce noisy labels, and the classifier you then rely on in exactly those categories is the worst one you have. Capacity scarcity does not merely slow enforcement; it degrades the thing meant to replace it.

4. When the frame holds, and when it misleads

The capacity frame rests on three claims, each testable on a company. First: review demand exceeds review capacity at the current action mix. True at Tevara by a factor of 2.36. False at Tappal, where 198 complaints a month is an afternoon's work for one analyst: its binding constraint is signal, not capacity, and telling Lukose to optimise his queue sends him to the wrong meeting. Second: the harmed party holds an account and a reporting path. True at Tevara. False at Tappal, where the harmed party is a stranger holding a phone. Third: exposure is mediated by a distribution mechanism the firm controls. True at Tevara, where ranking decides who sees what. Only partly true at Tappal, which controls send rate but not delivery — each message lands whole on first contact.

That third failure is where the frame misleads. Exposure-bounding buys time, and time is worth buying only when harm accumulates over an interval. A single threatening message to a single person is complete on arrival; there is no interval, so demotion, holds and staged reach are worth nothing, and an expected-cost calculation that trades a few of those against many wrongful removals is answering a question nobody asked. This is why Tier 1 at Tevara is run at ρ = 0.91 rather than optimised: for irreversible harm the correct posture is slack, which looks like waste on any dashboard measuring utilisation.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature firms actually do

Multi-product firms find enforcement keyed to the wrong object. Tevara's strike ledger is keyed to videos; its live-audio product has its own, and repeat offenders live in the seam. Mature firms keep a person-level enforcement ledger and accept that it is leaky. Two-sided products face a worse version: suspending a Tappal sender strands that sender's own customers mid-order, so practitioners suspend the capability and leave the account alive. In regulated settings the obligation splits: the Reserve Bank's digital-lending directions make recovery-call conduct the lender's compliance problem while the message leaves Tappal's infrastructure, and the telecom registry Tappal must use gives it a verified sender header but no conduct record. Hardware is harder still: there is no delete key, the levers are firmware and the sales channel, and the recall is the only removal.

AI-native products invert the structure: the model is both enforcement mechanism and abuse vector. A guardrail tuned on the prompt is evaded at the output. Mature practice runs separate input and output classifiers and treats a sudden fall in refusal rate as a detection failure rather than a product improvement. At the organisational seam the tell is ownership of the rate limiter: trust and safety reports through legal or operations, while λ is set by growth and μ by engineering. A programme that cannot ship a rate limit inside a quarter lacks the levers its name implies.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A service level with no service rate

Competent teams publish "harassment reviewed within 24 hours". An expert asks for μ in items a day and compares it with λ. Where ρ exceeds one the published figure describes the lucky items, and the queue's median age rises even as handle time falls. The tell is a dashboard reporting handle time but never arrivals against capacity.

Prevalence with no weighting

Tappal's abuse is 0.6 per cent of accounts and 8.4 per cent of messages — fourteen times, because abusive accounts send more. Both are true and they support opposite decisions: the first says the problem is marginal, the second that it is nearly a tenth of the product's output. An expert never quotes a prevalence without naming its weighting unit.

Detection that assumes the victim is a user

Report-driven detection is blind wherever the harmed party has no account. Tappal measured it: twelve accounts suspended in August had sent 2,31,000 messages and drawn 21 complaints, one per 11,000. The tell is a category flat for six quarters while the product grew: flatness is the signature of a measurement ceiling, not of control.

The reversibility illusion

The obvious reading is that a gentler action justifies a looser threshold. It does not: scaling an action's depth and duration scales the harm averted and the honest reach suppressed by the same factor, so the exchange rate stays p/(1−p). A reversible action buys an option — a window in which a second signal can arrive and the bet be placed again at a better price.

Reviewer agreement is the ceiling on everything

Tevara double-reviewed 400 harassment items in September; the two reviewers agreed on 316 of 400 (79.0 per cent). With each marking 30 per cent violating, chance agreement is 0.58 and Cohen's kappa is 0.50. A classifier reported at 88 per cent agreement with that label is measured against something two trained humans reproduce four times in five. Score it separately on the 316 agreed items and the 84 contested ones.

Appeals allocate accuracy to whoever can afford to ask

At Tevara, 46 per cent of actioned creators in the top earnings decile appealed; 3 per cent in the bottom decile did, and the overturn rate was 38 per cent in both. Appeals are therefore not an error measure but a demand curve, spending the scarcest reviewers on the richest users. The honest error estimate comes from re-reviewing a random sample of actions nobody appealed.

The report button is an adversarial surface

In the week of 14 July 2026, 1,240 harassment reports against 18 Tevara creators arrived from 47 accounts, about 26 each. The expert's reflex on a report spike is reporter concentration and history before content: a rule triggered by a count of reports has handed its denominator to the adversary.

Policy debt

Policy is written after incidents, so clauses accumulate faster than reviewers absorb them. Tevara's harassment policy went from 11 clauses in January 2026 to 34 in September; double-reviewed agreement fell from 86 per cent on 400 items in January to 79 per cent on 400 in September, a 7-point fall and 2.6 times the 2.7-point standard error of the difference. Rising policy precision and falling enforcement consistency are one event seen from two desks.

7. How the picture changes by product type and stage

In consumer social products exposure is the variable, so ranking is the enforcement system and removal is a special case of it. In B2B and enterprise software accounts are few, contracted and identifiable, so abuse is handled through verification, audit trails and account managers rather than queues — except that AI features broke this: one seat can now emit third-party harm at machine speed, which is Tappal's position. Marketplaces have two victims and two kinds of error at once, and must treat sellers as customers while screening them as suspects. Hardware has no delete key. AI products add harm classes with no content to remove and make the model its own adversary.

Stage changes which arithmetic binds. A seed-stage company with a hundred accounts should read everything by hand: full human review is a luxury of small λ. The decisive moment is the quarter in which λ crosses μ, because it arrives without announcement and the first symptom is a backlog, not a complaint. At scale the problem becomes consistency across hundreds of reviewers and several languages, plus statutory response machinery. What does not change, said plainly: the capacity arithmetic and the ladder of actions ordered by depth and duration are identical everywhere.

8. Three worked examples

Demotion as an option, not as mercy

Tevara's scam classifier dispositions 3,720 items a day that no human will see. At a measured precision of 61 per cent, 2,269 of them are violating and 1,451 are not. Reported videos accrue a mean 260 views an hour over their first 72 hours, so demotion at 92 per cent suppression for a 31-hour window costs a wrongly demoted video 7,415 views against 18,720 for a removal running the full window — 2.52 times. The exchange rate is unchanged; the stake is smaller. The value is in the second bet: of the 600 demoted items a day that pick up an independent signal inside the window, a sample found 142 of 160 violating (88.8 per cent).

A cap that bounds harm without classifying it

Of Tappal's 246 abusive accounts, 168 had registered within the previous 30 days: 168 of the 3,100 September registrations (5.4 per cent) against 78 of 37,900 established (0.2 per cent), a ratio of 26. Those 168 sent 14,44,800 messages over 1,848 account-days before suspension, 782 a day. A 500-a-day cap would have allowed at most 9,24,000 — a floor of 36.0 per cent on the reduction in delivered harmful messages, since 31 of the 168 never exceeded 500 in a day. The arithmetic is not where the estimate will fail: registration is free, so the adversary's answer is more accounts.

Where it failed: a rule whose denominator belonged to the attacker

Tevara's auto-hold rule fired when three harassment reports arrived on one video inside sixty minutes. In July 2026 the campaign above held videos from 14 of the 18 targeted creators for a median 26 hours, about 6,760 views each and 87,880 across the 13 later cleared; one hold was upheld. The failure was not model quality: the trigger counted reports, a quantity the adversary produced at will. The five-week recovery made reports count once per reporter cluster and the trigger scale with reach. Re-run on July's logs it would have held 2 of the 18 while still firing on 2,585 of the 2,840 holds that month that review later upheld (91.0 per cent).

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Service-level theatre

Warning sign: queue depth rising while median handle time improves. Diagnostic: what is μ in items a day, and does it exceed λ? Cost late: the backlog becomes unrecoverable and is auto-closed in bulk, destroying the label stream and the audit trail in one afternoon.

Enforcement drift

Warning sign: policy clause count rising, reviewer agreement falling. Diagnostic: re-label 200 archived decisions under today's policy and measure the overturn rate. Cost late: no decision can be defended to a regulator, because the firm's own reviewers do not reproduce it.

A blind harm class

Warning sign: a category flat for six quarters while the product grows. Diagnostic: where would a report come from, and does that person have an account? Cost late: the firm learns the problem's size from a journalist or a notice, and must then build measurement and remedy under a deadline.

Capacity bought as headcount

Warning sign: a hiring plan that scales linearly with volume. Diagnostic: what share of items is disposed by a reversible action, at what cost each? Cost late: unit economics never improve, and the first budget cut removes the Tier-1 slack because it looks idle.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Act first, adjudicate later. The strongest form: harm to a victim is irreversible while a wrongly actioned user can appeal, and exposure accrues in the first hours — 260 views an hour at Tevara. So act wide and fast at modest precision, and invest in the route back. It rests on an asymmetry of irreversibility, and is wrong if the route back does not work: if only 3 per cent of low-earning creators appeal, removal is irreversible for the people least able to absorb it.

Procedure before precision. The strongest form: a platform exercising state-like power over speech and livelihood owes notice, reasons and an appeal before acting; opaque enforcement produces quiet exit and invites statutory capture of policy. It is wrong where procedure costs latency the victim pays: a credible threat cannot wait for a notice period, which is why even its advocates carve out Tier 1 and then argue where Tier 1 ends.

Design it out. The strongest form: moderation is a tax levied on bad architecture, and the capacity arithmetic proves it, since any class with ρ above one must eventually change λ. Remove the affordance: no unsolicited contact from strangers, no unmetered reach for new accounts. It rests on the one piece of this field's mathematics nobody disputes, and is wrong when the affordance is the product: Tappal sells the ability to message many people quickly, and a firm cannot design out what it charges for.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this argues about thresholds. Someone who has internalised it asks what the action is, how deep and how long, who bears the error, and whether a second signal can arrive before the action becomes permanent. They quote a prevalence with its weighting attached and a service level with its service rate beside it. They treat reviewer agreement as the ceiling on every model claim. They compute a standard error before calling a gap a finding, and say "that is inside noise" where it is unwelcome. They know which harm classes they cannot see at all, and say so in the same sentence as the numbers they can. And they spend their political capital on λ — on registration friction, reach gating, rate limits — rather than on headcount, because headcount is the only lever that does not compound.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Lonappan did not ask for reviewers. She asked the growth team to gate payout eligibility behind account verification, on the pilot's own evidence: 684 of the 760 extra impersonation items a day (90.0 per cent) came from accounts registered during the pilot. An account that cannot earn until verified removes the payoff rather than the content. She reclassified impersonation from removal to earnings-hold plus demotion, which needs no notice draft and falls from 3.0 to 1.2 minutes an item. The programme's marginal volume is 8,700 less 3,000, or 5,700 extra items a day: 285 reviewer-hours at 3.0 minutes, 114 at 1.2, and 11.4 if the eligibility gate strips from the platform the same 90.0 per cent share of extra items the pilot cohort showed. And she replaced the 24-hour harassment service level with a published service rate: 3,300 of 6,000 items a day seen by a human. Evita Lasrado, Tevara's head of policy, signed the first two and objected to the third: publishing μ tells the adversary where nobody is looking.

Lukose shipped the cap — 500 messages a day for fourteen days, liftable on business verification — and accepted that it would bind roughly 124 of a month's 3,100 new registrations (4.0 per cent). He paired it with the lever Leelakrishnan had not proposed: a one-tap reporting link in every message footer, which in a 2,00,000-message test (two arms of 1,00,000) cut replies from 7,200 per lakh to 6,800 — 0.4 points, 3.6 times a 0.11-point standard error that treats messages as independent when in fact they cluster by account — and raised report yield from one per 11,000 harmful messages to one per 2,900.

1. Tappal's abuse is 0.6 per cent of accounts and 8.4 per cent of messages. Which belongs in the board pack, and what does that commit you to measuring next quarter?

2. Lonappan runs Tier 1 at ρ = 0.91 and spam at 31.25. Defend the slack to a finance director who can see two queues idle while another has a backlog.

3. If publishing a service rate tells the adversary where you are not looking, and withholding it lets your own organisation believe an arithmetically impossible promise, which cost would you take?

13. Going deeper

Accountability for what products do to people is the frame this sits inside: why a firm owes anything to a stranger it never contracted with. Content moderation and policy is where clause count turns into handling time. Guardrails and safety layers apply the same queue to model outputs, where λ is your own generation volume. Fraud and risk models supplies the scores and explains why precision is borrowed from the population a classifier is pointed at. User-generated content and trust and trust, ratings and reviews build the reputation layer that lets you act on accounts instead of items. Habit formation and attention, the Hook model and external and internal triggers explain how much of λ a product chooses. The Fogg behaviour model (B = MAT), variable rewards and investment and stored value close the loop: ability is the friction lever, and stored value is why a ban is expensive for the right users and free for the wrong ones.
case40v1-ethics.trust.safety:
Pavali Commerce: Three Weeks to Diwali

An Indian social-commerce marketplace decides what to do about the sellers it cannot see

1. Sunday night, Bengaluru

At 11:40 p.m. on Sunday 18 October 2026, Bhoomi Ikhare was still at the long table in Pavali Commerce's Indiranagar office, the air-conditioning off since ten. On her laptop sat eleven slides for the board meeting in Pune at 9:30 next morning. Ten were finished. The eleventh was titled Recommendation and held one bullet, which read <to be filled>.

Ikhare had run Product, Trust and Marketplace Integrity since the August board paper on fraud created the function — a paper she had written. Since then the complaint queue had not stopped growing, a three-city pilot had produced numbers her own data lead would not sign, and Diwali was on 8 November, three weeks away, with the festive code freeze beginning on 26 October. What she asked for on Monday was what Pavali would carry through its biggest selling fortnight.

The question put to her was simple: hold seller payouts nationally, or not. What she had was two ledgers of what looked like one fraud, differing by a factor of twenty, a model that would hold seven sellers outside the confirmed-bad set for every one inside it, a Dubai contract forbidding what the model implied, and a field team in Nagpur that had stopped forwarding complaints because, as its head put it, nothing good happened to the people who sent them.

2. How Pavali got here

Pavali Commerce Private Limited was founded in Pune in 2021 by Bhoopesh Ingaonkar on an observation about small-town trade: the person who sells to a household in Jalna is a woman that household already knows. Pavali gave her a catalogue, a shipping network and a margin. She brought the customers, in the places she already had them — her WhatsApp and Instagram groups and her building's women's association. By September 2026, 2,86,000 resellers had placed at least one order in the month, and Exhibit 1 shows where they were.

One decision from February 2024 constrains everything on Ikhare's eleventh slide. Pavali had to choose whether a reseller's buyer paid Pavali or paid the reseller. Forcing payment into the app would have made every rupee visible, and would also have required Pavali to hold customer money at scale and register as a payment aggregator with the Reserve Bank of India. Ingaonkar chose the other path. The reseller collects — cash, or a UPI transfer to her own handle — and pays Pavali for the goods. It was right for growth in towns where nobody wanted to type a card number into an app they had heard of last week. It is also why most of the money in Exhibit 2 never touched Pavali's rails, and why Pavali cannot reverse a rupee of it.

3. The industry

Reseller-led commerce in India is a volume business built on cheap data and vernacular interfaces. Meesho built the category; Flipkart and Reliance Retail have reseller programmes; ONDC has opened catalogue and logistics plumbing to anyone willing to integrate. Nobody competes on price alone: the margin a reseller keeps is the product. What a reseller actually sells, when she asks a neighbour for ₹600 before the parcel arrives, is her own standing in a group of forty women. That is the asset abuse destroys.

The regulatory surface is crowded. Pavali is an intermediary under the Information Technology Rules of 2021, which oblige it to name a grievance officer and open an appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee for a complainant it leaves unsatisfied; the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules of 2020 require a consumer complaint resolved within one month. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 governs what it may collect and how long it may keep it — which matters, because every version of the plan Ikhare is considering collects a selfie video from women who have already been verified once. And since April 2026 Pavali has licensed its platform to Pearlmont Retail Group LLC in Dubai, which brings a second jurisdiction, a second set of resellers, and a contract.

4. What happened

Figure 1 sets out the sequence. Complaints about advance payments that produced no parcel have existed since Pavali had resellers; the taxonomy got a dedicated off-platform payment code in November 2025. Through the spring of 2026 volume rose with the business and nobody treated it as a category. In February 2026 Pavali launched Pavali Live, video selling with in-app chat, and reseller acquisition accelerated.

By June the curve had steepened enough that Ikhare's team formed a view: popular resellers' accounts were being taken over and buyers were paying the thief. Pavali shipped device-binding and OTP hardening that month. In July support added a sub-code, group-admin impersonation, and the shape of the problem changed: the accounts named in complaints were mostly not hijacked. They were new accounts, opened with borrowed or rented documents, which had joined buying groups, built two weeks of plausible presence, collected advance payments for a Diwali-dated catalogue, and gone quiet. Exhibit 2 shows that sub-code only from July, because that is when it began to exist.

Two later findings bear on the August board paper. First, the paper reported "₹5.5 crore of fraud on Pavali" for the five months to 31 August. That figure is the buyer-stated column of Exhibit 2 — ₹549.6 lakh typed into a complaint form by people who had lost money, on complaints the ledger itself codes as off-platform payment — money that left a buyer's bank for a handle Pavali does not operate. A September de-duplication pass found 2,396 duplicate records among the 13,382 complaints logged from July to September, 17.9 per cent. Second: of the 13,617 off-platform complaints in the April-September window, 9,842 named an account that had never completed a single order on Pavali, 72.28 per cent of them.

5. The people

Bhoomi Ikhare, VP Product, Trust and Marketplace Integrity, Bengaluru. Owns Monday's recommendation and has stated no position to anyone. Her function exists because of the August paper, and the board remembers the ₹5.5 crore. She has not told it that she wrote that slide.

Bhoopesh Ingaonkar, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Wants the full package shipped before Diwali: "we are not going to be the app where women get cheated." His incentive is a Series C conversation that reopens in January. He has not circulated the lead investor's diligence list, which names trust and safety as a gating item.

Bhumit Irvekar, Director of Risk Data Science, Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Bengaluru. Built the v4 model and will not endorse the pilot as evidence for it. Wants a six-week randomised holdout, which puts launch past Diwali and past his own annual review. He has not pointed out that the cohort used to choose the 0.75 cut-off is the cohort Exhibit 5 is scored on.

Bhavinee Ilwale, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Her queue stands at thirty-one days against a one-month obligation, and she wants payouts held so the money is still there when a complaint is substantiated. She has not put in writing that 148 of the pilot's 774 appeals were never decided: they aged past seventy-two hours, released automatically, and appear in neither the upheld count of Exhibit 4 nor any rejected count.

Bhavyata Idgunkar, Principal Designer, Berlin, three and a half hours behind Bengaluru until the clocks change on 25 October. Her team owns the chat layer, and she argues it is the only intervention that touches the mechanism, while a payout hold "charges the poorest sellers for the platform's inability to see." In her own eleven moderated sessions in Nagpur, seven of the eleven participants got a handle past the block inside the session.

Balwant Itkar, Head of Sales, Platform Licensing, New Jersey. Opposes any payout change: the Pearlmont contract promises seller settlement within twenty-four hours of delivery confirmation, and he has two Gulf pitches live. He has not told Ingaonkar that Pearlmont's own compliance team asked for a payout hold in the Gulf in September.

Bhanu Irkhede, Head of Seller Community, Nagpur. Her objection is arithmetic: the mean September payout per active reseller was ₹5,989, and a seventy-two-hour hold in the fortnight resellers buy Diwali stock is working capital they do not have. She has a list of forty-one group administrators her field team believes are running the scheme, given on a promise of anonymity, and has not handed it over.

Bhavdeep Iravadkar, General Counsel and Grievance Officer, Mumbai. Holds that the binding risk is the one-month clock rather than the fraud: three complaints have already escalated to the Grievance Appellate Committee. He also holds that selfie-video re-verification needs a purpose and retention period Pavali has not written down.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 totals ₹831.3 lakh of buyer-stated loss over six months, and codes 13,617 of its 19,687 complaints, 69.17 per cent, as off-platform payment. Exhibit 3, covering the same six months, totals ₹40.3 lakh of disputed value. At the 0.75 cut-off Irvekar's team proposed — the second bar of Exhibit 6 — 6,760 sellers are held, 2.36 per cent of actives, carrying ₹518.7 lakh of payouts, 3.03 per cent of the month's payout value; 798 of the 6,760 are in the confirmed-bad set, a precision of 11.80 per cent.

7. Voices

"Hubballi is the only city where you shipped one thing. Nineteen complaints became sixteen. Three fewer on a base of nineteen is seven-tenths of a Poisson standard deviation. Put it on a slide if you insist; I will not call it an effect." Bhumit Irvekar, pilot read-out, 22 September
"Two-thirds of the holds that were appealed, we reversed. So we were wrong about those women, and they found out on a Tuesday when their money did not arrive. I keep being asked for the precision of the model. Ask me for the precision of the apology." Bhanu Irkhede, internal thread, 29 September
"We cannot promise Pearlmont a twenty-four-hour settlement and then put a seventy-two-hour hold in the same code path. Either the Gulf is carved out, in which case our story is that we protect Indian buyers less, or it is not, in which case read clause 9.4." Balwant Itkar, email to Ingaonkar, 6 October
"Every option on this list acts on a seller account. The woman collecting the money is in a group of two hundred people on a different app, and she is often not a seller at all until the week she decides to be. Who exactly are we holding?" Bhanu Irkhede, chat to Ikhare, 15 October
"I will take a selfie video from every reseller on the platform if it stops this. I would like somebody to write down, on one page, what we do with the videos afterwards, for how long, and who may look at them. Until that page exists I am not signing the DPIA." Bhavdeep Iravadkar, legal review, 12 October

8. The options as Ikhare sees them

Option A — ship the package nationally before the freeze. A seventy-two-hour payout hold on every seller scoring 0.75 or above, mandatory selfie-video re-verification before release, and the chat layer blocking payment handles and phone numbers in Pavali's own messaging. On September's population that holds 6,760 sellers a month carrying ₹518.7 lakh of payouts, and leaves ₹51.87 lakh of standing float, three days in thirty of the held value. Running cost is about ₹9.00 lakh a month: ₹6.70 lakh of appeal review at ₹190 a case on roughly 3,526 appeals, and ₹2.30 lakh of selfie checks at ₹34 each on 6,760 sellers. It needs 11 engineer-weeks. It does not change what happens inside a group that never opens Pavali.

Option B — hold the top band only. The 0.90 cut-off: 1,840 sellers, ₹146.2 lakh of payouts held, 486 of them in the confirmed-bad set and 1,354 not. It needs 4 engineer-weeks and ships before the freeze. It leaves 632 of the 1,118 confirmed-bad sellers unheld, and it leaves untouched any account too new to have a score.

Option C — leave payouts alone and act on the payment loop. Ship the chat layer, and add a buyer assurance of up to ₹2,000 an order on anything paid through Pavali's checkout. Priced on September's Exhibit 3 column, it covers ₹11.0 lakh of disputed value against ₹7.9 lakh already paid in goodwill, an incremental ₹3.1 lakh for the month, on the assumption that no disputed order exceeds the ₹2,000 cap and that seller recovery is unchanged. It needs 6 engineer-weeks. It pays nothing on money sent to a handle outside Pavali, which is the population Exhibit 2 counts.

Option D — hold the product still and move the governance. No payout change before Diwali. Publish a transparency report with Exhibits 2 and 3 side by side, seat an external panel of three to read rejected appeals, and cut the grievance clock to seven days by hiring four reviewers in Pune at ₹38,000 a month, ₹1.52 lakh in all. It needs no engineer-weeks. It leaves every mechanism in Exhibits 2 to 5 running as it is through the festive fortnight.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 9:30 a.m. on Monday 19 October in Pune. The festive code freeze runs from 26 October to 12 November; Diwali falls on 8 November. Engineering has seven people on the trust surface and one week before the freeze, which is 7 engineer-weeks, of which 2 are already committed to the Pearlmont integration, leaving 5.

The Pearlmont licence is ₹14.4 crore a year, ₹1.20 crore a month, plus a platform fee of 1.8 per cent on Gulf GMV, which on September's ₹31.6 crore was ₹56.88 lakh. Clause 9.4 sets seller settlement at twenty-four hours from delivery confirmation and a penalty of 2 per cent of the monthly licence fee, ₹2.40 lakh, for each month in breach. Pavali is not a payment aggregator and cannot reverse a UPI transfer between two private handles. Under the E-Commerce Rules the grievance clock is one month and Ilwale's queue is at thirty-one days. Irkhede's list of forty-one names was collected on a promise of anonymity, and Pavali's in-app chat logs are retained for ninety days, so nothing in a complaint logged before about 20 July can be checked against a conversation.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, what did Pavali lose between April and September 2026, and on whose books? Which ledger belongs in a board paper, and what would you write underneath it?
  2. Exhibit 5 gives a precision of 11.80 per cent at the 0.75 cut-off. What has to be true about the way "confirmed bad" was labelled for that figure to carry the meaning the board will take from it?
  3. What can and cannot be concluded from Exhibit 4 about the payout hold alone, and what would you have had to run instead?
  4. Price Option A and Option B for a reseller in Hubballi and for Pearlmont in Dubai. Who bears each cost, and which of those costs ever appears in Pavali's own profit and loss?
  5. What would an option that did not act on a seller account look like, and what evidence on these pages would tell Ikhare whether it is better?
  6. It is 9:30 on Monday morning. What should Ikhare do, and what exactly should she say to the board about the ₹5.5 crore, about Irkhede's forty-one names, and about what she still does not know?

11. Sunday night, continued

At ten past midnight Ikhare's phone showed a message from Irkhede, sent from Nagpur: a photograph of a handwritten page from a reseller's order book, two columns of names and amounts in Marathi, and under it the line she asked me what she should tell the people in her group. Ikhare put the phone face down. The eleventh slide was still open, and the cursor was still in the bullet. Outside, somebody was testing a string of Diwali lights against the balcony railing, and they came on all at once.
exp20v2-ethics.trust.safety:
Trust and Safety

Designing for the worst users without punishing the rest

1. A Monday in October

On Monday 12 October 2026, Rajiv Bangera opened a spreadsheet he did not want to read. Bangera ran trust and safety at Ishtam, a Kochi-based marketplace where people sell used phones, furniture and two-wheelers to strangers. The platform received about 1,00,000 new listings a week. A random sample of 5,000 incoming listings, drawn before any scoring and read line by line by his reviewers, had found 100 that were scams: a price too good to be true, a request to pay an "advance" by UPI, and a seller who vanished afterwards. That is 2.0 per cent, give or take 0.4 points at 95 per cent confidence. The audit sample also carried a second fact: 1,000 of the 5,000 listings came from accounts under 30 days old, and 70 of the 100 scams were among them.

Diwali fell on 8 November. Last year traffic had doubled for six weeks, and scammers had noticed. Ranjini Bhandary, who led seller support, wanted the opposite of what Bangera's fraud analyst wanted. The analyst proposed removing listings automatically at a stricter score. Bhandary pointed out that each wrongly removed listing was a real family selling a real sofa, and that her queue already held 400 angry tickets a week. If Bangera tightened too far, honest sellers would leave before the season. If he did not, buyers would lose money in the one fortnight they were most likely to try Ishtam for the first time. He had until Friday.

2. The idea

Trust and safety is the discipline of anticipating how a product's worst users will abuse it, and building detection, response and policy so that abuse is contained at a cost honest users can bear. The abuse comes in families: fraud (taking money by deceit), scams (fraud aimed at users rather than the platform), harassment (targeted hostility between users) and content harm (material that injures people or breaks the law).

The function took shape in the late 1990s, when online marketplaces and payments companies such as eBay and PayPal found that fraud was a product problem, not a customer-service problem, and set up teams that sat with engineers. Its founding insight is that open systems attract exploitation in proportion to their usefulness. The function now spans fraud analysts, policy writers, reviewers, engineers and lawyers, but its logic is economic: abuse is never zero, and the only question is who bears the residual. The sentence Bangera could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: every rule is a price paid by honest users for protection from dishonest ones, so we should set that price deliberately rather than discover it from complaints.

3. How it works

Figure 1 shows the mechanism Bangera inherited. Every listing receives a risk score, a number from a model or rule set estimating how likely it is to be abusive. Two cut-offs divide the scores into three bands. Above the upper one, the listing is removed automatically; below the lower one, it goes live; in between, a human reviewer decides. Removed sellers may appeal, and a second reviewer looks again.

Practitioners usually leave three steps implicit, and each is a place where a team's real behaviour departs from its diagram. First, someone must decide what counts as abuse, in writing, before any model is trained; the written policy is the label the model learns. Second, the reviewers' decisions become the training data, so reviewer inconsistency becomes model inconsistency. Third, the dashed line matters most, because it is the main route by which the system hears about scams that went live: they surface through buyer reports and refunds, weeks later, and those late labels are the main way it learns what it missed.

4. A worked example

Bangera had two candidate cut-offs for automatic removal. Cut-off A, the current one, caught 70 per cent of scams and wrongly removed 1 per cent of honest listings. Cut-off B, stricter, caught 85 per cent and wrongly removed 3 per cent. Those rates came from replaying each cut-off over the audit's labelled incoming listings, so the 70 and 85 per cent have scam listings as their base and the 1 and 3 per cent have honest listings as theirs. He priced the errors: a scam that goes live costs ₹6,000 on average in refunds and goodwill over the following 30 days; a wrongly removed honest listing costs ₹150 in expected lost seller activity. Both figures were estimates from last year's tickets, and he said so on the slide.

Share of removals that were scams = scams removed divided by all removals, for example 1,400 / (1,400 + 980) = 58.8%. Costs are the counts above multiplied by the stated unit cost.

At the audited prevalence, B is cheaper by ₹15.06 lakh a week (37.47 less 22.41). The reasoning: moving from A to B removes 300 more scams, worth ₹18.00 lakh, at the price of 1,960 more wrongful removals (2,940 less 980), worth ₹2.94 lakh. B wins as long as it costs fewer than 40 extra honest removals per extra scam stopped (6,000 divided by 150). Here the ratio is 1,960 / 300, or 6.5.

Now change one input. Suppose a payment-protection feature drives prevalence from 2.0 to 0.5 per cent, with all rates unchanged. B still wins, but only by ₹1.51 lakh (10.49 less 8.98), and the ratio is 1,990 extra honest removals per 75 extra scams, about 26.5. More tellingly, seven of every eight removals under B (2,985 of 3,410) are now honest listings. B's margin shrinks from ₹15.06 lakh to ₹1.51 lakh, and a cost above about ₹226 per wrongful removal (₹4.50 lakh of extra scam loss divided by 1,990) would reverse the choice.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

Volume is not prevalence

"We removed 40 per cent more listings" says nothing about harm. Prevalence is the share of listings that are abusive, measured by random sampling. Sampled at intake it was 2.0 per cent; sampled among live listings it is lower once enforcement works, 600 of 97,620, or 0.61 per cent, under cut-off A. Removals measure your activity; prevalence measures your outcome.

The base rate decides precision

Precision is the share of actions that were right; recall is the share of abuse caught. Table 1 shows that with unchanged recall and error rates, precision under B fell from 36.6 to 12.5 per cent as scams became rarer. A classifier does not carry its precision with it; it borrows it from the population it is pointed at, which is why the same model can be excellent on new accounts and poor on veterans.

Policy and enforcement are different things

A rule that forbids advance payments is policy. What the model actually removes is enforcement. The gap between them, found by auditing what stayed live against the written rule, is where most embarrassment lives, because the policy promises more than the system delivers.

Appeals measure less than you hope

The overturn rate on appeals understates false removals, because many sellers never appeal. It is a floor. The honest estimate comes from re-reviewing a random sample of removals, including those nobody appealed, with a reviewer who has not seen the first decision.

Severity changes the rule

A suspected counterfeit and a credible threat against a person do not deserve the same cut-off. Severe categories go to trained humans with a named escalation path, accepting delay and cost; low-severity ones can be automated more aggressively.

Adversaries adapt

Whatever you catch, you teach. Metrics measured last quarter describe last quarter's scammers, so a falling catch rate may mean a better attacker rather than a worse model. No audit tells you what a determined newcomer will try next, so the programme needs a standing habit of looking, not a one-time fix.

6. How it differs by product and by stage

In a consumer social product, the main harms are between users, harassment above all, and the signals are reports and block rates. In a B2B product, accounts are few, contracted and identifiable, so abuse is handled through verification at sign-up, audit trails and account managers; automated removal is rare. In a marketplace like Ishtam, abuse sits between two sides, so there are two victims and two kinds of error, and sellers must be treated as customers while being screened as suspects.

Stage matters as much. An early-stage company with one hundred sellers should read every flagged listing by hand and write the policy from what it sees; a model would have too few scams to learn from. A large company has the volume to need models, queues, language coverage and legal obligations, such as the grievance officer that India's 2021 intermediary rules require platforms to name, and the real challenge becomes consistency across hundreds of reviewers working in several languages, and keeping policy, engineering and support reading from the same definition of abuse.

7. Common mistakes

Celebrating removals

Symptom: the weekly dashboard rises while buyer complaints do too. Misunderstanding: activity treated as outcome. Cheapest diagnostic: sample 5,000 incoming listings before scoring and compare the scam share with last quarter; a live-listing sample reads lower and is not comparable.

One cut-off for everyone

Symptom: seller-support tickets cluster among long-standing sellers. Misunderstanding: assuming risk is uniform. Diagnostic: tabulate wrongful removals by account age; new accounts carry more risk and deserve a stricter rule than a five-year seller.

Reading the appeal rate as the error rate

Symptom: a reassuringly low overturn rate beside a sharp fall in new listings. Misunderstanding: assuming silent sellers were treated fairly. Diagnostic: re-review 200 removals nobody appealed.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Bangera's Friday slide shows prevalence with its interval, both error costs with their sources, and the break-even ratio. Cut-offs differ by account age. A grey band sends doubtful listings to reviewers rather than to the bin, and removed sellers see a specific reason and a one-tap appeal answered within two days. Reviewers are rotated off the most distressing categories after set intervals, and their disagreement rate is tracked, because inconsistent reviewers quietly corrupt the labels every future model learns from. A fresh audit is scheduled before anyone declares success, and the slide states which assumptions would reverse the choice.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Bangera chose cut-off B for accounts under 30 days old and kept A for established sellers. The audit showed where the risk sits: new accounts held 1,000 listings and 70 scams, a prevalence of 7.0 per cent, against 30 scams in 4,000 established listings, or 0.75 per cent. Assuming the same recall and error rates in both groups, B on the 20,000 new-account listings removes 1,190 of 1,400 scams and 558 honest ones, so 68.1 per cent of its removals are right. A on the 80,000 established listings removes 420 of 600 scams and 794 honest ones, so 34.6 per cent are right. The hybrid costs ₹25.43 lakh a week, ₹3.02 lakh more than applying B everywhere, but it spares 1,588 established sellers (2,382 less 794) from wrongful removal. On the stated ₹150, B alone would beat A even among established sellers (17.6 extra honest removals per extra scam stopped, under the 40 limit), so the hybrid rests on a judgement, not on the audit. That trade pays if a wrongly removed established seller costs the platform more than about ₹340 rather than ₹150 (₹5.40 lakh of extra scam loss divided by 1,588), and Bangera judged that a seller of five years is worth far more than that. He promised Bhandary a re-audit of 5,000 incoming listings in the second week of November, knowing it would arrive after the 8 November peak it was meant to guard, so he added a mid-week check of wrongful removals on 28 October and a rollback if wrongful removals among established sellers rose. He accepted that some honest newcomers would be inconvenienced, and wrote that cost on the slide instead of leaving it for support to discover.

To go further, study content moderation and policy, where the written rule is drafted; fraud and risk models, where scoring is built; and guardrails and safety layers, where the same logic is applied to AI systems.

Questions to sit with. First, which of Ishtam's users would you least want to be wrongly removed, and does your cut-off reflect that choice? Second, what would you have to observe, besides prevalence, to believe a falling scam rate came from your work and not from scammers moving elsewhere?
case20v1-ethics.trust.safety:
Naazuk: The Document at the Door

A decision case on trust and safety in at-home services

1. Opening

At 1:00 a.m. on Monday, 19 October 2026, Aryaman Humane unmuted himself in Toronto. "I can tell you how likely a first booking is to go wrong," he said, "but I cannot tell you what to do about it." It was 10:30 a.m. in Bengaluru, where Arpita Hiwale, head of trust and safety product at Naazuk, sat in a glass room in Indiranagar with the festival calendar on one wall and a printout of the Pune test on the other.

Naazuk sends beauticians into women's homes. By Friday, 23 October, Arpita had to tell the chief executive, Amey Hingne, which safeguard the app would carry into Diwali. Engineers in Bengaluru and Pune would start building on Monday, 26 October, and the release froze on 2 November (Figure 1). Whatever she chose, thousands of customers and providers would meet it within weeks.

2. Company background

Naazuk was founded in 2019 by Amey and a college friend after a plain complaint: a good beautician was hard to find, and a stranger at the door was hard to trust. It now operates in nine cities, from Bengaluru and Pune to Hyderabad, Chennai and Jaipur, with about 3,100 active providers. Almost all are self-employed women who set their own hours and keep 75 per cent of each booking. Customers book facials, waxing, mehendi and bridal make-up; the average visit is worth ₹1,200.

Competition is crowded. Urban Company is the national name in home services, neighbourhood salons take bookings on WhatsApp, and Nykaa has made premium beauty a mobile habit. Naazuk competes on beauty-only depth and on a visit that happens when promised. Payments run through UPI and Razorpay, though cash on the doorstep is still accepted. In the six months to September 2026 the platform made 6,60,000 provider visits worth ₹79.2 crore, of which Naazuk kept 25 per cent, ₹19.8 crore. Festival fortnights are the peak; last Diwali, bookings ran about 1.6 times the monthly average.

3. The situation

Providers report trouble through an in-app button, and Exhibit 1 sets out what they reported from April to September: 989 incidents in four types. Finance estimated the cash Naazuk absorbed on them, in refunds and goodwill payouts, at ₹9.6 lakh. The exit survey adds a second record. Of 410 providers who left in the half-year, 296 answered the exit survey, and 96 of those named safety.

For two weeks from 28 September, the company ran a randomised test in Pune. Half of new customers reaching checkout were asked to confirm identity through DigiLocker, the government's document wallet, before booking; the rest booked as usual. Exhibit 2 gives the result. Separately, Aryaman built a risk score that sorts each first booking into a low, medium or high band before a provider is dispatched. Exhibit 3 shows how the bands behaved when run back over the half-year.

The team sees the problem from different clocks. Aryaman works the Pune data after his Toronto day ends, nine and a half hours behind Bengaluru until clocks change on 1 November. Amey takes investor calls in Mumbai in the evenings ahead of a board meeting on 30 October. Abhilasha Hodarkar in Pune takes providers' calls from eight every morning.

4. The people

Amey Hingne, chief executive, Mumbai. He wants the festival quarter protected and a clean story for the 30 October board. "Every document we ask for is a customer we hand to Urban Company," he told Arpita. "I will not trade a Diwali for a form."

Abhilasha Hodarkar, Pune city head. She wants every new customer verified. She has not told Amey that providers have described eleven further cases of physical intimidation in Pune WhatsApp groups since April, none logged in the app, because the women feared losing bookings or being named to customers.

Archana Harmalkar, provider, Pune. Five years on the platform and a top-rated bridal artist. "I do not mind a form," she says. "I mind the door closing behind me." She believes the worst visits come after eight in the evening and wants to see who is waiting and be free to leave.

Aryaman Humane, data scientist, Toronto. He is proud of the score and wary of using it. Its strongest signal is that the customer's phone number is under ninety days old, which also describes students and newly arrived renters in Whitefield and Hinjewadi. "It measures newness," he says, "which is not the same as menace." He asks for a month of shadow running first.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: verify every new customer. Anyone placing a first booking confirms identity through DigiLocker. Naazuk would store only a verified name and age band, in line with the data-minimisation duty under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. The integration exists, and the step could ship in the first week of building. Its cost is the conversion gap in Exhibit 2. It leaves returning customers and any mid-visit emergency untouched.

Option B: tier the step by risk. First bookings in the low band book as today. The medium band must prepay by UPI or card; the high band must verify through DigiLocker before dispatch. Engineering estimates six working days and ₹14 lakh one-off, plus ₹1.2 lakh a month to run the score. It adds a rules service to maintain and leaves returning customers untouched.

Option C: add no customer step; protect the provider. A 24-hour safety desk run by a Hyderabad partner, at ₹32 lakh a quarter, watches live visits and answers an SOS button. Providers may leave any visit with full payout, and a single report suspends the customer's account and phone number. Customers meet no new friction. Fake bookings are still dispatched, and the desk reacts after the provider has arrived.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, who are the "worst users" Naazuk must design for, and who pays for their behaviour today?
  2. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, estimate how many customers each option burdens over six months and how many reports it might prevent. State your assumptions.
  3. What would you want to know about how Exhibits 1 to 3 were produced before relying on them?
  4. Which option do you take to Amey on Friday, what ships first, and what evidence would make you reverse it?

8. A note for the learner

Trust and safety asks how to design for the worst users without punishing the rest. Friction lands on many customers whose conversion a dashboard tracks; harm lands on a few providers who appear in no funnel. A well-reasoned answer names who is dangerous, prices friction and harm in the same units, and picks something it can reverse.

One defensible path is Option B, staged, with the cheapest parts of Option C. The worst behaviour concentrates in first bookings: 3.18 reports per 1,000 visits against 0.77, about four times as many, and 198 of 212 fake bookings. That justifies gating newcomers, but not all of them. Option A's seven and a half point fall in bookings per 100 sessions is 26 per cent of 29.0; applied to 2,00,000 first-booking visits it forgoes about 51,700 visits, near ₹6.2 crore of service value and ₹1.55 crore of revenue per half-year. Its apparent safety gain, 8 reports against 3, is too few events to separate from chance: a split this lopsided would arise about one time in four (probability 0.24) if visits alone governed it.

The score looks sharper, though it was fitted and evaluated on the same half-year. Medium and high bands hold 506 of 636 first-booking reports, 80 per cent, from 35 per cent of visits. Yet the high band's 306 reports sit on 20,000 visits, so more than 98 per cent of high-band visits drew no report, and reports undercount, as Abhilasha's eleven cases show. Those two facts argue for verifying only the high band, about 10 per cent of first-booking visits. Aryaman's month of shadow running will not fit before Diwali; a backtest of band assignment by area and phone age before 26 October can.

Pair this with the right to leave on full payout and one-report suspension, which protect the returning-customer cases that no gate reaches. Open a reporting route outside the app. Prepay half of medium-band customers first, so its cost is measured; stop it if their bookings per 100 sessions fall more than 26 per cent below the other half, the relative fall Exhibit 2 shows. Reverse high-band verification if more than 26 per cent of high-band bookings fail to reach dispatch, or if high-band reports do not fall within two weeks.
