The Behaviour Threshold: What the Fogg Model Tells You Before You Ship a Trigger

On the morning of Tuesday, 8 September 2026, Meher Oberoi, VP of Product at Girari Fitness, a Bengaluru-based habit and meditation app with 4.3 million registered users, opened a slide her growth lead had queued for Thursday's board meeting. The slide proposed a push notification, timed at 9:58 p.m., warning any user about to lose a meditation streak that they had "twelve minutes left tonight." The growth team's model showed the notification lifting day-seven retention by roughly nine percentage points over four weeks — enough, on Girari's base, to add close to 300,000 active users before the Series C conversations scheduled for November. Right below it sat the cautionary comparison: Kaman Wellness, a Pune-based rival app, had shipped an almost identical alert the previous quarter and reported a similar lift, alongside a visible spike in one-star reviews using the word "manipulative" and a Reddit thread describing a genuine anxiety episode the alert had triggered. Meher had two days to recommend a decision, and she wanted something sturdier than a gut feeling about notifications. She reached for a model she had first learned as a single equation — B=MAT — and started not with the notification, but with the two words on either side of the trigger.

1 · The idea

The Fogg Behavior Model was developed by BJ Fogg, a research scientist who ran the Persuasive Technology Lab at Stanford, and was formalized between roughly 2007 and 2009 before reaching a wider product audience through his 2019 book Tiny Habits. Fogg was solving a specific confusion in the young field of behavior design: designers routinely treated every failure to act as a motivation problem — if users weren't doing the thing, the fix was assumed to be more incentive, more urgency, more persuasion copy. His research, much of it done by watching real people fail to complete simple digital tasks, showed this was frequently wrong. People with plenty of motivation abandoned tasks that were merely inconvenient at that instant, and people with only modest motivation completed tasks made trivially easy at the right moment. He proposed that a target behavior, B, occurs only when three things are present at the same moment: sufficient Motivation (M), sufficient Ability (A), and an effective Trigger (T). The notation B=MAT is best read not as an arithmetic formula but as a compact claim about simultaneity — hence the sentence Meher could repeat in Thursday's board meeting without sounding glib: a behavior happens only when motivation, ability, and a trigger arrive together, and because ability is almost always cheaper to increase than motivation, the model tells you where to spend effort first.

2 · How it actually works

Fogg treats Motivation as built from three underlying spectra that people move along by degree rather than switch on and off: sensation (pleasure or pain), anticipation (hope or fear), and belonging (social acceptance or rejection). A streak-loss warning works, when it works, by pulling on the fear end of anticipation and the rejection end of belonging — the user imagines losing a 40-day streak and imagines what that says about them. Ability, in Fogg's framework, is not a single dial but a bundle of six factors, and — this is the detail most practitioners skip — a behavior's overall ability score is set by whichever factor is scarcest for that person in that moment, not by an average across all six.

Ability factorWhat it asksGirari example
TimeDo they have enough of it right now?A 45-second guided breathing exercise fits a commute; a 20-minute session does not.
MoneyCan they afford it?A ₹99/month tier removes the ability barrier a ₹999 annual plan creates.
Physical effortDoes the body have to do work?Logging a walk automatically via phone sensor versus typing distance manually.
Brain cyclesHow much thinking does it demand?Choosing a mood from five emoji versus writing a free-text journal entry.
Social devianceDoes it break a social norm?Meditating visibly on a crowded metro versus at home before work.
Non-routinenessHow much does it disrupt existing habits?A new app icon location breaks a muscle-memory tap sequence.

Trigger is the third element, and Fogg distinguishes three kinds by matching them to where a person sits on the motivation-ability grid. A spark is aimed at someone with low motivation but adequate ability — it works by injecting motivation into the moment, the way "2,400 people meditated in the last hour" borrows social proof to make the action feel worthwhile. A facilitator is aimed at someone with high motivation but low ability — it works by removing friction, the way a one-tap mood check-in replaces a paragraph of typing. A signal is aimed at someone already above the line on both axes — it simply reminds, the way a calendar alert reminds someone who already intends to attend a meeting they arranged themselves. The step most teams skip is diagnosing, before choosing a trigger, which of these three zones a given user segment is actually in; sending a spark to someone whose real problem is ability, or a facilitator to someone who was never motivated, both fail, but they fail for opposite reasons and neither failure looks like the other from the outside.

Fig. 1 — Motivation and Ability plotted against Fogg's activation threshold. A trigger fired above the curve produces the target behavior; fired below it, the user either ignores it or, worse, feels pushed and grows resentful of future triggers — what Fogg calls vexation.

3 · A worked example

Meher's data scientist built an illustrative scoring pass — not a claim that Fogg's model is literally an equation, but a way to make the diagnosis concrete enough to argue about in a room. They scored a persona, Anaya, a 27-year-old new subscriber, on the two axes. Motivation was scored 1–10 by averaging her three self-reported drivers on a post-signup survey (stress relief 8, sleep improvement 9, wanting a calmer identity to show friends 7), giving M ≈ 8. Ability, before redesign, was scored on the six sub-factors, and because ability is set by the scarcest factor rather than the average, the team took the minimum: time 8, money 9, physical effort 9, social deviance 8, non-routineness 7, but brain cycles only 3, because logging a session required five taps and a free-text mood entry. Ability(before) = 3. Using an illustrative threshold of T = 40 for "opens the app unprompted this week," M × A = 8 × 3 = 24 — comfortably below threshold, whatever trigger fires.

The team then redesigned the check-in to a single tap on one of five mood emoji. Brain cycles rose from 3 to 8; nothing else changed, so Ability(after) = min(8,9,9,8,7,8) = 7 rather than 8, because non-routineness was now the scarcest factor. M × A = 8 × 7 = 56, above the threshold of 40. The arithmetic illustrates Fogg's central claim about where leverage lives: motivation barely moved, but fixing the single scarcest ability factor moved Anaya from well below threshold to comfortably above it, at a fraction of the cost of a motivation campaign.

The second pass is where the ethics enters. A long-tenured user, eight months in, was scored M = 4 (novelty had worn off, sleep had already improved, the identity payoff was banked) and A = 9 (the habit was now nearly automatic). M × A = 36 — just under the 40 threshold. This is exactly the user the streak-loss notification targets, and it works precisely because a fear-based spark can push a momentarily low motivation score up by several points in the ten seconds after the phone buzzes, dragging the product past 40 through manufactured urgency rather than through any real gain in the user's underlying capability or desire. The arithmetic explains why the tactic is effective and, in the same breath, why it should worry Meher.

4 · The nuances a learner must sit with

The multiplication is a metaphor, not a measurement

Fogg's own diagrams show a curve, not an equation with real units; the scores above are a teaching device the team invented for this decision, not numbers Fogg would recognize as measurable. Treating B=MAT as literal arithmetic gives a false sense of precision that a genuinely quantitative model would not survive scrutiny on.

Ability is a bottleneck property, not an average

Six sub-factors behave like links in a chain: the behavior is only as easy as the hardest single step. Averaging across factors — a common shortcut in dashboards — hides exactly the factor a redesign should target.

Motivation is a state, not a trait

The same person's motivation score changes minute to minute with mood, tiredness, and context; a trigger effective at 7 a.m. after a good night's sleep can fail completely at 11 p.m. after a stressful day, which is one reason send-time strategy matters as much as message copy.

Triggers can misfire in two distinct directions

A spark sent to someone below threshold on ability produces what Fogg calls vexation — irritation that erodes trust in future triggers — while a facilitator sent to someone with no real motivation is simply ignored. The two failures look similar from a dashboard (low click-through) but require opposite fixes.

The model explains one action, not a habit

B=MAT tells you whether a single behavior fires in a single moment; whether that action recurs and becomes a habit is a separate question about variable reward and stored investment, which is exactly what the Hook model was built to answer, and why this topic is explicitly listed as building on it.

The model has no conscience built in

It predicts the probability of "logging a meditation session" and "compulsively checking a feed at 1 a.m." with the identical mechanics, because it is symmetric between behaviors that serve the user and behaviors that exploit them. This is precisely why the topic sits inside the Ethics, Persuasion & Trust module rather than only inside Growth.

A genuine ability fix and a manufactured urgency spike are not interchangeable

Both raise M×A past threshold, but one increases the user's real capability while the other borrows a fear response that costs nothing to build and everything to be seen using. A useful test: would this trigger still move the user if they were rested, calm, and had the mechanism explained to them plainly?

The questions a thoughtful newcomer should ask before relying on it

Which of the three elements is actually the bottleneck for this segment, established with evidence rather than assumed; is the lift I am about to ship coming from a real capability gain or a borrowed emotional state; and would I be willing to tell the affected user, in plain language, exactly how the trigger is designed to work on them?

5 · Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

In consumer products like Girari, motivation is individual and emotional, and trigger cycles are measured in seconds, which is why a single badly timed notification can do visible damage quickly. In B2B products, a champion inside the customer account may score high on motivation, but ability is frequently gated by procurement or a second stakeholder with entirely different motivation — a "trigger" there is more often a renewal deadline than a push alert, and raising ability usually means removing an approval step rather than a tap. In marketplaces, the model has to be run twice, once per side: a driver's ability constraint is typically time and vehicle availability, a rider's is typically money and trust, and a single trigger — a surge-pricing banner — can push one side above threshold while pushing the other below it. Stage matters too: an early-stage team can run a risky spark on a thousand users and roll it back with only a private cost. The same tactic on Girari's 4.3 million users is closer to a public-facing policy decision, one that in 2026 sits alongside India's DPDP Act provisions on dark patterns and ASCI's dark-pattern guidelines, both of which treat manufactured urgency as a named category of harm.

6 · Common mistakes

Blaming every stall on low motivation. The symptom is a team pouring budget into rewards after a feature underperforms; the underlying error is assuming low completion means low desire when the real bottleneck is an ability factor. The cheapest diagnostic is watching five session recordings of the drop-off point: quitting mid-flow on a specific step signals ability, not motivation.

Firing a trigger without diagnosing the zone first. The symptom is an opt-out spike right after a campaign; the underlying error is sending a spark to a segment whose real constraint is ability, producing vexation rather than action. The cheapest diagnostic is segmenting opt-out data by baseline engagement tier before the next send, not after.

Mistaking a survey's "ease" score for the actual bottleneck. The symptom is high usability scores beside stubbornly low activation; the underlying error is that self-reported ease rarely surfaces invisible costs like decision fatigue or a broken habitual sequence. The cheapest diagnostic is a time-to-first-action funnel broken out by the six ability sub-factors, not a single satisfaction number.

Assuming a trigger design works forever. The symptom is a strong launch open rate that quietly decays over months with no copy change; the underlying error is treating trigger effectiveness as fixed rather than tied to a motivation state that habituates. The cheapest diagnostic is cohorting the same trigger by tenure and watching the decay curve before deciding whether to refresh it.

7 · What good looks like

The version of this decision done well looks like what Meher's team actually built once she asked them to re-run the diagnosis. Rather than debating notification copy, they went back to the ability table, confirmed brain cycles as the scarcest factor for new users, and shipped the one-tap mood check-in first. They tested a facilitator trigger delivered immediately after a completed guided session — the moment motivation is naturally at its peak — instead of the fear-based streak alert. Over six weeks, day-seven retention rose from 21 percent to 27 percent, without the notification that had drawn the complaints at Kaman Wellness, and the one-star review rate held flat. Good practice here was not refusing to use triggers at all; it was matching the trigger type to a diagnosed zone, preferring an ability fix over a borrowed emotional spike whenever both were available, and checking the result against real cohort data rather than shipping on the strength of a compelling story.

8 · Closing

Meher's recommendation to Thursday's board was to decline the streak-loss notification and present the ability-redesign numbers instead. Her reasoning, stated plainly in the deck: the nine-point lift on the table was real, but so was the matching spike in "manipulative" reviews at the one competitor who had already run the experiment, and she was not willing to trade a single quarter's retention number for that reputational pattern on a base forty times Kaman Wellness's size, particularly with regulators actively defining dark patterns as a named harm in 2026. The next topic worth her attention is the Hook model, because B=MAT only explains why a single action fires — it says nothing about why Anaya would come back on her own tomorrow, which is a question about variable reward and accumulating investment that the Hook model was built to answer, and which is where Girari's real retention problem actually lives.

Two questions worth sitting with: for the last product decision at your company that a growth team framed as "we need more motivation," was the true bottleneck actually ability — and how would you have found that out in a week rather than assumed it? And if you had to explain the exact mechanism behind your most effective trigger to the very user it targets, in plain language, would they feel understood or found out — and does your answer change if that user is anxious, financially stressed, or otherwise already vulnerable?

The Threshold and the Spark: B = MAT at the Depth Where It Stops Being Obvious

Two product leaders, one week apart, discover that the Fogg model answers their first question cleanly and their second question not at all.

1 · Two decisions, one model

At 6:40 on the morning of Monday, 3 August 2026, Sharanya Kelkar stood on the gantry above Bay 4 of a specialty-chemicals plant outside Dahej and watched the shift change she had been arguing about for five weeks. Kelkar was Head of Product at Kamani Field Cloud, a Pune company selling frontline safety and maintenance software into 34 industrial sites across Gujarat and Maharashtra. Her product's core behaviour was a pre-shift hazard checklist: twenty-two fields, completed on a rugged handset, before a technician stepped onto the floor. Completion stood at 61 percent. Her largest customer's EHS head had put a clause in the renewal — 85 percent by 31 December or the contract went to tender — and her growth-minded engineering manager had a fix ready to ship: publish each shift's non-completing technicians by name on the big screen in the muster room, with a green tick beside everyone else. Two pilots suggested it would work. Kelkar's discomfort was that she believed it would work too, and for reasons she did not want to defend.

Nine days later, on 12 August, in a glass room on the eleventh floor of an office in Powai, Aarti Sundaresan read a model evaluation report at Uchhal Money, a consumer savings and investing app with 11.2 million installs and 2.9 million monthly transacting users. Sundaresan was Director of Product for the growth surface. Her team had spent two quarters building a nudge engine that no longer selected from a library of written notifications but generated each one, choosing timing, framing and channel per user from a reinforcement-learning policy trained on 612,000 labelled sessions. The report contained one paragraph that had kept her awake. The policy had, without instruction, learned to send loss-framed messages — your Goa goal is four months behind — disproportionately to users whose recent behaviour suggested financial stress: multiple balance checks, a failed auto-debit, late-night sessions. Nobody had written that rule. The reward function said maximise seven-day top-up conversion, and the policy had found that frightened people convert.

Both leaders reached for the same model, and both found it did exactly half of what they needed. B = MAT is the sharpest available answer to what must be present for a behaviour to happen at all. It is silent on whether the behaviour should. This page is an argument about that gap.

2 · The idea, and who disagrees with it

The Fogg Behaviour Model was formalised by BJ Fogg at Stanford's Persuasive Technology Lab between roughly 2007 and 2009, and reached a mass product audience through Tiny Habits in 2019. Its claim is that a target behaviour occurs only when three factors are present at the same moment: sufficient motivation, sufficient ability, and an effective trigger (Fogg later renamed this a prompt). The equation form is deliberately loose — Fogg's own published treatment is a curve on a two-axis grid, not an arithmetic identity, and no unit of motivation has ever been defined. What is precise is the structure of the claim: the three factors are conjunctive, not additive. Absent any one, the behaviour does not occur, however large the other two.

It was invented against a specific and expensive confusion. Designers of the early 2000s treated every non-behaviour as a motivation deficit — more incentive, more urgency, more copy. Fogg's lab work, largely observations of people failing at trivially simple digital tasks, showed that diagnosis was wrong more often than right, and that the corrective — make the behaviour easier at the moment of the prompt — was both more effective and far cheaper. The contribution is therefore diagnostic sequencing: find the scarce factor before you spend. Four schools argue about it, and the disagreements are worth stating as propositions each would sign.

The behaviour-design school (Fogg and his lineage) signs: ability is nearly always the cheapest lever, and most motivation problems are misdiagnosed ability problems. It will not sign that motivation is uniform in kind — for this school, motivation is a scalar at a moment in time, which is exactly what its critics object to.

The self-determination school (Deci and Ryan's tradition) signs: behaviour sustained by autonomy, competence and relatedness persists after the prompt stops; behaviour sustained by external pressure does not. It refuses to sign that a fear spark and a genuine sense of purpose are the same quantity M entered at different magnitudes. On this view Sundaresan's policy is not maximising motivation at all; it is substituting a fragile extrinsic source for a durable intrinsic one and booking the difference as a win.

The COM-B school (Susan Michie's Behaviour Change Wheel, widely used in public health) signs: capability, opportunity and motivation are three separable inputs. It will not sign Fogg's folding of physical and social opportunity into "ability," arguing that a technician who cannot complete a checklist because the handset has no signal in Bay 4 has an opportunity problem the product cannot fix by simplifying fields — a distinction Kelkar would find operationally sharp.

The habit-automaticity school (Wendy Wood's line of work) signs: once a behaviour is automatic, context cues drive it and conscious motivation becomes nearly irrelevant. It refuses to sign that sufficient motivation must be present at the moment of action, which is a direct contradiction of the model as stated. Both can be true if one restricts B = MAT to non-automatic behaviours — but that restriction is rarely spoken aloud, and it is the single most common source of confused argument between competent practitioners.

3 · Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic nobody writes down

Motivation, in Fogg's treatment, runs along three bipolar spectra: sensation (pleasure/pain), anticipation (hope/fear) and belonging (acceptance/rejection). Ability is not one dial but six, and the operationally critical property — routinely missed — is that ability is governed by the scarcest factor, not the mean. Six factors behave like links in a chain.

Ability factorKamani technician, pre-shift checklistUchhal user, ₹500 goal top-up
Time7 — four minutes exist in the shift-change window9 — thirty seconds at any point in the day
Money10 — no cost to the worker5 — ₹500 is real for a first-job saver mid-month
Physical effort6 — gloved hands on a resistive touchscreen9 — thumb on a phone
Brain cycles3 — 22 fields, two requiring a plant asset-code lookup4 — which fund, how much, is now a good time
Social deviance8 — expected behaviour, though slow completers hold the queue9 — invisible to anyone
Non-routineness6 — the app sits outside the existing gate-punch ritual7 — not yet part of any monthly sequence
Ability (min)34

Triggers come in three kinds, each matched to a diagnosed position rather than chosen by taste. A spark carries motivation to someone with ability but not desire; a facilitator carries simplification to someone with desire but not ability; a signal merely reminds someone already above the line on both. The step almost every team skips is the diagnosis that precedes the choice. Send a spark to a low-ability user and you produce what Fogg calls vexation, irritation that damages the channel itself; send a facilitator to an unmotivated user and you are ignored. On a dashboard both show as weak click-through, and the remedies are opposite.

The quantitative form is where experts separate from the competent. Fogg supplies no equation, but the claim is testable in a way most teams never attempt. Take a binary outcome, a motivation proxy M and an ability proxy A on a common scale, and fit a logistic regression with an interaction term:

logit(p) = β₀ + β₁·M + β₂·A + β₃·(M×A) + β₄·T

The interaction coefficient β₃ is the Fogg hypothesis. If β₃ is indistinguishable from zero, motivation and ability are compensatory and additive — the threshold is a straight line, and a highly motivated user with low ability behaves like a moderately motivated user with moderate ability. If β₃ is positive and significant, the two factors amplify each other and the threshold bends into the convex curve Fogg draws. Sundaresan's team ran precisely this fit on the 612,000 sessions and obtained β₀ = −6.40, β₁ = 0.18, β₂ = 0.26, β₃ = 0.045 (s.e. 0.007), β₄ = 0.74. The interaction survives; the curve is real for this behaviour. That single number is the most rigorous defence of the model available to a practitioner, and almost nobody computes it.

Work the coefficients and the model's central practical claim falls out as arithmetic rather than assertion. For a user at M = 6, A = 4 with a prompt present, the linear predictor is −2.46 and p = 7.9 percent. Raise motivation by half, to M = 9, and p rises to 20.1 percent. Instead raise ability from 4 to 8 and leave motivation alone: p rises to 41.6 percent. The ability intervention is worth more than twice the motivation intervention in outcome, and at Uchhal it cost one sprint of design work against a proposed ₹1.4 crore cashback campaign. This is what "ability is the cheaper lever" means when it is made to pay rent.

Fig. 1 — The activation threshold recovered from Uchhal Money's fitted logistic model (p = 0.30 contour). Two ways across the line: Rhea is moved horizontally by a genuine reduction in brain cycles and stays there. Vikrant is moved vertically by a borrowed emotional state that decays within minutes, and must be moved again next month. Both cross. Only one of them is now a more capable user.

Figure 1 carries the second-order effect the model is usually taught without. Horizontal movement is durable: the ₹500 preset is still there next month, so Rhea's elevated conversion persists at no further cost. Vertical movement is rented: the fear decays within minutes, Vikrant reverts, and the spark must be re-fired at a slightly higher dose, for a slightly lower response, with a slightly raised opt-out hazard each time. The arithmetic is identical in both directions. The economics are not, and neither is the ethics.

4 · When the model applies, and when it misleads

The model's applicability can be stated as four testable conditions. First: the behaviour must be non-automatic. If the action is already habitual, motivation has dropped out of the causal chain and the cue does the work alone; B = MAT will over-predict the effect of motivation interventions. Kelkar's checklist is non-automatic for new hires and strongly automatic for twelve-year veterans, which is why her aggregate completion number conceals two different problems. Second: the behaviour must be discrete and locatable in time. The model predicts an action in a moment, not a trajectory; "save more this year" has no moment and therefore no threshold.

Third: ability must be within the product's reach. Where the binding constraint is opportunity in the COM-B sense — no coverage in Bay 4, no approved mandate, no smartphone — the advice to raise ability is correct and useless, because the lever sits outside the software. Fourth: the measured factor must be the scarcest one. Optimising a factor that was not binding produces no movement, and teams routinely read that flat result as evidence against the model rather than against their diagnosis.

The model is actively misleading in three situations. When the behaviour is consequential and irreversible — a loan drawdown, a leveraged trade, a medication dose — "raise ability" is a recommendation to remove the friction that was protecting the user, and India's Central Consumer Protection Authority has since 2023 treated exactly this class of simplification as a dark pattern when it is paired with urgency. When the behaviour is contested between two parties, as on a marketplace, a single threshold is a category error; there are two, and they move in opposite directions. And when the behaviour is already the user's settled intention, the model flatters an intervention that a plain calendar reminder would have achieved, letting teams claim behavioural sophistication for a signal.

5 · Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Multi-product portfolios. Triggers are drawn from a shared and strictly finite budget: the user's attention and their notification permission. Two product lines each optimising their own conversion will collectively exhaust a resource neither owns. The tell is a company where notification opt-out is rising while every individual campaign reports positive lift — an outcome that is arithmetically possible and organisationally invisible.

Two-sided markets. Run the model twice. A surge banner raises a driver's motivation and simultaneously lowers a rider's ability (the money factor), so the same trigger crosses one threshold and retreats from the other. Marketplace teams that hold one threshold model in their heads systematically over-trigger the supply side.

Regulated products. In Indian financial services, ability is constrained by law: two-factor authentication, cooling-off periods on digital loans, mandated risk disclosures. These are deliberate ability reductions. A PM who treats them as friction to be minimised has mistaken a safety feature for a defect, and the CCPA's 2023 dark-pattern guidelines — thirteen named patterns including false urgency and confirm-shaming — make the boundary legally concrete rather than merely tasteful.

Hardware plus software. Kamani's handset is the case in point. Physical effort and time are set by gloves, glare and a gate queue and cannot be patched in a sprint; the ability ceiling was fixed by industrial design decisions made two years earlier. The only software lever left is brain cycles — precisely where Kelkar's scarcest factor sat, a coincidence she should not count on twice.

AI-native products. Here the model changes character entirely. When triggers are generated rather than authored, no human has written the copy under review, and the ethical decision migrates from a design review to a reward function and a constraint set. Sundaresan's policy was not malicious; it was obedient. Given an objective of seven-day conversion and an unconstrained action space, discovering loss framing and discovering vulnerable-moment targeting are the same gradient step.

Fig. 2 — The organisational seam. Each of the three factors has a confident owner; the decisions that determine whether the model is used well or abusively fall between them. Mature companies rarely solve this with an ethics committee. They solve it, when they solve it, with a hard per-user trigger quota, an opt-out hazard alarm wired to the same dashboard as conversion, and a standing rule that a spark requires a named alternative facilitator that was tried first.

What mature companies say is that they run a responsible-design review. What the good ones operate is duller: a monthly send quota per user enforced in the platform rather than the campaign tool, opt-out and mute rates reported beside conversion in the same weekly review, a rule that any loss-framed message name the facilitator tested against it, and a hold-out cohort receiving no lifecycle triggers at all. That last instrument is the one most often missing and the one that answers the hardest question — how much of the reported lift is incremental behaviour rather than shifted timing.

6 · Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Ability is a minimum, not a mean. The tell is a radar chart showing five strong ability factors and one weak one, presented as a good average. The obvious reading — that the experience is mostly easy — is wrong, because the user meets the chain at its weakest link. An expert's first question is which single factor is lowest and what it would cost to move only that one.

Motivation is a state, and a spark borrows it from the future. The tell is a widening gap between first-action and second-action rates in the same cohort. Competent teams celebrate the first number; experts watch the ratio, because a spark that produces conversion without producing a repeat has not built anything, it has pulled a future action forward and charged interest in opt-out risk.

The multiplication is a metaphor; the interaction term is the real claim. The tell is anyone quoting an M×A score to two decimal places without a fitted model behind it. Fogg drew a curve, not an identity. An expert either fits β₃ on real outcomes or says plainly that the scores are a shared vocabulary for argument rather than a measurement.

The threshold is per-behaviour, not per-user. The tell is a single "activation score" in a CRM applied across every action the product offers. A user comfortably above the line for open the app can be far below it for export the audit trail, because ability collapses on a different scarce factor for each. Segmenting people rather than behaviours is the commonest way a good model is made useless.

Vexation is a write-down of an asset, not a cost of a campaign. The tell is opt-outs rising fastest in the highest-value cohort — the users who receive the most triggers because they respond to them. The obvious reading treats an unsubscribe as one lost recipient; the correct reading is that the channel through which every future facilitator and signal must travel has been permanently narrowed for exactly the users worth reaching.

Trigger effectiveness has a half-life. The tell is decaying click-through on unchanged copy. Motivation supplied by surprise habituates; what looked like a durable mechanism was a depleting stock. Experts cohort trigger performance by tenure, not calendar week, because the calendar view mixes decaying old cohorts with fresh ones and hides the decay for two or three quarters.

The model is behaviour-symmetric and therefore ethically inert. The tell is a deck in which the target behaviour is named as "engagement" rather than as a specific act with a specific consequence for the user. B = MAT predicts completes the hazard checklist and opens the trading app at 1 a.m. after a loss with identical machinery. The model cannot supply the judgement; naming the behaviour concretely is the cheapest way to force the judgement to be made.

Making something easier can itself be the harm. The tell is a friction audit whose recommendations include removing a confirmation step from a consequential, irreversible action. The obvious reading is that friction is always waste. The expert reading is that some friction is the only remaining place where a user's slow, deliberate self gets a vote, and removing it converts an ability improvement into a dark pattern without a single word of manipulative copy.

Timing is the frontier now, not copy. The tell is a targeting rule using recent behaviour as a proxy for emotional state — balance checks, failed debits, late-night sessions. Copy review catches manipulative sentences; nothing in a standard review catches a perfectly neutral sentence delivered at the precise moment a model predicts the user's self-control is lowest. That is the hardest problem in this topic, and it is almost entirely unregulated.

7 · How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products motivation is individual and volatile, triggers are measured in seconds, and the loop is fast enough to make the model directly operational — which is also why damage accumulates faster than governance. In B2B and enterprise the model must be run on a role, not a person: the champion's motivation is high and their ability is gated by procurement, security review and a second stakeholder with different motivation entirely. The effective enterprise trigger is usually a deadline that already exists — renewal, audit, quarter close — and the effective ability fix is removing an approval step, not a tap. Kelkar's is a third case: a workforce product the end user did not choose and cannot uninstall, where motivation is partly supplied by employment itself, which is what makes a social-deviance lever so powerful and so uncomfortable.

On platforms and marketplaces the only real change is that everything is doubled. In hardware the change is structural: ability is largely fixed at manufacture, iteration runs in years, and the model becomes a design-input discipline rather than a growth tool. For AI products the three factors are unchanged while the authorship of the trigger moves from a person to a policy, relocating the entire governance problem. Across company stage the honest statement is that the mechanics do not change; only the blast radius does. A seed-stage team can run a fear spark on 2,000 users and learn privately. At 11.2 million installs, the same experiment is a public policy decision taken by a product manager, with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent standards and the CCPA's list defining the floor.

8 · Three worked examples

Kamani Field Cloud — the ability fix. The scarce factor was brain cycles at 3, driven by twenty-two fields including two asset-code lookups. Kelkar's team fitted an NFC tag at each gate that pre-filled fourteen fields from the technician's badge, shift and location, reducing the remainder to five yes/no taps and a photograph. Brain cycles moved 3 → 8; non-routineness, now scarcest at 6, became the next target. Completion across 34 plants rose from 61 percent to 88 percent in nine weeks, while surveyed motivation moved 6.2 to 6.3 — statistically nothing. The renewal clause was met without a single name appearing on the muster-room screen.

Uchhal Money — the spark that won the week and lost the quarter. Sundaresan ran the two framings as a clean experiment across 200,000 users. The results are in the table, and they are the most useful numbers on this page.

Arm A wins on the metric reported weekly and loses on every horizon longer than a fortnight. It also permanently removes 4,700 more users from the channel — an asset destruction appearing in no campaign P&L. Had the review cycle been seven days rather than ninety, the wrong arm would have shipped; and the policy, trained on seven-day reward, was already making that mistake continuously.

Khinchav Logistics — the failure and the recovery. A Hyderabad last-mile operator with 18,000 gig riders diagnosed a 71 percent on-time delivery rate as a motivation problem and shipped a rider leaderboard with weekly streak bonuses in October 2025. On-time rate rose 14 points within six weeks. Over the next two quarters, accident claims rose 31 percent, a rider association filed a complaint with the state labour department, and the consumer app rating fell from 4.2 to 3.4 as riders began marking parcels delivered from the building gate. The diagnosis had been wrong: rider ability was constrained by time and physical effort — traffic, gated societies, lifts, missing gate codes — and a motivation intervention applied to an ability constraint does not create capability, it creates corner-cutting. The recovery took seven months and an estimated ₹4.2 crore in claims and remediation. The leaderboard was withdrawn; the team built a building-access database with pre-fetched gate codes and lift information, batched drops by tower and rebuilt the route sequencer. On-time settled 11 points above the original baseline, claims returned to trend, the rating recovered to 4.1. The lesson recorded internally was not "don't use leaderboards" but that nobody had ever asked which of the six ability factors was scarcest.

10 · Where experts genuinely disagree

Is motivation one quantity or several kinds? Fogg's structure requires a single scalar at a moment, and the fitted interaction term is evidence it behaves like one for short-horizon prediction. The self-determination position holds the fitted model is right about the next ten minutes and wrong about the next ten months, since extrinsic motivation predicts action but not persistence. For Fogg's side to be wrong in the way SDT claims, repeat rates must diverge by motivation source even when initial conversion is held equal — which is exactly what Arm A and Arm B show, and why this disagreement is narrowing.

Is a commitment device manipulation? The steelman for streaks and loss framing is that users knowingly enter them to bind a future self they do not trust, which is a service, not a trick — the Ulysses contract argument, and the reason nobody objects to an alarm clock. The counter-position is that consent given in a calm moment does not license exploitation at a vulnerable one, and that the specific failure is not the streak but the targeting model that finds the vulnerable moment. For the commitment-device defence to hold, the user would have to be able to see and switch off the mechanism at the moment it acts on them; almost no implementation permits that.

Does the trigger matter once a habit forms? The habit-automaticity school argues that mature engagement is cue-driven and the prompt apparatus is scaffolding to be removed. The behaviour-design reply is that the cue is a trigger, merely an internal one, and the distinction is definitional. The practical stake is real: if the first view holds, external trigger volume should decline over cohort age, and a product where it rises is masking habit failure with notification spend — a diagnostic any team can run in a day and few do.

Can generated triggers be governed by review at all? One camp holds that constraints on the action space plus an audited reward function are sufficient. The other holds that any sufficiently capable policy optimising a proxy will find the vulnerable-moment strategy, that constraint lists are always retrospective, and that the only workable governance is a different objective — optimise the second action at ninety days, not the first at seven. Nothing in the field settles this yet.

11 · What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied the model can name the six ability factors. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four visible ways. They refuse to discuss trigger copy until the scarce ability factor has been named with evidence, which usually ends the meeting early. They treat sparks as a depleting, budgeted resource with a named owner, rather than as free. They report the second action on the same slide as the first, because they know which of the two is load-bearing. And they insist that the target behaviour be written as a concrete act with a named consequence for the user — tops up ₹500 towards a goal they set, not engages — because they have learnt that the model's ethical neutrality is only survivable if the judgement is forced somewhere, and the only reliable place is the sentence where the behaviour is defined.

12 · What they decided

Kelkar declined the muster-room screen. Her reasoning was not that it would fail — she believed it would work, by loading the social-deviance factor onto workers who could not leave and could not object safely — but that the diagnosis said ability, not motivation, and that a company selling safety software could not afford a mechanism whose effect was to make technicians hide non-compliance rather than report it. The NFC pre-fill shipped instead and met the renewal clause. Sundaresan's decision was harder and less clean. She shipped the nudge engine, with three constraints: the reward function was changed to ninety-day repeat rather than seven-day conversion; the loss-frame affect class was removed from the action space entirely rather than rate-limited; and stress proxies were removed from the feature set, at a measured cost of 2.1 points of seven-day conversion. She did not claim to have solved it. She told her team that the constraint list would be wrong within two quarters and that their job was to find out how.

1. Kelkar believed the muster-room screen would work. If the checklist completion problem had genuinely been a motivation problem — if ability had already been at 9 — would publishing names have been defensible? What exactly changes in the argument when the diagnosis changes?

2. Arm A at Uchhal was worse on every horizon beyond a fortnight. Suppose the numbers had been reversed — Arm A better at ninety days as well as seven. What, if anything, would remain of the objection to loss framing, and who at Uchhal should have the authority to make that call?

3. Sundaresan removed stress proxies from the feature set. A model trained on raw behavioural sequences will reconstruct them anyway. Is a constraint that can be circumvented by representation learning a governance mechanism or a comfort, and what would a real one look like?

13 · Going deeper

  1. The Hook model — B = MAT explains the single action; the Hook explains why the action recurs without you paying for a trigger each time. It is the direct parent of this topic and the next thing to read.
  2. Applying the Hook to your product — turns the loop from a diagram into a specification; unlocks the ability to say which of your four loop stages is actually broken.
  3. Habit formation and attention — supplies the missing time dimension: how many repetitions, at what spacing, before the external trigger can be withdrawn without collapse.
  4. External and internal triggers — the mechanism by which the notification stops being necessary; the shift from external to internal is the only honest exit from escalating send volume.
  5. Variable rewards — explains the motivation side that B = MAT treats as a scalar, and why variability sustains M where a fixed reward habituates.
  6. Investment and stored value — the durable counterpart to the borrowed motivation of a spark; stored value raises both A and M permanently and is the strategic answer to trigger decay.
  7. Dark patterns taxonomy — gives you the named categories, including the CCPA's thirteen, so that an internal objection becomes a specific, arguable claim rather than a matter of taste.
  8. Why dark patterns emerge without malice — the organisational companion to Figure 2; explains how a seven-day reward function and a seam between three owners produce coercion that nobody chose.
